Worst part ever. I thought, wow, Assassin's Creed! I will fight, I will climb, I will jump from roof to roof! No. This part is about run ridiculously far, ride a horse and see the story videos. And learn useless things, like hunting or making trade caravans.
- I had one good fight in game. Then I figured out, that I missed the point - I had to run away and jump off the cliff. The enemies are endless. So, the best fight was an accident.
- Buildings are far from each other, so you can't run by roofs. One-two-three houses and you have to make leap of faith  into a cart of rotten cabbage. So, there is no point to even climb anywhere. It does not make your way shorter or give you any fun.
- You have to run to the teleport point to activate it. Run a lot. And next time it still can be not available to jump to. If it is available, it's still annoying, because when you need to jump to NY, you jump 1. To the end of location. 2. Walk to the end and teleport to... 3. Middle land, where you must. 4. Jump to the end of it. 5. Turn back and walk to the edge/gate. 6. Hello NY, it was a fast travel!
- Viewing points gives you nothing useful, so I just skipped it
- Horses stuck at every stone and can't jump over basic obstacles. So it is not faster sometimes
- You will learn to handle the ship. To use it twice. You will learn economics and trades and use it not even once. You will learn hunting and forget it as a bad dream. This is, actually, very good. Useless things are skippable. As well, as videos.
- Nice try with ability to climb the mountains and trees. But I won the game and still not sure, where I can do it and where I can't.
- One assassin walks into the bar... And he slowly walks through the hall, slowly goes to the second floor and get to the NPC's table. Every time. Because he can't run inside the buildings.
- Incredible amount of re-runs and re-plays because of one idiotic wrong step. It is really annoying, when you can't do a simple, basic thing.
- The story. It is probably good, but lack of gameplay ruins it anyway
Of course, game can be played deeper and wider. All this side missions. NPC quests, hunting, trading... But I just wanted to end this torture as fast, as I can.

-terrible UI
-poorly explained / unexplained mechanics
-TOO MANY CUTSCENES
-missions are either a few seconds long or drag on for eternity
-there is always a 'correct' way to do each mission, if you stray or try your own method, prepare to rage
-'full sync' conditions are incredibly annoying and sometimes virtually impossible (chase a man through crowded alleys without touching anybody)
-protagonist voice acting is bland and slow and sounds mentally challenged, i cringed through all dialogue
-so much preachy self-righteousness, especially from SJW protagonist. eyerolls upon eyerolls
-ranged weapons are awful. in combat you will be lucky to get one shot off, it may or may not kill the target
-targeting enemies from a distance is awkward and difficult. if they move your target lock will probably break. you will probably air assassinate the wrong person many many times
-glitches and bugs (eg. combat music can get stuck on a loop even when not in combat, forever, unless you start a new mission; my convoy got stuck on 'attacked' and made one of the three slots permanently unavailable with no way to resolve; a few times during freerun i was magically thrown 60 feet in the air and died; sometimes a mission location that's supposed to be map marked will become unmarked and frustrating to search for)
-in combat it takes like a 12 strike sequence to put down a single guard, with 50% chance your sequence of stabs will be interrupted by another enemy striking you
-'streamlined' freerun using one button means no way to differentiate between types of movement (ie sprinting, jumping down to ground, leaping to catch another ledge, running up a wall) and many frustrating instances where the dude does what you did not intend
-too much dull filler content (mind-numbing underground labyrinths, lockpicking, large sections of map you have to explore by walking with nothing interesting to see, checkers and similar boring minigames, 'grinding' challenges where you have to perform various actions many times over, having to visit stores to manually send out convoys every couple minutes to sell items which takes like 400 clicks each time, hunting which is cool at first but ultimately pointless except for the grinding challenges and too easy.....)
there are some positives (environment, animations, animals, ships) but the negatives vastly outweigh them IMO. I did enjoy this game at times, but there were far too many annoyances sucking the fun out, and finishing it is a chore, especially for a completionist.

Sadly I can't recommend this game.
Pros: The mood, atmosphere and music for this game were all great. I love when games provide a lot of extra information in the form of notes and journals, and this game has a lot of it. Some of the puzzles were great.
Cons: A LOT of the puzzles often come down to random guesswork. There are also a lot of situations where if you don't drag your mouse across the entire screen, you won't find some small vital piece of something. This is just not a great puzzle game. Since this is the central gameplay, it should be more solid.
Some of the written material could've been better (the "Confrence Room" sign is one of the many notable editing errors). It felt like these materials were ambitious in scope, but could have used a lot more work. The books and magazines felt especially rushed.
Overall this game was more frustration and looking at walkthroughs than it was enjoyable gameplay.

I'm not an usual Point-and-click adventure player so at the start of the game I felt a bit lost. However, as I moved on and got to know more about the story, I became more engaged and things started to make a whole lot more sense.
The game graphics, sound effects, puzzles and documents all come together to effectively delivery an ominous and opressive atmosphere which very much matches the atmosphere you'd expect from a deserted bunker.
Some of the puzzles are quite accessible while others proved very challenging. You can solve all of them without resorting to guessing and random experimentation but some might have elements that confuse you more than they help you ("check button", I'm looking at you). Reading and paying attention to all the documentation and notice boards is critical to your success and make sure to note any unusual writings or numbers.
The story of the game was very engaging as you start to collect more data and more information about what was done at the facility and what happened. The ending, however, was kind of awkward and, to be honest, a frank letdown given the direction the story seemed to be taking. And while I appreciate when games/videos do not provide all the details so we are free to use our imagination to try and come up with reasons and explanations, I feel that this game, specially near the end, took many liberties in that regard. My playthrough took close to 5 hours but an expert P&C player might be able to do it in less time.
Overall, I'd give this a rating of 6/10. And a definite recommendation if you're a fan of the genre.

Now that I have played through the game once, I have to admit that I am rather disappointed by the final version of that game. the concept and screenshots presented in the greenlight campaign looked promising and made expectations rise that the developer is going to create a first person adventure, mixed with horror and/or mystery elements as well as the appearance of a fearable opponent/monster - set in the 1950's soviet union period.
Well, it took me about four hours to complete the game, and the end is, as some reviewers already stated, confusing and dissatisfying. The impression that I get is that the game was cut somewhere in the middle of the story line, for whatever reason. The end and what you experience minutes before just don't fit together.
Some players already said they found the puzzles hard to solve. I think that most of the time there is a logical way to solve them - you get a lot of information you need by reading the reports you find. I missed a clear signal that I really solved the puzzle - for example, when I got the right frequency on the radio.
About sound and graphics: Although the soundtrack is atmospheric and very generic, the places you visit are insensate and rigid. At one point, you inhalate some sarin which makes up some nice effects like a blur (no, not motion blur.) or blood red framing. but that's it.
Graphics are ok, but you don't go for the high end polygon count in a game like that.
One groundbreaking gameplay element that should be mentioned implicitly is the door-opening eyeball. You have waited a long time for developers to come up with some nice gameplay thingy that cuts the edge. Simply put the eyeball through a hole to get to the other side from where the door is locked, and the eye will open it for you. nice.
If you are not in for the eyeball, I cannot recommend this game at all.

I bought this game a long while back, but never got around to playing it. I'm not even sure if I've cleared the first area or not. I beat a demon chick, then quit shortly after it. From what I've played, the game is frustratingly difficult. The controls suck, with the act of jumping being religated to the z and c keys, meaning you'll keep accidentally hitting the x button, which is your attack.
The way enemies move almost guarentees that they'll hit you, and each of them deals a large chunk of your health. And I have no clue where the hitboxes are; so there's little consistency on whether you'll be hit or not. It'd be nice if the staff you were given fired a ranged attack. But no. It instead makes a little wall of white streaks in front of you that barely do any damage and all but require you to be in range of an enemy's attack.
Add that to the fact that the game is predominantly focused on ultra-precision, do this jump exactly or insta-die platforming over dozens of mini-sarlacc pits, stretchy arms that deal half your health, and demon cannons that fire at a rate slightly slower then the speed of sound. You'd think that the fact you're an angel with huge eagle wings would grant you some form of flight. But apparently you get less air-time then kangaroos.
Oh yeah, you get to take leaps of faith too. Have fun figuring out when. Not to mention sometimes, the game will have invisible walls that prevent you from walking to another screen.
And I was playing the game on normal difficulty (mortal mode). Under the easy difficulty (angel mode), the amount of benefits it gives is almost pandering. But as you go through the game, you'll see all of the checkpoints you would have got had you gone with easy mode. And the description for had mode (demon mode) sounded like what I ended up getting. I have no idea what this game would ask for on that setting.
Story wise (from the short bit I played), a big bad lizard-man from long ago was chained up in your... town? City?... Place where you live with a population of about 4 angels. And you and your friend decided to go throw rocks at him in his jail cell... ain't that likable. And he roars at you, causing you to fall back into a cartoonishly large switch that was just sitting on the wall behind you that instantly frees him. And the guards are nowhere to be seen because... your friend asked them to leave, I think. No big deal. They're only watching over a guy who can turn your place from paradise to hell in 6 seconds, who can supposedly only be stopped by an item was lost as soon as it defeated him long ago. Don't even bother putting bars around him. Those handcuffs will keep, you hope.
So yeah. You and your friend are idiots. The people who imprissoned the big bady were idiots. And now you get to do bs platforming and annoying combat to stop him. I'd say have fun, but you probably won't. If you're looking for a fun action, side-scrolling platformer like Cave Story or Shovel Knight, look elsewhere... or play those games. This is jump at the last pixel or die the game.

The game overall is pretty great. It's  a relentless but fair platformer with a few unique mechanics that allow for tonnes of clever level design. Everything is utilized fully to make for a lot of frustrating but rewarding fun.
Unfortunately the game is tainted by one major flaw: the flying sections. The game throws away every clever mechanic it teaches the player and instead puts you into a section of dodge the incoming objects and nothing else. These sections feel like a child's first Gamemaker game, which sucks because the rest of the game is so good.
If you can look past the flying sections, the real game is well worth the money. If the game was ever on sale it would be worth it even with the flying sections.
I'm only choosing to recommend this because I can't in good concience give a thumbs down to the best parts of the game. If you like Metroidvanias at all, you'll love most of what this game offers.

The game has potential, but I can't recommend it at the moment because the online multiplayer is too prone to breaking.  At times you'll get desynced and combat with other entities totally breaks for a few minutes until you finally resync.  But while that is happening, you can still move around and interact with things so you can totally bypass defenders, circumventing half the gameplay.
The game also has some rather bad hitching in the performance which happened for both me on my RX480 and my friend on his 1070ti.  If it hitches at a bad time you'll take hits or miss your shots and it is very annoying.  These aren't some bleeding edge graphics here, there is no excuse for that sort of performance issue on this kind of hardware.
The game isn't all bad though, and if not for these glaring issues I might have enjoyed it more.  The unlocking of percs and customizing your own classes is a nice touch.  The situations that arise in game can be pretty hilarious when big crazy fights break out because you accidentally got caught stealing from some guy.  The game is completely morally ambiguous as well.
If you are buying this to play split-screen locally, you might not run into some of this.  But I got this to play online co-op specifically but it is just too glitchy at the moment.  I plan to revisit this game down the road and should these issues get ironed out, I'll change my review.

Ducktales was a game I use to have when I was really young. I still have the game actually for my gameboy. Needless to say, I love the remastered version of it. Difficult for me at times, but who doesn't need a challenge sometimes?

I've never watched the DuckTales TV show, nor played the original game... but as soon as I saw the trailers I was hyped. The game is a remaster of the NES game DuckTales, with a beautiful new stylised look in HD. Not only that, but it has new modern remixes of the older tunes which sound great. The new cutscenes that were added have full voice acting by the original cast, which is an impressive feat in itself. Alan Young as Scrooge McDuck is still as good as always, and it's a joy to hear his voice acting.
The gameplay itself is exactly the same as the original NES game, which isn't a bad thing. The controls are solid and never feel unresponsive. The game itself feels like a new game, especially to somebody like me with no experience of the original. I found myself loving every moment, and I really connected with the characters and the world they existed in, despite having no experience of DuckTales previously.
My only gripe is the game's length. Despite the new level at the start of the game, the main story is only 2.5 hours long. The good thing is that you can choose to unlock all sorts of concept art and sketches for the game using the money you gain by playing the levels. Replaying levels never gets old, and there's an option to turn off cutscenes automatically if you want to just play the game, and also an option to have the original 8-bit music in the levels. I feel like I'll get many more hours out of the game just for the fun of playing the game.
If you're a fan of the DuckTales TV show, or the video game, you must get the game now. If you've had no experience with it before, but are interested, I recommend that you wait for a sale and pick it up then, as the length may not be enough to satisfy. Personally, I'm glad to have the game in my library.
Next time, pick a game worth remastering.

While the game retains the same gameplay and enjoyment of the original, it has some very giant flaws that I cannot believe or understand how the developers allowed to exist.
The first major flaw is the hit boxes. Either the enemy or Scrooge's hitboxes are way too liberal. Now, I'm not saying it needs to be pixel perfect, but it needs to be within reason of the pixels which, in many places, it is not even remotely close. So the hitboxes are really bad and loose in a lot of places.
The second major flaw is, for enemies that take multiple hits (See bosses), they get an invincibility to them after each damaging hit, which is completely reasonable, however they then become like ghosts and you can move through them. This is bad because often by the time you are getting away or through them, they come back into being solid and then hurt you, all because they don't retain their physical parameters during invicibility. This could have easily been resolved by either giving a shorter invicibility length or by simply making them not become ghost-like on hit.
Other than those two flaws, the game is very fun and quite enjoyable.

As a staple of my own childhood, DuckTales Remastered is a dream come true. The levels stay incredibly faithful to the original game's design, the graphics are crisp and colorful and the soundtrack is incredible. I would have said that WayForward did an amazing job, had it not been for one major flaw; the hit detection. This has been something that has plagued any "retro" style game, whether it be remakes of old games or brand new ones. The hit detection in DuckTales is not only poorly presented but also incredibly frustrating. For example, pogo-ing onto enemies with just outside of their hitbox results in you taking damage, even though graphically it shows itself as landing the hit. Another example is during the Amazon boss battle, there is a segment where his head will fly from the background to the foreground, making it tough to discern where he will land/hit, which results in the loss of a heart. With the old-style sensibility of restarting levels or boss battles once you lose your 3 hearts, this quickly reared its head as this game's Achilles Heel. DuckTales is a personally beloved franchise, be it the game or the show. I still highly recommend this game, but I feel WayForward made a huge mistake with not patching this issue before release.

Long story short, it sucks.
Long story long, Relive is one of the most fascinating failures I've seen on the Steam free market. I've never seen a game set out for one, simple, little task and not only divert its focus from that task, but sucks massive balls while doing so.
It's a game about CPR! So make a game about CPR!
Seriously, the training session is completely unncessary. It's literally a sequence cut out from Chapter 2, where all you do is just get told about the steps for CPR and watch some awkward animations of the character doing CPR. No interaction. Just questions and answers. I remember when I learned CPR in real life, I had to actually perform it on a dummy. Isn't there any way it could've at least made a mini game out of it?
And what's up with the story mode? It's awkwardly and slowly paced, with sluggish controls and incredibly pace-lengthening tasks that are so boring I started counting how many character's voices were generated by a computer. Basically, it's all the robots, although I'd guess that a couple of the humans act just as much like the robots in this game.
Basically, there's a big storm in Mars, you have to get out, but before you do you have to calmly walk through different corridors and single-handedly equip and prepare a ship for take off, so some lazy-a** crew can get to safety. Isn't it their job to prepare the ship? I was busy saving their crew's lives in the previous level, and also carried their box with data cores inside for them!
The sound is awful in this too... well, besides the voice-acting. There's no sound effects. For anything. No footsteps. No Mars-storm sounds. No crowbar-hitting-steel sounds. Just nothing. And it's really... really... boring.
Relive is a unique game. If you like bad games, this is sure to entertain your little masochistic self and for a lovely short 2 hours. But it's not fun. It's an absolute drudgery to complete. I'm giving Relive a 1/10.

In a proper and just world, Tera would've launched in 2004 and rewritten the MMO rulebook instead of WoW. I realize that I've just spewed outright blasphemy and am in extreme danger of being stricken down by a bolt of divine lightning, so let me explain. Traditional MMO combat – as popularized by Blizzard's genre-stomping behemoth – isn't exactly thrilling. While PvP and high-end PvE ratchet up the mobility factor a bit, leveling generally involves all the high-octane action that's typically associated with being a tree. That is to say, you root yourself in one spot and flip your brain switch firmly into the “Off” position. Tera, by contrast, requires skill-based swinging and fleet-footed acrobatics, leading to adrenaline-pumping last-second dodges against even the most mundane of foes. Also, which would you rather play as: an ugly old gnome or an adorable (and vaguely horrifying) dog person? I rest my case.

The missions were a bit repetive and not really difficult. Some main area forts have to be taken in but I used brute force instead of stealth which works very well, although it is not very assassin like.

Was the game epic? No. I preferred Brotherhood because of the better personality development and recognizable scenery. I would give it a 7/10.

Rainbow 6 Siege has satisfied my craving for a solid FPS that I haven’t felt since Bad Company 2, or Modern Warfare. It’s tactical, it’s fun, it has competitive elements, you just have to be willing to learn and put in the time to memorize the maps.
R6S has great gameplay. The controls, aiming, and movement all feel natural. The game modes I find exciting. I feel as if there are enough interesting characters that makes me want to play to unlock them. Speaking of unlocking characters, R6S has a fair model where the base game is ~$40 and that’s all you really need to pay. The maps are given to everyone, and the Year X (1, 2, 3) packs are all optional and more for development support. You do get the characters unlocked for free with those packs, but I feel like it would lessen the gameplay, and take away the drive to unlock things, if all were purchased. Another amazing aspect of R6S is the destructible environments allow for a huge variety of options when it comes to attacking/defending an area. In essence because of so many possibilities, no 2 games will really be alike.
I rated this an 9 due to 1 main factor subtracting from a perfect 10: Learning curve. I am coming into R6S nearly 2 years after its release, so I find myself at an extreme disadvantage when it comes to general knowledge about the game. I understand it’s probably like this for most games, but it’s even more so in R6S.
Graphics are solid. I noticed no parts in the game where I had to stop and just look at the scenery. They are not bad, but in 2017, when I am first starting, other FPSs like Destiny 2, clearly outclass it. If I was playing this on release, it might be different.
Audio reminds me of DICE games like Battlefield, but almost better. While BF does amazing with bullet sounds and environment, R6S excels with undistorted indoor/outdoor sounds that greatly add to the realism. The sound in R6S is what FPS games should be trying to achieve.
Content is good, but not anything amazing. In R6S there is Situations, which teach a player various aspects of the game. There are about 12 in total. Next is Terrorist Hunt, which is essentially PVE mode. You and 4 others Vs. NPCs in various game modes. The final mode is Multiplayer which is split into Casual and Ranked. I feel the content is sufficient enough, but it’s not varied enough where I can play this all day. Especially in ranked mode where there are less maps available.
R6S has great replay almost entirely due to the multiplayer being so varied, but at the same time I find it not perfect due to 1. The few modes available, and 2. The map restriction on ranked. Overall these are minor issues because I find the gameplay fun enough that I want to play. Another detrimental part might be if someone purchases all the Year packs, this would greatly shorten the amount of obstacles players can grind for and when unlockable are finished, people would be playing for rank improvements. I have about 40 hours into the game as of this writing, so maybe this will change as I unlock more things and have less of a desire to play. I’ll update if so.
I do recommend R6S. There are clear negatives, especially coming into the game this late, but I have enough fun with the game to make it my “Main” FPS since Call of Duty, and Battlefield have been a bit of a letdown in recent years.

For the $2 I spent on this game during a sale, I won't say it's bad. I certainly wouldn't pay its current full price of $13, though. Having only ever played pool before, snooker was an interesting change. After learning the basics of snooker quite easily from the game, I'll borrow the sage words from the cover of an Othello box to describe it: A minute to learn, a lifetime to master.
Pros:
+Easy to learn game with simple rules
+Simple, easy to understand interface
+Varying levels of opponent skill. Sometimes the round is really easy, sometimes really hard. A healthy dose of both throughout each tournament to keep it interesting.
+Other billiards type games when snooker gets to be a bit boring
Cons:
-Multiplayer is absolutely broken. Tried to connect 15 times, succeeded 3 times. If you want to buy this game for the multiplayer experience, don't. Period.
-The graphics aren't the greatest. Which is fine, you shouldn't be buying a snooker game to look for high definition graphics. Even so, sometimes you just can't avoid noticing people like this:
-When I mentioned a "healthy dose" of varying skill levels in tournaments, I half lied. Half the opponents are Jekyll Hyde behind a cue stick. Makes an awesome bounce off the wall that would make pros cry in one break; inexplicably sinks the wrong ball for absolutely NO REASON WHATSOEVER the next break.
-Mind-numbing physics - I cannot count the number of times I've aimed for the corner pocket and had my ball repeatedly bounce off the corner, going neither into the pocket nor back out onto the table. Once is amusing. Thrice is bemusing. 13th time is agonizing.
-Adding onto the above, the ball will never, EVER fly off the table from being hit too hard. If I could climb up onto the table and hit the ball with a golf club, it would never leave the surface of the table. Not really important, but just a petty annoyance of mine.
Closing statement: It's not a bad game. If it's under $10, it's worth the money. It's not polished, it's not pretty, but it's still entertaining. Just don't buy it for multiplayer.

It's a pretty decent game. The soundtrack is well written and consistent, it's updates are pretty packed, but the main attraction is the actual gameplay. There is a large variety of methods to complete an objective, like busting through the front door with guns blazing, strategising the stealthiest and most outwitting of plans, tampering with the air they breathe so they forcefully kill eachother, or hiring a team of criminals to do your bidding.
The locals act differently depending on your misdeeds. Specific actions can affect their opinion of you, and therefore the rest of the floor, so you have to decide how you'd interact with people too.
One thing I would point out is that the playstyle you want to use has to fit the character you pick, so choosing an offensive character would restrict you to that offensive style. Thankfully, the addition of custom characters lets you work around this, allowing you to mix and match your favourite aspects of a player.
You can also have fun messing around with the 'Mutators', basically altering the game's pace and/or difficulty with crazy stuff like a zombie apocalypse every level.
There's a lot of bugs and glitches in the game sometimes, and often make it necessary to restart the game, however the community constantly points these out for fixing.
I'd say it's worth the buy personally, but perhaps you could wait for a more stable and packed version in future.

Firstly, I came into this with really low expectations, I'm not really a fan of the assassin's creed series, but i've heard (from friends) that they're bad and getting progressively worse each year... the last one I played was either 1 or 2 (whichever the first open world one was). I really just bought this bc I have a weird fascination with ancient egypt and I couldn't pass up the chance check this out.
That said, I freaking love this game, in reality everything about it including the mechanics, story, combat etc. i'd consider all middle-of-the-road at best, but the fact is, the surroundings, atmosphere, etc. are just unreal. The world is huge and you can spend hours (and i have) just screwing off and ignoring the quests and story completely. I particularly enjoyed tomb-raiding some of the pyramids and tombs, and the atmospheric stuff like that is where this game really shines, like coming out of a dark tomb into the sunlight, the way the shadows play on the tomb walls when holding a torch or lighting a brazier(sp?), the sounds and experience of swimming underwater and then coming out, how you hallucinate weird things when out in the desert too long, the historical accuracy and how the city's feel so incredibly immersive etc. and the sound is done really well... The fun part for me was really just running around and exploring/looking at stuff, it's like going on a vacation.
So that's the good, heres the bad, everything else, like the story is just meh, the rpg-ish elements certainly were a good idea, and they set this game apart from others in the series but where they screwed up is the items to take advantage of it, unless you buy loot crates or items, you end up seeing the same blue items over and over, so literally i am using the same season-pack items i started out with 70 hours in. the controls are very poorly thought out for pc (but not impossible to get used to) combat can feel clunky, particularly parrying (it doesnt work well unless you're right on top of your opponent, and they really should have taken notes from the arkham or middle-earth games) and other things, like some of the perks don't work properly all the time, chain assassination's or chain adrenaline kills, a few of the bow skills (the bows, besides the predator one, feel bad in general)... one of my little niggles is they have all these cool cosmetic outfits, you also have this cool way of upgrading your armor, it looks different each teir you upgrade to, but only if you're wearing the regular armor, want to buy that armor from the store or use one of your dlc ones? those always look the same.
(Important for those w/ older or underpowered CPU)
Another one, and a major one so I'm giving it it's own paragraph, is that this game is optimized very poorly for pc. keep in mind this is running on a (gtx 1080/i7 6700k) rig that handles anything else with ease, (some examples... shadow of war on ultra-80-120fps, destiny 2 on ultra-120fps, wolfenstein on highest 80-120fps) but for whatever reason this game decides to divert a rediculous amount of the job to the processor, while the gpu even at ultra settings is only ever doing about half of what it is capable of... I've heard a few theories, like they are running 2 DRM platforms in the background, which seems probable, my theory is just that it is optimized badly, and forcing the cpu to do too much work while the gpu is working on half capacity. So while I get 100fps in destiny 2 at a packed-to-the gills event with 20+ players running around. this game averages around 60fps in crowded areas, and all the while my gpu is confused as to why it's not being utilized properly... the good news is you can turn all the settings up to ultra without negatively affecting your framerate, bc even then, the gpu is still only doing about half what it is capable of. if i was trying to run this on a rig with an i5 for example, i'm pretty sure i'd be getting drops into the area (30fps) that I consider unplayable. I'm not even sure what this is optimized for... I've seen this game on an XboneX and (inside alexandria/memphis/siwa/other busy areas) it looked like it was struggling... literally hurt my eyes (30fps), not seen it yet on a playstation but afaik the XboneX has better specs anyway. Like i said though, it runs fine on my rig but at times its right at the edge (60fps) of what I consider playable, and bc of the poor optimization, that can't be fixed by tweaking settings. I get pretty much the same framerate at low settings that i do with ultra.
So to sum it up, bad performance, meh story/combat/mechanics, freaking awesome ambiance/atmosphere/immersion. about the performance, it's a major flaw and it's broken but i don't see them fixing it, so i'd never reccommend to someone running less than an i7, but as long as you had that, i'd bet it'd run fine w/ a gtx 1060 or 980 or less, bc my 1080 isn't even working up a sweat. I probably also wouldn't reccomend this to a freind who was looking for a cool rpg/adventure type game unless they were specifically looking for an assassin's creed game, but i'd definitely reccommend it to anyone wanting to explore ancient egypt. So i'm giving it a thumbs up based on that, I bought this game to explore an area and part of history that I'm fascinated with and imo that's the one thing this game does really well.

Obviously, whether you'll enjoy it depends on how into board games with RPG elements you are (obviousy, they're pretty addictive to me), but as a recreation of the board game it's pretty sweet. The interface could be a little better and the AI could be better, but in the several games I played I didn't notice any noteworthy problems other than I wish the AI were a little more competitive. This is definitely much better played with human players.

Classic game brought to computer life.  Considering the table game is over $40, this is a bargain!
For those of you who try to compare this game to something like Hearthstone, all I can say is "Don't" because that is apples to oranges. All the strategy comes from what the cards give you, how well the dice treats you and how badly it treats your fellow players. In Hearthstone, unless you are playing with a starter deck, the strategy is the deck building and praying you get the cards you need out in time. Not unlike MtG. But with Talisman, you only have your class' benefits/drawbacks and MAYBE your choice of Runestones if you opted for that DLC. After that, you just have to watch the game unfold and as another reviewer put it, prepare for some serious "risk management". Also, this game has no time limit unless you set one.  Unless you set it up for sudden death (120 turns or less), all I can say is this party can go all night, so have 4 six-packs and a couple bottles of wine to enjoy with this game. I played one game, 3 players and 1 AI and each player, including the AI, each had a major setback and the game took 3 hours to conclude.
Might want to order out when playing this game. ALSO, for new players, turn off the timer so you can learn the cards. Had that issue when entering the Warlocks area, he offers 6 or so quests but the timer can time out while you are still reading the second card. This isn't chess. Its on by default, so check setting and turn it off because when it times out, you skip your turn.
With that said, the more real players, the better. The AI isn't always perfect and when an AI tries to use some spells or magic items, it can sometimes throw the game for a loop. I have only had this game actually crash TWICE in nearly 2 years I've owned it and only required a reboot from that once. Loops happen a little more often in which case you have to alt-tab out to desktop and shut down the program manually with Task Manager. But it is still worth the occassional headache.
The game seems very glitchy. Crashed around three times already after less than an hour of gameplay.  I'm not sure if I would recommend this to a friend.
Even with US2 out, I still picked this up (lack of funds) and I love it, even with a system like mine, it still stays above 30, amazing.

Don't get fooled by the positive reviews like i was. Everything about this game is very shallow.
There are 4 worlds(maps), but they aren't very big at all, they are actually rather small and the first world(Canyon) is actually rather tiny.
There are 30 cars, but they are all pretty much the same with next to NO diffrence in stats (There are no stats, all of the cars control the same except the later cars are sligtly faster then the beggining cars).
The only car stats is that the cars are devided in three categories: Light, Medium, Heavy. The problem is that they all control the same with the only difference being that the Light cars are a slightly faster, the Heavy cars are a slightly better at stunting and the Medium ones are somewhere in the middle(aleast from what i have seen, this is never explained in-game).
The mechanics are shallow. You can only do backflips, frontflips and move the car left or right doing 180, 360, 720 and 1080 turns midair(sorry, i don't know whats the real name of that trick if it even has one). The cars fly around on even the slightest bump and that can get annoying.
There are 6 minigames(events) that happen randomly in the game but most are very shallow. Here is why:
1. Find the ring event: There are always a few rings in every world, and when this event starts one of those rings turns blue and you have to get to it first in order to win.
The problem is that the player who is closest to the ring will probably win (unless the closest player makes some stupid mistake) so its completly luck based.
2. Racing event: All you have to do is go thru all of the checkpoints to win.
The problem is that ALL of these races take place on the flat terrain on the maps instead of useing any of the many props in the worlds so they are rather boring.
But the BIGGEST problem is that ALL of these races are very short, they last around 30 to 40 seconds. That happens because, again, the worlds are rather small.
3. Tag event: You have to stunt on as many of the props(and thus ''tag'' them) and you have to have the most props tagged before time runs out in order to win.
This event isn't actually all that bad. It makes sense that such an event exists since this game has alot of focus on stunting.
The only problem is that 2/4 worlds have specific places that you kinda have to go to in order to win cause they are filled with props.
4. Stunt event: Get the most amount of points by stunting before time ends.
This isn't HORRIBLE, but its shallow because you can easily win most of the matches by just doing the same stunt over and over again.
5. King of the crown: A random player gets the crown and has to keep it for 60 seconds to win, and the other players can win by hitting the player with the crown so they can take it.
It sounds good on paper but because of the mechanics and the fact that on even the slightest bump your car flyes around, it can be a pain sometimes to hit the guy with the crown, and 50% of the time the guy who randomly gets the crown at the start is the one who wins.
6. Coin collect event: Collect the most amount of coins before the time ends to win.
This one is completly fine, no real problems with it.
There are some bugs, most aren't all that annoying except the bug where you clip thru a prop and usually you are stuck there then you have to re-enter the world, thus you lose the event.
There is usually more then enough players in the game playing so don't ever enter an empty server(but sometimes when you are not playing at peak hours there won't be more then 6 players on any server).
There is no way to comunicate with other players.
The graphics are mobile tier(thats because this is a port of the mobile version of the game), but thats not important. What IS important is the sound, and the sounds are OK, but the music gets repetitive.
There is also a seprate Tank Battle mode, but its nohing special.
You start with the regular tank, you can buy 4 diffrent tank that all have diffrent stats(Yes, the tanks have actual stats).
You have around 5 VERY tiny areas that are in the sky, and the way you win is by shooting another player so that he flys out of the area and then that gets counted as a kill (yes, you just push them, they don't actually explode).
As you may see, the Tank Battle mode isn't all that great and there are other games (and mods for other games) that do a better job, but its not bad. Its OK.
But do you want to know the BIGGEST problem with the game? The game can be played for FREE on Android/Iphone AND it can be played for free on the web browser! So this game, even with the free copy, isn't worth 1 euro, let alone 5 ♥♥♥♥ING EUROS.
A mobile game on pc but it's worth the (very low) price.

An interesting adventure game which takes place in a research station on Mars, which has been breached by a nanite storm that threatens to destroy it. In this game you play as one of the crew members of said station, who needs to reunite with his fellow crew members and escape the station before it's destroyed.
What's interesting about this game isn't its depth or complexity; gameplay is quite simple, and follows the structure of traditional point-and-click adventures (where you look for different objects in order to progress and such), only that it's placed in a first person view; what's interesting is that a main point of this game is teaching the player basic CPR techniques, and I'd say it does a good job at that. It might not be the best way to learn it, but it does a good job of increasing awareness on how to act in situations that might require the use of CPR.
Other than that, the game is pretty short. It's still a good game, in my opinion, so I recommend it.

I loved the concept behind this game, but the execution was a little lacking. 70%
PROS
1. You learn CPR (I assume. I'm not medically trained, but to my novice self, this seemed like an accurate depiction)
2. Interesting art style
3. Cheery AI helpers!
4. It actually had a plot and gameplay outside the CPR training
CONS
1. The CPR learning section is kind of dull. It's not as interactive as it should be. I know clicking 30 times in a row might get annoying, but hey, it's more interactive.
2. "Interesting" art style. Some of the characters looked a tad creepy.
3. The robots didn't nearly have enough impact as they should have. When faced with the prospect (and related achievement) of losing my AI helper, I was only mildly distraught. I should be bawling at this point. Probably what might help is getting some voice work for this game. If I could hear the tinge of sadness creep in to its normally chipper tone, that'd be more impactful. And while I'm at it, all the humans could stand to gain voices, too. And environment sound effects. And... we'll just call it here before I completely derail this review.
4. The plot was kind of thin. The robots seem to insinuate that these nanobots were growing or evolving somehow, but that never is really resolved. Also, apparently the doctor just randomly has a crush on Mike that never goes anywhere. I was certain that one of them was going to die to get us off this station, but nothing nearly so dramatic happens. Also, gameplay is pretty slow as a whole. A time element while you're racing to save your buddies (for example) would have been a good addition.
Overall, I would recommend this game. However, my approval is less about the game itself and more about the concept and the potential it holds. Perhaps we could get a sequel in the future where you learn not only CPR but other medical techniques and apply it in a more combat or action-oriented setting while the gung-ho robots and solemn team members actually speak audibly to you. That, without a doubt, would be a 5-star game.
EDIT: The developers added some voice work. Hurray! The AI helper still isn't quite as cheery as I imagined, but just giving some of these characters voices really helps the game. There are a few sections that are still randomly mute (such as when you ask the Director for her room code), and it'd still be nice to get some atmospheric sounds, but this is definitely a step in the right direction.

While trying to make this game a bit more fun by including puzzles and involving some critical thinking (what little you would need, mostly to find the secrets ), it lacks the basic information about it's main purpose. Since I am from the USA, I do have my guidelines to go by and while researching for what the EU's version was....I wasn't able to find much. However, I believe the standards are the same. With that in mind, I'll break this down into 2 reviews.
1) The way the game describes to check to see if they're awake, by shaking them, especially where you had to do it on an a "player" in the game, could have killed them from trauma to the spinal cord. Common practice is to slap hard on the shoulds, not shake them.
2) Head-tilt chin-lift technique doesn't leave the mouth open, because you're literally pressing up on the jaw. Should be a step to open it and see if they just choked (doing CPR on a person who just passed out from isn't harmful but you should be checking to make sure that you're doing the right thing).
3) Many reasons why people don't do CPR is because the "rescue breaths", which aren't necessarily needed and not as important as keeping the blood flowing to the brain and heart. This information should have been included also. As with rescue breaths, you're to keep about 100 beats per minute and then 120 without the breaths.
4) It should have been explained better about the AED, and how you won't ALWAYS shock a person and should continue CPR inbetween the readings. It should also explain what the purpose of the AED is. Movies and games (including this one) make it seem that when a person's heart stops, you just need to shock them to bring them back to life. Which isn't true for most cases. Unless they are in ventricular fibrillation (v-fib) or (in some AEDs) ventricular tachycardia (v-tach), the AED won't shock. It should also explain to follow the vocal instructions of the AED and also the pads for both placement and when to do things. Also, if someone else brought it to you, then you should ask them to set it up while continuing CPR. By this game, once you get an AED, you're supposed to waste time putting it together, taking off the clothes (something else not 100% needed, just access to skin). and applying the pads. One person can do that while another person does compressions. The game itself says 3-5 minutes without oxygen and the brain starts to die. An unskilled person will take 5+ minutes to setup the AED.
1)   Ignoring the CPR faults, the game itself is pretty buggy. Tho for a free game it's not that bad. One thing kinda bugged me was during part 2,
I was trying to block the door with objects. Instead of pushing them aside, the doors just went through. them. No matter how many I placed infront of them.
2)  While voice acting would have been nice, the diaglog could have been improved, especially when interacting with any of the AIs. Particularly, during stage 2, you could keep asking any of the AIs that had options the same thing over and over again, with no change to 90% of the diaglog.
3)  You found the secrets, but only thing you could do with them is get a brief description of them. Would have been nice to been able to view something about them, especially since some where not that easy to find (but not that difficult either).
4)   The ending puzzle made no sense to be honest.
I know it's a game, but that made no sense were as the rest sorta made sense.

It's an interesting question: can you make a platform hell game - a genre that treats difficulty as a joke at the player's expense - feel serious in its intention to provide a tough but fair challenge? The answer offered by Wings of Vi is yes... with some reservations.
Though Wings of Vi pedigree traces its lineage back to masocore freeware games like I Wanna Be The Guy, you'll find none of the joke traps or obvious, gleeful sadism that made those games infamous. Vi plays its difficulty straight. Environmental hazards and new mechanics are typically introduced with a soft enough curve (relative to the rest of the game, anyways) to allow a degree of practice before their trickiest permutations appear. Bosses, though always difficult to beat, are rarely difficult to grasp mechanically. The game even places camera-scrolling demon eyes near complex platforming segments to let you survey their deathtraps in full heart-sinking glory. Wings of Vi wants you to understand its difficulty, not surprise you with it.
Wings of Vi hasn't completely escaped its roots, though. A few segments and bosses needle the player with demands for frustrating precision. You can almost envision the playtesting sessions where the developer played through a challenging section, mulled it over, then impishly dialed it an extra degree towards punishing. As you die repeatedly to platforms placed one hair past the comfortable apex of your jump, or laser timers one millisecond too short to clear, or bosses with one attack pattern past the realm of manageable, you may feel your skills flexing to close the gap, or you may feel like the goalposts were shifted to create it. What should be challenges of execution sometimes devolve into challenges of patience as you struggle to squeeze the last few frames of perfect inputs into a sequence of maneuvers you've long since figured out.
One thing I'd be remiss not to mention is the final boss, perhaps the most unnecessary dogpiling of player abuse I've ever witnessed. The aggressive and occasionally erratic movements, combined with its already trying attacks, would have been enough. To have to deal with these on a battlefield that's contstanly poisoning you, with sometimes poorly timed health orb spawns as your only remedy; on platforms that may summon pentacles that may set you on fire for standing near them, which can ruin one of the boss's few chances for free hits; and while juggling the enemies that spawn towards the end of the lengthy battle... it was all too much. That one fight alone took more than 8 hours of attempts and 700 deaths on NORMAL.
And yet, gripes aside, I would still narrowly recommend this game. The exhiliration I felt from beating it, even just on the medium difficulty, felt like earning a crown studded with the jewels of dozens of bested trials. Besides that, from going back on the easiest difficulty to earn the last few achievements I can say with confidence that Wings of Vi is thoughtful enough with its application of difficulty modifiers that anyone who knows at least to expect a high but generally above-board challenge should be able to find a difficulty that suits them.
Wings of Vi has its flaws, and I wouldn't recommend it even to most platformer fans. However, if your reaction to overcoming (sometimes unfairly) steep odds is more triumph than relief, you might want to give this angelic platform hell game a try.
It's challenging, but definitely worth the time and effort!

Urban Trial Freestyle isn't too bad of a game. The core things are there. The physics, upgrading your bike and the tracks are all good.
I'm running Windows 8.1 64-bit and the games stability was marginal at best. Sometimes it would crash once and then play fine for an indefinite amount of time. Other times it would crash at random over and over again and I just had to give up that day.
It also crashed every single time I got a Steam card for the game while playing.
I feel like the graphics engine wasn't optimized very well as I had to lower shadow settings and turn off AA. I have a GeForce GTX295. For the level of graphics in this game... it shouldn't be struggling at the max settings. I was able to get a constant 60FPS by lowering the shadow detail and turning off AA but i had to run it in 1920x1080.
Speaking of resolution. I have two 1440p monitors and i seemed to get slightly better stability when i set my resolution to match what I’d launch the game at.
It took me 10 hours to beat all the tracks, get all the cash bags and beat all the challenges.

*inhales* ok, here's the think about Da Orks: you won't have as simple a time as you will regular Armageddon. Now this is by no means a bad thing, quite the contrary it's good having a game that actually challenges you sometimes even on easier difficulties. However that all depends on HOW that difficulty is achieved. You see the difficulty spike from the original game to Da Orks is because Armageddon is a game that rewards accuracy and range, the Ork forces tend to have neither of those. The ork form of accuracy is shooting enough bullets until they hit. The way this is accomplished in game is by giving the orks more characters per unit.... for the infantry. This is where the main problem of the game arises, you see because while infantry have more characters and therefore more "shots" higher tier units such as tanks have just as many characters as the Imperial equivalent and fires just as much except the Imperium is more accurate. This leads to them landing more shots and by extension more damage than you. This can be offset by the fact that Orks can get rather Tanky armored forces faster than the Imperium does and thankfully the AI seems designed to go after units that have many characters in it that can't fight back as well/at all. this is where the rather versatile unit the Goff Guard come in. when you get them I recommend changing all your infantry into them since they have 40 characters, the most armor on an infantry, morale boost every turn to surrounding units, high vision, high mobility, more than DOUBLE accuracy compared to other infantry, they will rip just about any infantry/ space marine unit they get in combat with, and the computer is obsessed with shooting them first and always. This is because the Goff Guard fit into both of it's "priority targeting" algorithm: there's 40 characters in the unit and the farthest they can shoot is adjacent hexes.... yes you read that right the Goff Guard are equipped with the basic 20 damage "Slugga" pistol that has a range of 1. This means that on the computer's turn they will be shooting the GG without them able to launch retaliatory strikes. Remember that part though about these guys having armor? yeah they have 60 armor per character and as infantry units gain full cover from terrain. This means while they may take a lot of hits they can usually just tank through it and cause the computer to leave your other units alone. Now then on that note I will tell you that there are Ork units that actually get decent accuracy: the Skullhamma Battlefortress and Looted Baneblade spring to mind but there are others you get access to during the What If scenario we was robbed. You are gonna need them since these next three battles are no picnics with turn limits pushing 50 and an army of strong Imperial Guard and Space Marine units (special mention of the Salamander map since it's funnel maps on bridges ARGGGGH!). Notable of the new units you get access to are the mighty Gargants and Great Gargants! wait, you get access to Gargants and Great Gargants at the same time? what's even the point in regular Gargants then? well strangely enough you need them just as much as the Great Gargants. This is because the regular Gargants have less armor, mobility, and vision BUT! have better range, accuracy, and more shots than the Great versions. This means having the Greats on the front line and the regulars just behind them. Remember the tutorial campaign (which you really should play) that shows you that a DIVERSE force will deal with an opponent better than one that puts all it's power into a singular unit type. Remember to keep your Orks diverse and you should be able to have an easier time than some idiot who fielded almost nothing but Great Gargants (gosh I wonder what stupid review writer did that *cough*me*cough*). Anyway for someone who wants to play a bit more Armageddon or just wants to scratch that Orky itch I would recommend you pick this one up.

Joke Review:  Welcome to the male-on-male sexual harassment simulator.  The only game where you get to kiss men while they're passed out and grope their boobies while claiming you're giving them CPR.
Real Review:  Well, I thought to give this game a try.   It' not too bad, but it does not live-up to the feeling of panic, survival, horror, and possible combat that the trailer hints at which makes you think it'll be pretty long with a pretty good story....not quite.
You play the game as ERROR 404 (according to your apartment door) and get a message from your boss.  Lug around a
box of plot device data you cannot access throughout the base.   You are forced to learn CPR to continue through the base before putting it into practice one time.  The game's narrative isn't much and the dialogue seems to be a little wordy for an emergency situation through 4 chapters you'll finish in 1-2 hours.  (My log says 4-5 hours due to replaying to find an achievement)
Breakdown:
Chapter 1:
Wake up, pack your box, run away.  (Or as the video says... "Get your sh*t together!")
Chapter 2:  Mandatory CPR lesson after meticulous running around and puzzle solving.  (This will be your longest chapter, hands-down)
Chapter 3:  Cube physics that will make you wonder why they companion cube logic isn't good and why you're falling through boxes you're climbing.  Put your CPR into action.
Chapter 4:  Pack the ship, turn on the communications tower, escape.
Pros:
A noble cause for the purpose of CPR.
Run-around adventure.  (if you like that sort of thing)
Puzzles here and there along the way.
Decent usage of 3D models. (They look like they came out of Borderlands)
Free.
Achievements.
Cons:
A plot that isn't all that good.
Misleading trailer.
Although human models are decent, they're mostly ugly.   (Surprised the director is decent)
Glitchy (Box physics are not on par with Companion Cube physics in Portal)
Occassional freezes (during the CPR exam.  Do NOT choose "Wait for help", you'll wait forever)
Alt-tab on boot just to get the screen to display.
Personally, I was peeved about re-running through chapter 2 for an achievement (some of the time, the dialogue causes a freeze), but overall?  I've played worse.   Although I don't know if the usage of CPR is accurate in this game, I can at least say that it's attempt at educating gamers.
5/10.  Decent.  (Experiences may vary.)

I'm an avid fan of the DuckTales cartoon, but never played the original game, therefore my perspective comes from a non-nostolgic point of view.
The game manages to capture some of the same charm as I fell in love with in the cartoon, while it's limit is due to the confines of a platformer... Meaning, it doesn't have the same level of story as you'd find in an RPG or Adventure game. Each location/stage is decently sized, and enough hidden gems to make discoveries enjoyable. The difficulty is an odd mix, as the concepts of what to do seem quite easy, it often is a little harder to execute for the average gamer.  I believe that type of difficulty is a reflection of the 8-bit platformers of yesteryear, where they all were fairly difficult but that's what made the game rewarding.
Despite the game's moderate difficulty at times, it never left me frustrated enough to take away enjoyment. With this concept, the game also has a map to help guide you through seeking the items required to pass the levels. This helps give directlion and prevents the "what piece am I missing? I've searched everywhere!" feeling that many games leave you with.
The controls are quite simplistic, yet work quite effectively. It is smooth and even, allowing you to execute the moves and strategies you aim for.
The game also contains many  unlocks and goals to give plenty of replay value to the game, and make one strive to "unlock everything", which can give depth of purpose to a platformer as well.
The absolute best aspects of the game is the ovreall art- from the beautifully animated and true to the show characters, to the voice acting (including some of the original cast from the show), to the music and sound effects, as well as the dialog. It's really a gem!  The way the characters move and respond to the environment is great, making the characters have life instead of being mobile inanimate object. The sound effects and music help feed the environment and adventure, bringing an iconic feel yet remaining its own. And the interjections of story with the voice acting and dialog is fantastic! It happens frequently enough to bring it closer to the feel of the cartoon, caputring each character as they were originally portrayed. Each character talks like, sounds like, and acts in the same ways I would expect them to.
Summary: This game is very enjoyable and worth purchasing! The gameplay doesn't meet the same caliber of story that a modern adventure game would, but this game is a remake of a platformer, not a "new" game. It has the same rustic charm as games made during the orignal era, and captures the feel that any DuckTales fan would enjoy. Hopefully this game will spur some renewed interest in the series for the next generation, as this is a solid and enjoyable representation of what I'd expect from a Ducktales platformer.

A fantastic remake of a beloved 8-bit game. WayForward took what was a fairly simplistic, straightfoward platform game, and transformed it into a handful of mini-episodes of the DuckTales cartoon. It feels all the more authentic thanks to a fleshed-out script and full voice acting from many members of the original cast. Do the frequent cut scenes slow down the action considerably? Yeah. Is the game a little more shallow than you perhaps remember it being? Yes. But for me, these flaws were easily overlooked when I realized I was listening to Alan Young and June Foray (both of whom are in their nineties) performing the voices of Scrooge McDuck and Magica DeSpell again. It's the best nostalgia trip I've had in years.
It's not just the voices, though; the whole production is sublimely well done. The original idea to make Scrooge's cane a combination pogo stick/golf club was inspired, and the controls and feel of the NES game are replicated perfectly here even with the gorgeous new hand-drawn artwork. The developer retooled and modernized a few areas of the game, added in a new level here and a new challenge there, remixed all the original music, and topped everything off with reimagined boss fights that are both challenging and beautiful in 1080p. Hats off to you, WayForward... you're among the best in this business.

Introduction:
Although this game is a mobile port (which has cross platform support with mobile) that doesn't mean it's bad. Most mobile ports are absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥on steam but this one is decent. Now there is a reason it comes with a free copy is because it's overall more enjoyable with a friend because this game lacks content.
Price:
Let's be clear, this game is not worth the full price so don't go buying this full price grab it when it's on sale. I got this on sale of course and this game is worth around a dollar. Even though I say it lacks content I spent over 5 hours unlocking stuff which despite keeping me busy it didn't have the variety that would come with a higher price.
What it's about:
It's a game where you go around stunting with cars collecting points for flips, spins, and hitting beacons above the jump points. There are several stats to each car you unlock which are bought using ingame currency earned by winning random events and doing stunt jumps (beacons). You can level the stats to the cars by driving certain ways (explained later).  There is also a tank pvp gamemode which has hilarious impact physics which literatly send someone either flying in a random direction or simply flip them a bit.
Stats:
You have several stats on each car. Top speed which is leveled by driving fast, Acceleration which is leveled by accelerating from a near stop, handling which is leveled by drifting, and boost which is leveled by using your boost.
Most of these stats work well except when you're trying to level out all the cars at the end because acceleration can be quite annoying where all the other stats can be easily level grinded by drifting fast across ice.
Bugs and Functionality:
This game may play better on controller which I haven't tested. The annoying bug that you get use to is where you have to go to the esc menu to view you mouse which makes the onscreen garage button almost useless because it's hard to click without a mouse (although it's also in the esc menu). This is likely something left in from the mobile version for who knows what reason (touch screens maybe?).
There is also a bug where if you're on a different map then you friend and you try to join them using the steam friends list it will put you in the game but you'll be on the map you were on and not your friend's map where you'll see the cars driving around usually floating because of different map terrain and so on.
This game lacks graphics options which isn't much of an issue with this game. Why you might ask? This is because of it's mobile style and cross platform play. The game defaults to native resolution (you monitor resolution) so if that's an issue then avoid this game but overall it's not an issue. The game runs at 60 frames+ thankfully, and graphics are simple and would be pointless to change since requirements are low anyways due to it sharing online play and style with mobile.
Conclusion: Buy at sale price and use that gift copy to play with a friend and you'll use that sale price beyond it's value.

I really enjoy this game, the graphics take me straight back to the OG Pokemon, and it's almost like I get to stab that butthead who prevented you from entering Rout 1 before you talk to the Professor.
The premise of this Rogue Like is that a corrupt mayor has stolen all the booze in the city in order to fund a crime cyndicate that he is in charge of, and you must scale the city to stop him (and is a pretty decent statement about runaway capitalism). The city is appropriately separated into socioeconomic statuses and you must go through the slums all the way up to the 1%ers to kill the mayor.
The combat is an addictive balance of melee, guns and stealth, although I can't help but feel like the Soldier is the best character I've got so far. The Doctor was great for unlocking the Assassin, because I was able to chlorophorm everyone without detection, and the Gorilla was great for unlocking the wrestler because his dash attack still counts as using only your fist, but neither of those characters are able to use weapons (and the gorilla isn't even allowed in stores for hillariously obvious reasons). The Assassin's sword runs out of durability way too fast so you pretty much have to secure another weapon before it breaks, which is a drag. The Soldier however, has a helmet, guns, mines, grenades, and door demolishers. I'm working on unlockin the other chacters, but as it stands Soldier is mostly who I want too play, and the immbalance is worth mentioning; athough the gorilla is a strong second pick because give him a melee weapon and he can dash to one hit kill most things.
So far it feels a bit easier than Nuclear Throne, as I die a somewhat often to Big Bandit on floor one of NT, where as there was no boss at the last floor of the slums in this game. I would appreciate if I had to kill King Hobo to get out of the slums or something. It would make sense that the mayor employs the filthiest hobo to keep the slums down on their luck.
Also, it may be lost in the wall of settings text, but this game doesn't appear to have a mouse senistivty slider, and I had to go into my PC's mouse settings to adjusts, but hey thats an Early Access game for you.
Overall this game feels way more polished than a lot of early access games, and I gotta give props to the one guy developing it because he seems pretty responsive to the community, but more importantly he seems to have created a game that one person can manage. I see way to many tiny dev teams get swamped in what they want to accomplish.

Preface: DO NOT BUY THE STARTER EDITION ; EXPLAINED BELOW
I've been playing Siege since release and it'a game I ALWAYS come back too. I may take a break for a few weeks, but I'll always end up playing it again. It is an extremely fun tactical tacti-cool shooter that relies heavily on teamwork. It's like Search and Destroy from Call of Duty, except better in every way. You get one life, and to some that may be a turn off, but to most, it make it so you have to take every move carefully and think about what you're doing. This is one of the few games in the past few years where I've gotten both Season Passes the moment they went on sale, and haven't regretted it.
Starter Edition problems: There are 16 base operators that you can play, and with the Starter Edition, the operators cost  12,500 renown (compared to 500-2,000 renown for the operators in the Standard Edition). Starter Edition will immediately get access to two Operators, along with 600 R6 Credits to spend on two more Operators (or other unlocks) of their choice. The two initially available Operators are randomly chosen from a pool of six – Rook, Sledge, Ash, Fuze, Mute, and Smoke. That may seem like it's worth it; 2 random operators and 600 premium in game credits, but don't be fooled. The game is fun because of the variety of the operators you can play as, and with the Starter Edition, you're going to be stuck with a the same few FOR A LONG TIME. Each operator has a gadget  / special ability, and Ubisoft has done a good job that there are no overly overpowered or underpowered operators; every operator serves a purpose.
This game is one of my favorites, and it surprises me that it;s developed by Ubisoft because it has had AMAZING post launch support.

Warhammer 40,000: Armageddon – Da Orks (phew, that’s a long name!) is a turn based tactics game set in the Warhammer 40k universe. It’s also an almost perfect Panzer General game, but the player commands green skinned beasts instead of Axis or Allies units.
The basic gameplay is almost identical to Panzer General‘s (or rather, Slitherine‘s most excellent Panzer Corps, which was Panzer General in all but name) Players get a number of units (which increases as the campaign advances) and they have to overcome enemy forces using tactics, rather than sheer troop numbers. Every unit has different stats, and armchair commanders need to take into account unit weaknesses and terrain if they intend to make it past the first series of missions (by the way, the game can get quite hard even on the normal difficulty setting)
Objectives vary, but there’s always victory and resource points that must be captured before the turn limit ends (and defended, as the Imperium’s forces don’t take kindly to greenskins occupying their territory) Battles take place on familiar hex maps (hexagonal tiles can be turned on or off at will) and the game maps are highly detailed and succeed quite well in their task of showcasing a ruined planet in the far future of the Warhammer universe.
While it’s possible that new players may be able to play the game without reading the manual, I would encourage everyone to give it a look or maybe twenty, since it ends up being an invaluable source of information (and the in-game tutorial isn’t as in depth as I would have liked, an issue that also plagued the original Warhammer 40k: Armageddon) It’s not particularly long, sitting at a comfortable forty pages, and it does an admirable job at explaining the differences between different units, and the impact that the terrain can have on their combat effectiveness.
Speaking of units, the variety on offer is staggering. I could spend hours picking new ones for my armies, and they are all exquisitely detailed and competently animated.
Playing as the Orks brings some interesting tactical choices to light, as many units rely on close combat abilities. Sadly, most missions don’t really feel as if the player is in command of the WAAAGH! since the enemy forces are usually similar in numbers, if not superior.
The game’s Achilles’ heel is its dificulty, as it presents some rather sharp spikes, even at the normal difficulty setting (in all fairness, I haven’t tried turning the game down to easy, but its predecessor was TOO easy when I tried that, so I would think that isn’t a good solution to the problem at hand) Some people may find the challenge a bit too severe, and I wouldn’t blame them, though most of the problems seem to stem from the lack of good tutorials inside the game (which is why I highly recommend reading the manual)
Visually, the game is competent, but not extraordinary. The maps are highly detailed, as I said previously, and the units are all quite beautiful, with competent animations (though people not used to this kind of game may find them a bit too austere)  Sound design is also competent (with special mention to the voice overs used during the game’s many story panels) and hearing bolter fire, lascannon shots, or even listening to the units moving (they all have specific sounds) is always enjoyable. The soundtrack is serviceable, and it’s always in the background, never getting in the way of the action.
Strategy fans will get a great deal of enjoyment out of Warhammer 40,000: Armageddon – Da Orks, and 40k enthusiasts will get even more, due to the game’s faithful representation of the tabletop game’s units. It’s not perfect, and it’s sad that the development house didn’t include a better tutorial, since not all players will read the manual, but it is a welcome addition to the videogame branch of the Warhammer franchise.

Note: The game also features a multiplayer mode (of the Play by Mail type) but I did not get the opportunity to try it.
7.5/10 (Good)

Disclaimer: I received a review copy for Warhammer 40,000: Armageddon - Da Orks from Slitherine Group as part of their regular press release package to the public.
As a huge fan of WH40k: Armageddon, it's subsequent DLC packs (cept for Ork Hunters, didn't actually play that one) and a huge fan of DA ORKZ, you can imagine this new expansion was right up my alley. Seriously, WH40k: Armageddon was one of my favorite strategy titles of 2015.
So for the uninitiated, WH40k: Armageddon - Da Orks is a turn based war game in the same vein as Order of Battle, Panzer General, Panzer Corps or any variant you've seen of a Hex Based War game. The big difference here is it takes place in the Science Fantasy universe of Warhammer 40,000 and it centers on the conflict on the planet Armageddon from the Orkz perspective.
For those who don't want to read:
Gameplay First Impression
For those familiar with the Armageddon series of games from Slitherine, this is the list of major new features:
-Additional 150 new units (including my new favorite: Horned Squigs)
-A multiplayer skirmish mode that allows changing of variables in the initial set up of the game rather than playing preset scenarios (preset scenariors still included)
-A story line entirely focused on the Orky perspective including new alternative "what-if" scenarios.
-Completely stand-alone. You don't have to buy the base game or it's subsequent DLC's to play this new expansion.
So what's Good?
-Da Horned Squigs (Those deliciously overpowered little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s)
-More scenarios of the already fantastic game
-It's focused on Orkz. I've waited too long for this!
-The unit variety is astonishing to say the least. One of the biggest reasons this series continues to set a standard for future 40k Wargames.
-The heavy focus on Ork Heroes like da Mad Dok Grotsnik and G. Mag Uruk Thraka in the story.
-More of the same stuff that made the original game so fun.
-Unit detail is still damn good.
-You still have a few alternate divergences that can be made throughout the campaign.
-Seems like a good starting point for new players who are unwary about purchasing the complete edition of Warhammer 40k: Armageddon (the original).
The Not so Good?
-More of the same from the original game. This is a pro because the original was great. This is also a bit of a negative because it doesn't feel like there are features that change how battles are played out. It's pretty much the same, keeping the enemy at a distance and pummeling them down until their numbers are low enough to engage in close combat!
-The game is run on the same engine that ran Panzer Corps and the original Warhammer 40,000. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, I'm just sad there still aren't dynamic animations like you'll see in Order of Battle. It should be noted that the maps are detailed and the unit models are all quite detailed though, so the overall aesthetic pulls the game strongly through.
-I can't help but feel like I'm playing a lot of battles where the Imperium of Man outnumbers me. Dis iz odd cuz Da Orkz are da ones who shud be doin' da out numberin'! I want to be in command of a WAAAGH! like the Orkz that bashed against me in unending waves when I played the Steel Legion's side. Maybe as I play more into the story, I'll begin to see battles where there is a proper WAAAGH!
-The voice acting seems a bit less on par compared to the previous entries which were great and over the top sounding. It's not horrible by any means, mind you, just heavily filtered. I'd say more a meh than a negative, truly.
Final Verdict:
Despite my lengthy "not so good" section, it really is good. If you liked the original game, then you'll enjoy this one. If you're new to the series and looking to jump in, this is a great place to start at a cheaper price point. Would definitely recommend to War Game fans and Warhammer 40,000 fans alike.
