Had a lot higher hopes for the game based on comments, but it's really just only an okay game that TRIES to accomplish a lot but struggles in a lot of aspects too. Overall you'll have a great time playing the game but it loses the charm quick.
PROS
------
- The unique characters like the Zombie are REALLY fun and offer really unique and interesting gameplay in comparison to some of the other characters.
- The humor is great.
- Some interesting and well thought out ideas are in place like being able to poison characters to make them leave, or being able to bribe certain characters to do certain tasks for you.
- The items are pretty interesting for what they are and some of them are definitely unique and fun to use.
- The game feels like a unique experience compared to other games in this genre.
- The game runs great because of the low cost art style.
- Dedicated developer is always a plus, especially with how easy "Early Access" is to exploit.
CONS
---------
- $16.99 feels too expensive. Yes the developer is dedicated, yes there's an okay amount of content, but it exploits the grind aspect to say there's more content than there really is. Pixel graphics, a weak soundtrack, and some clever ideas aren't enough for that price tag.
- Half the characters are great, the other half are just kind of whatever. Some characters like the Hacker just feel very, very, very useless and uninteractive.
- VERY few NPC's. 30 minutes in you've seen every one of them and you basically already know what they all do.
- The inventory / HUD feels a bit clunky or ugly. Could be polished a bit and cleaned up.
- Not a whole lot of clever or sneaky interactions that you can find that aren't pretty obvious already.
- The maps are pretty boring. Very few things to interact with and once you've played a run or two you'll see nothing new from then on.
- The game takes a while to play through a run and a LOT of the run feels grindy before it gets interesting and possibly a bit difficult.
- Buying items doesn't feel very rewarding or useful. I kept finding that unless I needed that one clutch heal, then I was never, ever, ever using the item machines or shops.
- MOST items feel pretty pointless. A lot of the time you can get through a game solely by shooting your way through or using your fists without the need for any other items aside from food (healing).
- So many interactions either feel wonky or just flat out don't make sense. It doesn't feel as polished as it could be. Characters act uncharacteristically sometimes out of nowhere and there isn't a sense of.. "my gameplay sparks x reaction from characters." It's just alerting an enemy versus not alerting an enemy.
- Rewards and purchases with the currency feel.. wonky. Currency takes a while to get and most rewards feel too insignificant for you to want to buy or grind to buy. A lot of them you actually DON'T want to buy because it makes gameplay more inefficient with the way leveling up is designed. They don't offer interesting enough gameplay changes.
- The game isn't challenging unless YOU place some kind of challenge there for yourself, which basically means every run is some kind of Nuzlocke run. You're just looking for excuses to do things in certain ways.
- The game was made under the premise that you could play it however you want. That being said, the only method that makes sense is to go in guns blazing because you're still basically doing the same thing as the other methods. You want to hack that computer and have an edge in that regard with the Hacker? Doesn't matter, because computers are too easy to access, too easy to use, and you're left with no niche, purpose, or edge over any other character. They can do the same thing as you just as easily. Computers and certain things should've been made more difficult for the average character to access to give certain characters distinct niches. Right now they can all do the same thing as one another with ease (except for characters with special abilities).

Just finished playing this game to completion (upgrading all cars, etc), and I have to say it was pretty cool.
Items of note for you who are interested:
• It's an online game - you connet to servers (JP, EU or US based on your locale), so ultimately it's a multiplayer, like a simple version of Trackmania or similar.
• Graphically, it's not going to blow your socks off [mobile port I believe], but it makes up for that in charm, with 30 different vehicles, each with their own characteristics (engine sounds, horns, boost effects, handling).
• While only 4 tracks, and a tank battle level, there are various things you do in each one, from collecting coins, accumulating stunt points, racing, tagging objects, find the ring, and king of the crown, it doesn't get too boring if you like to be competitive, and in there to enjoy the game.
• No in level or lobby for chat! A MP game like this could benefit so much from this, would make it's stay a lot more welcome, something I'd come back to if it had this.
• There are a few glitches - getting stuck in certain places, points sometimes mess-up in the tag matches, and sometimes you lose connection to the server (that last one doesn't affect your progress, so don't freak out) - but I was able to overlook this as didn't have high expectations of a game that's only like $5
I really enjoyed this game, and if things like chat/interaction with players was added, more levels, and some of the glitches were fixed (points-glitch in particular), this would be something I'd see people stick around to play longer. Recommended game - 2-pack for $5 is a no-brainer - dive in with a mate, and get playing!

Okay, I looked back at my original review, and I made it around 10 minutes in. Now ive spent around 3 hours into the game, mostly for getting the cards. But, oh boy, has it not been worth it. Let me go over one of the most dissapointing part of the game.
First of all, it's a mobile game. Not saying thats bad, but the part that irritates me is that I found this game, for FREE, on Kongregate. Why would you pay 5 dollars for a download of a free Unity game?
Second. Ive been having plans to become a game designer for quite a long time by now. I have studied quite a few games, to learn what makes them good. But, the first step for me in my books is broken by this game, and laughs about it. Invisible walls. THERE IS AN ACHIEVEMENT FOR FALLING OFF THE WORLD. Who in their right mind would think that instead of programming invisible walls to the side of your level, you should instead reward the player for falling off the world? That's terrible for the devs! That makes them look lazy! I really just need someone to explain why they did that.
Third. It's basically just a watered down Tony Hawk game, alike to the new Pro Skater 5, without the glitches. The biggest problem for me is how to get points and XP. Sounds easy to make, right? They managed to make it extremely flawed. Yeah, it all looks good to kids, the target demographic here, but they can be exploited very easilly. For points? The tag game is the easiest thing in the game. To get a bunch of points, all you need to do is go off a ramp and hold down and left/right. Noone really realizes it, so I keep getting number 1 on each tag mission. Its very sad. Now, the XP system is a good idea how its pitched, but the fact that you can just drift and hold control to boost, and you rack up XP super fast, is just depressing. I really dont understand why it's that easy to abuse.
In total, NEVER buy this game. It's a mess of a game, and it's really not fun. I never really wana touch this game again. If you want to try it anyways, go search it up on Kongregate. And if you want an actual fun version, just play Tony Hawk's Underground 2, or even better, a mod for it called THUG Pro. It's super fun.

I love everything about this game.  It takes the feel of an old Capcom platformer, and breathes new life into the old formula.  If you're a fan of platformers, DuckTales, or even just solid gameplay, this game is for you.

As someone whose first videogame was DuckTales when I was 4 years old, I was excited about this remake ever since it first made its announcement.  I am very happy to say that I was not disappointed.  DuckTales Remastered is a perfect example of how to do a remake of an old-school game.
Controls are exactly the same to the point of my muscle memory working perfectly, the option to turn Hard Pogo on or off is a godsend, the music may be rather busy for some but I personally find to be a fantastically expansive soundtrack, the characters have all of their personality back with most of the original cast coming back in full flawless form, and lastly the difficulty still remains as an honestly tricky game on some parts.
If you think this is just the same old game from the NES, you're wrong.  It's even BETTER than that, with more expansive levels, mission objectives, a helpful little map system and a much more involving story that's just as kooky and carried away as the old episodes themselves, DuckTales Remastered made me relive my entire childhood in the span of just hours.  Buy it.  Love it.  Like a hurricane.

This game isn't finished. The developer is telling you it's finished, but it's not finished. Balance issues are everywhere and half the content is locked behind a  4-5 hour grindfest for each character. The level exp doesn't increase as the enemies get harder so you'll find yourself grinding the first level on repeat in order to get good gear.
The enemies don't get harder, they just get more health. At some point the extra damage means nothing to you except more grinding if you get hit.
Stats are unbalanced, and there are bad ones.
There's about 3-5 unique enemy AI, and they are copy and pasted into different designs.
The bosses have about 2 different AI shared among all of them.
The levels are boxes, always 2 boxes wide, and 3-4 boxes tall.
The exit is always in the top right.
Some of the rewards have such a huge grind that they're just not worth getting. The stories are bland and have no difficulty curve, just a difficulty steep wall to the boss fight. For a game where your life counts, it's pretty cheap.
However, the movement is addicting. Flying through the air, dodging projectiles left and right, you'll fly through levels with a euphoric speed. That's the one thing this game has got right, and nailed it. It's the only reason I will still play it. Also, the ultimate weapons he's locked away behind tons of grinding are a lot of fun, even if some are a lot better or worse than others.
This game had potential, and the developer took that potential and threw it under the rug.

This is the type of game that, the longer you play it, the more your realize it's not as good as it first felt.
The short story is, it starts hard, and ends nearly impossible. Long story is, it's doable, sure, but it requires a level of precision and memorization that starts to defy the "challenging yet fair" tagline the game flies. It becomes less of a tough game, and more of a droning grind of just doing the same tiny segment of level over and over and over until you do it exactly right.
It's not fun. There's a balance that games like Dark Souls nails perfectly; it's a tough game, but honestly an experienced player can breeze through it. Older games like Castlevania also get it right, the difficulty was more about your ability to go quite a distance with good play. Wings of Vi quickly devolves into challenging you to go a very, very short distance with PERFECT play. That's not satisfying gameplay, it's bashing your head against a wall until it works, and then you bash on the next wall.
I didn't finish the game, but I did get to the final boss. This was where my patience just ran out. I just didn't have the patience anymore to spend 30 minutes to an hour repeating the same 20 seconds of game content until I finally had the privaledge of seeing the next ten seconds of content to grind out in turn. The same process that had me feeling unfulfilled with the last several bosses.
I don't recommend the game. It starts strong, tough but reasonable, but the difficulty only goes up and up into the realm of the unreasonable.

(TL;DR at the bottom.)
First off, I bought the Starter Edition for about £6.50. Didn't have too much faith since it was Ubisoft, and was pretty much going in blind on the recommendation of a friend. Most of the reviews that mention Starter consider it worse than Hitler, because of the massively increased operator prices. If you've not seen the link or expanded the description, I'll do a shorter explanation.
Starter has a flat cost for each original operator of 12,500 renown (regular currency), compared to the 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 tier system for each Counter-Terror Unit (CTU) of Standard. You can buy the operators in any order you wish, and both versions have the same credit (premium currency) cost of 300. Post-launch operators can be purchased via the Year 1, 2, and 3 passes, with Y3 operators being available, free, a week early. Otherwise, they cost 25,000 renown or 600 credits in both versions. Both versions are hosted on the same servers and have the same features besides operator costs.
I played for about a week with my friend (aww, fwends) who taught me a lot of things - mainly map and operator knowledge - which helped a hell of a lot, since knowledge is a huge part of this game. If you don't have a teacher, go check out YouTube, because there's a few channels who do fairly good videos for beginners. Or you could always wing it, but prepare for a steeeeeeep learning curve.
After that week, I bought the third credit bundle for about £16, happy to spend more on a game that I'm still surprised isn't full AAA price. You could argue there's a bit of a pay to win structure there, but everything is unlockable without spending more, and the game isn't full price unless you want it to be, bar the post-launch operators. I'm also amazed that Ubi are still updating and producing new content going into the third year, showing that you can still stick with a game these days rather than releasing a sequel a year later.
On to gameplay. On the whole, it's good. Not military sim levels of realism, but not CoD or CSGO levels of arcade. 5v5 with 3 game modes - hostage, secure area, and bomb. The maps are well designed, but hilariously unrealisitc - there's a comical number of convenient air vents and floor hatches. Generally each operator has a gun that's just their best, and there's little reason not to use an ACOG scope on anything that'll take one. Saying that, I prefer some weapons with the holographic just because, but we'll move on. Guns can generally be ranked by fire rate, since headshots are one-hit kills, so the more rounds you can spray at your enemy's face, the better. Don't think this means the game is just spraying - if you can't aim, you ain't gonna enjoy much IMO. Damage still matters anywhere else though, and each operator has 4 points between armour and speed, either 3:1, 2:2, or 1:3. These matter because of how many non-headshots they can take, or how much noise they make moving around, and noise is integral in this game. It can give you advance warning of someone nearby, and save your life constantly. You can also get to know the gun sounds to a point that you can tell which operators are on the other team by them shooting. Like I said, information and knowledge is a huge part of this game. You'll learn maps as you play them, realise strategies and manouvers that happen all the time.
Now, the servers and net code are really worse than Hitler. Matchmaking is surprisingly fast, but load times are random as hell - someone can take over a minute to load after all the operators and spawn points are chosen, and it really isn't their fault. You'll swear you shot first, or hit about 5 headshots, but you still died. It'll happen. If there's anything wrong with this game, this is where the issues are. But it hasn't stopped me playing. Sure, the rage will come, but don't let it stop you. There's nothing better than getting a clutch or an ace. My first clutch made me feel proud. My first ace was also a clutch, and I'm damn well happy to say I jumped out of my chair, shouting and fist-pumping. This was in casual. I've not even played ranked yet, and I don't plan to either.
So for the TL;DR guys/girls/attack helicopters, this game is a genuine tactical shooter, where knowledge and information are as important as your ability to flick-shot. It gets updates often, and new content is still being produced into the third year. It's amazingly cheap for what is, in my mind, AAA quality. 5v5 contributes to basically every action being meaningful (so please don't reinforce between bomb sites, or roam with a 3 armour), and the maps are well designed that one decision can flip the round if the other team haven't safeguarded against it. I've had no issues with progression, and while I have bought credits, I can't see where I would have had issues. It isn't full price, so how can you complain about unlocking operators?

TL;DR? Basically the game is a terrible version of Tony Hawk games, and it's a sad attempt of a clone.
Okay, I looked back at my original review, and I made it around 10 minutes in. Now ive spent around 3 hours into the game, mostly for getting the cards. But, oh boy, has it not been worth it. Let me go over one of the most dissapointing part of the game.
First of all, it's a mobile game. Not saying thats bad, but the part that irritates me is that I found this game, for FREE, on Kongregate. Why would you pay 5 dollars for a download of a free Unity game?
Second. Ive been having plans to become a game designer for quite a long time by now. I have studied quite a few games, to learn what makes them good. But, the first step for me in my books is broken by this game, and laughs about it. Invisible walls. THERE IS AN ACHIEVEMENT FOR FALLING OFF THE WORLD. Who in their right mind would think that instead of programming invisible walls to the side of your level, you should instead reward the player for falling off the world? That's terrible for the devs! That makes them look lazy! I really just need someone to explain why they did that.
Third. It's basically just a watered down Tony Hawk game, alike to the new Pro Skater 5, without the glitches. The biggest problem for me is how to get points and XP. Sounds easy to make, right? They managed to make it extremely flawed. Yeah, it all looks good to kids, the target demographic here, but they can be exploited very easilly. For points? The tag game is the easiest thing in the game. To get a bunch of points, all you need to do is go off a ramp and hold down and left/right. Noone really realizes it, so I keep getting number 1 on each tag mission. Its very sad. Now, the XP system is a good idea how its pitched, but the fact that you can just drift and hold control to boost, and you rack up XP super fast, is just depressing. I really dont understand why it's that easy to abuse.
In total, NEVER buy this game. It's a mess of a game, and it's really not fun. I never really wana touch this game again. If you want to try it anyways, go search it up on Kongregate. And if you want an actual fun version, just play Tony Hawk's Underground 2, or even better, a mod for it called THUG Pro. It's super fun.

My steam collection seems like an uncharted territory full of titles that I've never heard of. Sometimes I just pick a random one, run it, and expect nothing. Optimism was never my strong suit after all. So, I run Crash Drive 2. Expecting the worst.
I entered the menu of the game, exhaled with irritation. Everything looked unpolished to the point that I felt like pressing quit instantly.
I am glad and lucky I did not. You see, yeah there are all kinds of problems here, interface wise. But, buuuuut, and that is a big but (I like that point in every review I write. I like it, and I cannot lie). The core gameplay mechanics are pure bliss, fun, or any other similar word you could put there to simulate a happy warm fuzzy feeling in your gut.
There is the stage, open not linear, and the players with their cars in it. Driving around, roaming freely. Then the events start to come, one after the other. King, with a crown and all, every other car chasing you to get it from you. The winner will be the one left wearing it proudly on his/her hood.
Stunt contest? Sure, there is that as well. Racing? Yeap, this is a random event that just may happen. Also it is the one event you can opt out for the round, if you wish.
Play play play this game, if you love fun racing titles. Do not let the sloppy interface put you off. The heart of Crash Drive 2 is golden.
One last thing. The in game invite friend system does not seem to work. You have to invite your friends via steam, in order to play with them. In fact the best way is to start a game and then the rest of the group join that game you created, via Steam not inside the Crash Drive 2 menu. Cumbersome? Yeap. Sloppy? Sure sure. But if you have friends who own the game you have to play it with them. If you do not have friends who own the game gift it to them. If you don't have friends, go make some. And then play Crash Drive 2 together.
Seems like fun, if your in to doing your own thing, or maybe competing with the other players. Cars are apparently indestructable, so not much to worry about, just enjoy it!
Ever want a barebones driving game you can mess around in, where the lack of polish is its charm? Look no further!

This game isn't finished. The developer is telling you it's finished, but it's not finished. Balance issues are everywhere and half the content is locked behind a  4-5 hour grindfest for each character. The level exp doesn't increase as the enemies get harder so you'll find yourself grinding the first level on repeat in order to get good gear.
The enemies don't get harder, they just get more health. At some point the extra damage means nothing to you except more grinding if you get hit.
Stats are unbalanced, and there are bad ones.
There's about 3-5 unique enemy AI, and they are copy and pasted into different designs.
The bosses have about 2 different AI shared among all of them.
The levels are boxes, always 2 boxes wide, and 3-4 boxes tall.
The exit is always in the top right.
Some of the rewards have such a huge grind that they're just not worth getting. The stories are bland and have no difficulty curve, just a difficulty steep wall to the boss fight. For a game where your life counts, it's pretty cheap.
However, the movement is addicting. Flying through the air, dodging projectiles left and right, you'll fly through levels with a euphoric speed. That's the one thing this game has got right, and nailed it. It's the only reason I will still play it. Also, the ultimate weapons he's locked away behind tons of grinding are a lot of fun, even if some are a lot better or worse than others.
This game had potential, and the developer took that potential and threw it under the rug.
The developer should finish their games

There are good video pool games out there. Games that have natural feeling controls, that actually remind you of stroking a pool cue. Games that add to the formula with innovative game modes that would be impossible in real life. Games that give you the fine control needed to make complex shots.
This is not one of those games.

This has to be the best snooker/pool simulator I have played. The game physics are very true to real life. The two improvements I would like to see would be more items in the shop, and a more varied audience and opponent model. As it is now the audience is always the same people sitting in the same seats, and there appears to be only one sitting model of the players which is always the same.

This is not a game I can honestly recommend with a clear conscience, although people looking for a Snooker simulation on Steam are going to find their options sorely limited; this is in fact the only one, but there are so many things that don't feel right with this game.
The AI difficulty can vary wildly within the same match, and even within the same frame, going from missing shots you'd think were unmissable to clearing the table unless you snooker your opponent on the break. The AI has no concept of shot selection either - in one example, the computer opponent had potted a red and ended up in the jaws of the middle pocket, completely unable to see pink and black. He them promptly nominated black (despite having an easy blue he could drop in to the opposite middle) and proceeded to play the cue ball directly into the jaw of the middle pocket, sending it careering around the table and missing everything. This happened 3 times in a row, at which point I was awarded the frame. Laughably bad.
Michaela Tabb, bless her heart. She's a good referee and a likable character on the Snooker and Pool circuit, but there's no visual representation of her in-game at all; she's been reduced to a disembodied voice with about as much emotion in her tone as GLaDOS in Portal. In some instances, the game doesn't even get the scores right - on more than one occasion, I've potted a red, followed by a pink (for a break of 7), only for the game to proudly announce that I'm on a break of 6. The only thing stopping poor Michaela from turning in her grave is that she isn't actually dead.
Sending the cue-ball in-off is a common occurrence, but one that seemingly happens at random, completely irrespective of how careful or otherwise you're playing. There is no consistency with shot power, with a 100% power shot sending the cue ball all the way around the table twice, but a 40% power shot is rarely enough to even pot the black off its spot.
Animations of the crowd clapping are horribly and obviously looped, the player character is never seen and has no character model, so you can forget about character customisation aside from the name, and the opposing player is only ever seen sat down at the side of the table while you make your break. Obviously it was too much to ask to animate a model of someone walking around a snooker table and playing a shot.
If you want a good snooker game on the PC, avoid this and buy Virtual Pool 4, which has a fantastic snooker game mode.

I purchased this for $1.39.  It's fun, but not without it's flaws.  I had to forfeit a match after scratching on a shot where the cue ball would not return to the table, so the game could proceed.   In this game if you have not played it, you earn credits to upgrade your cue, get different couloured chalk, etc.   I spent my credits on the auto-chalk feature, where the computer is supposed to chalk your cue before each shot.   I started failing on a lot of shots, and attributed the problem to not manually chalking my cue, even though | had this feature.
The ability to fine tune your shot would be enhanced if you could use a key stroke to fine tune the angle, rather than just adjusting the mouse.   Sometimes it's two or three minutes to get where you want to position the cue.
Lastly, this is an individual game, I am vain enough that | don't want anyone messing with my statistics.   It would have been nice if they could have added a feature where you could create other players, for friends to try the game.   You cannot lower the amount of frames played if you play 8 or 9 ball, every time you tap the button the frame count goes up.
It's fun, but I am glad I only paid $1.39.  If they update to improve some of these features I would recommend the game, as it is, your statistics do not really reflect your statistics with these flaws.

This game is painful. As someone with fond memories of the original product from my childhood, all I can say of this newer experience is that the developers did too good a job copying the original game... right down to the mechanics from 1990.

.
The only way you get through this game is by trying, and dying, a LOT. And starting from the very beginning, every single time. In a word, this game is hard. But it is not hard in the good challenging sense. It is hard in the frustratingly unfair, hair-pulling, rage-inducing sense.
Also annoying: Too plentiful and slow-paced cutscenes that you have to rewatch every single time, although you can also skip them every single time.
That said, it is beautiful to watch and listen to. But I know it's not something I'll be coming back to.
WayForward focused on the wrong things to upgrade for 2013, and it's a shame.

Its a fun mmo that reminds me a lot of Maplestory
It has some issues, which ill outline first:
You level up really fast. I played this a few years ago when you couldnt get to 65 in just a few days. Over 120 or so hours i spent to et to 49, i saw a vast game with lots of content. I played mostly solo and it was a great experience. You feel like an adventurer out doing random oddjobs for the good of the people. Back then i didnt see a TON of players, since most chose the mainstream dungeon raid rout to level up, i chose hardgrinding. However today, you can make a character and get to lv49 in a day with x2, maybe not even. Iv never been max level, so i cant say how much there is to do once you get there, but for everything before that, you basically skip it all.
Theres also the bit to extreme limit on character slots. 16 is the max per server, yet you only get 2 to start with. That dosnt let you really try any classes. According to most players, you should play a class to 65 before you decide weather or not you like it, and if thats the case, youd have to do this a myriad of times, while deleting any class beforehand that you worked up to 65. This is unless you paid 5$ like an absolute idiot to get another slot, are a founder (8 slots per server, and lots of other perks. 17$ average price), or used ingame gold (current price is 27k on average). The last 2 options by far being the best and admittedly not bad choices at all.
Now with that out of the way, i get to talk about why i recommend this game. The thing is that you get to meet a lot of people. Its a pretty popular mmo. The issue is the good classes are gender locked, so you often get horny ♥♥♥♥boys trying to get with you, disregarding the possibility that you could be a guy playing a female because you wanted to be a Ninja or a Brawler. Iv been told the economy is good, though iv never delved into merching, and a good economy is, for players like me, a very big selling point. Theres also apperantly a lot of endgame content. Outside of that theres a myriad of classes, which each play slightly better/worse/differently depending on your race. The community is pretty ok. Im not confident in saying its great because in pvp servers your likely to get railed by some upper for no reason, but i dont have many reasons to say its bad since i actually met a lot of cool people just yesterday (playing as a Ninja and copying others gets you a wide variety of responses). Oh, and lets not forget that as far as i can tell the game isnt p2w. From wat i see, paying dosnt get you any actual combat benefits outside of leveling faster. And most paying players usually buy cosmetics, which is almost exclusively what money is good for in this game. Take that as you will. Oh, lets also not forget the graphics are stunning

TERA falls into the trap that so many MMOs do today, which is great artists and programmers, but bad game designers.
The graphics are beautiful and inspired, everything looks polished and complex, if your computer can handle it I would recommend it based on the eye candy alone, but that is not everything in a game, especially an MMO.
I am one of those old MMO players who enjoyed the golden age of Ragnarok, and although that game is far from perfect, it has the same formula as TERA, amazing art, music, style, but absolutely terrible design, gameplay wise. But Ragnarok has better design overall.
What I mean by that is, TERA has no customization, once you select a race and class, everything else is set for you: your equips, your skills and your function in combat. Even though it is fun to block/evade enemy attacks and simply watching their animations is fun in itself, you can't ignore the fact that you are just doing what you are supposed to, there is a railroad and you can't think outside the box, experiment or even explore like you should in an MMO, you don't decide your attributes, your skills are mostly level locked so you don't have too many options (god forbid having options on an mmo!) and all the equipment upgrades are basically the same item as before but with a slightly bigger number or maybe some useless ability like 4% bonus damage or whatever...
I can't say a lot about the PvP part because I didn't play the game enough time to be a competitive PvP player.
I think of TERA more like an online action game with great graphics than an RPG, there are RPGs from 20 years ago with higher level of customization, if TERA managed to include these in the game, then it would definitely be considered one of the best of the genre. The video game industry needs better designers.

I've played every Assassins Creed game since AC2. I have not finished the game, but have about 20 hours into it and wanted to give you my honest feel for the game.
Pros:
Graphics: I run this game at 1440p and the graphics are nothing short of amazing.  The attention to the smallest of details here is hard to match.  Particle effects, day/night cycle, weather changes and water quality are some of the high points.
RPG-type Gameplay:  I was reticent about this aspect of the game, but it turned out to work really well.  Like many other games, it is important to not only complete main story elements but the side story elements as well in order to level for higher difficulty areas and to be able to progress the story.
Missions: The main story missions are well voice-acted and the story is engaging, which is above all else one of if not the most import aspects of an AC game (for me anyway).  The side missions here are welcomed and follow, to some degree, the Witcher 3.  By that I mean you have an ! exclamation point and that leads to nicely fleshed out side-quests that are mostly interesting and diverse.
Map Size/Density:  The map size here is massive.  I saw a video where a guy walked (not ran) across the map from end to end and it took 3 hours to do so.  Density is just right, in my opinion.  There are several cities and towns to explore along with the obvious POIs i.e. Great Pyramid etc.  If it was overly dense it wouldn't have been geographically/historically close to being correct.  What I'm saying is, it feels like they got it right proportionally.
THE CONS
Stutters/FPS drops:  I've got a 7700k, 1080ti, 32gb RAM, m.2 ssd etc etc and during some of the cut-scenes and other areas during gameplay I will drop to 20 FPS.  Otherwise, I run everything fully maxed at 140% screen resolution at 60-70 FPS at 1440p.
TL;DR: Taking the 2 year break between games has paid off.  They've done a great job incorporating many of the aspects of the AC franchise that we all know and love ala great story, great graphics and overall great gameplay (combat varyingly subjective.).  There are some CPU overusage issues which have reared their head occasionally and are known about and this issue will most likely be fixed in a future update.  It has not prevented me from enjoying the game, not one bit.  Highly recommended.  9/10.

Ubisoft has done it again creating a thrilling, intense, and "cluster charged" game with many tactics, but Ubisoft needs to work harder in optimization for others when a new operation is released. For example, Operation White Noise so far is very thrilling, but the only issue I am currently concerned about is frame loss due to poorly optimized routes looking in a certain direction on a map. I currently have a gaming laptop with an I7 skylake 6700 Processor, 8 gb of ram, and a GTX 960m with 4gb of vram. My computer handles games very well and can power through most like GTA V on Very High Settings, but again I am very concerned about the direction Ubisoft is going. This game is incredibly fun. While it isn't for everyone, I think those who are fans of grinding games and ARP's will love this game in general
There are a few pros and cons I want to list out:
Pros:
-The controls are really easy to use and learn, besides the 1-6 hotbar, but eventually even that becomes muscle memory
-Awesome soundtrack and visuals
-Gameplay and combat are super fun, especially when you have friends to help you out to take on tougher enemies.
-Barely any glitches or bugs that I have found.
-Different story lines give for lots of replayability and unique awards
-There's always a new challenge and that feeling of risk, which is super exhilarating in a video game
Cons:
-A very heavy grinding game. This is mainly a con for people who aren't a fan of that.
-It doesn't give you much of a tutorial besides one or two basic control commands. This isn't a complete con but it's rather irritating if you're just starting off.
-No health bars or names are listed while you're fighting an enemy, so you have to go a lot of googling if you get a quest that involves finding a specific enemy. (This should be added, in my opinion)
-Multiplayer uses Hamachi or other LAN programs to set up, so a steam invite option would be nice.
Other than that, this game is absolutely fantastic and my new favourite. I would definitely reccomend it.

It is very easy to praise this game, but be aware it suffers from bad first impressions.
First thing I want to point out, this game is NOT I want to be the guy or "rage games" like it, Wings of Vi is an incredibly hard platformer where carefully timed jumps, speed and timing matter. If I were to compare it to anything its more like the super dungeon in Cave Story, or star levels in Mario, only stretched out to an entire game. This games difficulty is FIRM but FAIR, and I love that.
Every zone/level has a unique gimmick to it making every area different, and getting new powers does not make the game easier, instead, levels adapt to your new powers and introduce challenges and platforming segments that test them and your ability to use them. The level design is absolutely wonderful in this regard, and it always keep you on your toes. The game definitely gets more fun as soon as your first power is introduced.
Enemies and bosses remind me of dark souls, in that they attack in a way and in patters where everything can be dodged and dealt with in a fair manner, you will take damage because you were too slow to dodge, or because you got greedy and tried to get extra hits in when you should have run away. The combat has it's own little rhythm and dance to it, and thats great too.
Visually the game is nice and stylized, bosses look good, animations look good, and everything runs buttery smooth. The games' music is fantastic, every boss has a unique theme, every level has playlist worthy music in it, its great.
On the negative side however, there seems to be a bug where when you slide your character will stand up randomly, and when you're dodging attacks this can lead to some unfair deaths, but it doesn't happen too often. The main problem is that everything I praised about the game, doesn't apply very much to the first level. Now, the platforming is still strict and well thought out, however every enemy type in the first level moves in a sporatic and chaotic fashion and do not have stun frames or knockback when you hit them. This leads to very cheap feeling opponents that deal damage to you in very unfair manners. With only a jump the platforming isn't very creative, so it does feel kind of dull jumping through levels in that regard, the music is nothing to write home about either. The boss fight is still good, but definitely the weakest out of all the bosses.
Overall, if you love super difficult platformers and want to test your skill this is the game for you, I highly recommend it, but beware, you have a rocky start before any of the real fun begins.

Honestly, this is one of the best purchases I've made all year. I normally can't stick with a game for more than a few hours before I start finding it boring, but I've unlocked every character, item and ability, and I'm still coming back to this game all the time thanks to the excellent create-a-class system. I don't normally write reviews, but I honestly lie awake some nights worrying that people don't understand that Streets of Rogue is a seriously awesome game. So let me tell you: Streets of Rogue? Seriously awesome game. You heard it here first. So sit down, buckle in, and crack open a boy with your cold ones whilst I explain to you /in detail/ exactly why and how damn much I reccomend this game on steam.
---
Plenty of games have tried to simplify the rogue-like genre to varying degrees of success, but I think the best way to understand SoR is as a procedurally generated immersive sim. The game handles combat, item hoarding and leveling up characters perfectly well, but the true beauty is the playground you're given to play in. The first few times I played, I died consistantly within the first three levels because I was running around at full pelt punching slum dwellers, scientists, doors, fridges, and anything else that I suspected might drop an item if I could only punch it the right way. Slowing down, I realised there are so many more interesting ways to play. For item collection quests, you don't have to kick the door down and punch the item out of it's holders' still-warm corpse. You can knock politely, offer the guy an item to trade, and be on your merry way. Or visit a drug dealer, spike his air-conditioning with a random drug and see what happens. Might poison him, might turn him invisible. Is he in a gang? Pick a fight with a rival gang, and lead them to him. Is he in a hideout? Find a hacker, pickpocket his hacking tool, and use it to set off poison gas and trap doors in his base. Half an hour in, you'll realise how fun it is to pick a class and take it's unique abilities for a spin to see just how many different ways you can skin a gun-toting cat guarding the item you need to exit the level and escape the unkillable robot death machine slowly stalking you across the map.
Even in beta, I still haven't seen all the games content- in part because of how balls-hard it can be, and in part because its so much fun just to screw around trying new characters or ideas out. Half of my runs end with me hitting exit, because I've just seen something happen that gave me an idea for an awesome new character build I had to make RIGHT NOW. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ fire spreads in this game?? Hold up, let me roll an arsonist class with a flamethrower, and oil barrel and a lighter. Secret Agent that mixes cyonide into drinks and loads a water pistol with rage inducing chemicals? Check. Player-made gang that gains a new member each level, but is attacked on sight by rival gangs? Checkion rings. Ancient vampire that's strong enough to punch a dude through an entire building's worth of walls, but can only heal by drinking blood? You get the idea- there's like, a ton of different ways to play the base game, and with the create-a-class mode, you can basically play however you want to. There are a few limitations with how creative you can get, but by and large, I've been able to make every character I've wanted to so far. PROTIP: Grab a buddy, turn on rogue-vision mode, and play co-op as the police officer class. You're basically playing a top-down S.W.A.T sequal.
At the moment, my only gripes are with a select few abilities or items that aren't fully explored and feel a bit useless. For example, you can play as a doctor that gets extra bang for his buck with medical items... all one of them. And I often go entire runs without encountering a med kit at all. The game features an awesome firespreading mechanic that takes into account flammable objects and oil spills- but its impossible to use oil to set anything on fire, as it can only be poured into empty spaces. There are a few cases like this where the game features content that isn't being used to its fullest- but unlike many beta/early access titles, they are small issues that I can absolutely see being addressed in future patches. The dev even has a form built into the pause menu so you can hit him up with suggestions and feedback the moment they pop into your head- and from what I've seen, these ideas genuinely get taken into account and often find their way into the bi-weekly update patches. The only other problem I have with the game is that there isn't more of it to go around- but with placeholders in the current version for character-specific missions, player-created gameplay mutators and more, I can see that changing very soon.
One criticism that tends to crop up in negative reviews is the lack of mission variety leading to repetitive gameplay. To an extent, this is true. You'll be given the same 3-4 mission types over and over again. Kill these guys, get this item, hit these switches, ad infinitum. But ultimately, if you are having repetitive playthroughs, it's because you keep doing the same thing every time. There is a ton of options at your disposal, and the game does a good job of rewarding (or necessitating) a varied approach to challenges. Limited ammo cappacity and frequent item rewards mean your best chance of survival will likely involve a few different gadgets, and you are rewarded bonus XP for pulling off missions without guns, weapons, or alarms. Ultimately, this is a psychological difference between forcing you to mix up your gameplay, and allowing you to. In the Splinter Cell games, each mission is mixed up with different requirements- use these weapons, trigger no alarms, complete the mission in this time limit. But at the end of the day, what are you doing every single time? Killing those dudes, grabbing those maguffins and hitting those switches, with varying degrees of flavour text thrown on top. Chosing not to do this in SoR is a design choice that leaves the creativity up to the player, not the developer. The game isn't going to tell you "Kill this guy with cunfusion gas, trigger no alarms". But you WILL find yourself with a vial of confusion gas in your pocket, tasked with killing a guy surrounded by fire pits and meat churners, and you can bet you'll get a bonus reward for killing him without weapons and without triggering alarms.
As it stands, I'd reccomend this game to just about anyone who can enjoy being left to make their own fun in sandbox games. It's a ton of fun in single player. It's awesome with a bud. It'll take you a long time to unlock everything. You'll have a lot of fun screwing about in the process. If the developer keeps to his plan of adding a ton more mission variety, more items and abilities, more characters and more interactions between all of these elements, this could easily be something I consider a masterpiece.
TL;DR:
If you the type of guy that boots up GTA SA, runs in the complete opposite direction of the mission marker and starts practicing safely landing airliners, this game is probably your jam. If you told your friends you'd finished Oblivion after Sean Bean turned into a firey winged god-lizard and killed Goro from Mortal Kombat, this probably isn't your jam, but its your own fault.
Definitely worth it, even with early access...

I love how the characters you can play in this game each make the game a completely different play experience.  A comedian telling jokes can get the owner of a locked door and safe to just give up their key to you, although I went into a room with some thugs who didn't like my humour when I told my joke and immediately killed me, so the jokes don't always go down that well.  But then playing a vampire where I have to drink the blood of innocents and making sure no-one else sees me doing it changes everything - and playing a zombie that everyone runs from or tries to kill and you need to get a zombie infection going on each level is yet another different experience.  Then add into that some random 'events' - the two I have come across so far are a radiation leak each 20 seconds that hurts people outdoors (which you can use to your advantage, but which has you scurrying from building to building) and a killer robot slowly chasing you whose missiles it shoots at you really hurt - but again can be used as an advantage to help you blow walls down.
My only request at this point is to allow characters to be upgraded.  There is an unlock system that lets you unlock new random inter-level rewards - but for casual players such as myself I would stick to the game longer if I can grind my character's stats higher and other improvements (such as improving special ability through upgrade tree).  There is a way to pay for starting items, but I don't like spending upgrade currency on single use items - I would rather grind permanent items (starting from weak and slowly upgrading to stronger) than just buying single use powerful items.
Overall this doesn't feel like an Early Access Game, it feels like a completed game.  Mind you at the time of writing this review I see the developer talking about improving Downtown area and until now I haven't managed to get that far in the game!

Suprisingly fun (given its low price point), colorful twin-stick shooter with a rich passive 'buffs' tree, and a variety of characters you can play as with different ranged/weapon specialties and unlocks, and a unique special attack/ability for each character. Some interesting variations in enemy AI behavior, and some interesting environmental hazards. A sprint/roll ability adds some movement variety.
Killing enemies drops green credits that you can pick up and use between levels to improve passive buffs. You get credits even if you die on a level. And this is *not* a roguelike/roguelite, so you keep your progression through the 60 handcrafted levels.
I haven't gotten far enough yet to try all the special abilities. One provides a protective shield around you. Another casts a sort of spell on surrounding enemies so that they take each other for a time. Another freezes nearby targets temporarily.
So far I prefer the Deep Waker Zero character for his bullet-hell like SMG weapon, which is so far what I have the most fun using in this. :)
Cons? imho, it's held back a bit imho by lack of terrain variety, absence of any interesting objectives (it's clear the map and find the portal) and generally very rudimentary sound FX. Which probably is just a function of a small budget. I think the basic twin-stick gameplay -- though I'm playing on kb/mouse -- is generally spot-on. :)
This is an Early Access title, so it'll be interesting to see how it evolves.

DuckTales Remastered is a testament to what a developer can do with an old title and WayForward does an absolutely stellar job in every department.
Graphics and animation are lovingly updated and re-created to make you feel that you are playing an interactive episode of the old TV show.  I could go on about this, but if you haven't watched the 'Duckumentaries' above (and on YouTube) they do a great job of showing the process they went through to update it.
Sound design is fantastic, but the game's music was the audio portion done with the most love of the original NES source material.  It is nothing short of beautiful and nostalgic.  The composer went above and beyond keeping close to original compositions, but updated them perfectly to full orchestrations.  I can not fathom how this could have been handled any better.  The calm, smoothness of the stage select music coupled with the act of performing a swan dive into Scrooge's money bin hit my nostalgia nerve very hard.  Nothing has pulled me back to the happiness of my childhood like that did in a long time.  The other impressive bit in the area of audio was the use of what I believe is the entire original voiceover cast from the cartoon which adds another layer of authenticity and enjoyment to this game.  And when I say everyone I mean all the way from Scrooge (Alan Young was 93 I believe when he recorded this) all the way down to Webigail and even Duckworth the butler has a couple of lines.
The gameplay remains wholly unchanged from the original.  The pogo can be a little frustrating every now and again, but it always was and isn't in any way crippling here.  Also, the addition of added difficulties is welcome since the original was very unforgiving in this area.  The main change is the addition of a whole new final level - Mount Vesuvius which takes the place of returning to Transylvania in the original.  A difficult final stage that is well conceived and fits in with the rest of the game well.  The final bit of the game after your battle with Dracula Duck is a homage to what the old 8-bit twitch reaction platformers could be.  The game is a tiny bit short, but that's hardly a criticism since the orignal was the same and only took more time due to the unforgiving difficulty.
Overall, this is a wonderful game for all ages, especially those old-school gamers of us in our 30s that loved these old 8-bit platformers.  I am definitely keeping my eye on anything WayForward does from here on because they clearly know how to make, not just a good game, but how to make it fun and its refreshing to see a developer who seems to really care about what they're doing versus raking in the cash as the primary motivator.  If they ever got their hands on Capcom's 8-bit MegaMan library (especially this same music composer) I would be all over that.

TERA has a ton of great elements, which make it a game with a lot of potential. Unfortunately, there are far too many deal breakers. This game is made for noobs.
The developers of this game have taken something that could have been really good and essentially cranked it down to "Very Easy Mode". If you're looking to walk around in a pretty forest killing helpless creatures, this game was made for you. I don't recommend this game to anyone looking for any level of challenge or mental stimulation.
Firstly, the dungeons are a total joke. Your party is made up of a tank, healer and DPS, but theres really no need for a tank or healer. Everyone can just face roll the dungeon on their own. It's a total cake walk. The hardest part of the dungeon is picking up all of your loot while still keeping up with your teammates who are sprinting through the instance. Players literally purchase their characters a pet that auto-loots so they are able to keep up.
Secondly, there are several overpowered classes that are super easy to play. For some of them your rotations don't even matter. On many classes you can just push any available button and you will do fine. On the other hand, some of the overpowered classes have some really interesting and dynamic skill sets. Unfortunately, the game chains abilities and you can just spam space bar. If you are playing one of these classes, you will quickly learn that space bar is the only button that matters. The TERA community has coined the term "Spacebar Hero" for these clases.
Now I'm sure all of the dedicated fans of this game will tell you:
1) Wait until end game and theres a bit of a challenge.
2) Don't play an OP class. Pick a hard one.
Both of which are ridiculous. Why on Earth would anyone play an underpowered class and then farm their butt off to keep up with the 12 year old who is smashing space bar? When games have overpowered, "spacebar hero" classes, it totally ruins all sense of competition.
As far as waiting until end game goes, there is nothing fun about grinding for 65 levels before you get to the "Moderately Challenging Mode".  How did it become industry standard that players are expected to invest 40+ hours in levelling tutorial before the fun starts at "end game?"
I really liked TERA for the first few hours that I played. Unfortunately the developers chose to water down the game and make it so easy that its not fun for even casual gamers. I'm really tired of the gaming industry making games so easy.

Roguelands is a Roguelike game with RPG elements. You go into levels, gather resources, battle monsters, defeat bosses, ETC.
In Roguelands you have 20 or so races (I haven't counted) and everytime you die you have a chance to unlock those races (Like Magicite) Some of the races start off with a diffrent starting weapon.
So how do you start the game? Well you go into the first level (There is a portal in your ship that teleports you to it) Once you're there, you murder everything in your path and begin leveling up. Then you gather resources with your drone, you just click on the rock/plant ETC. and your drone will mine it for you. Resources are inportant and the key to this game, i'll get to why later.
The game has magic, guns, armor, swords, and shields, to craft those items, you need emblems. Emblems are crafted by putting 10 resources (any kind) into the Emblem maker (Idk what it is called) and you craft the 10 resources of your pick and it crafts a Emblem of that resource, here is all the Emblems -
Now once you have 3 diffrent Emblems, you combine the 3 diffrent Emblems in the Anvil to make armor, weapons, or shields. Look on the Wiki to know the recipies.
I don't wanna spoil everything, so here is some Pros and Cons.
Pros
1. Good Combat
2. Good crafting system
3. Challenging
4. Classes you can choose (Gunner, blademaster, ETC.)
5. Addicting
6. Lots of weapons and armor
7. Lots of bosses and monsters
8. Levels/planets that you explore that are randomly generated
9. Multiplayer
Cons

Sat trying to fix the traffic in my city for 2 days now.

Despite many complaints (check the forums and negitive complaints) including my own the game still has bugs.  I've enjoyed this style of game since the first Simcity.  The bugs dont appear right away with a smaller city as such everything seems fine at first and the game is enjoyable.  After spending hours building your city up is when the issues start to become apparent.  Some people have managed to make a large city without issue but many have not so its hard to say where the problem lies.(different windows versions, certain DLC, etc)  This may explain all the positive reviews as most havent played long enough to have this issue and some were lucky enough that the issuesnever manifested on there system.  After spending hours building your city up is when the issues start to become apparent.  I have spent a lot of time on building multiple cities trying to narrow down the problems and insure that it wasn't my city design.  The first and main issue is garbage.  There is a great article in the forums on how its handled called "Garbage is Rubbish", however all those issues aren't game breakers.  As your city becomes larger the incinerators send out less and less trucks.  There is no logical reason for this to happen.  Many have suggested poor traffic layout is the issue but even if it were (its not in my case) it still has no logic.  "There is a traffic jam across town don't send out any garbage trucks across the entire city but pay everyone for the day."  Traffic is another whole issue that could take up a paragraph but again its not game breaking just unrealistic, annoying, and somewhat limits any creativity you may have in your city design.  With average happiness running close to 90%, traffic efficiency averaging around 90%, and 20 times the required incinerator capacity there shouldn't be any issues but it breaks somewhere between 150,000-300,000 population every time and garbage trucks just stop running across the entire city and of course the entire city collapses.  Crematoriums seem to have a silmilar issue but I've never had them get to the point of complete collapse.  Mods were added to see if any of them would help but they didn't.  Tech support was of no help and of course denied there was any issue.
While experimenting with the garbage issue I noticed something else.  Your net  income isn't entirely based on fixed game factors and adjusts itself.  I can only guess this is an attempt to maintain some semblence of difficulty and 'balance' so you can't let your game run for days to have a large bank account even if you design the perfect city.  At first I thought it might be my city design and management that my profits were never very large but as a lot of time and experimentation went on there is more to it.  The best example which was tried several times with different cities is that a good size city ran for a couple (real) days without making any changes and though the weekly income bounced around slightly it averaged out at pretty close to $0 and the overall bank account hadn't really changed very much.  A mod was added that quartered the garbage costs, the mod doesn't affect any other game mechanics and no other changes were made.  At the time garbage costs were around $200,000 so they quartered to $50,000.  In theory after this the net profit should average out to $150,000 but this wasn't the case.  Initially the profit jumps up to close to this amount but after a short while it settled in around an average profit of $15,000 and then stays there.  It seems no matter what was done it would never maintain anything over $20,000 average net profit for more than a short burst.
It's unfortunate that all my play time was basically beta testing instead of just playing and enjoying the game.
In closing this game has so much going for it and most of the issues it has are minor and could be overlooked if they could only fix the big issues.

I'm not a huge fan of snooker, but sometimes I like to play on slower, not typical arcade games like chess, snooker or golf, where you don't have to rush. I'm little bit surprised of some of the bad comments about this game. It's not perfect, but which game is? My score 9/10.
Pros:
-   Graphics. The balls, table, light looks surprisingly good. Looks like a real.
-   Sound effects are simple brilliant. You actually feel like in real game. If you miss a simple shot or you score a high points from very difficult position, audience react perfectly. I'm impressed how good job the developers did with this.
-   AI, in my opinion is really good. It not play like machine. Sometimes miss a simple shot (like you do), but sometimes can also surprise with a very good one (like you also do :-) So AI is really balanced. Maybe for the first time game looks easy, but try to win the whole competition :-)  When you play free game you can chose different difficulty level. So you can adjust this to your skills.
-   Is really easy to learn how to play this game. I'm not talking about actually the game rules, which are easy too, but about how to operate the cue, how to change positions or how to change the strength of the shot. I would say that the way how you operate it remind the snooker tablet games, where you don't have complicated interface.
-   Game assists like for example, which direction ball will go after shot ect.  Very helpful. You can turn them off or on if you like. If you are a hardcore player, turn them off.
Cons:
-  Some hardcore snooker players probably don't find in this game simulation touch of it. For them I think this game will be to simple in general. But like I said previously: try to win the competition.
-  Textures of the audience could be improved.
-  You can't actually see the player. So what you have is: table, balls, audience, cue and background. So there is no virtual player.

If you are after a snooker game then this a good game with a fair price and great graphics. But there a few things to note. First off you are probably going to want to leave the aiming guides turned on. This isn't cheating, it just compensates for the lack of depth perception that is inherent in virtual pool games, at least until there is a version that uses the oculus. If you stick to playing in first person it gives a fairly realistic feel and balance to the game. If you turn them off then you end up playing nearly every shot from the overhead camera view which makes if feel like an 8-bit arcade game. Also lining up the shots in the overhead view without the guides is so frustrating that you'll find yourself moving your head to strange angles and spending a few minutes on every shot to try and find the right line, only to miss by an inch or two anyway. Changing to the overhead view at all could be considered cheating but it is the only way to get a overview of the layout since you can't walk around the table while playing, something that I found lacking. There are also shots where the pool cue completely obstructs the view while in first person, which is odd since a little tranparency would have been an easy fix here. Changing to the overhead view is a must in this case.
To play you set the desired spin, cue angle and power level before clicking on a button to fire the shot. A mouse driven cue and power action is sorely missed here. Coupled with the guides it takes nearly all of the interactive feel of the game away. However, since spin, power and cue ball placement are so important in the game of snooker it still has its merits as a tactical game or training aid.
As mentioned in other reviews, the AI is inconsitent because they will play poorly for half a game and then trot out a break of 50 or more at the end. I also feel guilty when snookering the opponent since in many cases they will miss, at least in the early stages of a tournament, and it is so easy to force them to replay the shot and win the frame by default after the third miss. They simply don't change the shot they attempted the first time.
I'd recommend the game to anyone with a passion for snooker but I'd be raving about the game if these points were addressed. As it stands I'll just have to repeat that it is a good game with a fair price and great graphics.

The classic NES game "Ducktales"  gets an amazing makeover. The gameplay for the most part hasn't changed much, but I wouldn't have it any other way. I loved taking out enemies with a pogo cane/stick when I was a kid and I still do. It just doesn't get old. There is some variety added to the gameplay like the bosses' patterns being changed. I loved the DuckTales cartoon in the 1980s and so I hoped I'd like this remastered version of the original NES DuckTales game. Unfortunately, the developer failed to understand the current market and decided to design the game as if it were an NES game. Essentially, a lesson in frustration.
First, you can't save whenever and wherever you want. I realize many games do this today, but it's a poor design choice. All it does is increase the overall level of frustration and repetition in a game. We've had the capability to save our games when and where we wanted since 1984 (see King's Quest), yet in 2013, it's a rarity because game developers are lazy.
Second, the controls are awkward and that's even using a gamepad. The pogo jump, for instance, is hit-or-miss and rarely works right when you're attempting to do it over spikes or some other deadly landmass.
Third, it seems half the damn game is cutscenes. Don't get me wrong, I like a good story as I grew up on classic Sierra Online and LucasArts Adventure games, but these cutscenes are unskippable and the story involved is barely adequate, even for a game based on a cartoon.
[EDIT - I've been informed that cutscenes are now skippable. I don't know if this is a recent development or not, but considering I couldn't skip them, the above paragraph is remaining. That said, this factor should no longer be held against the game if cutscenes are indeed skippable.]
Now I know some people will say I'm being unfair, as this game is essentially a remake of the NES title. To them I reply: Deal with it. This isn't the same game. Yes, it's a remastered version, but it's not the same.
Changes have been made in every step of development, so there's no reason why a real save game mechanism, skippable cutscenes and a decent control scheme couldn't have made it into the works. Saying the NES game was like this is a poor argument, because the NES title had hardware limitations that modern consoles and PC do not.
So what's good about this game? Well, it's DuckTales (which I imagine means something to you if you bought it) and the original voice actors have come back to play the parts they did in the cartoon. In addition, for those who wanted a near-perfect replication of the NES title, this is a masterpiece.
In the end, I have to say I don't recommend this game. It's not terrible (I've certainly played worse), but it's very frustrating. While I'm sure that'll bring some gamers to a near ♥♥♥♥♥♥ state, it's far more likely that same level of frustration will drive most gamers away.

I recommend this game hesitantly, and I say hesitantly b/c you should not pay much more than the current summer sale (Jun 2014) price ($0.99) .
Let's start with the obvious. This game is an unabashed knock-off of Trials, the much heralded game which is literally the exact same thing. You're a motorbike rider trying to get through an obstacle course where the handling and physics of the bike are the crux to passing them. I look at this game as a cover version of a popular song. Rarely are cover versions better than the original, but once in a while an artist will do very well and have a hit of their own on their hands. This is not a hit, but it's at the very least curiously listenable.
There is not a lot of customization in this game. There is basically one bike that you upgrade various parts of using money you collect on the various tracks.
What I liked:
- I liked the background effects of the tracks. The NPCs include cops, various passersby, and occasionally people will try to throw things at you. There's even some explosions.
- It was $0.99 and it drops cards.
- Relatively small (about 800 mb) download.
- Its challenging.
What I didn't like
- It lacks depth. The tracks are repeated at the higher levels in places.
- Occasionally the bike handling/physics is wonky.
- The braking and reverse mechanic has to be used sometimes to get awkwardly placed money bags and can totally kill your time/momentum.
You can do a lot worse than spending a buck on this game. It's an unapologetic knock-off of the brilliant Trials series (the latest game in that series is Trials: Fusion) and it succeeds in replicating the gameplay of that series to a point. However, at the end of the day, why play this when I can just play Trials? It does nothing that series does better.
That being said, it's a buck, and with four card drops, you basically can get this game for $0.40 if you choose to sell those drops, even less if you get a foil.
Don't expect anything great, but if you know what you're getting into, there's a bit of entertainment to be found with this game.
If you do find that you like this game, or at the at the very least how it plays, do yourself a favor and pick up one of the entries in the Trials series.
Lots of fun for .99 and if you love MCs, stunting, but can't afford the repairs or loss of life, grab this game. However, there's not enough going on to justify $10............

> No lost pieces.
> No questionable owner / source of rules if pieces or books are missing. Even comes with a "house rules" setting if demanded or the sake of extra fun or defense of some paradigm.

> Easy tracking of statistics and view.
> Easy access to other players.
Cons -

It's a bit of a stretch, but this is a pretty okay game. Compared to other superior rogue-likes, it falls hard in areas, such as the lack of variety, weak story, weak animations and a complete lack of a tutorial.
However, there is one thing this game does very well, and once you find out about it, it carries the rest of the game and mitigates some of it's less than standard mechanics.
A very real sense of progression.
Having the ability to save your items in a chest and access them post-death is quite frankly pretty smart. I wouldn't say other rogue-likes should add this feature, (though some do), in Roguelands it just *works.* It's very much because of the crafting system, which I found very addicting figuring out all the recipes I could with the resources I was given. If I crafted a better weapon, I was presented with a choice to store it for another character for a head-start, or keep it and upgrade my current character.
Overall, if you enjoy rogue-likes, you'll most likely enjoy this one. However, if you have no experience/don't enjoy this kind of game, I don't recommend starting with this one.

A flawed gem. There's essentially two games here, a by the numbers focus group-made AAA game that spreads itself too thin and a game that actually tells an interesting story beyond the obvious. The combat is clunky, the pacing is awful (it takes HOURS to actually start the game properly), and the ending hours sputter and collapse, literally. But I was captivated by the presentation of a person of color in a leading role, especially as its set in Colonial America. Ratonhnhaké:ton (aka "Connor") was criticized for being dull and unlikeable, but how else would you expect someone in that position to take the role and still seem genuine? Connor has been discriminated, persecuted, and alienated throughout his life, and so responds by being serious and dutiful. He has to prove himself adequate at every turn just for his existance to be acknowledged, while at the same time trying to hold unto his principles and idealism. In the end the story takes a turn that, while historically accurate, still feels surprising given game's responsabilities as mainstream media.

Assassin's Creed III is the third main installment in the Assassin's Creed series. It features a new engine (AnvilNext) as well as a complete new set of animations and new assets. It is therefore a fresh new start in the series, with a new protagonist and yet still delivering the same narrative style and continuin the story of the previous games.
The AnvilNext engine was promoted for its ability to display enormous crowds, making the game's open world and cities feel much more alive. Additionally, it allows the game to display a great number of soldiers making historic battles (Battle of Bunker Hill, etc) much more believable. At least, that's what was stated during the promotional campaign.
The truth is that the developers have delivered on their promise when it comes to displaying civilians around the cities of Boston or New York, however, the main instance where you are actually seeing a legitimate battle taking place, at the Battle of Bunker Hill, is a joke.
Yes, there are quite a bit of NPCs rendered, however, they feel very static and the interaction is very limited, they are displayed on the background and you do not get to have a significant part in the action.
Next up, we have the infamous combat system of the AC games. If you are looking for a skill based combat which will challenge you throughout your experience, this is not it. It is based upon button mashing and counter kills. I don't think it is that much of a turnoff, but for some people it might be very boring and repetitive if not distracting.
I do not think AC3 is a bad game, there obviously was quite a bite of effort and love put into it, however I have a couple of main problems with it.
1 - The Tutorial
I have never seen a longer tutorial in a game before. It literally takes about 5-7 hours to compelete the entire sequences of the game which are designed to form the protagonist into the skilled Assassin he is meant to become. However, you might think that this might be dentrimental to his development as a character. Worry not, most of these sequences are simply narrated cutscenes in which you have no possible control over. Plainly said, the game is way too slow in its beginning.
2 - The Story
The story of this game is just not believable. Part of me thinks the game as a whole and especially towards the end was extremely rushed. The dialogues are bland and way too random. I cannot count the amount of Ex Machinas in this game in order to drive the narrative forward, such as random characters giving an answer to a plot point. The protagonist is annoying, and the main redeeming factor of the story is that the modern day elements of this particular AC games are actually very well executed and quite enjoyable.
All in all, AC3 is not a bad game and for its current price it deserves a try and you might find it quite fun. But do not expect a masterpiece.

9. Eat like a true Medjay.
