As a Pirate Captain lead your shipmates in settling an island and growing in power. Gather resources, build, trade, and train soldiers.
Everything is done indirectly by issuing orders to followers who might just not listen to the order. Followers need to be paid with gold too, otherwise they refuse to do anything. Other gameplay elements include fighting off natives as well as a growing imperial force. The Captain can fight and is stronger than normal units, and can be further enhanced with equipment obtainable through dungeon runs.
All this sounds nice however it's also extremely frustrating. Particularly with regards to orders on being followed.
There is no central storage of resources, everything is just kept in piles on the ground. As such, keeping track of stock is done by the pirates counting items and 'remembering' stock levels. What this means is that pirates are not always aware of just what is available, items can be stolen or procured without updating the totals. This in particular I found very frustrating as multiple times I ran into a situation where I had piles of stone but my workers claimed there wasn't enough stone and would not continue building. Or worse, they think there are no coins left and stop doing anything even though there are coin piles around.
As the world is randomly generated it may happen that only small islands are created and a colony has to be set up across many islands. Even then building space is limited and follows a sytem similar to that of the old Settlers games whereby each point on the map can only suport a building of up to a certain size depending on several factors. This limits what can be build on each island even more. Travel between islands is done by ship and only the captain (and his guard) can set sail. To establish a colony on a new island the ship is sacrificed to provide workers and raw materials. Setting up production lines across multiple islands requires a lot of micro management and effort to ensure pirates actually do what they're supposed to (see paragraph above).

I saw this and instantly wanted to play it! Everyone who grew up in the early years knew of these iconic train sets. I had them in the early 90s and even IKEA sells their own brand of wooden train set! Anyway, you have an engine to start and a single piece of track. The rest is entirely up to you.
The physics engine makes it fun to knock over blocks or boxes or just send your engine flying off the track. Build up or build down and then decorate it to make it your own. It’s simplistic, it’s relaxing, and it’s fun. Lose yourself in the nostalgia gameplay as you build up your little train town.
You start with a single engine on a piece of track. From there, you can add as many tracks as you see fit. You can access the Toy Box by hitting G to see all the neat things that can make your little train town stand out. Or maybe you’d rather keep it simple and prefer the look of the wood alone.
It’s up to you. Building is super easy with Left Click to lay track and Right Click to remove it. WASD moves you around, Q and E raises and lowers the camera as well as the track elevation, and T let’s you become the conductor! Control the speed of the train with W and S and track switching with A and D.
There are so many different buildings, structures, objects, and stations to put down with more being added. The developer is active on the discussion boards and the game is a blast to play in EA. I tend to lose myself just building and I do like that I get to ride in the trains and pick up passengers. The clear night environment is probably my favorite so far.
I love trains. I grew up on them with my dad building them in the basement. He’d buy me these wooden train sets when he came back from deployment. So, being able to relive my childhood, playing with one of my favorite toys as a kid without fear of losing my pieces is fantastic. The game is simple in its design, but fun to play. Especially if you have an eye for design and a love for building. The music does get a bit repetitive, but I wasn’t paying any attention to it since I was so focused on building.
The game controls well and as of this review, I haven’t heard mention of controller support or it’s limited at the moment. I’m excited for this game and to see what it can become. There are talks to be able to customize the color of tracks or engines and different types of train cars. Guess we’ll see!

This is a weak installment in the Assassin's Creed franchise and that weakness stems from the terrible protagonist, Connor. He is an unintelligent meathead who blunders along and is always reacting to problems rather than planning ahead and being proactive. It was very frustrating to play as such a tool of a character is who derided by other characters in game for his poor decision-making skills.
Part of the reason for my dislike is I compare him to Haytham, the character you control at the outset of the game, and while Haytham is competent, charismatic, and practical, Connor is none of those things. The entire Templar vs Assassin ideology finds fertile storytelling in this game but the Templars (the erstwhile villains) come across as very rational and pragmatic while the Assassins seem more like kids stamping their feet and saying "Stop liking things I don't like!"
The historical databse in-game was very fun to read, however, as you see the people and events of the American Revolution as viewed through the eyes of an Englishman. Enlightening and an educational read, as were the databases in previous games, so the game shines in this regard.
This is not a bad game, but it is a bad Assassin's Creed game. Good to play and see the modern day story unfold with Desmond and company but otherwise a bit off-putting. Combat is good, parkour is good, interesting crafting system (though I used little of it since I hate crafting but I can see the appeal), level design is beautiful, and the sound of your tomahawk smashing skulls never gets old. The previous installments with Ezio set the bar very high and despite this game's innovations, it fell flat for me because of story and the main character.

I suspect that I'm merely going to reiterate a number of things which other reviews have said - all six or ten of them which actually resemble "reviews", as opposed to love letters to the game's creator - so bear with me (no pun intended).  Oh, and I'll mostly be reiterating the NEGATIVE reviews, which is never a good thing.  The first thing which I feel I can safely say, in any case...is that this is hands-down MY LEAST FAVOURITE FREDDY GAME thus far.  By a LONG margin.

The general atmosphere of the game gets at least part-way there, but the gameplay suffers immensely from the simple fact of its CHIEF MECHANIC being questionably executed.  For ♥♥♥♥'s sake, I just got my ears syringed out a few weeks ago, and I'll be buggered if I can hear any of the so-called "audio cues" which my character lives-or-dies by (I certainly haven't heard any "breathing" as of yet, just faint shuffling and the like).
Let me put it another way:  I'm no good at the three earlier games, and certainly haven't managed to get all the way to the end of them - Night 4 is the most I've managed on any - but at least I by-and-largely "got" what it was that those games wanted me to do.  Sure, Mr Cawthon always throws in a few curve-balls as the nights progress, but I seriously didn't even feel like I won the first night of this instalment fair-and-square:  I got through it on the second go, after "getting jump-scared" at 4am on the first...but didn't feel that I "deserved" to survive to 6am the second time around any more than I felt that I "deserved" to get subsequently jump-scared at 3am the NEXT night!
I'm keenly listening out for the breathing or whatever, but seriously...how good do my HEADPHONES have to be?!  Even when I believe I've heard something, I for the life of me cannot tell WHICH of the three doors I'm supposed to be checking.  Sometimes I seem to fluke it, sure, but I certainly don't feel in "control" of my own fate.  It's naught but SHEER DUMB LUCK which seems to have decided how far I've progressed to date (though I do have a fair grip on how to look behind me regularly, to ensure that Foxy doesn't "take me" from behind, so the mechanics which resemble those from the earlier games still work well enough).
The game's problems don't end there, however.  For all its atmosphere, FNAF4 ultimately lacks SUSPENSE.  Suspense is precisely what makes so-called "jump-scares" scary - without a build-up, it's just an image and a sound effect - and the frenzied running back and forth of your character almost makes this feel more like a sports simulation with the occasional "BOO!" thrown in for good measure.  Also, as much as I love the idea of a game based around childhood fears - "Among the Sleep" being a shining example herein - the sudden shift from the Freddy Fazbear's Pizza franchises to a little boy's bedroom is...well, a tad abrupt, and a tiny bit perplexing.
Maybe it's just time for an ALL-NEW SERIES, Scott?  'Cause there's not much about this entry which doesn't stink of desperation and a growing lack of ideas.  I mean, let's be honest here.  You made one truly GREAT game, and two really bloody GOOD ones...so who are you exactly, Kim Jong-il?  Won't stop 'til you achieve complete world domination?!  Time for a fresh start and a rethink, methinks.

In short, despite the fact that I'm not very "good" at any of them, I still found the first three FNAF games to be surprisingly compelling; meaning that even when I was losing, they kept me coming back, and I either got up to - or agonisingly close to - Night 4 on all of them (hell, the first one, I think I've even managed the cusp of Night 5).  This one, I just plain-gave-up on Night 2.
Nothing about this game strikes me as "fair" to the player.  There's an incredibly similar game called Boogeyman - which came out some months AFTER this one, so I'm going to assume it took substantial cues from this, though it may in all fairness have been in development prior - but it deserves kudos, in any case, for executing much the same premise (sound cues and all) in a decidedly more successful manner.  Boogeyman, like earlier FNAF games, by-and-largely strikes me as hard-but-fair...whereas this is simply HARD, if not nigh-on IMPOSSIBLE.  Either that, or my recent ear-syringing damaged the very specific range of the aural spectrum which the sound effects of this game just happen to occupy, so I'll never get to "enjoy" this painfully pedantic and repetitive game the way that countless thousands of others (claim to) have.
This really, really pains me, 'cause I do believe that Scott Cawthon is a very talented dude and I look forward to any games he makes in the future.  BUT...after giving highly praising reviews to the first three games in this series...I'm sadly going to have to give this one a THUMBS-DOWN.  ♥♥♥♥♥ me to tears, it honestly does.  But for me, at least, this game is not even PLAYABLE.  And yes, I am writing this well after all the supposed "fixes" which Mr Cawthon made, so I can't even begin to imagine how "subtle" the sound effects were in the original release.  Oh, and I see that in-between releasing four games in less than a year, he's also managed to co-author a Freddy BOOK.  Guess the words "quality" and "control" don't loom too large in the Cawthon household...
Verdict: 4.5/10.

20+ hours in and I will most definitely be playing more. My review will be based on my gameplay experience and might change as I play more. The game's setting was most definitely the most attractive reason for me to buy this game. Running around in the huge open world of Ancient Egypt helping its people, hunting, gathering materials, getting randomly attacked by wildlife and of course enjoying the amazing graphics and using the hell out of photo mode.
The story so far has been interesting with Bayek as its main character, who seems to be quite cheerful compared to other AC main characters regardless of the tragedies he's been through. The story also seems to build up quite well introducing historically relevant figures, issues and myths and connecting them to the main plot over time. 
I was very skeptical of the combat system at first but after trying out different weapons and getting used to handling the new system I find it more rewarding. Being able to switch weapons mid-fight depending on what situation you're in and using your shield properly makes combat difficult and more enjoyable rather than running in and countering 20 opponents instantly killing them, now you have to think before engaging multiple enemies if it's feasible. The only main issue I've experienced with combat is the lock-on function. It doesn't seem to work like it's supposed to making me avoid it all together. 
One tiny issue that isn't relevant to everyone but that annoys me personally (being Egyptian and an Arabic speaker) is the mispronunciations of Arabic words. Especially by the character Layla Hassan. I believe if they couldn't get and Arab or Egyptian voice actor they didn't have to force Arabic words into the dialogue all it did was result in very cringey game moments. An example of this is when she says "Cheers" in Arabic its Fi-sihitik which ends being remarkably butchered to be Fi-sikkhhittik adding unrequired phlegms. Sorry for this tiny rant it just triggers me how often this happens. 
40 + hours in and still enjoying the game only a few new things to add.
There seems to be a limited number of killing animations. Seems to be about 1-2 animations per weapon as well as 4 animations for hidden blade kills. A larger number of various cool animations would've been appreciated.
On the other hand the amount of side quests, collectibles, forts, tombs, papyrus puzzles and other distractions is HUGE. Not to mention the presence of interesting details and facts of the ancient world that are represented throughout side quests.  If you are someone like me that gets distracted and sidetracked easily, It will take you a long time before you finish the game's story line (I haven't completed it yet).
Swimming, in my opinion, for the first time in the AC series is manevurable and fluid in terms of control.
The Arabic in future dialogues only gets worse =( ... Please STAHP!!!
In summary, the game has been extremely enjoyable so far with lots to see, many side quests, interesting story, an enjoyable combat and loot system and of course Senu the eagle.

: Awe-inspiring and beautiful artistic design impressively rendered with ridiculously far render distance. Egypt is gorgeously realized and a constant treat to explore and behold.
: The score is a very cool mix of appropriately Egyptian-inspired instrumentals, NPCs singing songs in the streets and fields, and the occasional contrasting trancy-techo that emphasizes Egypt's mystery, beauty, and diversity.
: More than most games, it's incredibly easy and simply fun to get lost in this game. You'll find yourself weaving in and out of taking out assassination targets for the story, completing hundreds of side quests (complete with arcs, cutscenes, voice-acting, and varied gameplay), raiding enemy forts for loot, exploring hidden tombs and solving lite puzzles, and on and on. This game keeps giving and giving, and I'm almost 70 hours in at this point with still plenty to do.
: The writing is fresh, the plot is simple and story is mercifully not full of itself. Bayek is, in my opinion, the most likeable and relatable character in any Assassin's Creed game thus far-- Ezio included. He's strong-willed, charasmatic, and full of heart. Through Bayek, you'll experience the birth of more than just the Creed as we knew it... only be sure to keep an open mind, because it doesn't go down the way you'd expect.
: The details in this game are honestly mind-blowing; this is true for gameplay nuances, world-building, story points, etc. This is a game you should NOT rush through, because you'll be doing it and yourself a disservice. Comparing this game to its predecessors is night and day-- this game shines where all others fell apart, and is just a great time through-and-through. It's never been more obvious that the involved dev studios listened to the feedback fans and otherwise have been throwing Ubisoft's way over the past few years. I have two complaints, and they're incredibly minor in the grand scheme of things: The HUD lacks the level of customization previous installments offered, which effectively forces all players to be exposed to elements of the HUD intended for younger or more casual players in the name of accessibility that more experienced players will find annoying. The aggressive anti-piracy measures on this game take a pretty large toll on CPUs, which is a huge bummer. It's a silly practice that only hurts people that paid for the game, because frankly pirates will always find a way to crack the game and bypass the DRM, at which point they are receiving a better expierence for free.
: Do not miss out on this game. HUD and DRM issues aside, this is absolutely worth every penny and will easily keep you entertained for at least 100 hours. I'm a long time fan, and over time I've become harsh on the series because I care; this game has far-and-away exceeded my expectations and I cannot wait to get more of this game and its direct sequel(s). Heartfelt thanks to the teams behind this installment, because you obviously bled for this game.

You know when Keanu Reeves always says "whoa"? I think he must have been looking at an early copy of this game.
I had no idea what to expect when I threw this in my cart just to raise my order level a couple of bucks. I love racing games; and the description sounded good. The idea of it being multi-player with random events almost turned me off; mostly because I think online multi-player does nothing but bring up the worst possible players in games...not to mention I wasn't worried about doing anything but driving cars.
Well, let me just say my mind was changed as soon as I started playing the game. The levels are in fact open, just not quite as large as you might be made to think. Still, there are tons of physics and gravity defying stuff you can do. Sure, events pop up randomly and you're automatically put in competition...but you're not forced to actually do anything. You can keep driving around doing your own thing, completely ignoring the fact there's an event going on. But the events are somewhat fun and sometimes trying to complete and win those involves a lot of driving around. You aren't forced to join actual races though; just events that continue to work in sandbox mode.
There are a lot of various cars, and you do have to level them up. You have the option of buying a max level; but I wouldn't do it. Leveling the cars up to max doesn't take very long; I was able to level several cars to max in less than the 3 hours I first played; for the most part driving the car around will help you boost it's four areas. Drifting maxes your handling ability, using nitro obviously boosts your nitro ability, actual acceleration increases your acceleration rating, and driving at top speed maxes out your top-speed rating. Just driving around doing drifts for 20 or 30 minutes in a car will get it's level quite high. Save your money for buying cars as you unlock them.
I still can't get over how addictively fun this game is. The controls of the car are quite simple...and in a way remind me of a lot of the other simple racers. You don't have 4000 controls you need to memorize to drive the thing, just a few basic commands and a lot of fun arcade-type handling. There seems to be plenty of stuff to do; although if the events aren't your deal...the levels may get boring after a while.
Still, for even the non-sale price; it's worth picking up a copy.

Should you actually manage to get off the ground with an online game, odds are good that something unfortunate will happen to someone and that person will ragequit, which invariably crashes the game as well.

When I was young, a friend of my dad's gave him a CD with an NES emulator and a bunch of games on it. I tried them all, but the two that I kept going back to were DuckTales and DuckTales 2. I had never known about the show, I didn't grow up with it, but the games were so much fun.
Fast forward to 2013 and the first DuckTales game gets a remastered release! Around its release, I had finally gotten around to watching the first few episodes of the original show. If you were a fan of the show, you're going to find a lot to love here. WayForward did a wonderful job capturing the essence of the show, making each of the game's levels feel like their own episodes! Scrooge (voiced by Alan Young, God rest his beautiful soul), Huey, Dewey, Louie, Webby, Mrs. Beakley, Launchpad, and more, they're all here! Thankfully WayForward later patched in the ability to skip cutscenes, so if you've already watched them or don't care for the story, you can skip past them.
DuckTales Remastered plays very similar to the original game. It's a platformer where Scrooge uses his pogo stick to traverse as well as to defeat enemies. Shovel Knight fans, this is where it all started. The game features an expandable health bar, secret treasures all over, and a brand-new level and boss fight for the Remastered version that wasn't in the original game! The controls are tight, and have also been modified just a little in order to make it easier on our fingers (though on the hardest difficulty, you'll be forced into the hard controls from the original game).
Most of all, the game's main composer, Jake Kaufman, knocked the soundtrack out of the park. He modernized all of the 8-bit chiptunes exactly how you would expect them to be modernized, and they sound glorious. He also created original tracks (particularly for the aforementioned new level and boss fight) and even chiptuned them as well, for an 8-bit music mode! Jake Kaufman has had lots of other work, including, of course, Shovel Knight, and he deserves every bit of praise given to him.
Retro platformers have gained a lot of love over the years, and DuckTales is absolutely no exception. If you're a fan of DuckTales or just platformers in general (especially Shovel Knight!), you owe it to yourself to experience DuckTales Remastered, woo-hoo!

Top notch voice acting and an adorable plot that fits beautifully with the theme of the show and the game.
This game is a 90s kid/retro gamer's dream. What they expect the remake of their favorite game to be. WayForward outdid themselves this time, so please, go pick it up.

Marking not only the 10th main installment, Assassin's Creed Origins was released just in time to stamp the 10 year anniversary of the much beloved franchise. For a decade now, players have entered the Animus in search of legendary treasure and ancient artifacts; exploring the sprawling city of Rome, sailing the seas of the Caribbean, witnessing the construction of colonial America, fighting in the French Revolution, and so much more in the shoes of classic, fan favorite assassins such as Altaïr, Ezio, and Edward. Origins has promised to deliver fans the story of how the Assassin Order began, and what better place to weave such a tale than that of ancient Egypt.
The primary story revolves around Bayek of Siwa, the last known Medjay of Egypt, during the Ptolemaic era and the final years of the empire; to put it in laymans terms, 49 BCE, and during the time of Cleopatra's rise to Pharaoh over her brother. Without going too in depth, as the story is exceedingly well crafted and should not be spoiled for anyone, Bayek's story is one of personal revenge, and beside him stands his wife, Aya. The vengeance quest sends Bayek to hunt down thirteen members of what is only known as The Order, while both parties help to serve Cleopatra, ensuring her rise to power while the malevolent force of Rome, ruled at the time by the tyrant Julias Ceaser, loom overhead. Though the description may sound a bit bland, trust me when I say that this synopsis is leaving out every single the juicy detail. However, the modern day story arc leaves much to be desired, and it may disappoint long-term fans to know that it does not pick up where Syndicate left off.
The land of ancient Egypt is absolutely awe-inspiring in every way imaginable. While thoughts of the land conjure images of neverending deserts and sand dunes, not even a recognizable fraction of Origin's land is made up of these fictitious imaginings. The map is extremely diverse, and it's filled with beautiful, busy cities, refreshing oases, and startling clashes of Egyptian, Greek, and Roman culture. Above all, the glorious landmarks and jaw-dropping statues are what really make the exploration in this title fun and interesting. Gamers can expect to visit the Great Sphinx, complete with nose and paint, as well as the three Pyramids of Giza which don their original smooth casings. Statues of old Pharaohs and gods stand towering over city streets and inside temples, while the cities and temples themselves are adorned with lavish carvings. Ubisoft really went all out with the intimate details in this game, and it's all incredibly commendable.
With a staggering 34 map sections to explore, over 120 main missions and side quests to complete, 58 synchronization points, and dozens upon dozens of locations with challenges to complete, one would be hard pressed to say that there's nothing to do in Assassin's Creed Origins. From exploring ancient tombs, to looting chests, killing certain enemies and animals, and even discovering secrets hidden by Minerva herself, there is easily over 60 hours of gameplay present for those who want to get their money's worth. Otherwise, the main story can be completed in about 12-15 hours, but the additional content should definitely not be missed. The side quests feel far from generic, and each of them feature dynamic characters that Bayek becomes aquainted with; some of the missions even turn into larger, more in-depth tasks. Origins is truly the first Assassin's Creed title that lacks an abundance of repetitious behavior, and all time constraints have been eliminated, which allows players to roam freely and take their time with any given mission.
Much like Unity and Syndicate, Origins does have a detailed RPG factor to it, complete with a multi-branching skill tree, weapons and shields with stats, many different mounts, and various outfits, all with three rarity qualities; legendary, rare, and common. This time around the outfits do not offer anything further than an aesthetic appeal, and neither do mounts, and there are an incredible amount of both to collect; Ubisoft even have additional ones that players can purchase with the infamous Helix credits, aka in-game currency bought with real-life cash. However, it's worth noting that the best weapons and shields in the game are not bought with microtransactions, so there's no pay wall standing in the way of Bayek being his best. Sadly, a lot of the skills are dismissable, especially the over-hyped animal taming that Ubisoft pushed at E3; in most cases, it's not even worth the effort.
Among the advancements, the entire control scheme has changed. There are no more convoluted parkour buttons, but rather one for ascending and one for descending; there's no longer even a run button, as Bayek moves at full speed at all times unless he's crouching. Being stealthy is a lot easier, even for clumsy fools like myself who can't hide in pitch dark. Ubisoft must've also taken a page from The Witcher 3, since there's now a "follow road" option for when Bayek is on his mount. It's a great option if one needs to get up and stretch, grab a drink, let the dog out, take a poo, whatever it may be, however there are times that this option can lead players straight into danger, and coming back to a random desynchronization is both irritating and disappointing. Eagle Vision also now has a new meaning, as Bayek uses his pet Senu to do all of the scouting and targeting.
With that all said, Assassin's Creed Origins runs on the AnvilNext 2.0 engine, which is also used by Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands, Steep, and both Assassin's Creed Unity and Syndicate. Many folks have compared Origins to Wildlands in terms of how it plays, and those people are not far off. Senu, the Eagle, does control with great similarity to the drone in Wildlands, and the overall control scheme and functionality of Origins feels extremely similar. It's also sad to say that both titles have abhorrent optimization, and a plethora of technical problems. On my i7-6700k/GTX 1080 rig, I saw frame rates as low as 45 and as high as 120, with a standard rate of 65-75; mind you, all settings were maxed and I was using 1080p resolution. The biggest clincher is why Origins devours a whopping 70-80% CPU usage while running, however. Twice the game hard-locked on me, as my CPU usage skyrocketed to 95% out of nowhere, and one time it was while I was attempting to shut the game down. A smaller downside to Origins is the lack of soundtrack and the bad quality of of the sound in general. While everyone's voice acting is top tier, especially Bayek's spot-on emotions, the quality of everything from voices to footsteps sounds compressed, especially when using a high quality 7.1 surround sound headset.
Disregarding its downfalls, Assassin's Creed Origins is the best installment in the franchise to date; in fact, it borders on Game of the Year quality. The map is easily 4-5 times bigger than any other entry, and it will take dozens of hours to polish off all of the side quests and location exploring. For once, it's worth paying the huge launch price of $80 CAD, as the hours played to price ratio comes in at about $1.25 per hour for a full completion run. Even the deulxe edition content is worth the extra $10, as the weapons given are the most powerful that gamers will encounter until the very end of the journey. As for performance, if you have a mid or low end rig, and you have a console, definitely consider picking it up on another platform instead; as Ubisoft's track record of fixing optimization is abysmal. PC gamers still rate the lowest of the low on their list, and that doesn't seem to be changing any time soon.

TLDR they turned AssCreed into Far Cry with incredibly shallow "RPG" mechanics. Compared to the last 2 AC games this game is much better. It disappoints in some areas but it isn't a garbage cringefest by any means, and I do not regret paying $60 for it. It has several layers of DRM, lootboxes, and microtransactions so it gets an automatic negative review.
It's a decent enough game and there's plenty of quests world to explore. The new combat compared to past AC games is a great improvement, but without a stamina bar to stop you from attacking forever it feels like babby's first Dark Souls. Even playing on hard the game is only really challenging when you're fighting dudes that are a higher level than you. The whole progression system is just a boring way to extend the life of the game. If you assassinate someone it should kill them, it shouldn't depend on the big number floating about the guys head and whether or not I've killed the 500 deer required to upgrade the hidden blade. There's no innovation with the progression system.
The RPG mechanics are minimal. I wouldn't even call it an RPG. There's an inventory system apparently but it's only used for quest items, random garbage you can sell, and the seven whole different types of crafting materials. Let me craft consumables that help me somehow. Make it so I die of heat in the desert unless I have water on me. The ability tree is pretty lackluster. You need to spend skill points to buy crafting materials from merchants, and even then it's not worth it. Mounts and outfits are just cosmetic, so the only thing left to spend your gold on is upgrading your weapons, which is stupidly expensive. There's no way you can afford to keep upgrading the same weapon through the entire game unless you spend actual money to buy gold. The rewards you get from chariot races and arena fights are pitiful. Upgrading weapons is pointless anyway (until you hit max level) because you'll just find better loot. Or more likely you'll just find the same weapon, but at whatever level you currently are.
Story wise, I just wanted this game to not be a cliched cringefest and it certainly accomplished that. The ending felt
Totally feels like they ripped out a chunk of the story and are gonna sell it as DLC. Look, what's there is good, but it needs more. Once you beat the game nothing changes. There's nothing new to do. There's no sending dudes on missions, no calling in dudes to help you, and worst of all there's no home base to upgrade to give you a passive income. I guess if they did that there would be no reason for you to spend actual money on gold. The modern day story

Other random thoughts/complaints. Can't use your own weapons in the arena fights, just whatever weapon the game gives you. The 3 baby arena fights you're required to do before every boss feel tacked on to make the arena stuff last longer. Most of the assassination targets are just guys hanging out in a generic enemy outpost. The tools you have and the number of ways you can take on an outpost leaves a lot to be desired. Most locations are just one off things that you'll never return to. The combat is nice and responsive but there's basically no variety in the executions and it wouldn't hurt to at least have some limb chopping or something to make it a little more brutal. Bigger weapons literally shrink in size when you put them away. No interesting traps or actually challenging puzzles in the tombs or pyramids. Bayek has literally 0 reaction when he sees First Civilization stuff. Can't climb the war elephants. War elephants are just one off bosses that you never see in the open world. Phylakes are very cool but are also one off things that don't respawn. The guided missile arrow is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing dumb and over powered but also pretty fun to use. Still no noteriety system. Controls are better and feel nice since you don't have to hold a button to sprint. No crowd blending for stealth kills. No big crowds like in Unity. Projectiles are much better. There are big areas of the desert that have literally nothing. Haven't seen it rain a single time. You can wear nothing but a bathrobe if you want. Only had two or three game breaking bugs in my whole playthrough which were fixed by reloading. The game looks great. The lighting is great.
I could go on forever talking about this game. The bar has been set pretty low since Ezio died, and even lower after Desmond died, so overall I'm happy with the game. It has some real good feeling moments, but it still lacks some of the charm of the old games (the microtransactions and lootboxes certainly don't help). It's a big game but it's mostly just full of generic open world Far Cry -esque trash. I've said a lot of bad things but it's still a fun game and I certainly got my money's worth. Hopefully the next game improves on everything that's here, but when dealing with Ubisoft you have to prepare to be disappointed ;)

Crash Drive 2 is a port of a mobile game to Steam and it's got a lot of ridiculous driving, crashing, spinning, and flipping.  But is it worth your time?  Let's find out in this review on Crash Drive 2.
Crash Drive 2 is a pretty simple game.  You pick your car, get out on a multiplayer course with other drivers, and complete objective based events.  The different events include setting a high score, tagging various objects, and being the first to reach a certain ring.  The game is pure mayhem and silly fun as you bump into other players and there's no consequence.  Cars take no damage and most of the time you will land on your wheels.  Even if you don't land upright, chances are you'll easily flip over.  There are five different levels and you must complete a few tasks in order to advance.  You'll have to set a high score, drive through all of the rings one time, and complete a number of events to unlock the next level.
So multiplayer is crucial and it's the point of the game.  Whenever you join a level you're instantly matchmade with other players so you never know who you'll end up with.  Am I really playing with PewDiePie? Probably not, but that's funny.
There's also a ton of different cars to unlock.  There's lightweight and fast sports cars, then there are big monster trucks and fire trucks.  The trucks are fun for crashing into your opponents, but the sports cars will let you get tons of air.  Oh Yeah!
There's also a crazy tank battle mode that you get to unlock later.  The tanks can shoot and you can blow your opponents away.  Tank battle mode is probably the craziest because you are on a floating platform and you get points by knocking other people off.  It's total mayhem. Tank battle mode is like a different game, but it's also fun to play.
The graphics are probably the weakest part of the game.  Since it's a mobile port, it doesn't take advantage of PC power and there are no advanced graphics settings.  Some of the texture are pretty bad, especially in the first level.  The barriers that surround the level are just like warped end points.  They could have done a better job with this.  The plus side is that it does run very well, I maxed out at 144 frames per second and didn't really experience any lag.
There were also a few bugs, I got stuck on a tree once or twice but I was able to reset my position by hitting start even though the game doesn't indicate this.  I also had some disconnects during multiplayer sessions.
Crash Drive 2 is only $5 on Steam so it may be fun to mess around and drive like a maniac for a bit.  If you like silly games and want to relax from a grueling shooter session, Crash Drive 2 can be a fun distraction. I like hard games as much as the next person, but the problem with a game like this is when it gets so hard that there is no skill progression. As previous reviewers have stated it is about getting the exact right combo of jumps, not about building the skill needed to intuitively understand a course.
That combined with the fact that the monsters behaviour is rediculously RNG-dependant and that there is almost no way to avoid taking damage results in a lack of satisfaction upon completing a level. You don't so much feel you're getting better as that you were lucky to get it on that try. Super Meat Boy, Super Hexagon etc. were consistant in that you would understand the mechanics and get better. This is just about giving it enough tries and eventually succeeding.
I don't recommend this game on the basis that there are better ways to spend your time, which include both a better story and more skill progression. In the end the game is rediculously short in content and it feels like the difficulty is there to mask the lack of polish rather than being a real selling point in and of itself.

***If you're on the fence about buying this game and are not a hardcore platformer, I recommend reading this review***
I'm going to start this review off by saying this is not a bad game. It's just a game made to appeal to a very specific niche of people: gamers who don't care for a story and want to play a frustratingly hard platformer.
While this game is not without its redeeming qualities (for a specific audience)  I found that within 15 minutes of buying the game I was regretting the purchase, and will likely be requesting a refund. So what's wrong with the game? For me, it was three main things:
1) Very weak story. The game starts off with a 10-second story in which you walk into Jeh Oul's prison, throw rocks at him, he's freed, makes the expected generic threat, and escapes. You step outside and everything's gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥ That's all the story you get. If you actually take time to explore the houses at the start of the game, you'll find just a little more backstory, but it's still not much. After that, you're dumped into the game without any real objective than "rescue my friend". While I understand the story is not the selling point of this game, I still found the lack of effort put into world building off-putting, as I wasn't inspired to try to beat this game, or to find out what comes next. For me, this was one of the main things that killed the game for me, as from moment one the game felt less like an adventure and more like something I was doing just to say I did it.
2) Difficulty. As I mentioned, the game is made to appeal to masochistic, platformer-loving gamers. While I have no issue with playing a difficult platformer, this game doesn't ease into the difficulty, which I felt was a huge issue. Within a minute of freeing the demon king, I found myself having to execute very difficult maneuvers that left less than a few milimeters for error, which quickly led to me getting frustrated as it took me an average of 2-3 minutes to move from checkpoint to checkpoint (the checkpoints, on normal at least, are not very far apart at all). The most irritating part is that it wasn't just one maneuver at a time, it was often a series of 2-3 jumps that needed perfect execution or you'd die. Given that the game had literally just started, and it likely only gets harder from the beginning onward, I found myself wondering what I was doing playing this game.
3) I got lost. As I mentioned in the first point, there's no real objective in this game. There's no arrow that says "go this way", there's no context to follow, you're literally just standing outside the prison and given a weapon. I decided to keep moving forward, a strategy which worked until the second miniboss (20 minutes in). After that, I encountered a dead end, with no indication as to where I should go next. It was at that point that I decided that this game wasn't for me. I don't mind mazes, but the other two points mentioned above, paired with the fact I was lost left me entirely uninterested in progressing further.
That's pretty much it. As far as mechanics, art, music, and gameplay go, I would say that it's all pretty good. Were the game executed better, I might be writing a positive review as it has the potential to be good. Unfortunately however, I'm not.

Lemme just preface this with two facts:
I hope you already know where I'm going with this. This isn't any platformer.
.
And that's why it's so good.
is a refreshing change, amongst a sea of mind-numbingly EASY games. And its the good kind of hard game - the kind that doesn't cheat. The rules are there, very clearly for the player. No save-zones that were traps all along, no pay-to-win DLC to beat a tough boss. Its you, the deathtrap-filled stage, and a massive boss at the end that will eat days of your time. But hour after hour of persistence, progress comes. Slowly, you git gud. And finally, the massive boss is defeated, and the hours of frustration reward you with happiness and pride. You won because you are skilled, and you are skilled because you are persistent. It feels
, and its a feeling I haven't felt in a long time with games.
The story is simple, but enough to keep you going. You are Vi, an angel, on a journey to fix a mistake you made that put the world at severe risk. Along the way, you'll defeat all sorts of bizarre, twisted demons and monstrosities, and meet other characters, which you can talk to and learn about the lore.
In addition to the platforming and story, there is also the exploration -
puts just a foot over the
genre, rewarding the player that goes beyond the beaten path with secret chests. These chests contain unlockable cosmetic items for your character, that can be customized at any time.
So, the result is two parallel challenges at the same time: To finish the tremendously difficult campaign, and to get 100% exploration and acquire all the customization pieces. The collection of unlockable pieces is quite big, and after some time it begins feeling like a dress-up game - on top of the platforming and exploration.

I've approached this title with as little expectations as possible, since I've heard the game sucks, Connor sucks and everything about it sucks.
Well colour me surprised. Not only did I enjoy the game tremendously story wise, not only I liked the ending (I've heard it sucks!), not only I didn't mind Connor being how he was (though yeah, he feels like unfinished business. He sounds lifeless,  but it's sort of understandable providing what past he came from. Yeah he could be more polished a protagonist, I'll give nay-sayers that).
Have to admit though this game has been (for me) completely taken by Templars. Because Haytham is magnificent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
To sum it up:
Cons:
- A lot of odd hatred toward the game. Connor not being Ezio is not a catastrophe, you know.
- Some things are basically useless, like stealing. You don't really need it for anything unlike in, say, AC I when it was useful for replenishing your stack of throwing knives.
- Again, all the pistols, swords and other weapons are just collectibles and visuals.
- Outfits, few are goods, most are ugly. Also, you have only few dyes to choose from, and if you put something other then default outfit, odd things happen with Connor's haircut in cutsceenes.
- Some 100% synch requirements are maddening.
- Lifeless Indian speech. Why there was no emotion in actors' voices is beyond me.
- Not many silly/creepy bugs AC I and AC II contained. I sort of remember them fondly.
- All right, Connor makes little sense sometimes and acts as if he didn't know what he wanted. Though, maybe he doesn't.
Pros:
- Awesome settings in awesome times. Alternative versions of historical events - me likey!
- Combat: I liked it always, I like it here, too. More brutal.
- Pretty ok-ish story. If devs haven't decided otherwise, it would create a good start for some AC in the future, taking off from where AC III ended.
- Ending speaking truth about human nature. (No wonder so many dislike it!)
- Characters. There are many interesting characters, even if main protagonist is not one of them.
- Music. It's epic.
- Places you visit are very authentic, climatic and alive.
- Explaining other side of the never ending conflict. I like it when it's not black and white, and like it or not, Templars make a lot of sense.
- NAVAL MISSIONS! Pure joy. Even if one of the hardest 100% syncs was one of them.
- You can hunt. I didn't enjoy that, but option is there and it is something new.
- Contains multiplaya.
All in all, it was good times.

Like most rogue-lites, you permanently unlock new things by dying, but luckily this kept on with Magicite's (Good length for a rogue-lite, by the way. 45 mintues. Nice stuff. Like it a lot. Was a pretty good game.) unlock mechanic of "25% Chance To Unlock After Doing X". So, upon losing a 3 hour run and not being incredibly pleased, you find that you've unlocked just 4 of the game's many, many unlocks. Not because requirements weren't met, but because there was only x % chance of said requirement actually unlocking anything.
As of yet, I haven't played this game much, and as much as I hate myself for it I will play it more in the future, and I'll probably enjoy it. But that's because I somewhat enjoy pressing the left mouse button over and over and over and over again to use slow weapons against rather creative enemies (I have more than just insults). If you don't like grinding, don't buy this. If you want a 40 minute lunch break game, don't play this.
BUT, this game does have positives, and if you want a hardcore (though very slow paced) experience, or a time sink that still sounds appealing after what I've said about it, I would recommend it. Sadly, there's no way I could recommend this to any sane person who values their time whatsoever.

Well, you will better see about colonists yourself, they are funny guys too.
Second feature I liked is a slow pace of the game. In most RTS you must hurry up from the start and put every worker and every resource in use, otherwise you can lose the game before meeting an enemy. Here this is not needed. In fact, I even lose couple of times because tried to build more building at once and ending with not having enough resorces to complete any of them. The rate of game increases after department from first island, but there is still enough time to explore the world, hunt a crocs, or just aimlessly sail seeking a possibility to steal something. But it's not like a sandboxes or RPGs - there is a serious enemy and he is gathering forces, so you can't grind infinitely.
I don't want to spoil the pleasure of discovering all game mechanics, for me it was very funny part of the game, but I think I must warn about most common mistake - trying to stay on first island and build everything there. The purpose of starting resources and starting island is to build a shipyard. Everything else - mines, mint etc. can wait, shipyard is vital. After building your first ship don't forget to save a game and you are free to go - explore, colonize new island to make a complex production chains, hunt aborigines, bite and claw colonists to take their excesses for your fast growing economics. There are also caves, they are completely different world with different rules, very dangerous (and that's not joke) but very rewarding.
By the way, the game have good support of windows-based tablets, just don't forget to enable correspondnig option in a settings menu.
To be honest, there are also some words of critique: settings menu is terrifiyng at sight. And a more serious problem - there is not much things to do after you managed to win a game. You can play the game with some self-imposed challenges, but other then that you have to get out of this wonderful universe. So i hope that author will make an extended release with increased difficulty mode, even though it is unlikely.

The longer you read, the more details add to the picture.
You start with small island and few buildings.
You expand on a larger island. Build even more buildings. Kill some things. Mine some ores. Burn some enemy buildings.
Then sail around and see even larger world, meet colonists, get your butt kicked, load, get your butt kicked again, load, wipe sweat, load, run away.
Find a cave. Delve in. Get your butt kicked. Load. Avoid enemies, delve even deeper.
Find a chest. Get eaten by bears. Load.
Find another chest full of royal treasure. Equip things. Try to leave the dungeon alive. Get eaten several times.
Now we're cooking!
By the time you reach this, colonists will have weapons and large city. There's a LOT of work and sabotage to do.
Remember to save often!

This game is clearly a prime example of an Early Access title done right; it released in a buggy, nigh on uplayable state, and 2 days later the devs have fixed most if not all issues, plus are very open to incorporating feedback/requests. Also is sparse on the customization options, but I expect that will improve with time.
For any who might be confused, the opbject of the game is to remove hexes from a playing field one space at a time, until the statue in the center falls. The player that causes it to drop is the loser. As hexes are removed the physics cause the remaining hexes to weaken, so there is some minor strategy involved.
All in all, I really enjoy this title, and can't wait to see how it progresses in the future!

This problem may be killing a certain perosn, obtaining an item, rescuing a poor soul, shutting something down, or a little bit of different things.  It's up to you to use your head and the resources provided by the level to accomplish these missions before moving onto the next floor.  Fail to plan ahead and suffer the consequences.

Sweet jelly belly jesus. Let me start off by saying, I have played every Five Night's at Freddy's game that has been released. I have seen every jump scare and played every nightmare mode. And this game trumps them all. This game is completely different from the rest. Prepare to die in a childlike nostalgia of horror. This game takes you back to those frightening nights when you were eight, huddled under the covers with your flashlight. First off, what's different? For one. the animitronics have gotten a complete remodel, and I am not talking FNAF 2 happy smiley remodel. It's like Satan decided to get into making robots. Secondly, you aren't a security guard watching cameras in an office. You are a child in his room on a dark night, relying only on sound and your flashlight to save you from horrifying nightmares. To me, that is what makes this game terrifying. Not just the jumpscares, but the darkness. You have no cameras to rely on, no visual cues. Your only hint as to whether or not you need to ♥♥♥♥ing hide is the sound of a robot's ghastly breathing or the creak of a door. And you better hope to god he isn't right in front of your face. I have not even beat this game. I haven't even gotten past night two. That is how terrifying this game is. I strongly recommend this to anyone that loves to be really scared. I don't mean temporarily in-the-moment jump scared, but I mean full on hoping-you-don't-die-when-you-turn-around kind of scared. I seriously think that if you have a weak heart or heart condition, DO NOT PLAY THIS.
Fun 5/5. Terror 10/5, Graphics 5/5, Mature 4/5, Worth the Price? Yes.

So I have never written a review on here before, but I feel obligated after listening to all of the bad reviews. I almost didn't buy  the game at all  because of all of the people who argue that they have elite computers that have to try too hard in order to play the game, or saying they couldn't play at all because of framerate, etc. I'll address some of the issues I have read, and then  leave a more positive review at the bottom.
I'm pretty positive most of the people who argue that their computer is overpowered and should be able to easily run the game, have a computer greater than mine and I completed the game with relatively no issue. I did have a couple crashes, but I changed some things to keep my computer cooler and the crash rate plummeted. I rarely, if ever, had a frame rate issue. No, my settings are not maxed, because I don't need to boost my own  ego and rate the game based on if my computer can play it on ultimate settings rather than the actual game itself. Most of the comments here that are negative, do say the game is great but they disliked something Ubisoft  did. Ubisoft has  virtually always screwed the customer somehow, but you  knew that before you bought the game and if you really didn't like them you would have stopped buying Assassin's Creed way  earlier in the franchise.
The next review I read was about having to rush to complete the community event. After the event became active, the players had a full week to get to the required level and complete the event. At no point at all did I rush through any part of the game, let alone the story, to achieve the level needed and complete the event in time. In fact, I have almost double the hours in the game as one of the posters who made this complain and took my time to complete literally everything. I have all of the achievments for Steam and all of the available ones compelted for the Ubisoft Club. I loved the game, the  view, and the  experience and I'm not understanding how anyone needed to rush when you were probably a quarter to half of the level requirement before the event came out because I even got the game late.
The last group of reviews I want to counter is the cost and the additional DLC.  I did buy the Gold Version for the season pass and I'm not at all put off by the company offering additional resources for more money. Why? Because they are not at all necessary. There are outfits and weapons available, which you can easily get equal to or better versions of by actually playing the game or some of the free options Ubisoft offers. The resources offered are literally called "Time Savers" as in when you are too lazy to grind like in any other RPG and get the things you want, you pay for the easy way out. I admittedly did use one of these items with the free Helix points you start with and so there is no loss to me, only a little boost. I will admit the resources can be short if you don't prioritize what you're spending them on, but without spoiling parts of the gameplay I can't really go further into that.  I guess that falls into the "feeling rushed" comment from earlier. If you actually want the items/upgrades it is very easy to simply work for them. Want vs Need. It's basic.
For the actual game, it is extremely large. There is nowhere within the map that you can't go; most buildings are open and you can climb virtually any mountain when walking to a destination. Some battle types were a little frustrating, but that was just a personal thing really and the game itself was great. The kill animations for all of the weapon types were awesome and well though out. You never end a  battle just dropping a guy and walking away. There is a bow and weapon combo for everyone.
The story line was very intriuging and after doing a little research I found there was actually a lot of truth to it (as in most of the Assassin's Creed games) and I enjoyed running into a lot of the historical figures and handling the plot twists throughout the game. The game also has a unique way of starting the Brotherhood since this was suppose to preceed the other games.
TL:DR, Game good, reviews bad.

Where do i start? The combat system has been upgraded imensely, your fights change from the typical stealthy assassin into a fully blown master of arms in just a few seconds depending on the situation at hand and it doesnt feel like a disadvantage like i experienced in the other assassins creeds, usually you'd be more focused on running away and hiding so you could come back to assassinate your enemies when they had lost interest in you, but in Origins its like a step up, its more engaing, you have a talent tree so you can focus on different styles and tactics which is brilliant.
You can be a full blown ranger, slow motion jumps whilst aiming with your bow, quickfire headshots taking out 4 people with your bow before anyones even notices! you can go all out warrior mode with a shield and a massive axe, or dual blades.. spears.. maces.. you name it. or you can chose to be tactical, sleeping darts, bombs, traps, etc. or all of the above for a master of all situations!
The world is absolutley enormous with NO LOADING screens! the world is beautiful and immersive. there is nowhere you cannot go, climb, explore.. if you get bored of questing, or you just want to explore, you will always find something interesting AND beneficial to your development - All whilst admiring the beauty of the world around you which is just a bonus.
The gear is upgradeable so you dont get stuck with crappy weapons and feel the need to search for 'The best items' you can choose something you like the look of and always keep upgrading it so you dont have to say goodbye to it which i think is really great. the gear is upgradeable with animal loots, like leather and hides etc.. there are loads of (cosmetic) outfits you can wear which means you dont look like an idiot with a really beautifull chest piece and some cruddy leather boots/gloves. you always look good, which is quite important for me in games.
the quests are good, the campaign doesnt feel like a grind that you cant wait to be over... its rewarding and fun. i guess the rest is up for you to experience! definitley worth the buy... there is a store where you can buy legendary weapons and gear but i have not found the need to purchase anything! im really bad for spending money on games, and with assassins creed i have literally not felt the need at all, which is good to know also.

So roguelands. Almost everything about this game is extremely fun, including the art style, the crafting system, the combat. But the most fun a person can have out of this game, or any game, is roguelands multiplayer. The multiplayer can be an absolute pain to set up, but last year during summer when I first found this game, a bunch of new players including I, put together a rougelands group in skype. This was absurdly fun, however it lasted only around 3 weeks. This is because of the lack of content that was in front of us at that time. We had already played through what the game had to offer in the first week or so. What do we do after that? We messed around and made new characters to bide time for new story lines and arena bosses. The update adding the starlight rebellion storyline was the end for us. We all played through the story line in a matter of a day, and it was back to screwing around. Slowly, people started to get tired and conflict within the group broke us apart. The good times that we had were forever solidified in our memories, and the plaguebeast, John. Overall, best experience I've ever had on a game, and I thank the creator for that. On to the actual review.

You really have to judge this game for what it is, and not expect it to be something that it isn't.
Firstly, it's in Early Access, so it's not finished yet. I'm sure there will be much more content as time goes on. Right now, if you're looking for some kind of sophisticated world-building game à la Cities: Skylines or Cities in Motion, you're going to be disappointed. In its current state, this is more of a toy than any kind of simulator. It's the toystore wooden train set you wanted as a kid. There are a few dozen props to be added to the sandbox-style world, plus a basic set of wooden track pieces, and that's it.
Secondly, it shows a lot of potential. Some of the items (loading and unloading points, for example) suggest that the devs are working on adding more complex mechanics to the game. New gamemodes and the ability to create scenarios for the Workshop seem to be in motion already.
With all of that said, what you
get with Tracks in its current form is absolutely charming. The little wooden passengers bopping around excitedly as you pull into a station or roll up next to a platform are adorable. Driving your train is a smooth and enjoyable experience. Graphics are very nice. A lot of care has obviously gone into each of the little props, from stations and platforms to fountains. The "Random House" function is great, adding variety to your scenery automatically by placing one of three different sized houses randomly each time you click. The music is relaxing and pleasant. You can already build multi-level networks and multiple types of stations, as well as crossovers that allow you to decide between multiple routes while driving.
All in all, I think that Tracks is a wonderfully charming little toy. It's enjoyable and relaxing to play with and shows a lot of promise for what's to come in future updates. The devs are clearly putting a lot of care into making it a visually appealing product rather than just focusing on creating as
content as possible, which is appreciated. I'm really impressed with it and can't wait to see where it goes.

The game is nice, it is really a change from them FPS shooters, and the 8-bit graphics is awesome. It plays out nice, and some basic features are added, like zooming, increasing play speed, pausing etc. It's thought out well, but even these features have some parts missing. Increasing speed only has one setting, and that is 3 times faster than usual. This feature bugs out sometimes and no difference in speed occurs.
The movement in the game is nice. That is, you play as the captain of your crew and you move around engaging with certain stuff. But, that feature bugs out aswell. Sometimes while moving, your character will just stop moving and glitch out in a certain building. When you try to move him to another direction, he will only move 1 STEP AT A TIME. This needs to be fixed too.
Building stuff is really hard. When you want to build a building, you only get the name of your building, and the cost. There is no information about what it does, and how much resource it will cost (like workers who need gold). Your only chance is the name it has, and that isn't that helpful either. When you can't build on a certain spot, your builder guy will find the best spot for this build. If there is nowhere available for it, the build will be cancelled. Rather than cancelling, I suggest that your builder guy would scope out the entire island you are in, and look if certain structures are built on the grounds that have the requirements of your wanted build. This would be much more helpful than cancelling the build right away, at least he should ask.
Combat. Combat is really difficult to accomplish. When somebody is engaged, the game creates blood sprites on the ground. This would be much trouble normally, but these blood sprites cover EVERYWHERE. While fighting, I couldn't see my character, or the enemy. This needs to be removed, or the blood should be reduced, or defense in this game would be so difficult. I haven't done much combat, but I can assure you that it is too difficult right now.
Overall, the cost of building structures, and the working cost of pirates are way too high for starting off. It isn't impossible, but while grinding those resources, I got constantly attacked and I had to destroy some structures to build the new one I wanted. I kept losing my men. This can be balanced by reducing the overall cost of buildings, or giving players more resources when they start. Or being able to dismantle and loot ships of people who attacked you might also be a good idea.
Also, there is no tutorial. None. You get a random text popup at the start of the game, and nothing else. Nothing is explained. You're expected to know everything off the start. I saw the game and immediately wanted to play, so I bought  it, installed it, and booted it up. When I got into a game, I wasn't asked If I wanted a tutorial.
The settings menu also needs a lot of explanation. A LOT.
To sum up, this game requires you to be experienced with this type of game. It is incomplete, and needs to be fixed. The fighting mechanic is bad, the building system requires much more than point and build. There is very limited resources, considering you spawn randomly on some islands which are so small, you can only fit like 3-4 buildings before you run out of space, which you need a LOT MORE. Nothing is explained in the game, which is essential in a game like this.
If you need a tl;dr, this is it here.
DO NOT BUY THIS GAME AT THIS STATE. IT IS INCOMPLETE, AND NEEDS MUCH FIXING.
NOTHING IS EXPLAINED IN THIS GAME. NOTHING.
THIS DOESN'T MEAN THAT YOU SHOULD NEVER LOOK AT THE GAME AGAIN. IT IS NICE, JUST NEEDS A BIT TWEAKING. I SUGGEST YOU LOOK AT IT AGAIN IN A FEW MONTHS.

This game provides a smooth and visceral twin stick shooter/beatemup roguelite, well balanced to make both melee and ranged combat interesting, and packed with emergent interactions.  But on top of that: randomly generated missions!  Streets of Rogue's random missions, most of which are of the infiltration-ey variety, combine with the generated urban settings to provide you with endless unique challenges, many of which give the modest and not overdone stealth mechanics a reason to exist.  I don't know if the random missions each level idea is original to this game, but it works amazingly well.  It's like taking the emergent complexity of a procedural dungeon crawl and squaring it.  I hope that many roguelite and roguelike developers shamelessly yoink this formula.
The game itself is somewhat of a mid length demo at this point, with the developer prioritizing a lot of core gameplay and engine functionality over making all the levels the game will eventually have.  I support this, because the foundation being built is rock solid, and I see even more awesomeness in this game's future building upon that.  If we ever get modding, be still my heart.
In any case, you'll have to get a fair bit of practice at the game before you can even notice that it's not complete.  Just getting through the first three sets of levels was hard before I had some solid strategies down, but definitely fun-hard.
There are great amounts of fun to be had from this game today.  The network co-op gameplay is great fun, though some sync issues are still being worked on, and the local co-op is too, with the ability to switch between split screen and single screen depending on how far apart you are.  It could be a bit better done... see SMBX for a stellar example... but it's still quite good.  And on top of being among a small elite group of stellar endlessly fun co-op games with both split screen and lan support, it's quite addictively fun to play all by myself as well.  Which can be a bit of a problem.

Serious review
Streets of Rogue is a randomly generation RPG rogue-like-like. (RIP)
It doesn't contain the elements of endless gameplay and leveling up your character into a god (Hopefully it will), but it has quirks and many ways to complete a quest. The replayablity of this game is so far only limited to character unlocks along with some unlockable traits and rewards for quests. Since it is still in dev, I respect that, as the game isn't finished and the dev most likely wants to hear feedback.
Good thing about character unlocks though is that it opens a whole new way to play the game. Such as playing with the gorilla you can tear through an entire level with your bare hands and not have to care to much about your character's weaknesses. Play as a hacker and you sneak around hacking computers making it so a person falls victim to their own traps. Play as a shapeshifter and completely abuse the ability to take someone over and use their abilities to accomplish your goals. Either way if you like to have several options on how to approach a task this is a fitting game.

God- Where do I even start?
The game itself is MASSIVELY REPLAYABLE, no two runs feel quite the exact same (even if you're traversing the same area, there's a bunch of randomly generated missions and structures to keep you entertained)
I frequently run through every nook and cranny of a level, causing as much chaos as possible, or gathering supplies through more subtle means. (By 'subtle,' I obviously mean electrocuting someone then snapping an explosive slave collar to their neck)
Let me just take a moment to describe SOME of the things you can do in this game.
You can hack most electronics, and make them do damn near whatever you please, including making fridges run!
You can cause a zombie apocalypse and feed on the flesh of your enemies to heal your wounds.
You can drug people with practically every status ailment in multiple ways (such as mixing it into a drink) and even chloroform them!
You could also play as a shapeshifter capable of possessing someone, shooting their friend, then running away as a firefight breaks out.
(Not to mention being able to create living suicide bombs forced to do your bidding)
EVERY class is viable in this game, as each one holds at least one unique trait that completely changes their playing style.
Oh, and by the way? All of the NPCs have their own unique behaviors that follow the logic of their classes (albeit with about a third of the health they normally do, in order to keep you from being overpowered by just one of them) so it's all fair grounds for fights! (Other things, too, but I'd rather not spoil everything for you)
Not only all of this, but the developer regularly responds to forums posts and tries to stay in touch with the game's community as much as possible, how awesome is that!?
Honestly? Comparing this game to other Early Access titles, I give it a 9/10, the huge updates are pretty much bi-weekly, and you get a bunch of bugfixes in-between. The only thing that prevents me from giving this a higher rating is the lack of a complete main mode (You can only access 3 areas at the moment) but even then, the dev is currently working on designing a new floor.
I cannot wait to see what this game is like in the future, and heavily recommend you give it a try.

Once a great MMORPG I feel like TERA is on a downhill slope from what it used to be, to a new player the MMO experience is fun and interesting, but the game suffers from repetitiveness during mid to late levels. Once players reach max level, they will be greeted by the terror that is TERA's endgame system.
I myself have around 1300 hours invested into the game, which the majority was spent talking to people in rest areas.
Pros:
+ Beautiful scenery & graphics (Good optimization when using lowest settings).
+ Multitude of classes.
+ Non tab target gameplay. (The combat in this game gets an A+)
+ Very in-depth character customization (w/ multiple races).
+ Options of PvE, Roleplay and Open world PvP servers.
+ BAM ("Big As Monsters") fights are interesting enough.
+ A large amount of areas to explore.
+ Not as pay to win as it could be. (With the exception to the dragons)
+ The level 60+ questline is entertaining.
+ Seasonal events.
+ A large amount of achievements with in-game rewards.
Cons:
---  THE ENDGAME SYSTEM (Section on that later on)
- CPU heavy, game can lag quite a lot.
- Four female gender-locked (with race locks) classes
- (Past personal issue) some classes outshine others by a large margin
- Some high end costumes/mounts are locked behind an RNG system. (Slightly favored as players can trade them using the auction house)
- Population issues (The game definitely spikes once new content is released, but there is little to no parties queueing endgame dungeons later on)
- To some, the mid to late levels can feel repetitive due to the quest system.
- 30GB+ Download
- As mentioned above around October they announced "Royal Dragon Mounts" which basically regenerate your HP and MP by 2%, and has a chance to double your critical chance. These are locked behind RNG boxes, but players were offered a way to farm these ingredients which would create one, but it had lesser stats than the RNG mount. This lead to this whole fiasco on the forums. With the publisher (EME) communicating little to none back to the community. (Basically P2W mounts)
Other:
+- Toxic community - I have seen people comment on the community as being toxic, I believe the community isn’t that bad, give or take global chat on each server.
+- A few differing modes of PvP, which from what I have heard, are uninteresting.
+- A certain race.
+- Slightly interesting crafting system.
-THE ENDGAME SYSTEM-
The worst thing I have against this game is the endgame system they have. The endgame system has players running dungeons daily to get gear. Each dungeon is blocked by an item level wall (item level is a number that corresponds to one’s equipment). Endgame gear consists of what I would say "4 tiers". Consisting of "beginner endgame gear", and then gear which you get from the "first endgame dungeon", the "second endgame dungeon", and the "over powered gear which is crafted from ingredients dropped from the hardest dungeon". Each requiring the previous gear to unlock the next dungeon.
Most of these dungeons are locked to have a certain amount of entries per day, or hour, resulting in players logging on to do their runs, log off, or interacting with the community. Following this, the content updates that are added to the game is the system I talked about earlier, with a new set of dungeons and gear that is stronger than the last, but following the same formula. This leads to the endgame feeling extremely repetitive, and I feel like they will never change the system (for example the endgame gear is abbreviated as VM, after the first set and is now currently at VM8/8.5).
Conclusion:
If you can get around the 30GB+ download size, I would say, give it a try and enjoy levelling a character at your own pace, enjoying the scenery and what TERA has to offer, but I feel like the repetitive endgame ruins TERA's overall experience.

Fun, but amazingly rough around the edges.
In theory it's a great game, and it is pretty fun to play, both factions are fairly well realized and have a decent degree of depth to them, but there is some major balancing issues.
The idea is that the Rebels will always have a numbers advantage to them over the Combine, but in practice it's fairly easily to match it as the Combine. The Combine in general have fairly strong units compared to the Rebels, and are a degree more pricey, but again still fairly easy to accumulate rendering any number advantage the Rebels have nearly moot. There are also a number of units both factions have that arn't quite as useful as others.
The Rebel's basic unit in particular is nearly useless, even when Zerg Rushed like they're supposed to be, and can also have a tendency to Friendly fire if not microed properly, whereas the Combine's Metro Cops always have some form of usage, whether it be setting up Turrets or releasing Manhacks for backup, and this is a theme throughout the game. The Combine are just better in nearly every way, but there is a certain satisfaction from overcoming them as the Rebels, but more often than not it feels a bit tedious to do so.
The game is also quite buggy. The AI is just... Stupid. Not the enemy AI, the unit AI. Very frequently they'll get stuck, disobey my "Hold Position" command, completely forget those abilities I put on Autocast, Crossbow Snipers JUST ♥♥♥♥ING REFUSE TO SHOOT ANYTHING THE TARGET IS RIGHT THERE WOULD YOU JUST SHOOT IT?!
The game also likes to crash.
A lot.
It'll crash in Offline play, Online play, more often than not it'll do so in the Singleplayer Missions. There's also no Save or Load for anything Offline related, so if your game decides to crash say...right as you're near the end of a mission you've already had to run multiple times because of crashes, you have to start right at the beginning once more.
And yet...I still recommend it. It's a Half Life RTS and despite its flaws, it has a lot of potential, the Devs are pretty good people, and the game itself is solid despite the numerous issues. It's definitely a Diamond in the rough though, but then again, it is a beta I suppose.
Seriously though, the crashing issue is ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous.
