Marking not only the 10th main installment, Assassin's Creed Origins was released just in time to stamp the 10 year anniversary of the much beloved franchise. For a decade now, players have entered the Animus in search of legendary treasure and ancient artifacts; exploring the sprawling city of Rome, sailing the seas of the Caribbean, witnessing the construction of colonial America, fighting in the French Revolution, and so much more in the shoes of classic, fan favorite assassins such as Altaïr, Ezio, and Edward. Origins has promised to deliver fans the story of how the Assassin Order began, and what better place to weave such a tale than that of ancient Egypt.
The primary story revolves around Bayek of Siwa, the last known Medjay of Egypt, during the Ptolemaic era and the final years of the empire; to put it in laymans terms, 49 BCE, and during the time of Cleopatra's rise to Pharaoh over her brother. Without going too in depth, as the story is exceedingly well crafted and should not be spoiled for anyone, Bayek's story is one of personal revenge, and beside him stands his wife, Aya. The vengeance quest sends Bayek to hunt down thirteen members of what is only known as The Order, while both parties help to serve Cleopatra, ensuring her rise to power while the malevolent force of Rome, ruled at the time by the tyrant Julias Ceaser, loom overhead. Though the description may sound a bit bland, trust me when I say that this synopsis is leaving out every single the juicy detail. However, the modern day story arc leaves much to be desired, and it may disappoint long-term fans to know that it does not pick up where Syndicate left off.
The land of ancient Egypt is absolutely awe-inspiring in every way imaginable. While thoughts of the land conjure images of neverending deserts and sand dunes, not even a recognizable fraction of Origin's land is made up of these fictitious imaginings. The map is extremely diverse, and it's filled with beautiful, busy cities, refreshing oases, and startling clashes of Egyptian, Greek, and Roman culture. Above all, the glorious landmarks and jaw-dropping statues are what really make the exploration in this title fun and interesting. Gamers can expect to visit the Great Sphinx, complete with nose and paint, as well as the three Pyramids of Giza which don their original smooth casings. Statues of old Pharaohs and gods stand towering over city streets and inside temples, while the cities and temples themselves are adorned with lavish carvings. Ubisoft really went all out with the intimate details in this game, and it's all incredibly commendable.
With a staggering 34 map sections to explore, over 120 main missions and side quests to complete, 58 synchronization points, and dozens upon dozens of locations with challenges to complete, one would be hard pressed to say that there's nothing to do in Assassin's Creed Origins. From exploring ancient tombs, to looting chests, killing certain enemies and animals, and even discovering secrets hidden by Minerva herself, there is easily over 60 hours of gameplay present for those who want to get their money's worth. Otherwise, the main story can be completed in about 12-15 hours, but the additional content should definitely not be missed. The side quests feel far from generic, and each of them feature dynamic characters that Bayek becomes aquainted with; some of the missions even turn into larger, more in-depth tasks. Origins is truly the first Assassin's Creed title that lacks an abundance of repetitious behavior, and all time constraints have been eliminated, which allows players to roam freely and take their time with any given mission.
Much like Unity and Syndicate, Origins does have a detailed RPG factor to it, complete with a multi-branching skill tree, weapons and shields with stats, many different mounts, and various outfits, all with three rarity qualities; legendary, rare, and common. This time around the outfits do not offer anything further than an aesthetic appeal, and neither do mounts, and there are an incredible amount of both to collect; Ubisoft even have additional ones that players can purchase with the infamous Helix credits, aka in-game currency bought with real-life cash. However, it's worth noting that the best weapons and shields in the game are not bought with microtransactions, so there's no pay wall standing in the way of Bayek being his best. Sadly, a lot of the skills are dismissable, especially the over-hyped animal taming that Ubisoft pushed at E3; in most cases, it's not even worth the effort.
Among the advancements, the entire control scheme has changed. There are no more convoluted parkour buttons, but rather one for ascending and one for descending; there's no longer even a run button, as Bayek moves at full speed at all times unless he's crouching. Being stealthy is a lot easier, even for clumsy fools like myself who can't hide in pitch dark. Ubisoft must've also taken a page from The Witcher 3, since there's now a "follow road" option for when Bayek is on his mount. It's a great option if one needs to get up and stretch, grab a drink, let the dog out, take a poo, whatever it may be, however there are times that this option can lead players straight into danger, and coming back to a random desynchronization is both irritating and disappointing. Eagle Vision also now has a new meaning, as Bayek uses his pet Senu to do all of the scouting and targeting.
With that all said, Assassin's Creed Origins runs on the AnvilNext 2.0 engine, which is also used by Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands, Steep, and both Assassin's Creed Unity and Syndicate. Many folks have compared Origins to Wildlands in terms of how it plays, and those people are not far off. Senu, the Eagle, does control with great similarity to the drone in Wildlands, and the overall control scheme and functionality of Origins feels extremely similar. It's also sad to say that both titles have abhorrent optimization, and a plethora of technical problems. On my i7-6700k/GTX 1080 rig, I saw frame rates as low as 45 and as high as 120, with a standard rate of 65-75; mind you, all settings were maxed and I was using 1080p resolution. The biggest clincher is why Origins devours a whopping 70-80% CPU usage while running, however. Twice the game hard-locked on me, as my CPU usage skyrocketed to 95% out of nowhere, and one time it was while I was attempting to shut the game down. A smaller downside to Origins is the lack of soundtrack and the bad quality of of the sound in general. While everyone's voice acting is top tier, especially Bayek's spot-on emotions, the quality of everything from voices to footsteps sounds compressed, especially when using a high quality 7.1 surround sound headset.
Disregarding its downfalls, Assassin's Creed Origins is the best installment in the franchise to date; in fact, it borders on Game of the Year quality. The map is easily 4-5 times bigger than any other entry, and it will take dozens of hours to polish off all of the side quests and location exploring. For once, it's worth paying the huge launch price of $80 CAD, as the hours played to price ratio comes in at about $1.25 per hour for a full completion run. Even the deulxe edition content is worth the extra $10, as the weapons given are the most powerful that gamers will encounter until the very end of the journey. As for performance, if you have a mid or low end rig, and you have a console, definitely consider picking it up on another platform instead; as Ubisoft's track record of fixing optimization is abysmal. PC gamers still rate the lowest of the low on their list, and that doesn't seem to be changing any time soon.

TLDR they turned AssCreed into Far Cry with incredibly shallow "RPG" mechanics. Compared to the last 2 AC games this game is much better. It disappoints in some areas but it isn't a garbage cringefest by any means, and I do not regret paying $60 for it. It has several layers of DRM, lootboxes, and microtransactions so it gets an automatic negative review.
It's a decent enough game and there's plenty of quests world to explore. The new combat compared to past AC games is a great improvement, but without a stamina bar to stop you from attacking forever it feels like babby's first Dark Souls. Even playing on hard the game is only really challenging when you're fighting dudes that are a higher level than you. The whole progression system is just a boring way to extend the life of the game. If you assassinate someone it should kill them, it shouldn't depend on the big number floating about the guys head and whether or not I've killed the 500 deer required to upgrade the hidden blade. There's no innovation with the progression system.
The RPG mechanics are minimal. I wouldn't even call it an RPG. There's an inventory system apparently but it's only used for quest items, random garbage you can sell, and the seven whole different types of crafting materials. Let me craft consumables that help me somehow. Make it so I die of heat in the desert unless I have water on me. The ability tree is pretty lackluster. You need to spend skill points to buy crafting materials from merchants, and even then it's not worth it. Mounts and outfits are just cosmetic, so the only thing left to spend your gold on is upgrading your weapons, which is stupidly expensive. There's no way you can afford to keep upgrading the same weapon through the entire game unless you spend actual money to buy gold. The rewards you get from chariot races and arena fights are pitiful. Upgrading weapons is pointless anyway (until you hit max level) because you'll just find better loot. Or more likely you'll just find the same weapon, but at whatever level you currently are.
Story wise, I just wanted this game to not be a cliched cringefest and it certainly accomplished that. The ending felt
Totally feels like they ripped out a chunk of the story and are gonna sell it as DLC. Look, what's there is good, but it needs more. Once you beat the game nothing changes. There's nothing new to do. There's no sending dudes on missions, no calling in dudes to help you, and worst of all there's no home base to upgrade to give you a passive income. I guess if they did that there would be no reason for you to spend actual money on gold. The modern day story

Other random thoughts/complaints. Can't use your own weapons in the arena fights, just whatever weapon the game gives you. The 3 baby arena fights you're required to do before every boss feel tacked on to make the arena stuff last longer. Most of the assassination targets are just guys hanging out in a generic enemy outpost. The tools you have and the number of ways you can take on an outpost leaves a lot to be desired. Most locations are just one off things that you'll never return to. The combat is nice and responsive but there's basically no variety in the executions and it wouldn't hurt to at least have some limb chopping or something to make it a little more brutal. Bigger weapons literally shrink in size when you put them away. No interesting traps or actually challenging puzzles in the tombs or pyramids. Bayek has literally 0 reaction when he sees First Civilization stuff. Can't climb the war elephants. War elephants are just one off bosses that you never see in the open world. Phylakes are very cool but are also one off things that don't respawn. The guided missile arrow is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing dumb and over powered but also pretty fun to use. Still no noteriety system. Controls are better and feel nice since you don't have to hold a button to sprint. No crowd blending for stealth kills. No big crowds like in Unity. Projectiles are much better. There are big areas of the desert that have literally nothing. Haven't seen it rain a single time. You can wear nothing but a bathrobe if you want. Only had two or three game breaking bugs in my whole playthrough which were fixed by reloading. The game looks great. The lighting is great.
I could go on forever talking about this game. The bar has been set pretty low since Ezio died, and even lower after Desmond died, so overall I'm happy with the game. It has some real good feeling moments, but it still lacks some of the charm of the old games (the microtransactions and lootboxes certainly don't help). It's a big game but it's mostly just full of generic open world Far Cry -esque trash. I've said a lot of bad things but it's still a fun game and I certainly got my money's worth. Hopefully the next game improves on everything that's here, but when dealing with Ubisoft you have to prepare to be disappointed ;)

To hell with the mixed reviews critics have been giving this game. To hell, I say! I found this reimagination of the classic NES DuckTales game to be a delightful and nostalgic adventure, invoking memories of when I played the game originally as well as memories of watching the cartoon on the Disney Afternoon.
The game was given a complete visual overhaul, with HD levels and backgrounds, fully animated character sprites, and wonderful use of effects and depth. The five original levels return, able to be played in any order! You no longer need to backtrack to other levels to open new areas once you'd found a certain item, which I imagine is to ease the confusion this caused in the original. The boss battles have been completely revamped, making full use of the environment around you. In addition, there is also a brand new final level that tests your mastery of the platforming mechanics.
The music for each level has been remixed, bringing the 8-bit classics up to date and giving them a much more orchestral feel. Another new feature is added storylines and cinematic sequences for each level, complete with full voice acting by most of the original cast of the television series. There's also extras and unlockables, like the in-game art gallery where you can unlock various rewards such as concept art and animation stills.
The developers put a lot of thought into these features, giving the players the option to use them or lose them in order to forge their own DuckTales experience. Don't like the new cinematics? You can skip them in the pause menu. Want to hear the old 8-bit soundtrack? There's an option for that. I think that WayForward has done an excellent job with creatively blending the NES game and the cartoon together. Whether you're a diehard fan of the original or a newbie looking to try it for the first time, DuckTales: Remastered is a much-appreciated remake that is truly worth its weight in gold.

This game is a great idea, but they have several rather serious issues, any one of which makes the game stupid.  As I said, the idea is great, so I'm saddened by the glaring flaws.
First, and probably most importantly, this game is very nearly entirely luck.  Yes, you get to make 2 choices about where you land each turn.  2 choices.  If you use spells, you can decide who to cast them on.  But you don't get to decide what spells you have, or when you get them.  This game would be a bazillion times more fun if they added a speed stat that let you move any number of spaces less than or equal to your speed, instead of rolling the die.  One of my favorite cards is a follower that "curses" you by making you only move 1 space each turn.  It gives me a unique sense of control in the game that I consider a major advantage.
Secondly, there are a lot of ways to (randomly and unexpectedly) lose that don't make any sense.  For example, if you ever, ever get turned into a toad, you've basically lost.  "But you haven't lost, yet."  Sure, sure, I can continue playing for the hour or so the game might continue in hopes of some shocking recovery... but honestly, why make a player randomly turn into a toad?  To my knowledge, there is no option to turn toads off.
Third, the game can last quite a while, and if you die early, the AI will slowly (even at max AI speed) complete each phase of each turn, dragging the game on far longer than any reasonably sane person would care to sit and watch the AI play.
I have fun playing this game, don't get me wrong.  But most of the time, I'm having fun thinking about what the game COULD be, rather than what it really is.  It pains me to have to say this, but I cannot recommend the game.

A neat digital rendition of a Talisman tabletop game. Unlike the "prologue" version, which is oriented towards the single-player experience, this one is primarily multiplayer, local or online.
In case you have never played the tabletop version, this game is somewhat like an RPG Monopoly. Dice-based, with some strategic decision making, but with few of those qualities that most gamers look for.
Not much of a depth to it, but the replay value is quite high. The rules are rather customisable and you may finish a run rather quickly.
The game does have occasional bugs (some spells can't be thrown and there are problems with Steam overlay compatibility in Win 7), but seeing as it was published recently, I expect the flaws to be ironed out rather soon.
While this is not going to be anyone's GOTY (you should get it during a sale or in a bundle), I recommend it for those chillout evenings with your family and friends.

I tried my best, I really did, but I couldn’t find a single thing about this game I liked. If you’re wondering what this game has in store, let me sum it up. A story mode that is mostly randomized levels rather than story and a “challenge mode” that is in no way challenging and takes 30 min. The game feels like it was made for one of those “24 hours to make a game” except this was the dev’s first game and he gave up half way.
Story mode is what I spent the most time playing and I’ll spend the most time talking about it. The story of imagine me is so boring, I got about 70% of the way and just gave up. The bad levels outweighed my interest in the story. From what I can tell it’s about a shy kid who you play as who is often bullied by other kids. I assume something terrible happens in the late story but as I said, the story is just too boring and the levels are just too bad that it discouraged me from finishing the game. The story is told in the stupidest way as well. After every level, you’ll get two or three sentences and that’s about it. There’s no animation, just words scrolling for about 15 seconds which is in no way worth the levels, which I will talk about next. My next point is the level design of story mode. There are two types of levels, boss fight’s, and the normal levels. Between each boss fight, there are what I’m pretty sure are 15 or so levels, which are the same thing over and over again, not to say they play similar, but to say they are literally the same exact level. The best way to describe the level generation is the game has 10x10 preset levels that are mix and matched to create one big level. This means that by the fifth room, you’ll start to say, “haven’t I seen this part of the level before?” and by the 20th, you’ll have a higher chance of having an exact copy of a previous room than not see one of the templates. This leads to the levels becoming boring, stagnant and just the same, but more importantly, the difficulty is non linear as the rooms are random and no new templates are added.  One level might be disgustingly hard, one that might take a few minutes but to the spike hell and complex maze that you got simply by the roll of the dice and the next could be a straight forward line to the finish with only a few, basic obstacles. The boss fights are better than the basic levels in that they aren’t randomized, but that doesn’t mean good. Often, parts of the level are left open with nothing but blank space. Each fight is different, yet easy, and unmemorable. Overall, when it comes to level design, I honestly think the game dev. put zero effort into programing and when it comes to story, he spent an hour writing it and then programed a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game for it and sold it for 3$
My next issue is how the game plays. The controls are comprised of basic wasd movement, and a system of arrows which you can shoot using the arrow keys. My big issue is with these arrows when it comes to playing a level. Arrows can be used for two things in this game, shooting blocks which will break if they have cracks and killing enemies. Arrows can be collected by finding them laying around levels or by killing enemies. My issue is that this may be the most interesting mechanic of the game which speaks volumes in that it’s simply an attack. If a single stagnate attack system which is still terrible, turns out to be the most interesting thing in your game, there’s an issue.
Another huge issue is that it is basically incomplete. The audio of the game is comprised of; jump sound, monster death, occasional sound from boss. These sounds probably took about 5 minutes to produce and record. The sprites are basic and look like they were made in photoshop. Hitboxes are so bad it’s hard to tell how far you need to be to avoid something. Overall most of the game feels incomplete and like no effort was put into it.
The challenge more was probably the best part of the game, but that doesn’t say much. I takes about 30 minutes to complete and is mostly just a smaller, slightly more well designed version of story mode.

Imagine Me lures the player in with a promise of challenging gameplay, interesting graphics and deep story but instead it turns out to be graphically challenged, unfairly hard, unresponsive, boring and overall a very
frustrating experience. No satisfaction. Not at all.

I have a wooden train set sitting around somewhere as a leftover from when I was younger. I forget how I found Tracks, but when I saw it I was surprised such a game even existed and bought it without a second thought. Playing with the infinite amount of track (and very lenient laws of physics) rekindled the nostalgic spark of imagination and wonder I always had when building my own tracks, and actually lets me live one of my childhood dreams of having just that: infinite track and more lenient laws of physics.
The Passengers mode even gave me an excuse to use my imagination a little more freely without feeling silly; they're actual little wooden figures that need to get from point A to point B, not invisible figments like what I'd played with as a child, so if you're concerned about this, don't be, although if you don't care, there's a completely clear environment where you can play to the heart's content of your inner child.
The gentle music in the background and the woodgrain of the tracks, trains, and passengers, as well as the design of the buildings and props, is all very relaxing. I've found myself sitting for [many {many}] hours on end just building, and being perfectly okay with that.
I don't have many complaints with the game, and those I do mostly have to do with the turnout/switching system. My physical set had a few more types of switch tracks than the game has to offer at this point, and when actually playing the role of Conductor actually getting the train to divert to a branch line can be a little unreliable.
Additionally, the tracks won't join properly on rare occasions, especially when using the straight elevation changing sections, which will cause the train to derail and fall through a track that otherwise looks like a perfectly solid section of track.
The game at the time of this post, however, is far from finished, and even in this early state is not only playable, but also enjoyable, so it's easy to look past them and have an idea of the direction in which this game is going. A direction I, and many others, all say is a good one.
If you had or always wanted a wooden train set as a kid (or even a plastic one like one of my old sets) and don't mind the occasional hiccup, then I highly recommend this game. If those hiccups are too discouraging, then add it to your wishlist, wait a month or so, and THEN buy the game. If you have a friend or child that is even moderately into trains, then buy them a copy of this game and they'll love you forever for it. The developers are still making improvements, are very attentive to the community, and are open to suggestions for additions & improvements, which is always a good thing.

Even for early access it's a pretty polished game. The looks work for it, it's simple, but entertaining.
Few skins could take it from wooden to industrial looking (hint hint Devs) if you like trains or if you have kids who like trains it's easy enough for them to play.
All in all its a visually appealing and kind of relaxing game. Looking forward to future updates

(Review made on August 8th, 2017)
(Small revision made about a minute later, whoops)
God- Where do I even start?
The game itself is MASSIVELY REPLAYABLE, no two runs feel quite the exact same (even if you're traversing the same area, there's a bunch of randomly generated missions and structures to keep you entertained)
I frequently run through every nook and cranny of a level, causing as much chaos as possible, or gathering supplies through more subtle means. (By 'subtle,' I obviously mean electrocuting someone then snapping an explosive slave collar to their neck)
Let me just take a moment to describe SOME of the things you can do in this game.
You can hack most electronics, and make them do damn near whatever you please, including making fridges run!
You can cause a zombie apocalypse and feed on the flesh of your enemies to heal your wounds.
You can drug people with practically every status ailment in multiple ways (such as mixing it into a drink) and even chloroform them!
You could also play as a shapeshifter capable of possessing someone, shooting their friend, then running away as a firefight breaks out.
(Not to mention being able to create living suicide bombs forced to do your bidding)
EVERY class is viable in this game, as each one holds at least one unique trait that completely changes their playing style.
Oh, and by the way? All of the NPCs have their own unique behaviors that follow the logic of their classes (albeit with about a third of the health they normally do, in order to keep you from being overpowered by just one of them) so it's all fair grounds for fights! (Other things, too, but I'd rather not spoil everything for you)
Not only all of this, but the developer regularly responds to forums posts and tries to stay in touch with the game's community as much as possible, how awesome is that!?
Honestly? Comparing this game to other Early Access titles, I give it a 9/10, the huge updates are pretty much bi-weekly, and you get a bunch of bugfixes in-between. The only thing that prevents me from giving this a higher rating is the lack of a complete main mode (You can only access 3 areas at the moment) but even then, the dev is currently working on designing a new floor.
I cannot wait to see what this game is like in the future, and heavily recommend you give it a try.

In Assassin's Creed I and II they gave us an open world limited by the technology of their age, and a core group of gameplay mechanics.  In Brotherhood and Revelations they restricted their open world to just one rich, culturally and geographically diverse location, choosing to make it larger and more immersive instead of giving multiple locations.  In Assassin's Creed III they pushed new limits and tested new ideas, like an assassin in the outdoors, hunting, in depth crafting, and naval mechanics.  In Black Flag they took the best of those ideas and crafted them into a massive, seamless open world held together by the sea itself.  In Rogue they gave us a new setting, with a new perspective on a story we never really got to know.  In Unity and Syndicate they again pushed new limits and tested new ideas, bringing back old ideas in a grand experimentation.  In Assassin's Creed: Origins they accomplish what they've been working toward for years; a true, completely immersive, open world experience driven by a rich narrative and held together by the sea of the desert.  There is rich diversity culturally, geographically, and even in the enemies you face, the wildlife you encounter, and the missions you go on.  No more grinding more of the same in a stale universe.  There is wonder in this game.  Even after beating it in a week, putting more hours into this game in seven days than I have into school all semster, there is still more for me to do.  More for me to explore, and I plan on going to find it all, because it is deeply rewarding.
*Side Note: I have not spent any money on the micro-transactions that are offered to the people who want them.  The game is 100% playable and complete without paying for anything extra, and that is a wonderous miracle in itself in this day and age.*

Ducktales Remastered is a remade version of the classic Ducktales video game from 1989. I didn't remember much of anything about the game or the show when playing, so anyone who's afraid that this game is purely nostalgia-driven can worry no longer. As for anyone who has played the original, I'm not sure how much stuff is new/old.
Ducktales Remastered is a classic platformer where your main goals are to make it to the end of a stage as well as collect as much money that appears as you can (you use this to buy art and music). Your moveset consists of pogoing on your cane (which jumps higher, nulls ground hazards, and can be used to attack) and hitting things from the side with your cane. Despite these basic controls, the game does a good job to employ them in the levels.
The game is fairly short, consisting of seven levels. But on my first time, the game took me several hours. The game as a whole looks beautiful. There are plenty of nooks and crannies to scramble around to collect gems, and I think the levels are well-designed overall. Each level even has different items in chests and the like depending of difficulty. The remastered music for each level is beautiful, but you can still listen to the original, 8-bit versions if you want.
Throughout the entire game, there are a bunch of cutscenes. And while the animations are fairly limited in these, they compliment the original voice-actors' voices. It feels like you're playing through an interactive DuckTales episode with each new level you visit. They're definitely charming and I've caught myself rewatching a few in future playthroughs. If you DIDN'T want to watch them again, you can chose to have most of the cutscenes skipped in future playthroughs. Scrooge also says a few lines throughout the game that are also charming albeit a bit annoying after multiple times.
As far as difficulty goes, the entire game seems balanced up until The End. You're given four difficulties: Easy, Medium, Hard and Extreme. Easy gives infinite lives and you take half-hearts in damage while the others have lives and you take full hearts of damage. Extreme has no saves throughout the entire game, so if you Game Over, you have to restart. I recommend starting on Hard if not Easy, since Medium was harder due to little/no life drops.
Now we get to my one huge problem with the game. The game stays at a nice level of difficulty throughout most of the game (some levels have tough bits, some bosses can cause trouble, etc). However, there are two segments after the final boss that I spent nearly two hours on trying to beat alone. First, there's this really tight upwards chase scene where you're likely to screw up a lot. Every time you lose the race, you lose a life. THEN, there's a segment where you need to quickly climb up ropes to avoid rising lava. However, a lot of the rope grabs are nearly-pixel perfect, and one screw-up means fiery death. Every time you Game Over (with 3-4 lives each chance) from those two points, you need to do the whole last level and final boss AGAIN. And with how unfairly difficult they are, you'll be doing it a lot if you're not on Easy. I refuse to play Extreme for this reason alone! If you don't like the idea of Game Over-ing, I highly recommend Easy first (if you want all achievements, you need to play it anyways for those 2 health upgrades), then moving onto Hard when you're used to everything.
Overall, DuckTales Remastered is a solid game that I would recommend at full price. As awful as it is, I won't let The End's unfairness spoil the rest of the game. I'm sure that, Ducktales fan or not, the game's level designs and mechanics will make any platformer fan happy while the music, art, and cutscenes will make it memorable. This was one of the worst boardgames I've played, as it is linear, without any tactical sense or strategy required, and being 95% luck based clearly does not help.
This is coming from a huge boardgame fan - having played quite a huge number of them (Descent, Arkham Horror, War of the Ring, Cosmic Encounter- to name a few).
My Gameplay Session - Played a warrior, not knowing the rules, rolls some dice. Rolls more dice, arrives at the center early because it seems to be the goal- doesn't have to spend a brainwave to think. Realized that I can't get to the middle without an item, attacked an AI and got the Talisman. Arrived middle, then a 30 minute snooze-fest of rolling dice while the enemies heal up and die so very very slowly.
I'm not saying that a good game needs to have some degree of complexity. I've enjoyed simple games like Ticket to Ride or Cleopatra, that at least its not a boring snooze fest. There is no immersion, I don't feel like a warrior, its just a label and gimmick, at the end of the days, Classes are just player modification that does very little to differentiate you from one another- you don't have to be smart about it, you just need to have half a brain and huge amounts of luck to do well in this game.

You play as the angel, Vi, and after screwing up and accidentally set a powerful demon free, it unleashes hell onto heaven and everywhere and you must fix everything back to normal.

If you consider yourself a hardcore gamer, you're obligated to play this. If you can't beat it on at least Mortal before giving up in frustration, your "hardcore" card is officially revoked.
Don't let the angel boobs, gorgeous retro graphics, or lighthearted-yet-awesome soundtrack fool you. This is easily the most difficult game I've ever played, and yet it manages to still be fair while being ridiculously hard. I've seen piles of angry rants about how stupidly unfair this game is and how Solgryn needs to die in a fire or something for being a terrible developer... and yet there are plenty of speedrunners out there who can beat it with double-digit deaths or fewer.
No, this game isn't "cheap" or "unfair". You're just BAD. And you're going to stay bad until you bite the bullet and pick up that controller (trust me, you want a controller) and start grinding away at the cursed castle in the sky until you figure out how to navigate all the flying demons and mounted chompers that seem to exist solely to make your gaming life miserable, then manage to execute the precise series of jumps and flutters that will get you from point A to point B without being devoured.
The first thing you'll notice is that this isn't one of those games that's nice to people who mess up. Sure, you can take a few hits from the enemies (even fewer on Demon mode), but fall into a chomper pit or black hole or even just jump-flutter instead of flutter-jump and you're instantly dead.
(Unless you're playing on Angel mode. You wimp.)
You're probably used to games that only kill you if you do something seriously wrong. This isn't one of those games. Even the simplest of platforming errors will get you sent back to the nearest checkpoint, which become scarcer and scarcer the higher you crank the difficulty. Speaking of checkpoints, they do fully heal you, but only if you aren't tagging the same one you just tagged. No "move forward, kill an enemy, go back to heal, repeat" nonsense here.
If you can survive the dastardly gauntlet of jumps and flutters and flying demons long enough, you'll get to try your hand at one of the several boss battles this game has to offer. Bosses in this game are incredibly well-done. You'll employ the same grinding away until you learn the pattern, then grinding again until you manage to execute the moves you need to execute in order to survive the varied attacks and whittle the bosses' health down... and then you hit the 40% health mark and the boss gets angry and the next attack wrecks you. Back to square one!
Some bosses are more focused on this repetitive grinding to defeat, whereas others are more RNG-based. The RNG ones are probably my least favorite, mainly because the sense of progress you get from learning the grindy bosses' patterns and seeing their health bars get lower and lower with each successive attempt isn't there when your progress on a boss is mainly determined by how long it takes for the boss to hit you with an unavoidable attack pattern... even though you'll quickly find that most unavoidable attack patterns stop being unavoidable as soon as you stop being BAD. Only a few truly unavoidable patterns exist in this game, and they're rare enough that if they do screw you over, you'll get another 10 tries or so at least before they happen again. Hopefully you'll beat the boss by then.
There isn't much of a story, but then again, this isn't exactly the kind of game you play for the story. It's the kind of story where you'll watch the cutscenes the first time through, go "oh, cool", then skip on every playthrough after the first.
The graphics are great. If you're a fan of the 16-bit style, you'll love Wings of Vi, and even if you aren't, you'll probably still be able to admit that its graphical presentation is of pretty good quality.
The soundtrack is done in the same 16-bit style as the graphics, and is equally impressive. You can buy the whole thing on the developer's website if you want, and IMO it's worth the purchase as far as video game OSTs go.
Overall score: 9.5/10

In the end UFT is a good game, but just not good enough. Pay a few [currency] more and buy Trials instead. And buy this in a sale later on.

Ah, I remember playing Ducktales way back on the NES. It was great and I still have fond memories of it. But I wasn't sure a remake would give me the same memories... On the one hand it's pretty much an exact remake of the original, but with improved graphics. On the other hand it' might not translate well enough, and, because of that, might scare gamers off. I'm sorry to say it's the latter.
First, let me talk about the things Ducktales does right.
The graphics haven been upgraded with 2D HD sprites in a 2.5D world. It looks excellent, even if the backgrounds don't fit with the rest of the graphics. I personally think it would've been better if it was entirely in 2D. But that's a different story. The levels are exact replicas of the originals. Epic !
The gameplay is also kept the same. It's tough. But not too tough. Back when I was a kid it literally took me hours to complete a level. Maybe it was because I was too young and didn't fully understand games just yet, maybe because games were really more difficult back then. Ducktales Remastered tested my patience when I had only just started it. I was rushing through levels carelessly and I died several times in a matter of minutes. This is a good thing, mind you. It makes the game feel old school, in a certain way.
But despite the game being somewhat difficult it's also very short. Levels can be finished within 30-60 minutes and since there are only 6 levels in total you should complete it in about 5 or 6 hours max.
Then the controls. The controls are pretty good, but jumping on your pogo stick doesn't seem to work all the time. Plenty of times have I tried jumping down, followed by a pogo stick jump and the game just didn't register the button being pressed. It cost me more health than intended.
Oh, and the voice acting... Man, the voice acting. The voice acting was cringeworthy. I understand it's based on the cartoon, but the dialogues in general were just terrible and childish. Same goes for the rest of the cutscenes. I skipped through them at one point because I couldn't take it anymore. Next time, no more voice acting please. Just a textbox would suffice.
And maybe it's my memory, but I remember secrets being secrets in the original. Secrets in the remake are pointed out in obvious ways. All that's missing is a big arrow pointing to it. Like I said, it might just be my memory but I remember this differently.
If I had to rate this game right now I'd give it a 6,5, or 7 at best.
Ducktales is a decent game and still kinda fun to play, even now and especially if you have never played the original. But wait for a sale instead, because the current price is once again too high. Also, I think the Castle Of Illusion remake might be better in comparison. Let's just wait for that.

Talisman may not be the most complicated game around or hold a candle to the newer deck-builders or RPGs, but it holds a lot of nostalgia for me from my middle and high school days.  I thought a few bucks on a Steam game versus a much larger amount thrown at a random eBayer was wise, but unfortunately the game falls short.
It's buggy, especially in online play.  Two games were all it took to decide this is best played as a local match.  Freezes, CTDs, and the inability to drop in on an existing game really killed the experience.
Playing against CPUs is no fun, either.  The rolls always seem to go in their favor.  Don't believe me?  I finally had a good match and got to the Crown of Command, but it took over twenty turns to win because I rolled a 3 or lower about 75% of the time.  A game I would have won swiftly in real life turned into a Sorceress almost making her way to the Valley of Fire all the way from the Outer Region.
If you're nostalgic for the game and don't mind the extra cash, you'll be a lot happier with the game in hand.  This isn't a cheap alternative, in my opinion, because you're best off inviting your friends over to play anyway.

This game is an mediocre at best timekiller with friends, but not much more than that. It really tries, bless its little heart, but overall the experience doesn't really justify the price tag.
STORY:
I think there's some semblence of story here, but its the same done before stuff you've seen in any game or movie or TV show etc. Not really bringing out anything new or interesting here. In addition to that mediocrity, many of the games important scenes can either be skipped entirely accidentally or even cut altogether due to how buggy this game can get. Multiplayer games bring out very strange interactions with many of the games core mechanics and can cause random deaths and story skips, really dampening the experience.
GAMEPLAY:
At first I was enjoying the limited controls and strange aiming patterns. I thought it was actually kind of interesting and refreshing. That being said, go back and play Magicite by this same developer. Notice anything similar? That's right! It's a copy paste of what made THAT game interesting. In addition, often times during this game, enemy hitboxes will not register hits, you will get hit by phantom damage that comes from nowhere, and there is no good tutorial. The game becomes trivial after a certain point up until the unfair and simply boring late game, where you are grinding for even the tiniest stat bonus or armor pieces in order to beat bosses that don't match how annoying it is to move your character. The controls are bad and make you feel like you did something wrong even when it was really just the character on the screen reacting to button prompts in time. Overall very disappointed in the lack of interesting things to do in this game.
PROMISES:
Any game that is funded on KickStarter will have some hiccups and maybe even some cut content at some point. However, in Roguelands case, most of what made the game originally interesting was cut for this strange RPG grinding simulator. Early build trailers show off a more robust crafting and XP system than the ones shown in the final build, and much more closely resembled Magicite (in a good way). More open world esque elements were shown off, like building a home or getting food. The ship in the final game is a shallow husk of those promises, and offers almost nothing intersting in the way of customization or gameplay changes. The space theme feels thrown together to justify why the hub area is so small and contains almost nothing of substance, and why you can just jump out of your ship and have nothing going on outside of it besides a moving background.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game even if it has a steep discount. Some masochistic RPG players may find some fun in the silly level of challenge (if you can even call it that) this game offers, but for most this is not worth your money or time.

This game is fun for a bit, to boot up and mess around with here and there. The pixel graphics and music are enjoyable, and the upgrade system (more health, stamina, speed, bleed damage, etc...) adds some variety to the gameplay. The game is a bit simplistic (which I don't mind) but the reason I don't recommend it is the limited mouse controls are annoyingly / unreliably implemented. Gameplay consists of you clicking / holding LMB to move your character around the screen toward the cursor as you dodge enemies while they constantly swarm you, with RMB being your attack / dash move (with the default character) to dispatch them or create some space between you. This is all well and good but there are often moments when your character will just not perform his RMB dash attack to evade the enemies. He just stands there with his♥♥♥♥♥♥in his hand and gets hit (or worse killed) by the enemies. This is caused because you have to fully release LMB, click RMB briefly to dash/attack then click / hold LMB again to begin moving once again. Due to the resolution and way you move your character by having him move toward the cursor, it feels like you have very little room to move once the enemies begin to fill the screen or will often accidentally dash slightly too far into an enemy and die. The holding of LMB to releasing to briefly press RMB rather than being able to just press RMB while holding LMB kills a lot of the fluidity of the game and feels inaccurate and unreliable. The game's title alludes to this being intrinsic to the gameplay, that you have to "Slash or Die" to make space to move around, but when the Slashing is so inconsistent your deaths are often frustrating. I suppose I could play more to "git gud" and learn its rhythms/hitboxes more, but I've found it to mostly just be a frustrating, idle distraction of a game with a poor interface.

I wanted to give this a thumbs-up after only a few hours of playing, but figured I'd wait until I finished it before doing one. Little did I know this would take a little longer than I thought, clocking in today at 4,038 deaths and just over 36 hours for my first playthrough on Mortal (normal) difficulty.
Keep in mind that Wings of Vi is straight-up difficult and challenging all the way through, getting progressively harder and harder. If you're looking for something you can breeze through effortlessly on your first try in a few hours or so, you might need to prepare yourself for something a bit different. It's very rewarding if you stick with it, and getting that one step closer towards progressing through a level or almost killing a boss feels very rewarding.
Wings of Vi is pretty awesome in all aspects. The controls feel responsive with various mechanics being introduced to the player as they progress, often teaching the player to make use of these properly before throwing them into the deep end. The gameplay never becomes stale or uninteresting, level designs are each unique and challenging in different ways and you get a great sense of satisfaction when you finally down a boss or get past that one room that you've been stuck on for a while. The art is pretty impressive too with some crazy good boss designs, and the music and sound effects blend in with the world and mechanics really nicely, with the Terrestrial Vale BGM probably claiming my favourite music track in the game alongside a couple of the boss themes.
If you're a fan of platformers or generally really challenging games, give this a shot without hestitation. If you're not a fan of either of this, still give it a shot because it's just really damn good.

The story with this game is practically infamous by now. So I won't waste time explaining its mediocre launch and Ubi's strive to fix the game or the fact that this game went from being a total letdown to a total success. Instead, I'll mention the one thing it does best - evoke tension in its players.
Not many feelings in modern multiplayer gaming quite match the heartpounding intensity that you'll experience in Siege. While it will never be the Rainbow 6: Patriots that we were teased with years ago, Siege has taken the tension soaked combat of its predecessors and amplified 10x by placing you in claustrophobic maps with five other thinking (most of the time), conscious players that are hunting you down, or vice versa.
One other element that makes Siege so addicting is the way in encourages creativity. Just about 60ish% of the map is destrucable, meaning you can approach the objective in multiple different ways. In a word, it makes every match unpredictable. Will Fuze launch explosive hockey pucks through the window near bomb or rain pucks from above through the wooden ceiling? Should I bust out some wall space with a shotty to give myself a peak hole or reinforce it in order to keep the enemy from firing in from that angle all together? Or is Sledge just going to Kool-aid man his way straight to the hostage and vault out to secure like a god damn olympic gold medalist with knack for gas masks? Anything can happen in a game of Siege, and it's intense as♥♥♥♥♥♥
One thing the game still suffers from is a maddeningly confusing marketplace. Although you can't purchase anything to improve your gameplay and it is by no means pay-2-win, it still baffels me how some things cost way more than others. Like, a cool♥♥♥♥♥skin I want for my primary costs just as much as a WHOLE NEW OPPERATOR ENTIRELY. So either purchase a new character who has new weapons, new abilities, new play style, or a skin that makes my gun look like it shoots plastic darts. Gee, tough call. Also the struggle to get 25000 renown to unlock one of the new operators without paying money is Destiny levels of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, except Destiny at least feels phenominal to play while Siege, by no means bad, still has a few issues to smoothen out with its gameplay. If vaulting and sprinting felt just a bit less clunky, I'd have no complaints.
Overall, I'd say this game is a must buy if you enjoy enthralling multiplayer tactics with a dose destructable environments and dank♥♥♥♥♥memes. The $15 starter edition is a safe choice, but I recommend getting the full version if you can and want to.

Imagine Me is agitated by its own existence. It can’t decide where to commit, patching on modes of play like a bad worker trying to explain their way out of a botched job by showing you all the little, trivial tasks they’ve completed instead. Right out of the gate Imagine Me tries its hand at procedurally generated level designs (it can’t be that hard, right? Everyone’s doing it). But once the algorithms start rolling and the levels actually come into existence, it’s immediately clear Imagine Me hasn’t the slightest clue what it’s doing.
Chunks of familiar levels become hastily adjoined to one another into an unplayable mess of broken hitboxes and impenetrable block mazes. It’s chaos of the highest degree, silent caverns filled only with the cries of my broken soul as I beat myself against a metaphorical wall trying to beat a game which is quite literally impossible to complete. Somewhere along the development pipeline it must have been clear that something had gone horrible wrong, but rather than rework the disastrous level generator into something functional, Imagine Me instead decides to abandon it altogether and starts building levels by hand (it worked for Mario, didn’t it?).
But much to my dismay Imagine Me hasn’t much of a knack for level designs, random or otherwise. At numerous points it almost appears as if whoever actually designed these levels fell asleep and never completed them, or otherwise became so bored with their own creation that they decided enough was enough and shipped whatever they had in front of them at the time. And thus we are left with 30 or so astoundingly dull and simplistic levels which play very much like the afterthought they were.
I might feel worse about the depths of Imagine Me’s failure if it didn’t seem so apathetic toward aspiring to even moderate quality (or functionality). Everything feels empty and tedious, leading you in circles until either the game breaks or you stop playing. Imagine Me is sloppy and dysfunctional, but I couldn’t say it seems to actually care.

Talisman may not be the most complicated game around or hold a candle to the newer deck-builders or RPGs, but it holds a lot of nostalgia for me from my middle and high school days.  I thought a few bucks on a Steam game versus a much larger amount thrown at a random eBayer was wise, but unfortunately the game falls short.
It's buggy, especially in online play.  Two games were all it took to decide this is best played as a local match.  Freezes, CTDs, and the inability to drop in on an existing game really killed the experience.
Playing against CPUs is no fun, either.  The rolls always seem to go in their favor.  Don't believe me?  I finally had a good match and got to the Crown of Command, but it took over twenty turns to win because I rolled a 3 or lower about 75% of the time.  A game I would have won swiftly in real life turned into a Sorceress almost making her way to the Valley of Fire all the way from the Outer Region.
If you're nostalgic for the game and don't mind the extra cash, you'll be a lot happier with the game in hand.  This isn't a cheap alternative, in my opinion, because you're best off inviting your friends over to play anyway.

I really wish that I could recommend this game. The first 5-20~ hours are fun, but then it basically just devolves into grinding. The crafting system is great, it has very satisfying and "cool" combat, you actually feel like you are getting more powerful as time goes on, but once you progress past the harder worlds, it just becomes repetitive. First of all, Ultimate Weapons. These are weapons, or armour, that either have very good stats, or a special trait, like it shooting an extra projectile or something. This seems like a great idea, but to do this, you need a "level 10" weapon. The only way to get this weapon is to basically clear a stage over, and over again. Even the later stages don't increase xp drops much. There are probably almost 1 hundred ultimate weapons and armour, but in a normal playthrough, you probably will only experience one of them.
Secondly, the enemies seem pretty repetitive. Some enemies seem like they were ripped strait off of Magicite, his previous game, while others just aren't fun. A diffucult enemy in this game means that it does a lot a damage, and has a lot of health. Not that its attacks are diffucult, or that it actually takes skill to defeat. And again, the enemies are really repetitive. All of the enemies in this game boil down to it has a melee attack, or it has a ranged attack, occasionally having a combination of both. Fighting numerous amounts of these each level can be quite tedius.
Lastly, health stats are very diffuclt to come by. In this game, you can choose a build for stats when you level up. If you choose, for example, tech and melee, when you level up you will get one point in both stats. This means that if you don't choose health as one of those stats, your health bar barely increases at all. by level 40, you might only have 20 health, when you are fighting enemies that deal 15 damage. This really restricts the type of builds you can succeed in, severely limiting your options for sucessful builds.
Again, I really would love to give this game a upvote, but this really isn't a great concept to begin with, not to mention having somewhat bad execution by the developer.

With the core premise of shooting around bisecting Ghosts n' Goblins monsters, you'd think it'd be hard to make a mediocre game.
You'd be wrong.
First of all, enjoy reminding the game of your preferred language between English and Russian, as it won't remember what you told it last time. Then, Slash or Die continues to demonstrate its high-school level programming with the global tactic of "Enemies just come at you", providing a ludicrously un-fun startup phase of you being too slow to avoid many attacks and needing to pause after every dash, which has a finite but unclear length and doesn't appear possible to lengthen. As early as the third level, enemies which are killed or kill you purely by RNG are introduced, as there's an arbitrary miss chance on ghosts, which deal contact damage. The first boss seems more complex, but also has completely broken hitboxes.
All of this is scored by an obnoxiously loud, uncustomizable soundtrack you can only change the volume of in rapidly flying amounts, not that the sound is the only component lacking options, as your hero upgrades are all just "more damage" when you oneshot everything but the boss after taking your first level in damage.
But my biggest problem with the game, and the thing which enables me to write it off even at my early stage of gameplay, is the fact that you can't attack while moving. You must stop, stand still, and press the attack button, or have your attack erased by your movement, leaving a nice juicy opening for whiff, tank, or RNG miss punishes on you. To my knowledge, you don't regain health, either, so you get to savor that for your entire run each game. It doesn't help that there's no indication of exhaustion until AFTER you try to attack with no stamina.
There are implications of other characters, but if the content gets better later, why make it suck up front? I don't owe anyone a tithe of my patience; make the game good, then make it get better. Nobody should have to unlock the game not sucking.
UPDATE: I've unlocked the first additional class, and tried Survival to find that it uses another.
Both suck. The Barbarian seems to go a set distance in the direction you click, then deliver an AoE attack at his destination, which would be fine were it not for the aforementioned miss chance on the ghost enemies and complete lack of precision for positioning. Survival uses the Samurai, which is just the starting class with no ability to level up and more RNG effects, making Survival pointless. Individual characters must gain their OWN souls (which don't come at an acceptable rate), meaning every new character starts the game over. If the developers were selling souls, I'd accuse them of gouging for them.
The audio implementaion is also bad, as a song will fade out, then just start over.

While I haven't beaten the game, I'm very close to the end, judging by the wiki and various other articles on the internet.
Wings of Vi has been described as a tough-as-nails, pixel perfect precision platformer. That's a pretty good description but there's quite a bit of combat, too. At first, you'll only be able to use a melee attack that has short range, but a wide attack radius. It's pretty easy to use and works well. Eventually you'll acquire a ranged attack as well. It uses the same button as the melee attack. The melee attack will activate automatically if there is an enemy in range, otherwise, you'll fire your ranged attack. At first I was skeptical of how well this would work, but it actually works very well, so I applaud the dev for doing a good job on this. The combat is relatively straightforward, you just need to hit things until they die, and not get hit yourself. Running into enemies hurts you, as usual. Obviously, combat can sometimes get more complicated when you fight bosses, but it never gets over-the-top convoluted. Speaking of the bosses, they're very unique. All of them are very different from each other and fun to fight (usually). Additionally, the intro to the boss is automatically skipped when you re-fight it, so you don't have to watch the same intro over and over again when you die over and over again. Another thing the dev did right is balancing hazards from enemies and the environment. In many games, such as the Mega Man games, the environment will often pose a much more serious threat to the player than enemies. Thankfully, they're balanced in Wings of Vi, so enemies are never a joke.
Another thing I liked in Wings of Vi was the amount of secrets to find. If you go out of your way to explore every nook and cranny, you can find treasure chests that contain items that you can use to customize Vi, the angel you play as. Most of the items seemed pretty distasteful to me, such as turning Vi's head into a giant eyeball or giving her a bony tail, but there were a few that seemed nice. The items don't actually change the way Vi controls; they're purely cosmetic alterations.
The music is nice as well. I particularly like the Amethyst and Dark Annihilator tracks. All of the tracks are at the very least decent, and the music is a real treat.
Unfortunately, that's where the good things end.
Pixel perfect is no exaggeration in some parts. Don't get me wrong, I love hard games. I've beaten Spelunky the special, extra hard way at least 7 times, gotten golden god on Super Meat Boy, beaten Super Ghouls n Ghosts... the list goes on. But Wings of Vi, without a doubt, is the hardest game I've ever played; sometimes for the wrong reasons.
As said before, there's the pixel-perfect precision. The timing required for some jumps is ridiculous, and you may die hundreds of times just trying to clear one jump. There's only so many times I can smash my face against a brick wall before it stops being fun. Dedication is one thing but actually enjoying this is another.
"But you can change the difficulty to an easier mode if you're having a hard time!"
This would be a valid argument, except there are still parts that require pixel perfect precision, even on easy mode. Easy mode makes checkpoints more frequent, and makes bosses have less health and attacks,  and adds platforms to some areas that require precise midair navigation. This is very appreciated, but it doesn't alleviate all of the issues, and some parts still require ridiculous precision.
This problem is compounded by the fact that the hit detection is wonky. If you're going to make a game that heavily relies on precision, then having wonky hit detection is an absolute no-no. One part requires you to wait until the absolute last moment to execute a jump over a hazard; too late and you'll touch spikes, too early and you'll  collide with an overhang. The thing is, Vi would sometimes be killed even if her sprite did not intersect the spikes' sprite. It would be very clear that she wouldn't be touching the sprites, because Vi freezes when she dies. Several parts requires you to do a mid-air dash past a one-hit-kill hazard. Quite often, Vi would dash past it, only to teleport backwards and have her death animation play over the hazard.  On one occasion I actually fell THROUGH a hazard and off the map. It's completely unacceptable.
Another problem with the platforming is that sometimes, the game doesn't respond to button input. This seems to be particularly bad with the action button; a button used for sliding, dashing, and fluttering. Probably about 1 out of 20 times I would try to do something like dash multiple times in a row it would flutter instead, or when I tried to flutter after dashing, it simply wouldn't do anything at all.
This is a little bit of a nitpick, but I found it to be annoying. One hazard will cause Vi's death animation to play directly over it; it's a sort of mouth in the ground that eats Vi. The thing is, if it's located at the edge of a platform, and you brush the side of the platform, you'll teleport on top of the mouth thing and die. Obviously this makes no sense, and should be changed.
Another thing I didn't like is the art style. Too many indie games adopt a pixel-art style. I don't have a huge problem with it, but I would prefer game developers to just add their art in normally. Better yet, add the option to use filters in the game.
Despite the fact that the game is a 2D platformer with a pixel-art style, this game has performance issues. My PC isn't the best, it's just a FX8320 and a 260X, but it's at least decent, and should be more than enough to handle a game like this. But it isn't. The frame rate drops to as low as 15 FPS frequently in later areas. You shouldn't need an elite PC to play an indie game with a pixel-art style. The poor optimization is completely unacceptable. The developer did try to fix the frame rate issues- by breaking one of the big areas into several parts. But it still lags badly. Again, completely unacceptable.
I think I've mentioned everything. At it's core, it's not a bad game. It doesn't require any major revamp, it just needs some polish. If the hit detection, button input, and optimization were fixed, I would definitely recommend this game. As it is now, though, I can't recommend it. Until further updates are released, I'd recommend you stay away.

There are plenty of cheap, retro styled, action oriented games in Steam. And you're probably wondering (like I was) whether this game falls into the "Devil Daggers" category or in the "Cash grab, better to avoid" category. In my opinion it falls firmly into the first category. It's a decent coffee break type of game that is best enjoyed in short bursts.
The basic idea is that you survive wave after wave of increasingly difficult enemies and you have to defeat a boss at the end of every level (there are three levels in total). You move around by keeping the left mouse button pressed and moving the cursor around. Your character will then follow the cursor. By letting go of the left mouse button and pressing the right mouse button you'll do a dash attack in the direction of the cursor that will hurt any enemy you come into contact with. Some enemies can be killed with just one hit, others require two hits and some enemies have a 50% chance of blocking or evading your attack.
The game tends to make a bad first impression, because your character starts out pretty weak and you might feel overwhelmed by the number of enemies on screen. Please do not let yourself be discouraged by this. Every time you kill an enemy you'll pick up their soul (in the shape of a glowing orb) and all the souls you have collected when you die, can be used as currency to upgrade your character. You can upgrade the walking speed, number of lives, power of your attack and the number of dashes you can make before having to wait until your stamina has filled up again. This makes a huge difference in how you play the game. After you beat the first boss, you'll unlock a second character, which plays slightly different. And after beating the first two bosses you'll unlock the third character who has a different skill set as well. There is also a survival mode where you'll play as the samurai who also has a unique fighting style.
I compared this game to Devil Daggers for a good reason, because this game requires a similar skill set. It's not about clicking as fast as you can. It's about situational awareness and setting yourself up so you can slash as many enemies as you can before being exhausted. And you also have to dodge enemy attacks, projectiles and prioritize which enemies to attack first. It really is one of those 'easy to learn, difficult to master' type of games. If you think ahead and react quickly you can reach the first boss in a few minutes. Make a few mistakes too many and you'll die again and again.
In conclusion: if you enjoy action oriented games like Devil Daggers, then give Slash or Die a chance. It's a nice diversity to play during a short break, but don't be surprised if you suddenly realize it's three in the morning and you should really, really go to bed. It can get addictive.

A difficult action platformer which has great boss design and simple controls.  You get to play as a cute, sexy angel on a mission to kill an evil demon, save the world, and collect all of the pieces you need to make the perfect outfit.  There is a system to save, name, and load outfits you make from different pieces, and you collect pieces by beating bosses, beating bosses without getting hit, and finding chests which are usually hidden and/or hard to get to.  The difficulty curve keeps me feeling accomplished whenever I make it to a checkpoint or beat a new boss.  Vi will also amuse people who like references whenever you find a chest with a sectet.  There are leaderboards for speedrunners and people who like to compete for the best score, but if you just want to play for fun you aren't pressured to be competitive.  The OST and aesthetic are also pretty nice.
The issues I have are pretty minor.  The bigger problem is a bug which sometimes allows the player to fall out of the world.  It doesn't happen very frequently and can be "fixed" by pressing the respawn key, but it is kinda annoying.  I also don't see much reason to switch from the default weapon in most cases.  Lust is good before you can shoot the orbs of purity, but everything but the default weapon feels weak or awkward after that.  And my most minor complaint is that I would really like to Have Fiola's dress.  I always liked how a blue dress looks with black cat ears.
Overall, I would say this game is worth your time if you enjoy challenging platformers, interesting boss fights, and unlocking items to play dressup with the character you control.

Let me preface by saying that Tracks the Game is in Early Access, there are things that may or may not be changed until it's finalized in the official release.
Tracks the game is based on the wooden train sets like Brio and Thomas the Tank Engine toys. Building a rail networks, getting passengers is the name of the game. The game includes three modes; Free-Play, Passengers, and Frieght. Because it is in early access, I can see that there is a high ceiling of potential when it comes to creativity surrounding the community. I'll talk about that later on.
Free Play is the sandbox mode of the game, using unlimited resources, you can build a rail network that can be as big or small as you wish. While there is no objective, free play allows players to let their minds loose in designing their track layout.
Passengers is a small game mode at the moment where the player has to build a station platform near some passengers and build a track to get them to the station. It is a simple game, but it allows open-ended solutions to the 5-or-so missions it provides.
Personally, getting the train at full speed to stop at the platforms and stations perfectly has been a personal challenge for me.
At the moment, Frieght is an unrelease game mode that has yet to be implemented. Other than knowing it as the third gamemode, I cannot delve further into it.
The music of the game ressonates the inner kind in myself, building layouts in the small kids' room of the house all day. I think it would be better if there were more songs added to the list so that there is a little more variety. Otherwise, I would have it off for an ambient effect.
The sounds for the train rolling full-speed across the tracks is very satifying. I would hope the developers add some hollow wooden clinking noises betweem the passengers, to placing objects, to the cars pushing against each other to really
the wood asthetic.
Tracks-The Game features two rooms to choose from and build in.
The first room is a pink-ish/beige-ish, featureless room (akin to Garry's Mod's "gm_flatgrass." It is an open cube that allows the player to freely build layouts without any restrictions apart from the room boundaries (which in itself is well more than plentiful).
The second room called "Modern Apartment." You can infer that this room resembles modern apartment that features furnishings, tables, chairs, TVs, pitcures, counters, shelves, flooring, and pretty much anything you would find in an apartment. This room restricts some track layout, but forces the player to get creative when building their layout in free play and Passenger Mode
I mentioned earlier that the game could benefit from a community-driven Steam Workshop if we were to take a page from Garry's Mod. Not only would some creative aspects be handled by the community, it would allow the developers to focus on other parts of the game. Maybe some of the more popular addons could be implemented as official releases by the Dev. team.
People would be able to submit rooms, layouts, track pieces, trains, traincars, scenery, and themes that could spice-up an otherwise, normal wooden set.

In Assassin's Creed I and II they gave us an open world limited by the technology of their age, and a core group of gameplay mechanics.  In Brotherhood and Revelations they restricted their open world to just one rich, culturally and geographically diverse location, choosing to make it larger and more immersive instead of giving multiple locations.  In Assassin's Creed III they pushed new limits and tested new ideas, like an assassin in the outdoors, hunting, in depth crafting, and naval mechanics.  In Black Flag they took the best of those ideas and crafted them into a massive, seamless open world held together by the sea itself.  In Rogue they gave us a new setting, with a new perspective on a story we never really got to know.  In Unity and Syndicate they again pushed new limits and tested new ideas, bringing back old ideas in a grand experimentation.  In Assassin's Creed: Origins they accomplish what they've been working toward for years; a true, completely immersive, open world experience driven by a rich narrative and held together by the sea of the desert.  There is rich diversity culturally, geographically, and even in the enemies you face, the wildlife you encounter, and the missions you go on.  No more grinding more of the same in a stale universe.  There is wonder in this game.  Even after beating it in a week, putting more hours into this game in seven days than I have into school all semster, there is still more for me to do.  More for me to explore, and I plan on going to find it all, because it is deeply rewarding.
*Side Note: I have not spent any money on the micro-transactions that are offered to the people who want them.  The game is 100% playable and complete without paying for anything extra, and that is a wonderous miracle in itself in this day and age.*

I want to like this game, and I'm trying. I had the boardgame version of Talisman and several of its expansions years ago, and played it a lot. The biggest problem I've encountered with this version is the usability. Spell casting, for example, is kind of dreadful. Several times I have tried to cast spells--even after learning the system of queueing spells--and had them not cast; I have accidentally cast spells when I simply wanted to read the text to see what they do, wasting them; and I have tried casting spells at the times that are indicated in the text, only to find out, nope, that was not the right time to cast it.
Important information text from the game is ill placed at the top of the screen in a box that is not prominent and doesn't stand out.
There are an awful lot of confirmation clicks as well--too many in some cases. Also, sometimes the confirmation text is not the best. For example, when you're learning the game and you view your followers, the "Dismiss" option can leave you wondering, Wait, will that dismiss my follower? Dismiss is a term in gaming that, in my experience, has always been used to get rid of followers. A better term for getting rid of message windows is simply "Close."
I hope there are improvements to the game design. I find myself more often frustrated than having fun when I play it currently.

I like what the game tries to do, but actual execution is poor.
A couple of things:
1: A lot of the game is cruel. Progress to a certain point, only to be knocked all the way back. I won't go into too many details so as to not ruin anyone's first playthrough, but the game unnecessarily takes longer than it should.
2: Buggy! We encountered the following bugs in the original & frostmarch expansion:
Bug 1: Player is unable to finish their turn because they can't perform an action, i.e. discarding a card.
Bug 2: If you quit the game (such as to clear out the error in Bug 1) and then rehost, the AI encounters a bug where it will not perform its turn until the timer completely winds down. The only way to prevent this from completely ruining your game is setting the timeout for each player's turn at 30 seconds, then at least you only wait 30 seconds.
Bug 3: Finishing quests. There are some items that are INCREDIBLY picky as to the order you complete them, so much so that it won't always be apparent. i.e. if you pick up the false grail, you are required to visit the Castle to discard it. However, you can only discard it during a certain action while visiting the castle. It's easier to see in action than it is to explain, but let's chalk up to poor game mechanics.
3: Sometimes awfully boring, depending on what class you pick. A lot of these classes (i.e. the ones that don't draw spells) are highly dependent on landing on tiles that have associated actions that they can complete. Unfortunately, this isn't always the case. This game seems to highly favor the spellcasters, because the spells allow you to overcome or encounter things that being a melee-focused character would not. This is unfortunate.
Overall, would not recommend. Played through it twice, and we all found each session very obnoxious at a certain point. It was always one of the three items above, though.
