This game is a job simulator in a wasted city full of crime and murder.
Except that you are not only a barkeeper/policeman/drug dealer/shopkeeper/investment banker/comedian etc., but also a spy for a government opposing rebel faction that kinda has no idea what they're doing.
So while making your way through the devastated distopia of the games city world you also need to fulfill crucial mission objective orders straight from your rebel HQ. The fun thing about that is that there's literally millions of ways of doing that, and depending on what job you're educated in there's even more ways with every playthrough.
For example: HQ orders to get a harddrive from the shopkeeper in town. Now, you could kill the shopkeeper and take it, or you could just threaten him to do just that if he doesn't give it to you right now, or you could give him a very valuable item in exchange. But if you are a shopkeeper yourself you can just buy it from him, if you are a thief you can steal it from him, if you are a slavemaster you can enslave him and make him give it to you, and this whole variability makes the game incredibly fun and long-living.
Other than the missions which are well planned in theory and well executed in practice, the game is all about the player being able to do whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they want. I especially like freeing gorillas from science labs while there's still scientists in there with them. Welp.

I got this as part of the tinyBuild Bundle, that being said if I had been able to play even a demo of world 1-1 I would've been okay with paying full price. This game is the perfect balance of the stealth, run and gun, party, and roguelite genres.
TLDR;
Streets of Rouge is my go to for couch co-op, especially since it makes cooperation completely voluntary. The story is silly, the humor is funny/broad enough for most parties; however, the gameplay is the selling point. A vast amount of approachs for any playstyle out there. All in all this is a lovely arcadesque couch co-op.
PROS:
+Insanely fun co-op
+Satifying sound design
+Diverse styles of approach to combat, developed further by traits
+Co-op goes from shared-screen to split screen fluidly
+4 player co-op, hybridizing online and offline
+Entertaining AI
+Dialogue lines are funny
+Progression system is pretty fun
+All characters have diverse play styles and seem to cover all the bases of said play styles for rouge-likes/rouge-lites
+Diverse weapons and Buffs continue to diversify approaches
+Dev that responds to feedback within minutes (litterally)
NEUTRAL:
+/-Game uses 'random' humor at times(I like it but SO did not)
+/-Music is good, but not memorable
+/-Mutators are both really good and really annoying, depending on which you get
+/-Lack of content at the moment (the game is updated every week though, consistently too)
+/-RNG hurts sometimes, but that's the way the news goes
CONS:
-All Partners are effected by the actions of a single player (cops stay aggro at all players if a crime is witnessed)
-Quests can be failed due to RNG
I highly suggest this game with at least one friend especially if you enjoy local co-op games

Wings of Vi is a very brutal experience, you'll likely find that the difficulty ramps up faster than you can learn the game, meaning you'll have to crank out repetitive grinding to overcome some areas, boss fights especially are showstoppers, as they're both tanky and spammy, so you'll need to dissect their patterns to nigh perfection if you want to progress. However Wings of Vi never pulls cheap shots, everything is approriately telegraphed so the amount of foresight required to beat obstacles is sparce, however if it's a laid back sunday platformer you're looking for, I'd look elsewhere.
Note that the game does have difficulty settings: "easy" is a lot more gratious, but by no means any kind of autowin, Grynsoft has voiced an interest in trying to soften the experience on "easy" difficulty to accomodate a broader audience though, I'll update this review if any significant progress happens on that front.
The platforming elements of Wings of Vi are heavily vested in both precision, timing as well as resource management: Using the right actions, at the right spots and in the right amount. You'll mainly be working with two mechanics: Jumping and fluttering. Jumping is a familiar friend and it works as you'd expect, with the exception that a lot of obstacles will require you to drop off the edge and then jump to manuveur below a platforming section, midair jumps of this sort count towards the same charge as a ground jump does, so learning the distinction of when to use one or the other becomes a vital choice. The flutter works as a sort of midair glide with a slight amount of lift, which you'll want to use when you want a greater amount of horizontal (rather than vertical) traverse.
While the platforming elements are mainly static, the combat feels somewhat more dynamic and RNG-based, where you have to learn the behaviour and patterns of enemies and react to them rather than use memorization. The boss fights have some RNG too, where which pattern (and subpattern) the boss cycles to is randomized, but the patterns themselves can be dissected and memorized in full, the boss fights are extremely engaging and fun, with a weighty feel of tension to them as you slowly and surely wear them down after having practiced the ordeal religiously.
The controls are extremely tight, midair control has a nice sweave to it, the flutter works as a counterstop, falling speed is light and feather-like, though the resource management part of the controls may feel unintuitive at first.
The game has a very pleasant and vibrant aesthetic with sleek-lined and fluid spritework, the music has delightful chiptunes and groovy waltz, sometimes with a bit of an apocalyptic intermix, the sound work is meaty and gritty to accomodate the demonic side to the story and the dialogue is witty and charming.
Wings of Vi is a well-realized platformer, with tight controls, difficult but imaginative platforming and a pleasing style, it's a grand adventure through a variety of themes, a little quirky and self-ironic and shouldn't be missed by any platforming fan looking for a challenge, highly recommended.

Crazy hard platformer that's really rewarding. You start out with nothing but a wimpy attack and a single jump that can be executed at any time, on the ground or falling. You then gain more abilities as you progress through the game, and instead of getting easier as a result, the dev's use this to add continually harder sections. It has a very megaman feel in both difficulty and how it controls. Like megaman you're quite heavy and this took some getting used to as I generally play games like They Bleed Pixels which is very floaty. Some of the boss fights also have a cadance much like megaman boss fights, both in their timing and in memorizing their abilities. Unlike megaman though the bosses in Vi use their attacks randomly making each attempt different enough that you can't memorize the pattern of their attacks.
They also let you customize your appearance, which I'm a total sucker for. These are unlocked throughout the game either through story events or finding secret chests.
Dying is pretty painless aside from a solidly difficult checkpoint system. It doesn't respawn you automatically, but you can respawn at will with the press of a button. So while you have to quickly tap the button every time you die, there's no waiting around for death or respawn animations.
The devs are also really awesome. Back when they were having trouble with save corruptions, one of them added me on steam and gave me a new save file at the exact checkpoint I was at! Seriously good people. I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

OFFICIAL REVIEW
I am 96 hours into the game, finished the entirety of it including the main storyline, sidequests, and all locations on hard mode. I've never actually been an AC fan (In fact I hated them for the most part), though I've played the previous games apart from rogue, unity, and syndicate and all I can honestly say is that the AC Formula prior to Origins is plain straight-out repetitive. Assassin's Creed and the concept known as "CONSISTENTLY FUN", never seemed to have coupled with one another. Until now however, with Origins. To site a few repetitive activites in the original formula:
- Trailing missions (Follow this guy for 20-30 mins and if he sees you no matter how close you are to finishing the trailing mission, you get desync'ed)
-Side activities particularly assassination contracts with no substance (There is no compelling backstory to motivate the player. Sometimes, there's no story at all. LMAO)
- Long♥♥♥♥♥modern day sequences that break the immersion of being an assassin from a specific time period
- Beautiful recreation of historical landscapes though lacking the flavor it needs to captivate the player and by captivate I mean to truly be enticing and not just a mere one-time glance.
- Laughably unchallenging Combat System that only kept me interested for the first 10 mins of experiencing it. After that I realized two buttons only mattered in combat; Counter and Attack (= Counterattack).
- All in all, too linear which always kept the player on a short leash.
With those factors listed, I want to explain briefly how the revamped AC formula of Origins have addressed the past insipid experienceI had with the AC Series:
- (Bummer for AC fans, I know, but hear me out) No more social stealth BUT THAT MEANS NO MORE BORING♥♥♥♥♥TRAILING MISSIONS THAT ARE BASICALLY UGL's or (Unnecessary game lengtheners). No more blending in with the crowd because you're not trailing anyone anymore. Though it was useful in terms of escaping pursuing guards, I'll admit. But I'll accept that compromise any day so as to completely remove the ♥♥♥♥-faced trailing missions.
- Sidequests (that'rs right they're no longer called missions) now are actually story-driven which makes the experience a whole lot better. Gone are the days when I have to senselessly assassinate someone without even knowing why I had to do it.
- The modern day sequences (Yes there is a modern day story in Origins, not sure if that's spoiler-worthy tho) is actually quite decent tho not as decent as Desmond's I'll say but the point here is that it does not over stay its welcome unlike previous modern day stories, so yeah, immersion-breaking problems are addressed here.
- Not only is recreated ancient Egypt of AC Origins a landmark to behold, it's also alive and breathing. The AI system (tho clunky at times) have specific schedules each tailored to the grand fabric of a truly immersive Open World. Heck, even the animals hunt and eat corpses of guards that are thrown by fellow guards on duty in the river. It's so detailed you can even see the mummification process in Memphis. And of course, it's not just a one-time glance anymore, with the addition of Photo mode, this game has entered my personal list of top 5 Open Worlds.
- Now I know a lot of hatred for this game is due to the new combat system, but it feels and plays better than it looks. If anything, it's way better by a hundredfold than the previous combat system wherein a baby could basically master it in a few seconds. It takes time getting used to it but once you get the hang of it, it's altogether very rewarding.
- This game have finally given the player so much freedom that I'm happily an AC fan now who looks forward to future titles. Black flag did a great job at the Open Seas exploration tho it still lacked the necessary aspects in terms of the freedom from a true sandbox experience derived from an Open World game. I'm just glad AC is no longer linear, the series always had huge potential had it been an open world from the very beginning. Historical landscapes easily explorable anytime without the hindrance of loading screens is what makes this game a truly fine experience.

This game is a job simulator in a wasted city full of crime and murder.
Except that you are not only a barkeeper/policeman/drug dealer/shopkeeper/investment banker/comedian etc., but also a spy for a government opposing rebel faction that kinda has no idea what they're doing.
So while making your way through the devastated distopia of the games city world you also need to fulfill crucial mission objective orders straight from your rebel HQ. The fun thing about that is that there's literally millions of ways of doing that, and depending on what job you're educated in there's even more ways with every playthrough.
For example: HQ orders to get a harddrive from the shopkeeper in town. Now, you could kill the shopkeeper and take it, or you could just threaten him to do just that if he doesn't give it to you right now, or you could give him a very valuable item in exchange. But if you are a shopkeeper yourself you can just buy it from him, if you are a thief you can steal it from him, if you are a slavemaster you can enslave him and make him give it to you, and this whole variability makes the game incredibly fun and long-living.
Other than the missions which are well planned in theory and well executed in practice, the game is all about the player being able to do whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they want. I especially like freeing gorillas from science labs while there's still scientists in there with them. Welp.

So, anyone wanting more info about this game, he's a rundown of story and what to expect.
You're a part of a crew that is rebelling against a dodgy mayor. So, you'll have to do a whole bunch of random missions to get by. These could be operating some machines at a certain location, maybe a mission where you must take out someone or even rescue someone or something from somewhere, once you do these, you can move on to the next level.
If you earn enough XP points, you can pick a perk to carry on with you for the rest of the game. Try and survive if you can, at this moment of time there are 9 levels but fortunately the endless mode can help provide more gameplay. We know that this is all getting extended and updated later in time.
now, generally during missions there are going to be some obstacles or people who don’t want you to achieve these things. And how you solve these problems comes down to your style of play, which is most likely represented by the class you pick. There's already heaps to pick from and judging from the open spaces there's probably going to be more added. All classes have distinctive styles of game plays, strengths, weaknesses. You know the deal...
The thing I think is cool is just how these classes are based on a mix of every day modern work careers to fantasy and weird.
You can play this single player, online with some buddies or even local co-op too and how you play is up to you. There's a lot of freedom in completing missions from being stealthy, going loud and destroying everyone or if you're clever you might even be able to talk your way into getting other people to do the job for you while you sit back eating bacon cheeseburgers.

Camera is obnoxious and is going to be your biggest cause of death. You can't see an enemy until he is pretty much 0.1 second away from you, so you have to resort to using slow-mo (part of the shooting mechanic) for the whole game (except final boss), which is tedious, especially when you have to click on your character to charge your shot and not just by pressing anywhere on the screen.
The movement response is also a big problem in the game. I don't mind that I have to break, and that it takes a while before turning from left to right, that's fine. But what really bugs me is the jump. There are no limits how many times you can jump after you are already airborne, but it just gives you a bit of velocity, which is quickly diminished by gravity, so you have to spam the jump button to climb up. It would be much better if the jump would work the same as the rest of the movement controls.
Level design is very basic and fits well the simplistic style of the game, but has a quickly thrown thogether feel. There are a lot of extra levels, almost as many as in the 'main' game and to my surprise these are designed much better, are more challenging and diverse.
Bosses are the only enemies in the game, and each of them is unique. However they can mostly be tricked and beaten easily, by just keeping them out of the screen and shooting at them, and they don't really resonate with their names.
Now the whole story fits well around the game concept and is mostly biblical. The whole game is constructed around david vs. goliath story, since david is small and has a simple weapon against their oversized and mighty enemies, hence the game name.
However levels/bosses are named after deadly sins and while some of them do act according to their representations, most of them don't. To me, names feel forced since there are no such references in the original david and goliath story. I guess we could say, that goliath is represented by the whole 'evil' of the universe you have to beat, but I don't know... Maybe I'm taking it too literal.
Overall even with the extra levels, the game falls short. Bad camera and controls increase the difficulty of already challenging game. At the end, it just feels like a game that works better on mobiles.

So, I don't really know what to call this game... I'm going to try though. To me, it feels like a very unique bullethell with physics and neat mechanics. Theres not much else to it, but the uniqueness stems off its slow down mechanic. The slow down mechanic allows you to aim and shoot, however it comes with a negative as well. Whenever you shoot, you'll be brought back to slightly faster speed than before, leaving you a little vulnerable for a short moment. The games gameplay overall is just this specifically, but with different unique "bosses" that have different things going on in each level, as well as neat ways to beat them.
Pros:
- Fun and definitely a unique experience
- Easy to pick up, hard to fully understand/master

Cons:
- A bit buggy at times, although fixable if you just look in discussion.
- Although the game mechanics are amazing, I feel as if one or two levels were just too tedious, and were pretty disorienting.
Overall David. is a great game thats easy to pick up, fun to play and brings a pretty unique gaming experience for a really low price. It has some issues with some bugs(just play windowed mode) and well, some levels are a little disorienting(one I can think off the top of my head). This is a really unique game thats super fun to play. I had a blast playing this basically the whole time(Which... never really happens for me).

Arcane preRaise, unlike Arcane RERaise, manages to be very slightly more competent than the previous game in the series, and comes up to the still worthless level of Arcane Raise. The weird monetization finally improves slightly with the mutually exclusive DLC characters, with there being a somewhat sensible assortment of 6, one of each gender/class combination, while the cheat item pack is about as mediocre as it was in Arcane REraise.
Meanwhile, the game still has no original assets, almost no story, a bare minimum of mechanics (2 characters in fixed classes from the first game, all items available from a shop somewhat early into the game), and is just over half an hour long with or without the booster pack, even picking up all chests, which I almost assuredly didn't need to do. Unlike Arcane RERaise, there's no real challenging fights unless you stumble into the part of the map where Demons and Succubi spawn too quickly.
To similarly sum up the entire game as I did for the first: after a tutorial featuring mechanics that don't actually exist in the game (e.g. potential punishment for retreating from fights, vehicles) that you have to confirm twice in a row that you want to play through, due to it being copied from the previous games without removing the confirmation screen, you are dumped into a house full of people who turn into zombies and skeletons or explode when you talk to them, get outside, have a second (or third) character join your party, then clear out a large village-style map full of chests of money and XP while occasionally ducking into the shop to buy equipment and +attack items at 200 a pop / 99 for 19800, enjoy the sound of consuming items 99 times in a row, then enter a building marked "Demon Lair" and fight the final boss, hitting it for 4000 damage five or so times. Unlike Arcane RERaise, you are actually treated to a new message appropriate to this game for beating the final boss, but it's just "Congratulations! You have defeated the boss."
Oh, and you get 36 achievements, probably also all stock art, once you get out of the house full of zombies.
In conclusion, no. Still irredeemable, and the last of this series I've ended up with a copy of, because I learned my lesson and the Occult Raise games appear to be even worse.

This has so far been the worst visual novel I have ever read.
Story: A boy is sent to a virtual world as a result of his dad's VR experiment gone wrong and he must now save the citizens of this world from certain doom. Honestly, it's the kind of story an 8 year-old could have written. It's uninteresting and very cliché, and frankly, there's not much else to say about it. It just sucks. Also, it ends on such a stupid cliffhanger, that I feel like they either ran out of a budget, or they got completely bored of making this game. Props for it being short, at least. ~ 2/10
Art: There's something seriously wrong with the art here. I'm pretty sure they used at least 3 different artists for the art because some images look completely different from the style of another. It's super inconsistent, and worst of all, none of the art is even that good anyway. Also, seeing as this is an ecchi visual novel, they somehow thought it'd be a great idea for every female (beside's the MC's mother) to have the biggest pair of ta-ta's you will ever see in your life. It just doesn't work and I found it more humorous than "sexy." ~ 2/10
That's pretty much all I have to say about it. There's no spoken dialogue and even though it's short, it still feels like it drags on because of how boring it is.

Burokku Girls is a rather impressive light ecchi novel. It's got some rather interesting characters framed around a world that may seem cliche on the outside. But deep down the game has a lot of heart. It's true that the game has adult themes and sexual content that is in step and stride with the ecchi genre, but it is also a game that has a lot of heart and drive behind it. These games are not just ecchi focused. Silver Cow Studio wanted to build a world, a universe, something to house their characters. And they put a lot of work into them.
The games are very text heavy, there's a lot to read. But if you put the time and effort into them to enjoy the characters and the worlds for what they are, both this and Time Tenshi are amazing.
There's not much in the choices or gameplay. These are novels with some nice artwork and some interactive animations. A rather nice soundtrack, beautiful backgrounds and some sexy fun.
If you've played Time Tenshi, you'll probably like Burokku Girls. Likewise, if you like this, you'll probably like Time Tenshi. The quality and care between the games are virtually the same.
I support Silver Cow Studio, and hope they continue to make more of these.

While I had heard of Home, the "unique horror adventure" released by Benjamin Rivers in 2012, I hadn't played it until September 2016 (part of a Humble Bundle). Let's not mince words here, calling Home a "unique horror adventure" would be like calling Super Mario Bros. "an epic tale of a humble man that battles the forces of evil in the name of love", which is laughable. Homesucks as a game and sucks as interactive storytelling medium.
From the start, it did not endear me to it by requesting I turn off the lights, use headphones, and play the game in one sitting. In fact, it seemed to imply that I had to play the game in one sitting, which would've annoyed me any further. But still, I felt annoyed it had the gall to tell me all that.
Listen. You do not tell me how I play my games. If you have to tell me the lights off and use headphones to create an "atmosphere", you're doing it wrong. You can leave the lights on and the jump scares in FNAF and it can still scare the bejeezus out of you and I'm not missing out on anything.
The pacing of the game plods along. Apparently you can't walk and hold the flashlight up at the same time, and the little guy you control moves extremely slowly with no run button in site. The latter is explained in-game as the main character ("Sweater Vest Guy") gets hurt and limps along, but unless Sweater Vest Guy has some sort of crippling neurological injury that disallows him to walk and hold the flashlight up at the same time, it's a horrible design and one of the things that harms the game.
From the beginning, you can already guess that HE was the killer all along (and references to the character's job loss and alcohol-induced sleepwalking seem to support that), but there's also some sort of contradicting "death list" found in underground tunnels just to mess with your mind and introduce some further fake ambiguity, all of which leads nowhere.
At the end of the game, Sweater Vest Guy will likely commit suicide (whether or not the player character really believes it was he who committed the murders) instead of offering a choice like running away or turning yourself into the police (there is a way to just "slip away", either by a complicated process of picking up and not picking up certain things...or by just quitting during the credits and continuing there). Not that such a choice had a lot of emotional impact. It's hard to feel sympathy for a goofy-looking ginger with two pixels for eyes and a sweater vest, but that only makes presentation even worse--I say the death of Sweater Vest Guy is meaningless based on the way he looks, but keep in mind I also was moved to tears during Final Fantasy VI, and that was sprite art as well.
I don't know Benjamin Rivers. I have no idea if he's a pretentious hack or a halfway decent guy who made a game that I just didn't really like. But if I ever meet him in person or online and voice my displeasure about the game's poor "storyline", I would be irritated if he said something like, "But ambiguity is the NATURE of the game!" then I would tell him this: "If you introduce disparate plot threads and then refuse to wrap them up or try to connect them in a logical sense, then you are not a genius, you're just lazy." But to be fair, Ben Rivers never actually said that to my knowledge, so until I have it on record that he said this, then it's still 0-0, he still may be a pretentious hack, but he at least hasn't directly insulted my intelligence.
If you have hopes for a good solid storyline, then forget it. Benjamin Rivers has a middle finger toward you if that's you're thing. I'm feeling charitable enough to say that it is okay enough for the 90 or so minutes it runs, but it was a time in my life when I was unemployed and played video games all day. I wouldn't waste time with it today, especially how slow the pacing is. Yeah, it's only $3 on Steam, but that's still far too much for what he's asking. Your money is better spent elsewhere.

When I picked this title up I really didn't know what to expect. It's not reviewed on any of the main adventure games websites and there aren't many reviews on Steam.
When I started it up I was asked whether I wanted to play it on Easy or Hard. I chose Easy as I didn't want to get stuck and it appears that the actual adventure gameplay is the same. The Hard difficulty level just affects the complexity of some sliders / picture puzzles.
On beginning the game itself, the introduction was very simple with just a few paragraphs in a diary to read about how my character got to the island. I thought at this point that it was a little too simple and lame. The story itself is quite bare bones, but it holds interest for the duration.
What I really liked about this game was the wonderful ambient, relaxing music. It's from Cyan Music and it really fitted the solitary exploration and puzzling of the game well. Other sounds in the game are the natural sounds of nature. There is no voice acting as there is nobody at all to speak to and this does not detract at all from the experience.
The graphics are simple but very effective, from snow scenes that give you a sense of the cold to plenty of water scenes and lush jungle / rainforest.
The interface is very user friendly.  Combining objects couldn't be simpler and the whole game is very intuitive. Hot spots do need careful searching though, though again there is help in the form of an eye icon that lights up all hotspots.
I completed the game in 2 and a half hours and did not use any of the available hints. It could be completed faster with the help of the built in hint system, but where's the fun in that?
I am not interested in Steam achievements, but for those that seek out 100% success, this game should be very straightforward in 2 playthroughs at each difficulty setting.
I can recommend this game for a peaceful two to three hours experience.

Foremost: David. is fun. You play a square with a rubber band gun of sorts, trying to best a series of boss rooms. That being said, David. has many problems and it's not the thin, but easily ignored storyline. Rather, it's the game's abitrary difficulty.
The game starts off very easy, most players should have no problem beating the first levels within their first couple of attempts. Even on "Very" difficulty, the game's hardest setting, which changes little but reduce the number of hits you can take to zero.
But the difficulty ramps up quickly, mainly due to the minimal overview the game gives you over each level and its challenge(s) at each level's start. The camera is centered on the main foe in the beginning, trying to give you an idea of what you're facing, but often doesn't show your character. Later levels require you to react quickly from the start to stand a chance. The way each level is introduced disorientates the player, forcing him to make his first move blindly to trigger the camera to snap back to him, all the while the challenge has already started. A good example is the "Anxt" level, where
.
Worse is that victory or defeat often feel arbitrary. Enemies are either too dumb (e.g. the "Wolf" level, where
) or too intelligent (basically everything that shoots you). This is part of a another problem David. has, that is controls.
To shoot you need to click on your character. However, survival requires you to jump around so much and so quickly, that skill is not needed to aim at your enemy but to click on yourself. Especially situations with many enemies become frustrating and feel unfair quickly as surviving often is a matter of getting off a shot or not to clear the way. Aiming on enemies, luckily, is very easy as the game goes into a sort of slow motion when you charge your shot. However it feels like the slow motion slows you down more than it does those around you. For example, enemies bound to charge over your head can correct their trajectory much more quickly in slow motion. It's as if they're given time to think.
David. is fun. Mostly, because it's challenging. Unfortunately it is for the wrong reasons.

Burokku Girls is a visual novel about breasts. As the story goes, you’re a young man trying out your genius father’s ultra-immersive VR simulator. Absolutely nothing happens, and you go home.
That would actually be more surprising than what really happens, which is that you get sucked into the game itself with no way to return home. Within minutes you’re tripping over some big-boobed warrior lady and being attacked by fireball slinging mind-controlled minions. There’s a PLOT that involves some women from beneath the ground who are trying to take over the world, and it does get surprisingly dark at times. The writing was decent most times but occasionally plodded along with humdrum details and dialogue. You probably aren’t here for the writing. There are a bevvy of characters, including aforementioned warrior lady, flirtatious bunny girl with magic powers that defy explanation, and some kind of tsundere Senran Kagura escapee. There are just a few choices to make throughout the story, so you're going to need a hand free at some points to actually pick one.
Some of the CGs look a little wonky, but the art is generally clean and well done. I cannot believe I’m actually seriously reviewing this. Sometimes I felt that the Minecraft-esque blocky backgrounds were too different stylistically from the otherwise colorful art. There is also no nudity, but that never stopped me from enjoying myself before. Yes, you could see more with a google search but that’s not the POINT, okay?
As for the music, the game cycles through a handful of tracks that are forgettable for the most part, although I really liked one or two of them. At the very least there's nothing here so offensive to the eardrum as to reduce my opinion of Burokku Girls.
The ending is a cliffhanger, which is to be expected (according to my friend who is a fan of Silver Cow Studio games and big boobs in general), but I felt like things were just getting interesting.
I’m recommending it on the basis that if you know what this is and it still sounds appealing, you’ll like it.

I went ahead and made something of a first impressions / review for Arcane (pre)Raise on my YouTube channel. I'll leave the link here if anyone fancies seeing the "fun" I had with this game, but I've also summarized my experience below.
Being one of a trilogy...wait, scratch that. Being one of three games currently on Steam, with 3 more AND a visual novel on (the now dead) Greenlight, you'd expect this game to be rich with story and history - what happened before, what's happening to the characters now, and where will it lead?! ...NO. No story. You wake up, the characters says you have to hurry, another says you need to close a portal, and that's it. No reason why and no back stories.
But there are plenty of other characters to add to the game if you're willing to pay MORE THAN THE PRICE OF THE BASE GAME! And of course there's no stories for them either (that I can tell - there was no way I was buying any of the DLCs to find out).
This game is just filled with random encounters/battles, with no logical balancing other than "the higher level you are, the higher level the enemies you'll face." This is logical, but it's just a set level of scaling depending on your general progress through the game. By this I mean the enemies you first meet, straight away, aren't balanced for someone just starting the game, and they remain the same difficulty until you hit a certain level that introduces the new group of enemies. And as far as I can tell it's just a case of there being a mix of one group at first, then you hit that magic level marker and then there's the second group and that's it - there's no gradual build of enemies or multiple tiers.
And speaking of the character leveling - this is achieved simply by walking around the TINY map and opening chests. You can escape the majority of encounters, but the chests are where the real character building lies. You can get up at least one level with every 2 chests, and they're everywhere! Also, going back to the DLCs, they contain 50,000 EXP each, so you can pay (again, more than the price of the base game EACH) to further level your characters.
I only played it for the length that I did for the sake of the video I made to review the game. I had made my mind up within half and hour, but I didn't want people to think I didn't give it a chance. So I did. And the more I played the more bored and frustrated I got with the game, and generally angry I got about it's very existence.
DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!

Welcome to the newest frontier in gaming: battles and scenes at the scale of armies and fleets, all active at once with no trickery around loading screens or off-screen abstractions.
Star Swarm is a real-time demo of Oxide Games’ Nitrous engine, which pits two AI-controlled fleets against each other in a furious space battle. Originally conceived as an internal stress test, Oxide decided to release Star Swarm so that the public can share our vision of what we think the future of gaming can be. The simulation in Star Swarm shows off Nitrous’ ability to have thousands of individual units onscreen at once, each running their own physics, AI, pathfinding, and threat assessments.
Note that Star Swarm is not a deterministic simulation -- the AI and everything else is being computed in real time, so you will get slightly different results from multiple executions even on the same hardware. Unfortunately, achieving 100% determinism with the highly threaded nature of the Nitrous engine is an unrealistic goal.
The Nitrous engine is already in use for three games currently in production: an unannounced title from Oxide Games, Stardock’s Star Control reboot, and Mohawk Games’ upcoming game codenamed Mars. Nitrous is also available for licensing to interested game developers.
You’ve got to see it to believe it. Download Star Swarm for free now to see what your gaming PC can do with the next-generation Nitrous engine.

I'm trying really, really hard to love this game, but I just can't. Despite absolutely loving the first ten hours or so, the more I play it the more annoyed I get. Here's why.
The setting and main story are boring. They had 3000 years of Egyptian history to pick from and they gave us the least interesting choice possible. I sure hope you like Romans, Greeks and the same Cleopatra/Caesar story you've heard a million times, cause that's all you're gonna get. Egyptians? Not really. The civil war story is short with no build up and the historical characters are decidedly unhistorical and very unengaging. Ptolemy and Pompey are both on screen for probably less than two minutes total, and neither get any development. Caesar is the least Caesar I've ever seen, and the main bad guy comes out of nowhere and is completely unengaging. The Assassin/Templar story has never been more unwelcome and uninteresting.
Cleopatra is the only decent NPC in the game.
On top of all that the terrible modern day sections are back in full force.
That said, Bayek is a great character and his vengeance story is excellent. Aya is also pretty good, but she gets derailed by being so heavily involved in the mess of the main story. If they had focussed on the vengeance quest and exploring the beautiful open world they created, and had they relegated Caesar story to a fun background element, it would have been much better.
The gameplay itself is clunky and not very fun. Bayek feels very awkward to control both in and out of combat. The climbing is very stiff and the free running element is almost nonexistent. The only real tactic enemies use is to stun Bayek and go to town on him, so almost every time your best off just sniping them with a bow and avoiding the tedious combat all together. At least in previous titles the dodge/parry/kill system could almost feel zen and relaxing. This is just annoying.
The last little annoyance is their lootbox and timed event systems. This is a full priced AAA exclusively single player game and they still want to nickle and dime you for rare equipment and the only themed costumes in the game, and control the timing and conditions of how you access the content.
Get it when its on sale because the historical sandbox really is both beautiful and fun, and if you want some real Ancient Egyptian fun until then go pick up Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy instead.

I usually give games a few days of play before reviewing them. But I think I've seen enough. Home is an 8-bit looking pixel horror adventure game. It pretty much operates like all the old point and click acventures of old. It tells you on boot to turn out all the lights...and put on headphones. Fair enough. I do agree that games which favor spookiness need to be played in a certain way...at a certain time. This one does it so it can clip-clop loud footsteps and doorcreaks at you. Pretty much insistently and annoyingly. It does so so in-your-face that when you click on a door to move through it it shows you a pixelated door opening in full screen with accompanying LOUD door creak. Same with going up and down stairs. That...really...makes me laugh after awhile. But not funny haha. Funny as in...I can't believe they thought this worked. You start off in mystery house during a rainstorm without knowing how you got there. You do the same point and click searching and picking up and using things you always do in these. But nothing happens. Nothing is scary. In the occasional room there is a noise, a slamming, mysterious whisper but at this point I don't really read it as having anything to do with the story or the game itself. But more oooooo dev is trying to scare me with spooky sounds. Not thrilled by the puzzles thus far. And really not thrilled that once I got past a certain part, it won't let me go back and check out a door that I missed. Isn't a big point of adventure games that they are freeflowing? YOu can go visit and explore places? Read their descriptions? Enjoy the atmosphere? Well here is another fact of this game. It has laughable bugs. When I got bored I saved the game. WHen I started it up again and hit continue...TWO of me were on the screen. That's right. My character (the protagonist) is on the screen normally but since I restarted it had two copies of it. Once I went into the next room it went away. So like I already was thinking this didn't have someone helping with content. NOw I know it didn't have anyone testing it either. The story is what could have saved this. Events could have saved this. But neither have occurred.
Edit: I've now finished the game...one run thru of it. I have to correct myself. The save bug does NOT go away. It is revealed when you use the mouse to move. You will always have two of yourself walking around the room once you restart. Now let's talk about the writing. Let's just drop this logic problem...At the beginning...you are trying to get out of the house. You come to a front door and...you can't leave...because there is furniture stacked in front of it! Why can't you just move the furniture like everyone else would do? There are lots of things like this. Also this game is written as if it was written in the past. This gimmick does not work. At all. It makes the game seems wishy washy. Makes it seem like nothing you do matters and that you aren't really trying to solve anything. Which I guess you aren't. It is telling the story and whatever you do is fine. That's the story. So there is no emotional impact for anything at all since you take it where you want. Someone also mentioned the achievements. Yes...the achievements also make no sense. And many bits at the end don't really make sense either. This needed so much more polish. It really is a grind.

Would end my story by leaving again.

WARNING: This game is REALLY hard, even on the easiest mode. You will die. You will die over and over and over and over again. If you rage, I strongly recommend you do not play this game.
That being said, this game is amazing. The controls are tight, the game is well made (not including the problems at launch, which many many games have), and most of all, it is a ton of fun. The tech in this game is really solid. Sliding, jumping, ranged attacks, melee attacks, double jump, flutter, and much more. Honestly, this game not only does an amazing job with the tech introduced throughout the game, but it also is really good at giving "easy" obstacles to practice the new tech, and ramping up from there. I felt like every part I played in the game was possible. Nothing felt stupidly difficult, jsut really REALLY hard. There were a couple parts I was getting really salty on, but I managed to overcome them. I'm near the end of the game now, and even though I have lost to the same boss probably an upward 300 times, I am still enjoying myself each fight.
And on top of all that? Completely unnecessary content in the form of character customization. This game has so much great platforming and numerous fun bosses, it feels like customization is something the game didn't even need, but it is very appreciatted. Sure, it probably isn't difficult to make these simple customizations (the cosmetic ones, of course), it still was something the game didn't even need to be amazing, it just makes the game that more amazing, and adds a lot of replayability in the form of returning to levels and collecting missed items and secrets.
I give this game a 10/10. As an avid Boshy fan, I can say this game is even better then Boshy. Keep it up Solgryn, I'll continue to follow you through all your game development.
TL;DR: If you don't rage, like difficult platforming/bosses, and like being a super kawaii angel, GET THIS GAME.

Yet another game that makes me wish there were some middle ground when it comes to reviewing. I will recommend David., but it's a soft yes.
This game is challenging, but for the wrong reasons. The controls are the biggest problem. David's maneuverability is tricky and can be sluggish. In a game where every second counts, this often means a quick end to the run. On top of frustrating controls, enemy AI is very strong. The easy Okay Mode is fine and is a light, healthy challenge on its own, but the more difficult Very Mode throws you into levels with smart, aggressive enemies and only one hit on your health. I don't mind enemies that put up a good fight, but when you're so handicapped by poor controls and instant death, the game gets old fast.
Overall I do like the game and the concept, it looks nice, the levels are unique and creative, and the arena, separate from the story/progression, is by far the most enjoyable aspect. (The final boss is also pretty sweet, and satisfying to unlock.) If the controls were better I'd give this game a solid recommendation. As it is, if you're up for a challenge and don't mind the kind of game where there's no hand-holding and the runs are short because you're dying quickly and frequently, I'd say go ahead and grab this if you catch it on sale.

It also does a fantastic job of showing how much better you’re getting and subtly teaching you. At the start of the game, I thought there would be no way I could beat the ‘very’ stages in order to get to the end but after playing the stage where your orbs are stranded about, I managed to figure out how to aim them based off their orbit around the ‘firing zone’. From there the game only got more rewarding as I practiced time shots looking at both the target and the orbs.
The Atari/polygonal style, the atmosphere, the sound effects, the retro music the simple yet interpretable story!
I’ve only spent a little time with David but it was a blast, and there’s still an endless mode and few levels left to beat on Very!

David is a 2d minimalist action physics little game.
You are David, a little texture-less square. You are gifted with a weapon that shoots M&Ms upon charging up, and it slows time too giving you bullet-time action to defeat other texture-less objects while navigating texture-less levels.
Some levels offer cool ideas and challenges, and others put you face-2-face against bosses.
Many levels are really fun.
There's also an Arena mode, basically a survivor mode, where you keep defeating incoming enemies until you die.
Your awards upon completing certain levels are.............hats!!
Altough i really wanted to like the game. But the sluggish controls and the camera make the game super frustrating and doing levels on "very" difficulty (I don't know why the dev called the difficulties modes as "Okay" and "Very", he could use Easy and Hard".
David has an unpredictable movements. When i want him to up, he sometimes don't go up. When i want him to go right/left quickly to evade enemies, he do so extremely slowly i die, and sometimes he go so fast when i just wanted him to strafe a little and evade, ending up dying by another enemy.
The camera in the final boss battle is fixed on him, so if he got far from you, you will be off-screen, and enemies will you have an easy time killing you.
Although a minor issue, but the game hud is off and mis-aligned from the actual resolution. There's a tiny button above the screen that you can't press on it, but if you press on the upper-right corner, it will open. Same for "game over" screen.
These flaws are even more annoying if you want to get all the achievements.
If the developer wanted to tweak this game with smoother controls and optimizing the game for bigger resolutions to fix the hud, I'm sure the game will be perfect for what it is.
And uh, game can be beaten in 1.5~2 hours, more if you want to do achievements.
Game isn't expensive, the price is good. but I will leave it for your judgement to buy it on sale or not.

If you look at the screenshots up there, that is pretty much what you get. They mixed SAO, Minecraft, and fanservice in order to attract the demographic of ecchi anime gamers. Sometimes it looks like they literally ripped Minecraft screenshots to put in the game.
Art isn't bad, but is sometimes inconsistent since they use at least three artists and their styles are sometimes not consistent with each other. This is especially true in the colouring and shading. If you're bothered by this, it will probably throw you off, though I only saw it happen once in the time I played. Also, you are not going to see anybody with less than a DD bust in this game, unless it's literally the MC's mom. If you want variety, this isn't the place for you.
There is nothing special about the story since it's just a vehicle to get you to the boobs. The writing is sometimes awkward, and there are more adjectives for things than you can shake your purple prose bible at. I will give them props for having some creativity with the world (literally called Burokku) though they mostly used Minecraft elements to justify it.
I am not usually into ecchi, but I do like ecchi with good stories or comedic writing. In this case, this was just not for me. But if you're part of the aforementioned demographic and are OK with just going for the fanservice, give it a go.
Edit: In case you guys want a preview of what the game looks like, I did a playthrough of the first half of the game.

First things first:  There are boobs everywhere.  They will be shoved in your face all the time.  Your character will inadvertantly grope every single one at some point, or have his face mashed in the middle.  All the time.  At least twice per character.  There is some plot reason behind why they're so massive, but it's left down to maybe two lines and dropped for the rest of the game.
The VN is very linear, with only two "branches" that I saw.  I'm sure the first one had no effect on the story, and the second just changes your ending.
The writing itself isn't actually that bad.  They took a Minecraft-esque world and made it believable, with characters that live in it.  The MC gets an eleventh hour super power that is actually pretty cool and actually frightens half of the good guys that see him use it.
The downside is actually what the developers focused on too heavily.  The sex appeal.  Yea, you're going to draw in crowds with it, but the Sakura series already took care of that.  Nobody really wants giant mammaries all over the place.  Had the chesticles not been such a focal point, with writer spending more time fleshing out plotlines than describing a pair of breats in two paragraphs, it would've turned out much better.

I was surprised to see that Home got mixed reviews here on steam. I read some of the negative reviews and I am honestly not sure if we played the same game. Stale gameplay? Confusing narrative? Limited scope?
Home is one of the best indie horror games I have yet played. I like pixel graphics, but I was sceptical if a pixelated game could create a dense and frightening atmosphere needed for a horror game.
It did.
The game is short. It is kind of the whole deal. You are trying to get home and figure out what happened in the last couple of hours. The tension while you slowly uncover the last night piece by piece is amazing. The story plays out differently each time and it is cool to see what tiny little decision you made had an impact on the entire story.

Although I didn't mind, it seems from the mixed reviews that it may be useful to know what you're getting into with Home. You, the player, play an integral part in how the story unfolds and ultimately ends. These choices are yours and if you'd rather not make them, which is fair enough, then Home is not the game for you.
If you quite fancy a choose-your-own-adventure (and ending) with a darker theme, then Home may be the game for you. In terms of horror, it's more horror story, or psychological, than actual scares. It takes about an hour and a half to complete, but has replay value given the choices (though I do wonder if your progress may be barred by choosing not to do things, which would lead to a frustrating experience - might be something to test out on a replay).
If it sounds like it might appeal, then I'd recommend giving it a go.
Good atmosphere to start, but it's just ultimately too short, and the extremely limited scope makes it more of a walking simulator than a game.

Sadly, this game did not match my expectations.  Perhaps I've been spoiled by other games with a similar nature, but this felt too bland and repetitive, not to mention it is surprisingly taxing on my computer.  Perhaps you can hide behind the early access curtain, but this felt more like an overglorified Flash game.
For a game that advertises variety, you see the same thing over and over.  The enemies quickly become familiar, and the weapons quickly become tired.  Three weapons with the same general mechanic do not "play and feel unique".  It's your standard set of light/fast, medium, and heavy/slow.  Plus three other weapons that, through a quick Google search, appear to be similar in nature with very minor variations.  I was disappointed.
The powerups are slow to come by, and a lot of them feel pretty useless.  The most useful one was a simple weapon upgrade for damage.  There were flashier ones out there for sure, but they were either very rare to come by, or their help was minimal at best, or both.
Perhaps I had a certain vision for this game that I did not get when I played it.  When I heard procedurally-generated, with a unique variety of weapons, I thought I'd be getting a different gameplay experience every time.  That's the point, right?  But I did not get that experience.
This is not a bad game by any stretch, but it certainly did not blow me away.  Maybe if it's on sale for a couple of bucks it would be worth getting... maybe.  But at full price, no.  For ten bucks, there are much better games out there.

Specs: GTX 1070 Founders Edition, I7 7700K, 32gb 3200 DDR4 Ram
Graphics: Visually this game is stunning to me but may not be for others. There is so much detail that has been put into this world that its easy to get imersed in the game itself. There are some glitches that can break that imersion but I have come across none that are game breaking in my play through so far.
Gameplay: Outside of the new combat system most will fill right at home when it comes to the formula of the game and its controls. The major change they made this time around is the combat system. Gone are the days of guards sitting back and you pick them off one at a time. There is a bit of a learning curve when it comes to this new system but once you have it down you are set. The side quest have also seen a bit of an overhaul and this game is full of them. No longer are they boring chores to work through rather some have interesting stories of their own. These storeis themselves add to the imersion of the world as well further ingrossing you in it.
Concerns: Other users have been pointing out performance issues and I have seem to be lucky in that I have not had many. My specs are listed above so you can compare parts to performance. This is not to say that I am running around at a consistant 140 FPS but I am not dipping below 80 so I will take it.  With more action on the screen comes slight drops but nothing that ruins the game.
Conclusion: Based on what I have played so far I can reccomend this game to not only my friends but anyone else. If you are looking for a world to get lost in then this will be the game for you. Be sure though that you have the time to sink into it as doing everything that there is to do requires a lot of time from what I have seen so far.

Not experiencing any of the performance issues alot of users here are, though I guess it's largely dependant on your system. In my case, I get a stable 60FPS at 1920x1080 with these specs:
- 256GB 850 EVO
- GTX 970
- i7 7700k
Game itself is pretty great, looks absolutely stunning, gameplay is streamlined and smooth and doesn't get stale quickly like other Assassin's Creed titles.
I actually like the new combat style, it's nice that they've diverged from the old parry and kill, batman-esque fighting. Your character now progresses in a meaningful way, with a skill point system much like any other RPG, points go in the direction of either Hunter (bows), Fighter (melee balls to the walls), Tool Dude Guy (use traps and shiz).
Story is engaging and seems well written and narrated, though I'm not too deep into it yet. Cutscenes follow suite in visual style and actually tell a great story.
Here are some negatives;
Micro transaction should not be in a £50 game. This isn't as big a deal as it sound, the things you can buy aren't even important, and are mostly negligible. If you don't buy them, it won't take away from your enjoyment at all. There's still something that pisses me off about it. This and the fact that they have so many ♥♥♥♥ing versions, i.e Deluxe Edition, Gold Edition... etc. Classic ubisoft trying to grab as much cash as possible.
There are also a few bugs, they aren't so bad, but still I shouldn't notice several bugs in the first few hours of a game.
Forcing uplay also sucks.. blah blah.. you get the idea, the usual crap that comes with ubishit games.
Overall I think it's important to realize that a fair amount of the negative reviews here are from people experiencing performance issues. If you're reading the reviews to figure out whether or not this is a good game; it is... if it runs for you.
Buy it, see if it runs okay, if it doesn't, refund.

Assassin's Creed III gets forgotten very easily being precursor to Black Flag which set the world on fire, but I personally prefer this one. In my previous reviews of Assassin's Creed games I suggested that some of the series' main (now underused) strengths were it's era-specific attention to detail and it's (slightly liberal) historical accuracies. I feel like the makers of this game took a lot of care to acurately depict Colonial America, more so than any other game I can think of and as a lover of history, I was loving that. Playing a key role in the Boston Tea-Party was thrilling, despite being British myself and committing absolute sacrilege by wasting tea.
I liked Connor too, the main character, kid was brutal as ♥♥♥♥. Plus we meet Haytham Kenway for the first time, one of the more interesting and divisive character's in Assassin's Creed lore. Although the game is overlong and can be tedious, it's a real contender for my favourite AC game. The sea-battles were underdevoloped but ambitious none-the-less, the voice acting is second to none and it really is a blockbuster experience in gaming, despite being slightly underwhelming.
If you're interested in accurate but loose depictions of history, this is a truly thrilling hit.

I'm trying really, really hard to love this game, but I just can't. Despite absolutely loving the first ten hours or so, the more I play it the more annoyed I get. Here's why.
The setting and main story are boring. They had 3000 years of Egyptian history to pick from and they gave us the least interesting choice possible. I sure hope you like Romans, Greeks and the same Cleopatra/Caesar story you've heard a million times, cause that's all you're gonna get. Egyptians? Not really. The civil war story is short with no build up and the historical characters are decidedly unhistorical and very unengaging. Ptolemy and Pompey are both on screen for probably less than two minutes total, and neither get any development. Caesar is the least Caesar I've ever seen, and the main bad guy comes out of nowhere and is completely unengaging. The Assassin/Templar story has never been more unwelcome and uninteresting.
Cleopatra is the only decent NPC in the game.
On top of all that the terrible modern day sections are back in full force.
That said, Bayek is a great character and his vengeance story is excellent. Aya is also pretty good, but she gets derailed by being so heavily involved in the mess of the main story. If they had focussed on the vengeance quest and exploring the beautiful open world they created, and had they relegated Caesar story to a fun background element, it would have been much better.
The gameplay itself is clunky and not very fun. Bayek feels very awkward to control both in and out of combat. The climbing is very stiff and the free running element is almost nonexistent. The only real tactic enemies use is to stun Bayek and go to town on him, so almost every time your best off just sniping them with a bow and avoiding the tedious combat all together. At least in previous titles the dodge/parry/kill system could almost feel zen and relaxing. This is just annoying.
The last little annoyance is their lootbox and timed event systems. This is a full priced AAA exclusively single player game and they still want to nickle and dime you for rare equipment and the only themed costumes in the game, and control the timing and conditions of how you access the content.
Get it when its on sale because the historical sandbox really is both beautiful and fun, and if you want some real Ancient Egyptian fun until then go pick up Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy instead.

Surprisingly good game, up there with AssCreed 2 in terms of quality and reviving the series. The game shamelessly rips off successful game design ideas from other games, and benefits from it immensely.
AssCreed doesn't feel like a cakewalk any more, difficulty settings and a change of combat system means you can no longer take down an entire crowd of enemies by simply spamming counter-attacks, multiple soldiers WILL take you down if you aren't careful. Stealth is therefore a necessary survival mechanic rather than an optional self-restriction.
Writing seems solid so far, Bayek is neither a brooding edgelord like Shay "I make my own luck" Cormac or a one-dimensional wiseguy like Ezio or that the MC from Unity who was only trying to get laid.
Visuals are nice, colours are really vibrant and the different environments do feel different.
Side activities don't feel contrived and repetitive (at least so far). Sidequests make sense from a writing perspective, collectibles are more involved than simply "find 100 feathers hidden around the city"

You will also in some dungeon encounter mini boss and ofc at the very end a boss.
Once a dungeon is done you can spend gold on upgrading your light attack or heavy or your passive. During your run you might also encounter a shop where you can buy potions such as an ekstra life or hp.

I've played for 15+ hours. I usually launch Roguelands from the "Commonapp" Steam directory without first launching Steam and thus Steam didn't record the vast majority of my play time. I have 3 chars that finished the storyline and unlocked all the race, avatars and recipes.
Summary: UNFINISHED. UNPOLISHED. UNPROFESSIONAL. DON'T BUY FOR MORE THAN 2 DOLLARS. Gets old VERY fast. Worlds are all the same. Multiplayer is difficult to set up. EVERYTHING WAS NERFED TO THE GROUND. Great music.
Full review: This is going to be a TL;DR because it's hard to appreciate how bad the game is without some context, so try to read through this to understand!
Unfinished, unpolished, unprofessional:
The dev has released an unfinished game then abandoned it, and has already moved on to another mobile game instead of finishing and polishing Roguelands. Instead, this game delivers on very little of what the original promises. Half of all the building material you find DON'T HAVE A PURPOSE YET. There is literally NO DIFFERENCE between many of the items besides cosmetic, probably because the dev hasn't finished them.
Very old very fast:
Literally every world has the same layout. They're just retextured. I have to admit the enemies do look different, but most of them use the same type of attacks and AI so it still feels the same, just graphically updated like some terrible HD remaster. The game starts with a refreshing novelty that really draws you in for the first hour or two, when you're learning to get the hang of the game. THEN it goes downhill from there because the game is unfinished and you run out of fun new things to find and discover.
Frustrating Multiplayer:
This game is only good with multiplayer. BUT! There is no lobby. You cannot find random players. You must play with people that you LAN with OR you need to get a third party program like Hamachi. Sometimes you even need to do port forwarding, which you can't if you don't have access to the your router, like dorm rooms or shared wifi.
NERFED:
I understand grinding, but you have to be rewarded for doing it. Otherwise, we'd all just stay in real life. The game used to be playable, you could have as much HP as you could level up, and skills did damage. But all the viable skills and items were nerfed (to be fair some DID need to be nerfed), and now you can only have 100 HP no matter what class you are. Does that make sense to you? The strength and vitality MELEE warrior has 100 max HP. THE GLASS CANNON RANGED GUN MAGE ALSO HAS 100 MAX HP. There's no such thing as defense, so somehow the dev thinks it is a good idea to not give warriors any benefit for being in melee range at all times. Keep in mind that later monsters do 20+ damage on contact.
The music is great though. I have to say that the first two hours of the game I was enamored by the atmosphere enhanced by the music.

First off, let me start by saying that I have played the game to near completion and am currently sitting at what looks to be one of the final battles of the game. As of this moment, I had to receive a save file from a developer twice to progress beyond points that were impossible in the current build of the game due to poorly thought out architecture in the game's "easy" mode known as Angel Mode.
The game, as of this moment is a bit crippled by launch day blues which, let's be honest, it can happen to the best of us. In it's current state, however, the game is completely unbeatable. That battle I'm on, as well as another one, seem to be impossible in their current states. One I could not finish as I had depleted the boss's health bars and they simply didn't die, and in the case I'm at? Well, the boss softlocks, and what I mean by that is upon defeating it it's collision box vanishes and no more damage can be done to it while it simply floats doing nothing.
I tried several times defeating the boss in numerous ways, and none of them worked rendering it impossible for me to clear the game. While I'd like to say those are the only oversights, that's not true. I've run into other odd things like becoming stuck inside the architecture at numerous points in the game and, horrifyingly enough, an endless death loop that requires restarting the entire game to avoid.
In it's current state, even for fans of hardcore platformers tailored to make you tear your hair out, the game just isn't quite there. If you're truly into these style of games, I'd strongly suggest waiting a week or two for all the bugs and kinks to be patched out. On the other end of the spectrum, I can't recommend this for anyone that's looking for a fun nor fair challenge as even on the easiest difficulty, dying to 3-4 attacks from any given enemy is common, and many segments feel pinpoint pixel precise rather than offering new and exciting challenges for the player to tackle.
Again, the latter complaint is just my humble opinion, but coupled with the other issues that are occuring I'd advise staying away from this game, at least for a little while until all the kinks are hopefully worked out.
EDIT: As of this moment, the bugs have indeed been fixed. A lot of optimizations have come into play, there are still some issues here and there. I have indeed finished since, however I still can't recommend the game on personal principles. Many of the complaints on design stand from a personal standpoint and my opinion stands that I personally wouldn't recommend this game. However, fans of pixel precision and spending hours gleefully hitting the R key will now find a lot to enjoy!

I've played TERA since it's Korean launch, had moved to North American servers, and I'm going to give some insight for anyone interested...
Don't play TERA. It's a Korean grinder, the community is comparable to EVE Onlines or League of Legends. In other words, terminal cancer. The graphics are lovely, the world can be quite immersive, and customization is okay for it's time, but it's major flaw is the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor optimization. As for the combat, it's quite nice and feels rewarding. The issue past that is the ever present genderlocking of classes.
The base classes of the game, being Lancer (tank), Slayer (DPS), Warrior (evasion tank/sustained DPS), Sorcerer (DPS), Archer (DPS), Mystic (support DPS/healer), Berserker (tank/DPS), and Priest (healer) are available to all races and genders, meanwhile classes such as Reaper (DPS), Ninja (DPS), Brawler (tank), and Gunner (DPS) are gender and race locked specifically. So if you wanted to punch something to death as a buff rock man, tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ you're stuck playing as a human female in skimpy "armor."
Another biggie, especially if you're looking more into PvP action, is that PvP is dead. Recent changes equalized all PvP battlegrounds, so if you're gearing for PvP, you've wasted your time because that gear doesn't apply anywhere outside of open world. Outside of Kumas Royale, which will be accessable at level 20, most battlegrounds are inactive. What used to be one of the most played battlegrounds, Corsairs Stronghold, takes almost two hours for a queue to pop, if not more.
What this game does great is only the combat. Dungeon runs are quite fun, and boss mechanics are something to look out for; especially in Ruinous Manor, Lilith's Keep, and Shadow Sanguiary. Dungeons are also presented with normal and hard modes. Hard mode dungeons really test your reaction time and skill... or whether your computer and ping are garbage or not. That's a thing too. Endgame is quite run of the mill. Every few months, grind for new gear, enchant, pray to RNG gods, rinse, and repeat.
For the lore lovers, you will be heavily dissappointed here. Lore is all but forgotten until there's a smidgen of plot at endgame, which isn't even worth it in my book as a hardcore lore hunter in mmos. The game used to have a pretty nice story and was well paced so you could see all the locations and vistas you want without that feeling of being pushed towards the end. I've brought this up, as well as many other players, with the result being "you think you want this but you don't" as a reply.
Overall, I recommend this game only if you want good combat. Otherwise, go play Guild Wars 2 or something, or one of those new mmos with a company that gives a damn about it's playerbase and listens to them. Don't give money to a company that doesn't care about the state of their game or the people who support it.

I like this type of games, third person MMORPGs. So I was excited when I first started playing TERA.
I started as an archer because in my experience, archers can get very powerful and I was in a PvP server. Archer felt rather weak, constantly dying, partly due to my lack of experience in the game. So I made a brawler, shame you can only make female brawlers but it gets the job done.
DISCLAIMER: THIS IS FROM A F2P POINT OF VIEW. I HAVE NOT, AND MOST LIKELY WILL NOT, SPEND ANY REAL WORLD MONEY IN THIS GAME.
Pros:
Leveling up: Rather easy to level up by yourself. No need for a party unless you're doing a dungeon.
Not that hard to understand: Ignoring lore, stories and what not, you can eventually learn how to make weapons, gear, accesories without anyone's help which is great because a lot of people can be toxic/not willing to help new players (but that's not exclusive to TERA community).
Fun combat: It is rather easy to beat enemies by yourself without requiring much, if any heals. You eventually get good combos which you can learn to use to exploit their maximum benefit/potential.
Weapons/Gear: Weapons and gear are rather generic looking (i.e. Female characters wear almost nothing, while male characters are basically covered head to toes). It's really easy to learn to differentiate which item is more powerful than others thus helping you upgrade your gear. There's no need to refine/enchant it (whatever it's called) until you reach max level.
Control: Its controllers are rather common (WASD for movement), the only thing I found weird but grew on me was that you have to press the Esc key to move the mouse around your HUD (i.e. for Options, and logging out and what not).

Cons:
Dungeons: It can take a while to get a party for a dungeon, there's rarely any decent explanation of what to do in the dungeon even for first-timers.
Items/Drops: When you receive items, drops or rewards, there's hardly any explanation on the item's description. You might be selling something really valuable on the Trade Broker/Auction house that might be useful to you or a friend later in the game. (I have most likely made this mistake with items I received early in the game. I already have over 1k gold, at level 5x).
Weapons/Gear: While I did list this as a pro, there's also a downside. Endgame gear and weaponry can be pretty expensive in many games but from what I've heard, in TERA, this is really bad. Endgame weapon for your class can be rather "cheap", but enchanting/refining it to its highest potential is stupidly expensive. Don't know how much of an upgrade it might be but it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to see it making a big difference in the price, especially for the go-getters.
