Mini Ninjas is a kids game where you play as Hiro, the Kuji magic wielding ninja tasked to destroy the Evil Samurai Warlord. Along your quest, you will find and rescue your fellow ninjas, Futo (the hammer guy), Shun (the archer), Suzume(the flute girl), Tora(the claw guy) and Kunoichi (the spear girl). Why an adult is playing this is totally unexplainable.
Gameplay-wise, you should be using a controller. You can alternate between the different ninjas that you have rescued with Hiro being the main ninja. Only Hiro can use Kuji Magic. Each ninja comes with a different way of fighting. Hiro uses a sword and Kuji Magic and his special attack will 1-hit KO any small samurai. Futo uses a hammer and is used to kill big armoured samurai. Suzume hits enemies with a flute and her special attack is to make enemies dance. Shun uses a bow and arrow to kill ranged enemies and his special is to fire an exploding arrow. Tora uses claws and his special attack is running around really fast and damaging anyone who touches him. Kunoichi uses a spear and her special attack is to spin around.
There is a stealth option in this game but it is very unnecessary. Most of the time you are given 2 paths to move onto the next area. One will avoid the enemy and the other will go straight through them. You will find yourself simply killing all the enemies in the way with Hiro's special attack.
The bosses are all quicktime battles where you try to press whatever key appears on the screen and/or rapidly press the X/A button. Every boss only needs to be hit 3 times for you to win. Only the Evil Samurai Warlord is a non-quicktime battle and requires you to use Kuji Magic to kill him. Meteor Storm made it simple enough.
There are collectibles like plants, which have an in-game use for crafting potions. You can buy the crafting potion recipes from a Tengu using coins. You collect coins by breaking jars and enemy tents. The potions do basic things like refilling your health, Ki and special attacks but they also come in the form of burping potions, arrow reflecting potions and essence of fish. These non-standard potions make me enjoy the game a little more.
Kuji Magics are diverse at the beginning when you can inhabit animals, search for shrines, light and summon bushes to hide in. However, most of them are generic damage spells like lightning, tornado, meteor storm and fireball.
Conclusion, it's an okay game since this is for kids. You will most likely get the feeling that this game is just barely passable. The difficulty is perfect for the little ones. The game has the potential to be greatly improved. For the studio that made hitman, stealth is really sub-par in this game.
Note: The developer is IO Interactive, a studio in Coppenhgen, Denmark. They were bought over by Square Enix. They are best known for the Hitman series.
1. Cute Game
All the little samurais going "Nin, Nin, Nin, Ninja".
2. Quite a Few Mechanics
I like how there are so many different ideas put into the Kuji spells, ninja special attacks and itemization. There is even cool stuff that you can do with the bamboo hat and fishing too.
3. Bob Sledding
For some reason, I enjoyed that part a lot.
4. Big Koi Fishing
I loved the ride.
5. Funny Potions
The non-standard potions are quite cute. Also, arrow reflecting was super useful.
6. Ninja Backstories
I liked those a lot.
1. Lack of Use for Other Characters
Throughout the entire game, you will only ever need to use 3 heroes. Hiro for killing, Shun for ranged killing and Futo for killing big armoured baddies. I had no need for Suzume, Tora or Kunoichi.
2. The Bottom Right Of the Screen is For Kuji Magic Only
Since only Hiro can use Kuji Magic, the bottom right is totally wasted with any of the other characters.
3. Big Empty Spaces
Big castle then big empty spaces outside.
4. Hitbox Glitches
When you hit an arrow tower or crate, you will notice that Futo's, Suzume's, Tora's and Kunoichi's hit boxes are extremely hard to connect despite their weapons swinging all over the place.
5. No Experience Given For Choosing the Path of Stealth
If you don't kill enemies, you don't get experience points. So, who would choose the path of stealth?
6. Repetitive Kuji Spells
Most spells seems to fall into aim-the-circle-at-the-enemy category. Only spells like Spirit Form,
7. Spirit Form is Really Just For Bear Form
Crane is a joke since it can't fly. All the small critters don't serve any use as there are no secret areas to access with tiny critters. You simply use the bear to one-hit enemies.
8. No Swimming
All that water with nothing to do underneatth.
9. Stealth is Very Lame
Squatting in the grass, hiding in a bush or summoning a bush to hide in. That's all a ninja can do? What happened to swimming with a reed in your mouth?
10. Snoring With the Ninja Assassin
Was this one on purpose? Did the developer really use a snore to voice over the ninja assassin? They must have been really bored with after a certain point.
1. Different Enemies
Small samurai, big samurai, flute monk, ghost, ninja assassin. It stops there. Seems okay but I think more could have been done.
1. Improve Other Character Usage
a. Futo could break walls with his hammer.
b. Suzume could summon animals to fight for you with her flute or put enemies to sleep
c. Tora can climb special walls with vines with his claws and move up and down on them
d. Kunoichi can high jump to special locations by using her spear as a pole. Her special attack never misses and can break blocks.
2. More Rewards for the Stealth Route
You are not rewarded for choosing the path of stealth.

Good game.  Hopefully, there will be more content, with machineguns, cavalry, and other things being added on latter.  The Devs have promised multiplayer, so there is that to look forward to as well.
The good:
The Artillery is very good at killing swathes of men.
The war is a big stalemate at times, a dynamic tug of war.  There aren't many games that do that so well.  Most times it is just all in one big battle, after which there is then a rout and destruction of the base.
The Atmosphere is decent as well.  It really gives you a feel of scale, when you have masses of men building pontoons over the marsh, taking a hospital, and shells that actually hit and get stopped by the trees.  The trenches spawn barbed wire, and engineers dig new trenches out of holes in the ground.
The bad:
The graphics look awful.  Not that I care, but some people do.  One thing of note is that the enemy is just a recolored version of your own troops.  Sometimes, the planes and tanks look pretty similar, and I'm sure someone who is red-green color blind will have trouble distinguishing between the units.
This is doubly so in that you can litterally not tell how many units are on top of each other.  In my opinion, this is skub, but I'm putting it as a notch against the game.  My reasoning is that it might simulate the fact that during the smoke and fog, you might not be able to tell how many troops are in the trenches.
It is hard to see what you are supposed to be doing at times.  For example, in the early missions, you get nothing but Infantry in trenches.  It becomes a struggle to defeat the enemy.
Snipers don't seem to do anything against entrentched infantry and other snipers.  They just sit behind the lines taking shots that do litterally nothing.
Compared to most of the other games in the genre, the unit selection is decent.  But I'm missing my MGs, Sturmtruppen, officers, and lobster armor men, cavalry, and grenadiers.
The game is pretty easy with all the units unlocked.  Obviously, somebody will figure out the pro-strats in this type of game very quickly when they are familiar with this type of game, but I've gotten pretty far in on normal with little to no challenge.
Last thing, is that the game lacks a setting.  Campaigns are labeled, but other than that everything is abstracted.  A good example is the game trenches II.  Every campaign mission in trenches is themed after an actual battle.  All this game needs are battles that have names people can look up and say, "Hey, cool, this map has a lot of mud and rain, just like in the battle of the Somme".
A good example is naming one of the maps the Battle of Mons and limiting the game to infantry, snipers, and artillery, and possibly limiting the trenches on the map.  Then the enemy would have a massive resource advantage, where they'd storm through with infantry.
Final Verdict:
It is free.  Go play it to learn about WW1 a bit in a semi-historical fashion.  Hopefully, it will get better as time goes on.

So first off I have to say that the multiplayer is so buggy glitchy laggy that it was near impossible to all get into a room, this is the first review with 2 video parts as it became necessary.
Part 1 - The Setup
If you watch the Video some of the apparent bugs in this game for steam is the volume control is set SO LOUD as you start the game, even when you change the settings the volume EXPLODES then adjusts to your settings at the menu, Next was the problem with the Online play... when trying to make a room and invite people we were never all able to stay in the same room people crashed got kicked black screened and more occurred, Then we discovered the search feature which allowed us to all get into a room together... ONLY because no one was playing this game at all we managed to always get a room together, which was a plus ONLY in this situation. After getting that working we never did get around to checking out the tutorial, until the end of the next video. but now that we finally got in here is where the gameplay actually started!
Here is my groups actual game play, and DAMN this game is much harder then you would expect even with a group of players.
As our adventure began we found out shortly that death is easy... reviving is hard... and there is not enough lives to save us. Using the WASD controls AND mouse made it an interesting experience, We also learned what those torches did in the beginning of the game, they seem to be game modifiers for more or less points? But as we ventured on we died, A LOT and we missed jumping A LOT, this whole game was a massive fest of hordes which I liked, but how squishy we all were 4 of us you would think would survive better against the masses, but if you choose the bow, you were dead 10x over. Working through the crashes and bugs there were many features which would have been helpful due to the instability. This game is NOT fully functional but it is a PROMISING GAME for a dungeon crawler... but it lacked the MAIN thing I want in a dungeon crawler... LOOT, DROPS. GOODIES... powerups... All that ever fell was GOLD and BEER. which is nice, but you never had enough health and you NEVER found enough gold. I wanted Armor Weapons accessories, EXP and so much more from this style of game that just did not exist. which made the game redundant with no REAL thing to aim for, as all weapons that you can buy from the hero shop cost SO MANY GEMS it was insane. And the lack of a driving story made me less inclined to continue. as well as you get a shop to buy health and lives... THEN it sends you through a DEATH MAZE to get to the boss... But enough of that as you get the ide here are the pros and cons.
Pros:
- Fun character designs and colors (looks a lot like castle crashers tho)
- randomly generated dungeons and dangers
- Multiplayer for added fun
- Gold is always split so no one is left out!
- fun skills and concepts such as Picking up your friends or enemies, and stacking up for skills tornado
- The funny Quotes the narrator says at the beginning of a dungeon
- Adorably FEARSOME enemies,
- Great textures and environments!
Cons:
- NO VOLUME CONTROL IN GAME, or options
- Tutorial is broken, you cannot jump until you hit ESC and resume, and yet does not teach you the skills you need to survive.
- Sound is WAY TOO LOUD, should either be quieter or be defaulted to a lower volume to be turned up as needed
- Narrator has 1 line in the beginning and then nothing
- There is NO STORY, no reason, no goal explained.
- Not enough gold
- Not enough lives
- No loot, armor, weapons ANYTHING, that drops except gold and beer.
- UNSTABLE MULTIPLAYER, this was the biggest kick in the shorts, it was so difficult to get into a multiplayer game it had to be a separate video!
- If a player disconnected they could not come back, which was a huge damage to our playing because we had to start over.
- Overall lacked any depth
- All characters had the same skills, it would seem a better plan to have everyone have a useful SPECIAL skill or different weapons.
- to Play without crashing I had to play in WINDOW mode in order to do so. I do not know what caused that.
So as I write this review I would have to say it is mostly negative...   but I honestly believe this game can be something GREAT... but it has a lot of things it needs to be a Dungeon crawler, Items, inventory, rarities, Reasons to make it re-playable and customizable, it needs a story, in this case a REALLY STUPID FUNNY STORY that makes no real sense as to why it matters. Things to drive the payers to keep going rack up hours collect items, because I have no real desire to play the game alone, and it is too difficult to find people to play with in it's current state. More voices taunts comments between characters, just in general it needs more.... if this game had more people playing it I would keep playing it as it evolves... but it needs new things right now to really give me the desire. With all of the crashing and unable to connect and errors my other people were having it was such a chore to play we almost quit before we started. I WILL recommend this game as it is worth a multiplayer at home experience just as a time waster between other things... but the potential this game has ... this game is less then 10% of what it could be. it needs more people because being able to get your team through the search feature showed NO ONE is playing this on steam currently.and the chances of me getting this exact team back together to play with me is very slim after this experience. its a great on the couch home game as it is now... but to make it worth your money it needs a lot of work. But this game concept of yours is sound. I really did enjoy the game for what it is, but I would become a die hard fan if it became so much more then this.

Super Dungeon Bros strikes me as a light-hearted & accessible rogue-like/lite isometric hack-&-slash ARPG-lite that's aimed more at casual fun rather than hardcore grinding... but that does not mean it's easy.
Here are some of my first impressions after my initial few hours playing Super Dungeon Bros (purchased myself directly through Steam for Windows on Nov. 5, 2016 & played solo/local using a wired/USB Xbox 360 controller/gamepad).
+ Simple to pick-up-&-play.
+ Good visuals, audio, controls, action, atmosphere, & functional quality/stability for the price.
+ Vibrant comical fantasy art design.
+ Well-designed user interface.
+ The overall "fun factor" is there for me (though I know "fun factor" is very subjective).
- Hordes of many types of enemies (close-range/melee, long-range/shooters, traps, etc.) often cover the screen, leaving you no room to safely maneuver and unable to attack/escape without taking lots of damage (and/or dying).
- When you melee (sword/hammer) attack, you stand still momentarily, which leaves you vulnerable to the legions of slashing enemies, flying arrows/beams, & traps all simultaneously coming at you from every direction.
- I feel like there's a slight delay (extra/long frame data?) between each distinct player action (attack, jump, grab-&-throw, dodge/roll, move, etc.) that makes combat less fluid than I wish it was. This brief delay continually leaves me vulnerable to more enemy attacks. A more rapid flow/transition between my actions could really help deal with enemy mobs better.
- The game spams big mobs of enemies, but players have no effective "spamable" attacks or moves.
- The rate that summoners spawn new minions is too fast. After dispatching a round of summoned minions, there's no time to attack & eliminate the summoner because he instantly spawns more minions infinitely. This makes an area with multiple summoners virtually impossible to pass (for me). After eliminating summoned minions, there should be a delay before the summoner can spawn more minions.
- Despite the twin-stick-shooter-style controls & mechanics, strafing (moving one direction while aiming & attacking in another direction) is significantly slower than normal non-strafing movement.
- Some enemies appear to have a damaging aura around them, and the sword's & hammer's ranges appear to be too short to attack those enemies without taking damage yourself (or maybe I'm just going about it wrong).
- Ranged enemies can attack you from upstairs/downstairs, but your ranged attacks cannot reach enemies that are upstairs/downstairs.
- The initial crossbow's small ammo capacity, weak damage, & eternal reload time makes the weapon woefully inadequate. It constantly leaves you helplessly running from mobs waiting to reload.
- Achievements don't seem to pop until you close/exit the game.
-- The best way I can think of to try to describe what I think is the biggest fundamental problem with much of the combat in this game is what seems to me like (in fighting game parlance) unfavorable frame data... For example: you swing your weapon to attack an enemy & (hypothetically) say it takes 30 frames for your attack animation to complete; you are locked into that entire 30 frames of attack animation & unable to do anything else until after it completes entirely; but a few frames after you've initiated your attack & before your attack connects with your target, the enemy you're attacking (or multiple other enemies in the screen-spanning mob) takes a shot at you with their own attack that (hypothetically) takes 20 frames to complete (10 frames faster than your own attack); you cannot avoid taking that damage because you're still locked (& can't even move) in your own attack animation while you're being attacked. This puts you at a vulnerable disadvantage every time you attack, especially heavy attacks, and/or attacking with hammers, and/or when dealing with hordes of enemies. I would love to see this re-balanced somehow, either by speeding up (reducing) the player's attack frames, or maybe by giving players some way to cancel out of their attacks before they complete (perhaps with the dodge/roll move), or maybe by some way of having player attacks interrupt/cancel enemy attacks, or maybe even by giving the player some invulnerability frames while attacking, or by some other better solution.
• Faster flow/transition between player actions (shorten/decrease frames/delay between actions).
• Faster strafing
• Ability to repeatedly dodge/roll more before waiting (dizzy) to recharge the dodge/roll ability, along with faster recharge of dodge/roll ability.
• Instead of finger-cramping button mashing, let players hold down an attack button to automatically swing melee (sword/hammer) attacks repeatedly.
• Ability to attack while jumping.
• Free pick-ups to recharge your ultimate attack (or auto-regenerating ultimate charge).
• More health pick-ups (or more frequently/easily-obtained health/armor power-ups/buffs, or auto-regenerating health).
• More noticeable indicators when the player takes damage (the first couple times I died, I didn't even realize I had been taking hits).
• Longer "magnetic" reach/distance to pull in coins/pick-ups.
• Access to game options from pause menu while playing.
• Built-in configurable frame-rate cap/limiter option.
• Built-in support for borderless full-screen window option. (I have not yet had any issues with Alt+Enter to switch between full-screen & windowed, nor any issues yet with Alt+Tab to switch back-&-forth between the game & other apps.)
So far, Super Dungeon Bros has definitely been fun enough to make me want to keep playing more. The game delivers on its claims, and it works without crashing/freezing or suffering from major game-breaking defects (for me, so far). I've tried playing public/online co-op, but I guess there aren't enough players yet (so soon after launch), as the game doesn't match me with anyone after several minutes of waiting in a lobby.
As it is (at launch), I think Super Dungeon Bros is a reasonably well-made & decently fun little indie game... but if some simple improvements to some of the game's basic mechanics were to be updated/patched in (like some of the items I previously mentioned above), I think this game could explode into something spectacularly addictive. :)
Of course, this is all just my opinion based on my own preferences. Others may have different opinions & preferences.
(I may edit/update this review later as I progress further in the game and/or as the game evolves.)
• Jump... As the game's title hints (for retro gaming fans), you can jump on some enemies to inflict a small amount of damage. If you get surrounded & trapped by a swarm of enemies closing in around you, try to jump on them & over them to get away. Holding the jump button while moving is sometimes a good way to bounce around & avoid enemy attacks.
• The Howling Gale Wand is one of the first unlockable weapons, and I have found it to be the most useful weapon in the initial arsenal, as it combines infinite (no-reloading-needed) piercing ranged attacks with close-quarters melee attacks, along with a minor heal in its ultimate attack.
• I haven't noticed any functional differences between playable characters, just visual/cosmetic & audio (spoken lines/taunts) differences. Your stats & abilities appear to be affected only by your weapon choice, not your character choice.
Good luck & have fun.

Tera, as a long time MMO player, I have mixed feelings on Tera at this point.  The tutorial is fine, gets you through within 30 minutes.  So far at the lower levels the game is pretty Vanilla, Easy to kill monsters, not finding a lot of challenge in the go kill x of mob and collect x of a thingy.  The story line is OK, it keeps you moving forward, and there are constant awards to entice you to keep moving along.
At the end of the day you can play for free, but you are of course limited to character slots and I am sure a few other things that I have yet to discover.  The elite membership does have some advantages but have yet to buy into dropping 15$ US  amonth for some extra gold and experience.  Of course the travel map and a faster mount is always enticing.
There is a good variety of player types, some are easier than others.  I have enjoyed the ninja and gunner class, tried the socerer not so much.  Like most mature MMO's this game keeps you moving along until end game.  I suspect that if you dropped a bit of real world cash you could hit max level in a day or two.
There is no lack of things to do, lots of quests, including daily's for added rewards, dungons and pvp. Through the low level PVP was pretty sad as  you are transported into a crib like area that looks very cartoony as a panda with a diaper and it is basically kill the boss before the other team kills him.  have to say not alot of fun.

Nothing to dislike about this game if you like MMO in anime setting.  It is not a WOW killer by any means.  But there were people playing had no issues finding dungeon groups.  This game does not break the mold of MMOs, but it is nice,
7.5/10 I think it is solid game, that will offer the casual gamer a good MMO experience, I would rate it a bit higher, but not a fan of anime style games and the look of the avatars.   But that is my hang up.

This is a masterpiece.
That's it, it's all I can say about this game. This for me is what The Witcher 3 is allegedly for its horde of fans. The developers took almost every mechanic that makes open-world games fun - great sidequests, freedom of exploration and parkour, Far Cry-esque bases, different combat styles for different weapons, RPG-styled loot and progression, even minigames - hippodrome races and gladiator fights (left out Nemesis system from SoM/SoW though, which is a shame - it would've been perfect for Phylake bosses) and put them all into Ancient Egypt, which is so masterfully recreated, it's unreal. From the Great Pyramids to the Lighthouse of Alexandria, from roman colonies to seas of sand, from ancient tombs to shores of the Nile - it's the most diverse and beautiful open world created in games, ever. This is the first game that made me
to not use fast travel, because of great "autopilot" system that guides your mount to the destination while you can just take in the world. And take screenshots.
But it's not only big open-world stuff this game is great at, it's the little things too. I can talk about this game's hidden features and details for hours, like, being able to pet cats or feed your eagle or putting on/taking off your hood/helmet. But the one I can't not mention is papyrus puzzles. These are little texts containing a description of a specific place in the world, and if you manage to find it, you'll find a treasure. There is no dot on the map for those, and you won't see them with eagle vision - you actually have to read the hints and look for a place completely on your own. In the decade of "press X to win"-mentality this was quite an unexpected (but very welcome) kind of side-activity for sure.
In short: buy it. Yesterday. A week ago. Preorder it for all I care - it is worth it. And it's coming from someone who never played an AC title before and didn't even like ancient Egypt much (I definitely do now though). I've played through it twice, 100%-ing it on the second run, and it took me 100 hours. And I still want more stuff to do, I don't feel "done" with it yet. I will surely look forward to updates/expansions/sequels.

This is an absolutely lovely game, and by far one of the best platformers I've played here on Steam. I'd even go as far as say it's one of the best platformers of recent times, up there with classics like Super Meat Boy. The reason I bring up Super Meat Boy is that, like that game, this game is also very difficult. As stated in the game's description "Wings of Vi is a challenging 2D platformer...", and it means it. Do not pick this game up expecting some walk in the park that you can simply breeze through. It takes quiet a while to get into the game's mechanics, mainly the drop-jumping and floating which you get a little later on. For me it took maybe 2 hours or so of platforming before I got anywhere near decent, and once I thought I had got aquainted with it, the game handed me another powerup and gave me a bunch of new challenges to overcome. It does a good job of showing you what you can and cannot do with said abilities, and does its best to ease you into it which it also does a decent job of. Some rooms may seem impossible at first, but if you experiment with which order you use your abilities in, be it dropping down from a ledge, then floating a bit and finishing it off with a doublejump, or maybe dashing at the start for some extra momentum and instead jumping early for some good height before you begin floating, it's really fun trying your way forward until you find that one combination which seems to work and perfecting it until you complete the task at hand and may continue onward.
The game looks gorgeous with beautifully drawn and well animated pixel art, an interesting array of characters and from what I've seen so far a fairly good set of enemies as well. The game also features massive bosses which may feel like yet another huge difficulty spike, and may get you stuck on them for a while, but never in such a way that it feels unfair. You simply need to try again and again until you figure out what to do and how to do it, and when you succeed it feels great!
For people who are accustomed to the platformers of today, this might seem like an impossible, cruel and downright idiotic experience. But to those who enjoy the challenge of older platformers, or those who simply are willing to give the game a chance and aren't too afraid of a challenge, I recommend this game whole heartedly. It has got what seems like quiet a lot of content, several difficulty modes, (Yes you can play on an equivalent of Easy, I have not tried it yet so I cannot say if it is still difficult but the option is there at least), Unlockable accessories which you can customize your heroine with; ranging from wings, hats and dresses to tails, glasses and hairstyles. (You can even unlock different companions who follow you around.)
The game is, so far at least, straightforward so it's not really a Metroidvania type game, but the upgrades you obtain help you progress in new and cool ways and help keep the game refreshing. Exploring a bit and jumping off where the game doesn't seem to lead you often awards you with a chest filled with collectibles. The devs weren't sure exaclty how long the game could be, which is understandable since it is a very skill focused game, and someone who learns fast and is a master at platforming will beat the game much faster than someone who takes a few tries to get it right (That's me), but somewhere around 20 hours could be expected. So far I am 5 hours in and only 20% complete from the looks of it, so seems pretty much spot on.
The game's soundtrack isn't extremely outstanding in my opinion, but it makes every stage feel different and keeps you going despite how frustrating some of the rooms can be at times. A few of the tracks are really nice to listen to by themselves as well, so I do hope the soundtrack makes it way to Steam. I would likely pick it up.
If you aren't afraid of a challenge, and feel you could fancy a bit of oldschool platforming, pick this game up! It is definitely worth the price and will likely be worth replaying more than once!

An exercise in frustration from a designer that's just not very good.
No, I didn't get very far because having my time wasted is just tiresome.
The primary mechanic is a drop-jump, where you can jump anywhere in midair, but only once. This means basically every jump you think you MIGHT be able to make...you can't. Unless you run off the ledge, then jump in midair for that extra foot of boost. So every time you just approach a jump like any sensible game, you're going to be short. And die. And forced to replay a section.
Then you get a flutter-feather item that allows you to hover briefly, and immediately are forced to use it to snake between instant-kill traps on the top and bottom. If you mess up? Yes, you're replaying a section again.
The instant-kill traps are chained in succession immediately after you get the flutter item, meaning you're going to be forced to replay the same bits over and over right when a powerup should be FUN: When you get to play around with it and see how your skillset has expanded. Instead any enjoyment you'd derive from a new item and new exploration/manoeuvre ability is killed by immediately being told you have to be an expert with it, or else you're going to hit your head against the wall.
Even in the short amount I played, I ran into three seperate enemies/obstacles that were invulnerable, but still reacted and appeared to take damage when attacked...only displaying a "0" showed me they weren't taking damage. This is honestly unacceptable. If you can't damage an enemy MAKE THAT PLAIN via another type of reaction. If they're never killable, make them not able to be hit at all. If you can do it, later, somehow...use some kind of "bounce off" where it's plain you're hitting but just unable to injure.
Add to this enemies that fly around rapidly, take multiple hits, and who aren't hitstunned so they simply run through your attacks and hit you...and you have a recipe for tremendous frustration at the designer.
At this point I just became frustrated and quit, I'm unwilling/unable to force myself through the bad design any more in order to try to find the "good" in the game.
Could have used actual playtesting from someone not interested in how "hardcore" they are. I'd recommend it to no-one.
Addendum: All the comments I'm receiving are "You suck at this genre, so get good." Maybe I do. But maybe people would like to know beforehand what the game is like, for people who don't excel in this particular genre of game. It isn't noted anywhere in particular that the game is extremely difficult in a particularly genre-specific manner. It just looks like a 2D platformer with some well-done visuals.
If you know you like this type of game, my review isn't going to be useful. If you aren't aware what sort of game this is, and you don't like that type of game? It's probably going to be useful. That's why this review is here.

First of all, I want to point out that this is not a bad game. Not quite. There are many things done very well, and it has lots and lots of decent ideas. But then again, it was Ubisoft who made that game, and as we well know they have to screw something up sooner or later. And they did. And so, the wasted potential of Assassins Creed III pours right out of the screen.
Let's start with good things, though. It has a great setting. I am honestly surprised that there are very few companies who decided to use western or semi-western times to set their game in. Although I don't know if this one qualifies as one set in the Wild West, it does have native americans, so for me, it counts.
I wish it was not, but I have to admit that this is as close as we are gonna get to a good game in those climates on PCs... with exeption of Activision's GUN of course.
Moving on. This game has hunting. And it is awesome. For a while, at least. It is really well done, and can be used as an easy way to make some money. Includes everything, baits, trapping, and air assassination performed on deer.
The environments are as good as you would expect from an AC game. Pretty when you look at them, and while traversing the landscape you will find lots of ways to use it to your advantage. You can hide in bushes, too, which is cool.
Connor's weaponry has some variety to it, too. You get a tomahawk, a rope dart, whatever that is, poison darts, a flintlock pistol, or even two, and you can even use a musket, and you get all your standard AC stuff.
One thing that bugs me, is that Connor does not have to aim down the sights. He just fires, and hits. Every time. But he is an Assassin, so I will let that slide.
But all the good things about this game get pounded into dirt by it's controls. Remember how in AC2 you had four buttons to work with? Legs, head, hand and high profile? Well, here you got one. For all those functions. It makes it impossible to choose what you want to do in some spots, when you have two options. It is borderline random.
Fighting bad guys feels how it should though. You got your counter attack, combos, all that stuff, and stats of your weapon sometimes even matter. It is a somewhat decent aspect of this game.
Let's talk about the protagonist now. Connor. He is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥. I don't like him. I honestly wish that I could play through entire game as the templars. Oh, did I mention? You don't even meet Connor until you are one-third into the game! Okay, enough with the spoilers.
It does have open world, too... but it sucks. Compared to AC2 or other similiar titles, like Prototype, or Red Dead Redemption (not released on PCs, **** you, Rockstar), it feels empty. It has some intresting sidequests, like Captain's Kidd Treasures, but most of them are boring. Like assassination contracts. You don't get a single target to whom you need to get to and kill. You get five nameless dudes, who sometimes get a map marker, and sometimes they don't. It really isn't what I expected, and I was disappointed.
What I kept coming back for, were the naval missions. Sailing near the coast of US of A was a really nice experience, and ship battles were very well done too... which is why they made Assassins Creed IV. And if you want ships, you shoud buy four, not three. But it was done in three, and I respect that.
Also, you can climb trees, now. Thank you, Rebecca. I have waited long enough.
The multiplayer mode is there, but it couldn't hold your attention for too long. It is somewhat better than the previous one, but not that much of an improvement.
As you play through the game you will get that strange feeling. You will know that all of that could, and should, have been done better. If they gave it more time, it could be a really good game. But sadly, they didn't.
The game was much shorter than I anticipated. I beat the main story in one night. Almost. Again, I will compare it to it's predecessor, AC2. Remember the net of all the big fishes in there? It was cool. You had something to pursue. In three, you have five dudes. One of them is just a mercenary. That is what I call laziness, ladies and gentlemen.
Overall, this game is not terrible. It is not even bad. Closer to unfinished, but decent, still. Nearly impossibly hard to 100% it, and a bit frustrating, but decent. And yet, it is not as good as previous one. And I am not talking about Revelations or Brotherhood. Those do not count. If you want the best in series, better get Assassins Creed 2. If you own an XBOX360 or PS3, buy Red Dead Redemption. I can't honestly recommend this game at full price, but if you find it for 10 euro, you might want to pick it up. It is not a bad experience.
Assassin's Creed III gets my six out of ten.

This game is what happens when devs get it right _and_ have fun doing it.
Although short and aimed more at a younger audience, Mini Ninjas is a fantastic and fun adventure through an imaginary Japan. The controls are well thought-out, intuitive and introduced at a nice pace. The scenery is a sort of faux-cell shading, but pleasant to look at.
There are 5 different characters, which you unlock as you progress through the game. Each come with their own skills and super moves and you'll be using at least 3 of these characters to get the most from the game, depending on the situation. The main character is also capable of casting various spells, which you also unlock as you progress.
The fighting and pseudo parkour are fun enough to keep one entertained all the way to the final boss, however there are also items to collect, spell shrines to find, jizo statues to discover and animals to free... all tallied in a handy pause menu list for the perfectionist.
Play-through time is just shy of 8 hours, and it could easily be sped through in 6, however, I skipped a spell and only managed to get all Jizo statues in 2 of the levels, so there's room to re-visit and explore every nook and cranny.
Overall, 9/10. Will probably play again in a year or so.

TL:DR Has a promising start setting up a potentially intersting story and atmosphere but never delivers on that potential
Home starts off really well. Your character wakes up in a room with a dead body and no idea of what happened or how he got there. The atmosphere feels really tense at the begin with you only able to see within the circle of light from your flashlight as you explore the otherwise almost completely dark surroundings. However as you play you'll find there isnt anything that will attack you or present any danger to your character and this sort of kills the tension a bit. You spend the game just going through doors and reading the snippets of text when you interact with glowing objects. There are some light puzzles but nothing that will challenge you in the slightest.
You are expected to piece together what has happened from the bits of text you read when you interact with objects however the end of the game (without spoiling things too much) makes this redundant by asking you to make your own conclusion. This would be fine if the stuff you learn throughout the game added up to a intriguing story but it doesn't. Instead its all vague and a bit cliched and it feels more like laziness on the part of the devs to come up without a good story with a great conclusion.
Good points:
- the beginning is quite good even if the rest of the game doesnt fall through.
Bad points:

This game is actually pretty fun despite its maddening flaws. It is easy to pick up and has enough customization to keep it interesting, but not so much to be overwhelming and slow everything down. The graphics are simple but serve it well.
I have rage quit this game quite a few times, but still come back and find myself  keep wanting to play it.
My number one gripe is the randomization of everything everytime you start it. I like a certain amount of unpredictability, which is why I tend to ignore complaints in game reviews whining about the "RNG" , but this game is just too random sometimes.
You start with a random amount of money and upgrade points, and you never know what kind of enemies are going to be spawned in different sectors. Its not uncommon to start with barely enough points to get weak weapons on a single ship and jump to the first sector where an enemy flagship armada destroys you on your first turn before you can even attempt to flee.
You also have to grind quite a bit to get the XP to unlock better ships, and they won't open up until you have lost which kind of sucks when you are actually doing well and have a decent cash reserve going.
Despite this, I got the game on a pretty steep discount for 99 cents and still keep coming back to hopefully overcome the odds, so it feels like a good purchase that I have no regrets about.
Plus the space combat is pretty fun especially when you have a few ships in your fleet armed with good weapons.
As always I also appreciate the devs for providing a Linux port that runs flawless for me.

This game has the potential to be better than FTL and SPAZ put together, which in a way it is both of these things but just isn't better than either.  SPAZ has more story, faster paced and more responsive combat and better controls, and FTL has better ship to ship combat and Roguelike elements. Both of the other games have better weapons overall but that's more to do with their in-game economy and construction as obtaining GOOD weapons in this game is basically RNG.
There's something just frustrating about having your ship get roflstomped by a ship with a third of your shields and a quarter of your health simply because it had a gun that stopped your ship's movement (which doesn't have any UI feedback besides the sudden inexplicable STOP of your ship), and then also has a bunch of repair drones, and is somehow able to fire 6 missile salvoes in rapid succession. And then you have to jump out and hope you can land next to a friendly space station to repair. I’d only managed to kill this rather minor ship (and I assume it’s minor as the game also doesn’t have any real indicators of ship power beyond obvious differences in size) after hopping out and building a fellow other ship and loading it up with guns and then going back for a 2v1, and then I still nearly died.
I suppose people might justify these instances where you run into these difficulty walls by saying “it's a Roguelike”, but with FTL the setting felt like these encounters were supposed to be this way through the setup of the story, and with SPAZ you had your mothership to rebuild and try again. In this one you die and get some XP to then unlock other ships, to which the new one I tried turned out to be incredibly worse than the starting ship. I would love to see some kind of overall ‘captain’ leveling that grants small boosts to ships that you use, maybe unlocking additional fleet slots, or giving bonus level/scrap points. Something that can make going through the next game a bit more possible.
All in all I think this game has some real good potential, enough to be better than SPAZ and FTL put together and my hope is that the devs are working on such. It would also be neat somehow if multiplayer could be added, but I can understand the difficulty of doing such so I wouldn’t blame the devs for never putting it in. Improvements to the player “level” for small upgrades to future games would be great, faster and more responsive combat would also work (SPAZ for an ideal), Fix up the UI so that EVERYTHING gives some kind of visual feedback to the player. If the devs still work on these things then I think they’ll have a game that would be really awesome, instead of the ‘alright’ game they have now.

This game is great fun for all who enjoy being bad at things.
Why is that?
Because no matter how good you are, chances are you can never do a perfect run and successfully salvage all the anamatronics.  It's not necessary, and the first few are not even that difficult once you understand all the mechanics.  The problem is that the last few are close to impossible, if they're even possible at all.
The rules are unclear to start with, and they change as you go along:
Freddy will only attack you when you put the paper up or presumably wait too long after the prompts stop, but Baby will attack during the prompt
Everything else is managable, I've even got a Macro for the Basketball Minigame so you can get perfect scores for extra cash.  Even the night shifts are fairly easy because you can keep retrying.
The real kicker, though? It saves immediately when you fail a salvage, forcing you to replay from the start for another chance.  Even exiting the game immediately upon the jump scare will usually result in starting on the next day.
One simple game mechanic ruins the whole game for me, personally, but aside from this nitpick the game is amazing and easily worth the money they didn't charge us for.  Thank scott for producing this game, and I highly suggest players try it out and do a peaceful run.

I'm not one to give up on games, but this is the first one I have asked to refund.
Sure, my playtime is short, but it is mainly due to the controls feeling off, and the camera not showing where my target is.
For once, I found a game difficult not because it was supposed to be, but because of some gameplay issues.

I really wanted to like David and not just because I was able to purchase it for 59 cents. The idea is fascinating. It's different... but it falls short. The biggest issue I had, and the reason why I requested a refund, is that it's clearly and unmistakingly a mobile port and a bad one at that.
The controls are still predominantly oriented for a touch screen. The primary (and only) attack requires you to precisely click in the middle of "David" while you're jumping all over the place. You then have to hold it and then flick it in the right direction. This would be all fine and dandy on a phone, but I imagine most gamers don't have touchscreen monitors.
"Partial Controller Support" is laughable. You can move around and jump... but I couldn't determine any way to attack with the controller. This is a major oversight by the developer.
I'm deeply disappointed because I WANTED this to be a great game, and I think it could have been had the developer spent some time actually adapting it to non-touchscreen platform beyond binding a few movements.
Additionally, the graphics were grating. They are bright and overly simplistic. I know that's the style the game is going for, but I didn't find them charming like I had hoped. Maybe had the overall experience been better I wouldn't mind as much.

Well, this is my first review for any game on steam, but felt Tera is deserving of my first recommended game review. I have been playing MMOs for a while (WoW, GW, AoC, WH, Neverwinter, Eve, Rift, Knight, LotrO, etc, etc..), but I have to say after playing about 24 hours, this is a GREAT MMO.
-The best/newest classes restricited to Elin or other female races. 0 male restricted classes.
- Grinding through quests can be repetitive.
-The stats on the loot while leveling all seem rather standard. The same stats on each piece of gear, just different values with minor other differences.
-Some of the textures are old or outdated.
-Almost all of the costumes on the shop are ♥♥♥♥♥♥/troll outfits.
-Somewhat low population base, mainly due to the population being spread over 3 (main) servers.
- Kumas is just....terrible...
- Leveling is TOO fast. Myself being a hardcore fan of Vanilla WoW, while doing dungeons or pvp you can gain levels at insane rates. Took me about 3-4 days of running dungeons with my friends to get level 42.
- Tons of races/classes to choose from
- Tons of custimization (glyphs, etc)
- Addicting combat, think of it like a mix between Smite + Witcher 3, but then add more skills than you know what to do with.
- Mostly balanced classes in PvP/PvE (excluding all the new ones - Ninja, Gunner)
- EXTREMELY fun to play with friends. If you have a group of people to do dungeons with constantly, you will never have to do a single repetitive quest in the entire game. I think the last time I did a quest was level...19? Been going with 3 people (healer, tank, dps) and can clear the 5 man dungeons despite the challenge.
- Boss mechanics remind me SO much of vanilla WoW. Very fun, and causes you to strategize before (or during in my case) each fight.
- FREE TO PLAY, very little pay to win aspects compared to most games.
- Beautiful and varied environment/bosses/dungeons. Almost every new instance or zone we got to would immidiately trigger the "Wow look at that" moment.
- Sense of exploration - Never before have I felt the desire to just explore the world and the environment.
- Flying mounts!
- Battlegrounds.
- Guild v. Guild pvp.
- New 30 man raid coming out.
OVERALL SCORE: 9/10
As of right now these are all the main points I can think of, I will be able to add to the list whenever my crew gets to end game at 65. Like I said, if you are a hardcore MMO raider like I am, you will definitely enjoy this game. Don't be afraid to try the game out if you are a solo player! Make your toon on Ascension Valley, and give my toon Thcflowsinme a whisper! We are always looking for more to play with.

You will then need to click on Device Manager under Devices and Printers. Under Device Manager, click the arrow next to Human Interface Devices. Right click and disable HID-compliant consumer control device and HID-compliant system controller.
This fix also works for Prototype 2 except you may need to disable all HID- compliant listings.

Battlevoid Harbinger sends you on a journey through space to cleanse star systems from alien ships and free your people. Each new star system comes with a different main mission and different aliens.
The game is simple to learn but hard to master. You start with a single ship, equip it with weapons and upgrades and head out to warfare.
Destroyed ships leave scrap and energy knots. Both can be used to upgrade your equipment or buy new gear.
You can trade with friendly space stations and accept missions. Completing missions earns you more scrap and energy knots.
Once you collected enough scrap you can buy more ships. Your fleet can consist of a maximum of three ships. Depending on the ship type some ships can be equipped with hanger bays, allowing you to build smaller vessels on your carrier or destroyer.
Clever selection of weapon types and equipment, like shield or hull generator, will become more and more important as you adventure through new star systems. Different type of aliens use different technology and different weapons and every time you jump into a new system the enemies become tougher.
The range between the weakest weapons and the strongest weapons is tremendous. Ships equipped with strong weapons can kill you in seconds. Regrettably, there's no comparable defence system to these kind of weapons which will ultimately always lead to a very fast and unexpected death.
Dying means permadeath. You only have one life. Death comes fast and is often very frustrating and seems unfair. Out of nowhere a group of heavy ships arrives in your sector and blows your fleet into space in a matter of seconds. You have to replay the game many times in order to learn which weapon and ship setup works best. The game can be very difficult and frustrating at times. Nevertheless I always found myself coming back to retry.
Battlevoid Harbinger is the very enjoyable and highly addictive game that comes with the well known 'only one more round' effect. Nevertheless my recommendation of this game is restricted. It took me 25 hours to beat the game on easy difficulty for the very first time and IMO it seems almost impossible to beat the game on normal difficulty, leave away hard difficulty. It seems like a basic concept of the game to not let you win. This strongly effects the otherwise clearly positive experience with this game in a negative way.
Pros:
- highly addictive
- simple but nice graphics
- simple to learn
- 2 x speed
Cons:
- hard to master
- you are unlikely to win
- quite frustrating every time you lose
- no save files
- permadeath
- limited types of missions
- unspectacular end of game (if you manage)
- scripted events move the camera out of focus during battles (very annoying)
- ship escort achievements are all broken

This could perhaps be considered a simple game, but hits on a lot of important themes found from other games. It is a good game for leaving and picking up later at another time, yet it has enough depth to it from being brainlessly boring.
The game is perhaps most similar to FTL but without a hunger clock and more focused on a squad of ships, one serving as your flagship. You enter a level with several sectors and a goal - usually defeating some end boss. Their are aliens but you don't seem to have any joining your squad of ships (you can use their weaponry though).
The game can be a bit of a random draw at times; while at other times you can grind your way to victory if you so choose. There are things like little side quests and mercenaries to hire but they are mostly just distractions.
I would probably best recommend this game for your phone if you are choosing for a specific platform, then for a computer.

I really want to start with what I feel about Home, does well.
It’s a game about exploring a small town after some sort of event has left it empty, a ghost town if you will. Part of the charm is learning what happened here. The music and sound effects do a nice job of accopaining the mystique of it all.
It also has a nice neat art style. It’s not like it’s the most amazing thing you’ve ever seen but it's not different enough to be something memorable (To most people the worse thing you can accuse art style  of being is bad, but to it's worse to be forgettale).
Then there is what I don’t like about it.
First off, it breaks the cardinal rule of gaming, it’s not really fun to play. In fact there isn’t much to do except wander around scene to scene (read; rooms/areas) getting snib bits of information on what the hell is going on. That’s it. That's the whole game. I had the same issue with “We’ve all Gone to the Rapture.” It’s a 2D walking simulator with virtually no puzzles at all. And by the time you get to the end, (I’m not sure many of you will bother to play it that long), you’re sort of done with it. Keeping in mind this game is only 2.99 and goes on sale sometimes. For what it is, it’s really not bad. Which as my father would say, "Not exactly a compliment." I give it a luke warm 5 out of 10 for trying to do something cool but missing the wow factor that would’ve made it a must play that I would feel better recomending to people. This being said though, if you like peaceful creepy games, Home will be fun for you.

David. is a one-trick platformer—you have your biblical slingshot which you use to sling shot against your foes—but it's a pretty good trick. Controls take some getting used to, at least with keyboard and mouse, but it's a manageable learning curve. Enemies and levels are varied enough in form and tactics to keep the platforming and combat interesting,  and there are enough levels and secrets to make the purchase worth the small price. Add in achievements for perfect runs (i.e. taking no damage), leaderboards for speedrunning, and an endless Arena challenge mode, and there's enough to keep you playing past the first run through.

is a really strange game that features simplistic, yet jarring visuals and a reflex-based click-to-shoot system. You play as a square named David in a bright geometric world, apparently sent there by an unseen deity to combat other evil (read: pointier) shapes. David can't touch the enemies directly, but can charge orbs of energy to fire upon them. While charging, David also reveals his ability to slow time. (This is a very special square.)
Though, let me also make very clear that the controls for this game are (intentionally)
. The physics of this game really like to defy you and it will take a little getting used to. The controls are heavily oriented toward reflex, as evil triangles and rhombuses will fling themselves at you at alarming speeds.
Within the game, there are only a dozen levels and a meager amount of achievements to earn (most of which are simply for beating the game). Yet, it should generate some serious challenge just to beat those levels to begin with. There is little replayability outside of the "Arena" mode, which is basically a room with endless enemy spawns and a leaderboard for total kills. Personally: 4 hours, all levels beaten, all achievements earned.
The music is nothing special. Kind of bland. Repetitive. Visually, the game is very jarring, with areas of extreme dark juxtaposed near blinding white. If you have sensitive eyes like me, this game
strain your vision. The screenshots provided on the store page are the extent of how this game will look: you might find it interesting, you might not.
It's a cool game. Very short; small world; no story--appeal lies in the gameplay and visuals. The physics are overtly designed to be infuriating, but the overall feel and aesthetic is whimsical. It's a cheap game anyway, and worth a pick up if you have a few hours to waste. I had fun.

If you're like me and what draws you most to the AC series are the history-based narratives, then I see no reason not to get this game. It's a great story and a good chance to brush up on US history, plus it felt like a lot of gameplay elements had been improved. In general, the major fault with the game in my opinion is that if you stray too far from the main storyline, things quickly start to feel dull and pointless. I thoroughly enjoyed this game but almost exclusively for its main quest.
Ironically, I feel it's partly
the side activities were optional that they were tedious, in the sense that, had they been cleverly included in the story as an more intricate part of gameplay, this could have become something I wanted to do as opposed to something that I decided to dismiss. In Black Flag, for instance, upgrading the ship didn't feel like a chore--I wanted to do so because I use the ship all the time for basic travel and exploring.
Having to wade through the tunnels to unlock fast-travel in the cities is a pain. And there aren't enough fast-travel locations in the massive Frontier region in my opinion (where the fact they decided to implement a stamina system for the horses was an added negative, considering). I guess some would argue that travelling through the world is part of the game, but personally I might have been more inclined to take on side quests and explore with the knowledge that this would ultimately help make travelling faster (e.g. by having all viewpoints become fast-travel once visited).
Taking out auto-follow is a baffling decision in my opinion--I was really glad to see that appear in AC:R as I could now focus on dialogue while walking, shame it's gone.
The ledger system seems intriguing but ultimately is dismissed as it's not engaging enough in the sense it's not really worth the trouble (e.g. I knew it allowed you to create larger pouches, which I would always buy in previous games, but in this instance I just couldn't be bothered and decided to instead welcome to added challenge of having smaller ammo available).

This game is a gem. Back when it was the nintendo DS era I picked up a this game called "Mini Ninjas" I loved the hell out of it. Now, 8 years later I go on a nostalgic trip and rediscover this game on steam. I fell in love with it all over again.
Pros:
-Large open world levels of lush and beautiful settings of dynasty era Japan
-Has replayability with all the hidden or non hidden objectives in each level which you need to get if you want to ace the level
-Clean/easy on the eye artsytle that compliments the setting of the worlds perfectly
-Multiple characters to choose from,
you can choose out of 6 characters which you unlock as you play all with their own weapons and specials
-Many different ways to aproach each level.
You have a choice of fighting with magic (Kuiji), fighting head on with just your sword (depends on which character you pick), Or you can just not fight at all and stealth your way through the level. The stealth component involves you climbing rooftops and landscapes, hiding between bushes and snow piles, using smoke bombs and special camo magic, and timing your way out of enemy vision
-Relaxing and just good fun
Cons:
- Camera angle. for the most part the camera angle is good and balanced but then there are always some parts of the levels that really mess up the camera specially in tight spaced parkour areas.
- You can only play as Hiro (main protaginist) when facing the bosses in boss levels.
- some levels leave you with no option but to fight and dont allow stealth.
- The swimming and sailing on boat can be very frustrating. Swimming is a slow painful process and when on your boat you can easily lose control and just crash into everything.
- The combat is very simple and provides no challenge unless you are facing the ninja minions or the mage minions
Overall Mini Ninjas is a beautiful and simple stealth and combat inspired game set in a lush Japanese dynasty era that provides you with a relaxing yet still action filled gameplay experience.
9/10

Streets of Rogue is a brilliant, hilarious, and refreshing game.
I have over 300 hours in Nuclear Throne, and Streets of Rogue gives a fresh take on the familiar gameplay. The level set-up is the same concept, with each area split up into three floors. Instead of killing every enemy to proceed, you have to accomplish a set of missions. Each floor is its own city. An assortment of people, buildings, police, and crimelords comes together to create plenty of hilarious interactions, and leaves the player plenty of room for creativity in how they want to solve their missions.
There is a wealth of character class variety, with each class having its own distinct gameplay styles. Whether you play the Cop, handcuffing criminals and not harming innocents, or the Gorilla, who is happy to destroy the entire city, the class you choose has an enormous impact on the gameplay.

There are a lot of people who would praise the simplicity of this game.  I am not one of them.  I enjoy simple gaphics games like Thomas was Alone, or games like Super Meat Boy where the mechanics are very simplistic but the gameplay is centered around doing them as perfectly as possible.  I would say that this game is almost some weird ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the two that should be disowned by both parents.  Except THAT concept sounds incredible, whereas this is...not.
To start, let me explain the controls.  WASD movement - W is jump, and S seems to make you fall faster.  You have inifinite double jump, which takes a bit to get used to.  You have control of your left and right motion while in the air as well, and the jump height is dependnent on how long you hold down W.  The control scheme feels more suited to a top down game than something that plays more like a platformer.
To attack, you must click on your character, and then drag the mouse in the direction you wish to fling
I'm not sure what the projectile is, but it is part of you.  While you're doing this, time for everything in the world slows down.  This means that your feedback on jumping and other movement changes while you are charging an attack.  Usually. Enemy shots appear to not be affected, though, which makes dodging those annoying.  And you will autoshoot if you charge too long.
There is an option for using a controller, but it's horrible.  The right stick moves the mouse pointer around, and one of the triggers acts like a click and hold.  It is unplayable, which is sad, because a controller scheme using a flick movement on the right stick to attack (maybe even hold Right trigger, flick the stick after it is charged) would be a gigantic improvement over what you're stuck with.
There appears to be no camera control whatsover, and your character does not stay centered in the screen.   The camera likes to zoom in so far that more often than not, you cannot see your enemy.  This means that not only are you dragging the mouse around, you are sometimes moving in slow-mo and to "reload" you have to get the mouse pointer back to your sprite.  And as you can't see your foe, you end up flailing around randomly and hoping you hit it.
This is fine if you aren't playing on "Very" difficulty, which should really be named "Hard" like every other game out there would have done.  You see, you jump from being able to take many hits on the normal (easy?) game mode to not being able to take a single hit on the harder mode.  If the camera wasn't zoomed in so far, you could at least work on your defensive skills, but by the time you see your target it is too late anyway.
So why am I complaining about the harder mode?  Well, because regular mode is boringly easy.  Once I figured out the awkward control scheme, the regular difficulty has very little challenge.  This isn't Super Meat Boy, either, where the challenge is to figure out the perfect run- I attempted the one of the stages on hard repeatedly, and minor differences in my movement created a very different response from the enemy, some of which left me in an undodgable position.
There is a difficulty progression from level to level, but it seems to be based around adding in more obstacles that you can't see until it is too late than truly making the game harder.

This game was released in 2012, wasn't a gamer then...now playing it on a high end PC feels still new and fresh, of course there are differences in the graphical options (Ex: HBAO +) with current gen games but still this runs like a heavy graphical game.
Pro's:
Playing for 88 hrs made me analyze this game in a very detailed manner comparing this game with the current AC games.
- Campaign story feels solid with the introduction of Ratenkhaoe:ke or Connor Kenway s/o Haytem Kenway. The journey which Connor takes to make him a full fledged assassin is awesome.
- For a 2012 game, the graphical aspect of the game is breathtaking. Shout out to the team in Ubisoft for bringing such a game. Its still a very high ended game that requires a decent graphic card to run on high setting as well a good system to sustain the game and for multitasking purpose.
- Missions are well balanced, the money system is more balanced that the current AC Games, {AC Unity : 2 million franc} {AC syndicate: 270,000 pounds} in a/c.
- Naval missions and DLC's are fun extra part of the game.
- choice of outfits and weapons are reasonable, though AC Unity was the best in terms of weapons choices.
- Recruitment and side bodyguards are useful in big missions or fighting multiple enemies or tough enemies {Ex: Grenadier or Hessian}
- Combat mechanism is fast and engaging though personal preference of Assassin's Creed Rogue
Con's
- There is still lots of glitches in the game, sometime combat mechanism of countering an enemy doesn't work , thus usage of secondary weapons become necessary
- People who had issues with Uplay being outdated didn't think about installing Uplay first then installing the game through steam, and this wasn't notified to steam for an alternate way to play AC III.
- Levelling the artisians is explained no where in the game, I had to browse through IGN and steam community to get the solution.
- Multiplayer seems new and odd, doesn't look interesting, maybe i am not used to it.
Overall this is a must buy game if you are a Assassins Creed player or someone new to the community who wants to try this game
Cheers

Set against the soft, lush backdrop of imaginary Japanese wilderness,
succeeds on the back of its level design, which consists largely of wide, open expanses joined not only by the path the game sets for you, but also by a myriad of hidden passages, all hiding their own little secrets.
does the thing
pretends to do, where you can choose stealth or a head-on approach, except unlike
, the stealthy approach to
generally consists of sticking to tall grass and staying away from patrols of the samurai who serve as antagonists rather than sneaking about and killing them one by one. Sneaking around the edges of an area means you'll usually stumble upon a stream which you can quickly ride past your enemies, or maybe a hidden cave where you'll find a magical shrine to give you a new power. Technically speaking it's a linear experience, but the levels are open-ended enough to create a sense of exploration without exhausting players with the massive, empty spaces of a big-budget sandbox.
As the young ninja-in-training Hiro, you set out from your idyllic home in the mountains to defeat Ashida - an evil magician and warlord who transforms forest animals into samurai grunts for his army. Throughout the game you pick up other members of Hiro's ninja clan, each with their own special abilities. Hiro is the only character who can use magic spells, whilst the hammer-wielding Futo is great for crowd-control in combat and the archer Shun can get the drop on enemies. Some characters are more useful than others. For instance, Tora's special ability allows him to run very fast across wide open spaces, which is useful almost exclusively in the area where he is initially unlocked. Similarly, Kunoichi's spear is like a worse version of Futo's hammer and Suzume uses music from her flute to temporarily disable groups of enemies, which would be great if it weren't for the fact that the time it takes for the flute's animation to kick in and start doing it's thing is - in most cases - longer than the time it would take to win the fight using a stronger character. The levels are divided loosely into segments; the game starts with a set of levels in an expansive forest, followed by a riverlands area (in which Hiro's large hat can be adorably used as a boat) and a mountainous, snowy zone towards the end. At the end of each segment is a large castle, which you are free to break into as you choose and make your way to the boss. These castles are often the best levels in
, with strings of lamps offering a stealthy route over the courtyards full of samurai, whose numbers make for challenging fights if you choose to face them in a head-on confrontation. Each castle has it's own gimmick, with the 'night' castle coming to mind as an example of some of the game's best level design, with towers and passageways making for a wide open playground coupled with some impressive visuals as you traverse a massive chasm via an enemy-laden bridge or row your hat-boat through the castle's various moats. Other shining example of
superior level design is the introductory level to the 'riverlands' segment. Set in expansive rice fields flooded by the samurai, there's a memorable hidden temple tucked away in a partially-submerged bamboo forest with stalks of bamboo extending into a canopy of leaves that obscures the sky. It's little moments like these - sitting on the water and fishing or sneaking through the reeds on the shores of a river filled with lanterns - that create a sense that this world exists outside the boundaries of the game's levels.
Despite 'ninja' being in the title,
isn't a game about stealth killing enemies. In fact, the surprise attack that you can perform while in stealth alerts nearby enemies immediately, instigating combat, and demanding an almost purist approach to the game - if you want to kill somebody, you have to fight, and if it's stealth you want, you can't be sneakily killing enemies. It's refreshing to see a game not afraid to actually lock you into an approach; it's great to be able to choose either sneaking or brawling, but 99% of the time you'll just use stealth and then switch to an all-out approach once you ♥♥♥♥ that up.
has no room for swapping out your play style - you have to decide right at the beginning of an encounter whether it's fight or flight that you'll be opting for, which is a uniquely prohibitive style of gameplay that surprisingly works out in the game's favour thanks to its' provision of tools effective for either approach. If you
want to play it stealthy, use a magic spell to transform into a rabbit and walk right past enemies without arousing suspicion. If it's combat you're after, there are different types of bombs and destructive spells available for easier killings, all purchasable from your friendly neighbourhood bird man. Unfortunately, most of these combat upgrades aren't at all necessary - combat isn't the most challenging affair, which is to expected from a game so obviously geared towards younger audiences. Even on the highest difficulty and in spite of a super slow block button that never blocks anything, most fights are pretty easy even without the use of magic and bombs. A lot of the combat that you'll be engaging in is either with groups of samurai patrolling along roads or in arenas where you have no choice but to fight. These arenas are the most genuinely challenging fights in
, as the game will often throw several enemy types at you at once, like archers with exploding arrows, a ghost that resurrects dead enemies and a huge, lumbering giant that can only be killed by Futo.
doesn't often throw enough people at you to create a real challenge, but when it does it becomes a tense brawl of tiny, clinking swords and bombs that go 'pop' as you juggle the arrows flying at you, samurai chasing you down with swords and the giant with the club that ponderously stomps towards you through the whole thing. The big fights are a testament to one of
' two strongest aspects - the calm, quiet tranquillity of the game's wide open levels and the frenzy that is it's combat. At it's core, though, what makes
feel so much more real and satisfying than other sandbox stealth action titles is the dedication to keeping it's wide, open levels distinctly separate from one another over a huge, empty open world to explore. This is why
feels like a real, genuine world that can be explored while retaining the straightforward, easy-to-follow linearity of a traditionally structured action-adventure.

I think the game is meant to appeal to a very particular audience. That being said, it's not for me. Here's why. When you die, you lose everything that wasn't stored away. That also includes all character progress. The stuff you did store away is available to the next character you create. But then, if they use it (which means they're not storing it), there's a good chance they'll die and lose it anyway. So why would I ever want to use my best gear if there's a good chance I'll lose it? And what's the point of having good gear if I'm too afraid to use it because there's a chance I'll lose it. To me, it just feels like I'm collecting things for the sake of collecting things and never really making progress.
It should be noted that as you play and die, you will unlock new races, outfits, and augments, which do provide a small boost to your freshly created character. But for me, it's not enough to really make me feel like I'm making progress.
If not for the fact that I lose everything when I die, I'd probably love this game. It's got crafting, and character creation, a bit of exploration, loot, base building, 8-bit graphics... everything, for me, that makes a great game.
I know it may kinda go against the premise of the game, but if they would just provide maybe a single-player only option to disable perma-death, then I think it would make this game vastly more enjoyable to a much larger audience.

That's the biggest miss for me, if the game stuck to one storyline and worked on it a bit more then maybe it could have worked out better. This is a really great action rogulite, even in early access.
It's like if Vlambeer (Nuclear Throne, Luftrausers) created Risk of Rain.
Much like Risk of Rain, the game is about fighting waves of enemies while collecting powerups that stack with eachother. Every match has a slow build up to a crazy endgame.
Unlike Risk of Rain however, there is no activating of teleporters or hunting down the last remaining enemies. Cavern Kings is significantly faster and lets you continue to the next area whenever you want (though that's not a very good strategy!). The game lets you destroy the environment with items, which lends the game to battles that feel more dynamic.
In some ways Cavern Kings does feel a little derivative (you'll encounter enemies and powerups which act very similar to enemies in Risk of Rain) but the game's mechanics are different enough that this never feels like a problem.
Overall this is a great game in early-access. If you're still on the fence, I believe there is a free demo available on itch.io!

Oh gods where to start...
Well, first I should say I loved the past FATE games. My personal favorite being the first. But the others I enjoyed just as much if not more. Anyways, onto the review.
I love how the kept the same feel and didn't upgrade the graphics that much or not at all. Brings back the feel for the previous FATE games.
The combat seems a bit more difficult (at least to me) and for good reason. With the introduction of AI companions is quite the bold move to make. It feels flawed. But not impossible to take advantage of.
Ok, so to the companions. for the first 10 levels their price is around 8000 gold to 30000 gold. After that it's much more expensive. Their skills and stats aren't as good as the main character clearly. And their spear, sword, crit, etc skills. They didn't put skill points into specific skills. Kinda all over the place. And their stats can't be changed or can you level them from level one like some companion based games i've played. But I enjoy it none the less.
Pet stuff the same... New items, new spells, and a new potion/charm of revival for your companions. And I think there's multiplayer stuff (haven't gotten to that yet). Enemies seem tougher now. Either that or my gear is crap lol.
The amount of enemies in one area has changed a lot too. Seems like it was doubled. But it's no problem for spellcasters or strong melee weapon users (AKA power attacks). The new weapons are very cool too. New swords, axes, and so on.
Very simplistic game with graphics of a potato Mark3. But a very enjoyable classic series.
The only thing I wish this game had was some awesome music.
But despite that, I'd give this a 8.5/10. Hours of fun. Hours of farming. Hours worth of enchanting BS.
