Recommended with some reservations. First, obviously I enjoy this game. I've played quite a few hours, and I've gotten my money's worth...
That said, there's a lot of room for improvement. The balance is way off, for starters. You'll occasionally be so completely outclassed in the early to mid game that it's almost silly. This is even more true at Normal difficulty, which feels crazy difficult. I haven't bothered with "hard" yet. Then, in the late game, you'll find yourself so absurdly overpowered that the enemies don't even have a chance.
The environmental hazards are either boring or annoying, but never really interesting.
The ship types aren't diverse enough, There's really no difference to the way the different ships play, aside from starting with hangars and fighters or not. And once you've bought your first formation ship, you'll have covered all your bases.
The story is barely, barely there, and while it suggests some interesting ideas, it's basically just a few totally ignorable text boxes at the beginning and end of each map.
The enemies, also, really aren't all that different. Knowing the difference in what weapons they favor is only relevant for the first map, and by then you have the start of a fleet and it doesn't matter at all what weapons your enemies use.
There is zero element of choice anywhere in this game. The quests are meaninglessly generic.
Also, why can't I just right-click on enemies to call up the selector wheel that lets me target them with all my ships? Why do I have to click on my ship, then on the enemies?
I feel like the creators came up with an engaging and easy to use set of basic systems. Then they built half a game around those systems. I think this game has a lot of promise, and I'm still enjoying it, but my interest is definitely going to wane way faster than with some of the other games in this genre. I really hope we get to see a sequel that keeps what works about this game and builds a richer world and experience on top of it.

I have played BH on the iPad since it first launched .  It has been and still is among my favorites.  The port to Steam seems to have sucked nearly all of the enjoyment from the game.
1)  Selecting a target in the mobile version is  a single click.  Here it takes two clicks.  A LftClick on the firing ship then a RtClick on the target.  If the player can indeed click on the target.  Click targeting is touchy to say the least.  Which brings us to:
2)  RtClick command is overloaded.  Not only does RtClick  tell a ship where to shoot it RtClick also tells the ship where to move.  So a missed click can send that ship precisely where you don't want it to go.  Coupling that with a somewhat small click target  ships frequently are headed to the wrong place.
3)  Controls are scattered about the edges of the screen resulting in a lot of wasted & unnecessary pointer movement.   There are many good reasons to cluster game controls. There most obvious being that it allows the player to keep his focus on the action. There are few good reasons to spread them across the entire real estate of the screen.   Perhaps none.
4)  Ship speeds are a bit slow on a mobile.  On a 27" monitor they are excruciatingly slow.
5)  Game balance is poor; even worse than the mobile version where game balance is precarious to say the least.  The worst balance issue is the ship speed.  All enemy ships are faster than all player ships.  All of them. This is especially annoying with regard to Carriers.  Historically naval carriers have been, and are, amond the fastest ships in the fleet.  The earliest carriers were in fact converted fast cruisers.  The job of the carrier is to get there"the fastest with the mostest"
6)  Formation following doesn't work well but then it doesn't work well on the mobile version either.
The devs have a new project that is taking most , if not all, of their attention.  They said that they have no interest in putting more work into BH.  That's too bad because the best advertisment for a game is a history of prior successes.  The worst is a weak port.
I'll continue playing & enjoying BH on my iPad and highly reccommend it.  I cannot say the same for the Steam version.

PROS
+ Randomized levels with randomized objectives keeps things fresh
+ Tons of items, traps, NPCs and factions to interact with

+ Witty writing and humor

CONS

- Purchasing upgrades between runs feels shallow (items and skills are added to possible rewards)

What it is:
A challenging physics-based platformer arena. Your abilities include double-jumping, and a bullet-time charge-shot that fires a wad of little balls which gradually return to you. The game consists of a stage select screen, and a series of boss fights with unique platform arrangements and conditions. Each enemy is made up of a bunch of small parts that want to eat you, and you have to figure out how to avoid its attacks while trying to shoot it without making your situation worse. You are offered two difficulties on each boss: start with a health bar, or one-hit death.
Pros:
A unique challenge. Inexpensive.
Cons:
Extremely simple.

If you know what you're getting into (lo-fi psychological narrative experiment, with adventure/horror elements), then this is a gem for $3.00. Especially since you can play through it multiple ways to arrive at different endings. It's a little like a "choose your own adventure" book, although there's a unique twist: because of the character's amnesia and unreliable memories, a lot of the choices aren't about actions or decisions, they're really interpretations of an ambiguous scenario. This is actually rather original and brilliant. Also, pretty neat how such a seemingly "simple" game tracks many minor decisions and discoveries and item pick-ups throughout a playthrough, then in the finale asks how you want to interpret it all.
The mixed reviews I feel are mostly due to one reason only: people don't like to feel confused. The plot, however you choose to progress/interpret it, is kind of convoluted, and you will probably feel confused at different points (its ok). Important thing is, the game is not nonsensical. It would've been nicer if at the end, once everything is being rehashed and tied up and re-interpreted, if there was just a little bit more detail or clues provided by the game (especially re: how that "first man" could possibly fit in), if it was a little less the player's responsibility to figure it all out. Hope that's a fair critique, because I do understand what the developer was going for.
Once you beat it, check out:
. Major "spoilers."
PS: I think I overlooked another reason this great game got mixed reviews. It was/is misrepresented. The top tags for this game are Horror and Adventure, whereas it would be better tagged as Story-Rich, or Story-Driven, and as a type of Interactive Fiction. The developer himself acknowledged he was inspired by the Visual Novel genre. Yet he also wanted to create a great deal of "hype" and player investment in the game and its universe, so he really stressed the "horror" element. Not that there aren't some nice scares and plenty of general spookiness/dread/unease throughout. But it all boils down to this: this game isn't about "horror" and it isn't about "adventure" ... It may not even be a "game," exactly - it's an experiment in narrative form, and it's about the fallability of memory, and fatally subjective interpretations of events. It all boils down to the final few questions where you're asked to decide what you/your protagonist believes went down. The "boss" in this "game" is basically your own mind/conscience, and, surprisingly, it can still kill you.
10/10 Would be confused/uncertain/delluded/quesy about my own actions again.

This is a cautious recommend.
The game has an incredible grind. You unlock new ships one by one as you gain experience. Experience is gained solely through playing the game, win or lose. The most efficient way to gain experience is by just grinding out hard mode, which makes the earlier levels utterly brutal.
Once you get to around level 17? Around when you unlock the BSE Harbinger and the Valiant, the game opens up and becomes more fun.
There's not a whole lot of gameplay depth, especially at the tactical level. There's a decent amount of ship loadout planning, and most of the decisions you make in-game are between combat encounters, where you choose how to allocate the game's two main resources: scrap for buying new weapons or ships, and skill points for upgrading your weapons.
The combat itself is the weakest part of the game. it has a very, very mobile feel. You only have control of the movement of your ships, but positioning barely matters. The main issue is the combat maps are small, and the ships' turning and movement speeds are very low compared to the way damage output and weapon range is balanced. If you are poorly positioned, you're going to suffer and repositioning rarely matters or is practical. Your ships aren't responsive enough for changes in positioning to do anything for you.
At the strategic level, you're shown what systems you can warp to next and what ships lie in wait there. Each system/combat map is divided into a 3x3 grid, and you can choose where you want to warp in based on that. This is crucial so you don't end up warping in on top of a space station or something. You're also shown whether enemy ships will be moving to another station during the next turn. You can either move to a new system, or wait at your current one to see how enemy ships move.
There's a very basic quest system mostly made up of "go here", "kill that", and "bring this item here" tasks.
My biggest complaint aside from the initial grind is inconsistent difficulty spiking. This is a symptom of a lot of rogue-likes, but it's still frustrating. Playthroughs can be as short as fifteen minutes if you die early, or as long as three hours if you make it to the last starmap. Losing late in the game to some random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you can't react to is infuriating.
That's really about it. It's a fun game that doesn't require a lot of thought, and is definitely worth it for the cost...if you can last through the initial grind (took me about nine hours spread out over a year or so).

There are plenty of ships to choose from and also unlock at the beginning of the game.  Although at the time of this writing the Carrier ships are far better than the starships that cannot hold fighter planes and/or drones.
Loads of replayability as each and every time you play, the map is much different than the last.  Believe me when I say this is a good thing because you will be ending up dying horribly more often than not.
Position matters!!  Where you jump into the sector and how you have your formation could mean the difference between a bad or a good battle.
Huge variety of weapons.  This actually plays an important part of your strategy since some turrets shoot farther than others.   You could even place shorter range burst fire guns on your ship to destroy your opponents as you warp in right on top of them to gain the advantage!
There is only one bad thing that I can note:
Once in a while, there are times where you will die no matter what you do.  Example:  I got caught in an EMP storm right before the tough boss battle and I could not move and had to wait 4 times straight in the same sector  before being overwhelmed by enemy ship battles.

Now, I won't claim I have much experience with space battle game, but this is a really challenging game that forces you to make careful decision or die.   Btw, you don't have save points in game (except when you exit the game and come back), so if you die in a sequence, you have to start another sequence, with a new ship of base stat.  Personnally, I like this design, because it makes every decision matters, and is part of the challenge of the game.  Or if you are maso, you will love it when the game tears apart your fleet, ... again and again ... until you git gud. In that regard, it is kind of like dark soul, but at least, you earn experience through each game sequence that you complete, either by dying or succesfully completing the main objective. With more exp and level, you can start a new game sequence on a randomly generated map starting with a better initial spaceship, and repeat the process.  So dying isn't exactly time wasted.
I would really like to see the developper increase the scale of the space battles, that is, giving players more than just 3 ships and adjust the enemy fleet size accordingly to balance things out.  The space battles are already pretty fun, but they can become very epic if only we have more space ships... I mean, more pews, the better

Anyway, careful not to die in space, and still die, cause the game still kills you even if you got gud, cause its challenging like that.  FUN GAME, serious, no sarcasm.

A strategy game built around the Half-Life universe-- and a pretty good one at that. My first RTS was Halo Wars for the xbox 360, so when I got this I was surprised at the amount of freedom compared to HW.
There are two sides that you can pick from: combine or resistance. combine's units are overpowered, but the unit cap is much lower and they cost much more than the rebels, which balances the scales a bit-- the rebels are spamming weak units early on, while with the combine you build up your army and defenses more slowly until you get your heavy units that can tough through just about anything. This makes it so that each team is working toward a different goal-- combine are defending themselves while the rebels are trying to destroy the combine early on through sheer numbers before they get striders and other heavy units.
The one thing that I really don't like about it is the price.

It's a good example of a great RTS. Did I mention it's free? Yeah, an RTS complete with fully working online, skirmish and an in-game campaign based on the best-selling Half-Life 2 series that is completely free with no microtransactions.
There are a few things I'd change if it were up to me, but these are little things that don't draw away from the great gameplay.
My only concern is the pathing, which is a bit bugged as most of the time units will try to get through a narrow gap and not realise that they cannot get through in which case they will continuously try to get through which can often lead to even more units being blocked.
Great game, I wish more people played online though.

I bought Cosmic DJ in the Humble Bundle Summer Sale. I think I paid around £0.69 for it and for that price it both entertained and annoyed me for a while.
The game has 5 pros I can think of.
Cut Scenes
I think the cut scenes are the best thing about the game and they had me laughing quite a few times. Steve3 is what made the cut scenes entertaining.
Music
The backing tracks in the levels are actually really good as standalone tracks.
Sliders
I really like the fact there were volume sliders, that I did not expect and they were great for muting unwanted instruments.
Exporting
Anything you create can be exported as an mp3 which is great.
Price
It was very cheap when I bought it and I think it was a fair price, I don't think I would pay full price for it though.
There are 4 main cons when it comes to gameplay.
Instruments
I was limited to a only a handful of different instruments to choose from and though the majority were nice sounds some of them would not fit into anything that was playing so I just ended up muting them. Each stage used slight variations of the exact same instruments which got very repetitive.
Notation
I could not make my own melodies or basslines, instead I was limited to 4 predetermined notes/hits which sometimes clashed with the backing track. Because the backing tracks were basically full tracks already they could end up sounding far too busy when your own notes/hits were added.
Mandatory number of notes
I did not like having to have a mandatory number of notes in the sequencer to be able to move to the next section. Sometimes the instruments or notation were sounding far too busy but I still needed a certain number of notes to carry on, when that happened I would just mute an instrument and put in as many notes as possible to get to the next section. This felt like the only way to progress without making something that sounded way too busy and this took the fun out of the game.
Steve4
Steve4 just ruined everything with his incredibly annoying voice.
Maybe I'm taking a casual music based game too seriously or maybe because I do quite a bit of music production I've come to expect too much when it comes to any sort of music creation. Either way I feel like the game was a bit of a let down, a mildly entertaining let down.
Even though it has it's faults I would still recommend the game to anyone with a passing interest in music creation or some time to waste.
At the time of this review the price for this game is £0.49, it's worth it for that price

Being a Scott Cawthon game, this was always going to be more than it first appeared, and so much more it is! This review contains game element spoilers, but no story or lore spoilers. I would highly recommend going in completely blind, if that's at all possible...
This title initially presents itself as an old Atari era arcade style game where you design your pizza and then feed hungry children. The game then breaks (literally) into what it's actually all about.
Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria Simulator (being called FNaF 6 by players everywhere...) combines the usual elements of the previous FNaF titles; survival horror and 8-bit minigames chocked full of easter eggs, hidden lore, and animatronics galore, with the NEW element of designing and running your very own Fazbear Entertainment franchised restaurant. You're given the opportunity to buy a small building complete with electricity, tables and benches. You're then tasked to buy items that increase your effectiveness as a successful client trap, take on sponsors and their money, and upgrade to larger and more modern restaurants over five days. This part of the game I find to be most enjoyable, aiming to maximise my restaurant's Atmosphere, Health & Safety, Entertainment, and Bonus Revenue stats without increasing my Liability (a stat which governs how likely you are to be sued). Don't forget to playtest your new attractions! Buying, upgrading, and playing your own games will add to your Fazbear Rating and give you extra funds. They may also yield other rewards...
Once you're finished with the design aspect of your restaurant, you will be taken into the oh-so-familiar office space where you will have to complete a list of tasks including ordering paper cups, printing menus, and remotely unclogging toilets? This is made infinitely easier without any dangerous animatronics on the premises, and that is actually a viable way to play the game. For those wanting a challenge, and for fans of the series desperate to understand more of the often confusing and hole-filled plot of FNaF however, prepare to become a paranoid anxious frustrated terrified wreck. Your tasks create a lot of noise, noise that will undoubtedly attract the attention of anything roaming the airvents. You'll love your sponsor's money, but you will despise their forced ads.
The final element to the game is truly unnerving. Paragraph 4 of your terms of employment with Fazbear Entertainment Inc. states that you have "special obligations" to check outside the premises every evening and bring in any animatronics you may find out there, take them to a particularly eerie backroom, and play audio prompts to them, documenting any responses. You're also given a tazer... in case you feel the rundown robot is becoming too "unstable". You ARE given a choice to throw the animatronic back into the alley, but where's the fun in that?! There are finer nuances to this game mechanic which you'll need to master in order to receive a sizeable cash injection for your restaurant. Suffice it to say that your heart will not thank you.
Those seeking some form of closure on this series and it's twisted lore will have to play smart in order to unlock all the backstory previously unknown, hidden within certain attractions. They will have to salvage all found animatronics and survive the office tasks, and will be rewarded. Those looking to just enjoy a fun and often times scary game, this game is perfect for them, and it's free!
It's FREE, guys... at least give it a try?

It's hard to recommend David. enough.
It's an incredibly abstract twin-stick style shooter with unique mechanics. A few are:
- Infinite double jumping. Tt's double in that the longer you hold the key the higher you go, so spamming jump (as you want to do from the getgo) is largely ineffective.
- Rubber-banding bullets that are only effective for a few frames. While you're charging them time slows down, allowing you to precicely aim. When you fire the enemies speed up before you do making it tricky to use.
- Truly unique bosses.
- After you beat those unique bosses you get a run-of-the-mill but extremely fun arena mode that lets you spend your high score on upgrades. Don't beat your high score? No new toys.
Visually it's geometric, clean, and easily conveys meaning through color (water is dark, you can't go through red walls, etc.) It can get hecktic, and busy, but the time-slow mechanic keeps it from being -too- overwhelming (though, you'll certainly be overwhelmed for a while).
On the negative side, the controls are slippery. It's difficult even to pass through the doorways in the game, and the physics are unpredictable. The time lag you experence after firing is part of it, but you carry significantly more moment out of the time-slow than the game suggests. Often times I felt as if I was being sucked to one side of the map until I got used to it.
To me, these flaws add to the challenge in a meaningful and significant way. It allows the game to flow at a breakneck pace, while allowing you to manage that pace on your own, but without giving you full control. A misclick will mean a loss of health if not death which keeps you from getting complacent.
Best of all, it's easy to pick up and play for a few minutes at a time, but it remains engaging for much longer than it's simple mechanics and feel would suggest.
It's hard to find a better value for the price. Buy this right now.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
Streets of rogue is a pixel-style rogue-lite title by developer Matt Dabrowski and published by tinyBuild. The objective is to traverse each procedurally generated city until the end in order to find and kill the mayor. The game also features cooperative play, both locally and via the internet. The title has a comedic theme both in game-play, dialogue, and story-telling. The game also has RPG elements as well as action, brawler, and stealth game-play mechanics, all of which depend on the player's play style, and the class they choose.
--------

Art is very subjective, especially when it comes to pixel-style games. Streets of Rogue has very charming visuals, and even has good effects and animations. All classes have their own design so when things get hectic on the screen, it's a little easier to distinguish the player from the other characters. That being said, things will still become visually cluttered at times, though this is to be expected due to the chaotic nature of the game. Each city is procedurally generated and as the player advances to each new city, the buildings and terrain designs will change depending on the type of city. The game should run fine on any low to mid-tier system, as it's not very demanding on the CPU or graphics card.
--------

The sound effects of the game are decent, they get the job done, but where the sound assets really shine, are within the game's soundtrack. The music within the game is great. Composed by Craig Barnes, the soundtrack has very funky, dance-y, blood pumping tunes for each stage of the game. The music very much fits the theme of the game, and is also very well done.
--------

The base mechanics of the game are pretty straight forward. The character moves around with the arrow keys, uses their equipped item with the left mouse button, activates their special ability with the right mouse button (if they have one), and uses the number keys for items within the hot-key bar. Things will get a little more complicated depending on the class that is chosen. Classes have their own benefits as well as disadvantages. The different classes will have different traits, abilities and starting items that can really affect the way the game is played. New classes can be unlocked by completing certain objectives. The player will level up by completing various tasks, and will be able to choose new traits upon doing so.
The game ends when the player dies but progression remains in the form of "chicken nuggets". Nuggets can be found throughout the game and are a form of persistent currency. They can be used to purchase new traits, quest rewards, starting items and other upgrades at the resistance headquarters/main hub. There are also mutators within the game can can be toggled to further change the game-play experience.
Each stage has objectives the player must complete in order to move onto the next area. These objectives are also randomly generated. Usually, the objectives have many ways to complete them. When an objective involves another character or NPC, the player can bribe them, trade with them, threaten them, or just straight up kill them. Some missions could also involve escorting an NPC or sabotaging a building. The player can also recruit other NPCs to fight alongside them.
There are many items within the game that do cool and crazy things. Knowing when to use certain equipment or tools does have some strategic thought involved. That being said, almost all terrain is breakable, and almost all NPCs can be interacted with (or attacked).
--------
The game is a lot of fun. I can't wait to see what else comes out of their early access in terms of content for the game. As mentioned earlier, the soundtrack is really good, and I also recommended getting the OST for it. The OST isn't complete, but will continue to add tracks as the game adds content and new stages. Co-op seems like it could be a lot of fun with friends, though online play might be a little too hectic. This is because without proper communication, I feel like everyone would be all over the place and uncoordinated. The game does receive consistent updates and is overall a fun experience.
Thanks to Matt Dabrowski for giving me the opportunity to review the title, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

While Assassin's Creed 3 may not be the best game in the series, it's still worth playing through.
The simplification of climbing and the architectural poverty of Boston and New York compared to the cities from the earlier games lead to parcour turning from the essential element of the game to something secondary and much less important.
The fighting system also got re-worked and is a bit simpler.
What I really enjoyed about this game is that it is huge. I mean, HUGE. You have a lot of things to do, a lot of side quest to complete and a lot of stuff to collect. Building your own homestead was the most enjoyable experience to me.
Aside from that, I found the trading system more realistic and more interesting. While in previous games you just made renovations and then collected the money after some time pass, here you have to craft items, to discover traders and to send convoys, taking the risk.
Naval missions are also abundant in Assassin's Creed 3, and they are quire well-done. It was a fresh and pleasant experience.
Still, there is also a downside to having so many things to do. You can easily forget about the main storyline. And the thing is... The storyline doesn't seem to be one of the strong points of this game. I wouldn't go so far as to say that it is bad or boring, but I just couldn't keep myself from feeling that something was lacking, when I was playing. Yes, there is one powerful twist in the story that happens pretty early in the game, but after that it seems like a lesson on the history of the American Revolution with the protagonist participating in every event that had any significance.
Speaking of the theme, I'm not really interested in the period of the American Revolution, but, nevertheless, I enjoyed reading witty comments of Shaun about the events and the characters.
All in all, this is definitely a worthy addition to the collection of any true Assassin. Surely, it has its ups and downs, but there is a high chance you'll be able to find something interesting for you to do.

Lambda Wars is a base building RTS that derives heavily from Starcraft. Its primary features are base building mechanics, unit micromanagement, resource gathering and a well developed tech tree. Units are intended to be used en masse, while more powerful individual units are reserved for the end game. The gameplay is well paced and feels similar to that of the Starcraft and Warcraft series.
My pros and cons list is as follows:
Pros:
-Creative unit designs
-Well balanced units
-A coherant tech tree
-Progressive base building mechanics
-Combat mechanics that include a balanced mix of micro and macro managing (i.e, units can throw grenades, the vortigaunts have a variety of powers that each individual unit can deploy)
-Competent animation
Cons:
-The turrets are finicky (they may not fire on a unit because it's slightly out of their range or obscured by a piece of cover)
-The game will occasionally lag when the screen is filled up with units
-Some units feel useless (mainly the scouts)
-Uncreative maps
-Not enough units (some units, especially the rebel's mid tier fighters, are just reskinned or slightly upgraded versions of early game units)
-No vehicles (yet?)
Overall: The game is still in beta and it definitely shows, however, it has definite potential to become one of the better indie RTS games out there. The units are competently balanced and the base building mechanics are excellently done. There are minor gameplay quirks and the graphical design is overall rather lackluster. There's also a small number of units total and no vehicles, but the units currently in the game are well balanced. Besides these errors, the game's mechanics feel decently polished and the game is playable in its current state, moreso than some officially released RTSs.
Score: 5/10. This is not a bad score, but the game is missing certain features that would raise it higher. This is a playable beta title that strays from the toxic early release model and presents well designed and engaging RTS gameplay.

This is a game where you explore tiles on a 5x5 grid on each level looking for the key to the exit door, until you either get killed by the monsters you uncover, or finish the run. If you die, your grave occupies the level you died on, and by finding it your characters have a chance of getting stronger. There are four character types each with four unique abilities, and as you progress through the game, your characters get stronger.
I don't think it's really a puzzle game, but if you have a few minutes to kill then there are worse ways to spend those minutes. You can save your progress in the dungeon and come back to it later if you need to, so you don't have to finish a run in one sitting.
It's important to note, though, that the developer appears to have abandoned the game at this point. There are lingering bugs, such as the black market owner's text bubble being illegible, and a few other non-game-breaking issues, but nothing i'd be inclined to call severe, and nothing that's likely going to get fixed.
Give it a purchase and see if it's to your taste. If it's not, then make use of the refund system to get your money back. Personally, I'm enjoying it.

This shouldn't be called horror, and that's its biggest mistake, if you ask me.
For many, I suspect, horror involves more explicit terrifying elements than corpses and the shifting sounds of buildings. In this respect, this game is far more of a psychological thriller than it is a horror game. Perhaps, it might be said, this is one of the very few thriller titles to be found in games, since it makes the decision to exclude both combat
any direct enemy confrontations. As other reviews indicate, despite mentioning that you choose the ending, the absence of any indication of whether you truly confront the cause of all the events led them to disappointment.
However, while I can understand this perspective, I think that the game stands up well enough on its own, with the interesting use of interaction with objects influencing the narrative, to get by with this. In fact, the very real recognition of your presence at certain points makes this an especially interesting title to me, whereas for others it seemed a copout. It wasn't the most graceful integration of the player's involvement, admittedly, but it was closer in tune to what I had hoped Deadly Premonition would do, if familiar with that title.
Either way, for as cheap and short as it is, and for what seems to me very decent quality (sound design/writing/artistically), I'd say this title is a steal if you're interested in games that experiment with interactive narratives.

"Home: A Unique Horror Story", is a game that doesn't play off the standard definition of horror being something to scare you, but rather something to shock you. This is a game like no other game I've played before (keep in mind I don't play a lot of indie games) and I walked away from it pleased with the gaming expereince I had. I'm a gamer that loves rich stories, and while this is a short game, taking me only 2 hours to beat at a leisurely pace, it definitely succeeds in being a game with a story I won't forget. You're thrown into the story head first as you wake up at night in a strange house you don't remember entering, with a flashlight by your feet, and a throbbing pain in your head. You must find your way home, and as you do you discover more and more about your character and the life they live. What's really cool about this game is that the information you learn as you go along doesn't necessarily define the protaganist, but rather helps the player create an opinion of who they might be. Each player can interpret what is going on for themselves to create their own ideas of what is happening in the story and how it really ends, which I think is what makes this game really unique and fun. With classic pixelated graphics I feel this helps the gamer focus more on what's happening to them in their story rather then how the game looks, which I really liked. I did a full let's play of this game in only 4 episodes on my YouTube channel, so if you're unsure if this is the kinda game you wanna buy hop over to my videos here on Steam and give the first episode or two a look.

About half of any good horror story will be a mystery.  The best of those stories let the reader infer what has happened behind closed door, instead of directly stating it.  Usually, around the time readers piece together the puzzle to solve the mystery, they start to realize the picture they're putting together is about something terrifying.  "Home" realizes this, and capitalizes on it in a superb way.
It must be noted that this game is not for everyone.  There is no action present on screen, and there aren't even any enemies to fight directly.  Some people may not even want to classify it as a game in the traditional sense.  In fact, they may be right.  Among other things, this is a story that is being told, and the player takes the role of one of the story tellers.  The best horror stories let the reader infer what the author meant, allowing the individual reader to fill in the gaps with things that unnerve them specifically.  "Home" takes the next step by letting the 'reader' decide how their own interpretation of the past events will shape the future of the story.
I recommend this game to those who enjoy a good slow-burn creepy story.  However, if you're looking to romp around and blast heads off of zombies, then this game will not satisfy you.

There are many who have compared this game to FTL. As a very passional FTL veteran (well over 1000 hours played), I would agree with this relationship - it's clear that elements of this game are inspired by FTL: the sector-hopping map, asteroid & nebula sectors, friendly & enemy battlestations (at least in the advanced edition of FTL), scrap as a commodity - and most importantly, the overall story arc of attempting to save a galaxy by "making-it" to the end of a series of maps and defeating a final enemy (although here, with less of a predictable cast of characters).
However, the perspective is certainly different. While in FTL, I commanded a single ship through various comical hurdles, becoming quite attached to my mighty mantis raiders and my lone zoltan who never got to leave the engine room. they leveled up, my ship gained dynamically altering augmentations, and I was responsible for everything from the timing of my glaive beam shot to ordering my stoic rockman to get out of a room that had been vented to open space.
Here, I am no longer a captain - I am the admiral of a triumvirate of starfaring vessels, built up painstakingly from skirmishes and pitched battles. I can't control individual crew members, because my responsibility is so much greater - I command squadrons of fighters, damn it, and the lives of tens of thousands of human crew surge forth and fall back on my word. This is a high value game, both in time and money, and very fun.

Early on the game can be a little tough, especially since the universe is procedurally generated and you can get some bad breaks.  But using caution and repairing at space stations you can eventually become a steam-roller of galactic doom, slicing through enemy fleets.  Playing around with the various weapons is enjoying, and once you can equip death rays and giant plasma cannons you can destroy capital ships in seconds.
You're going to occasionally lose ship in battle, but the game is forgiving enough that you can always build up to purchase a replacement and equip it effectively.
The game loads quickly, is rock solid stable, easy to control, flexible in configuration, and shows nothing of it's mobile roots.
All said and done, the only downside I can legitimately claim is that it ends right when you've got an amazing fleet you really have grown fond of.  But that's what endless mode is for...

After 2.3 hours I decided to write a review.
TLDR - If you like Lemmings you will like this.
Pros- Fluid gameplay. The bombs consistently react the same which was my big concern for gameplay. Aesthetically the game is nice to look at and has a sort of vintage feel. Original music. Surprisingly clever challenges later on.
Cons- There is only 2 speeds to play the game at (normal and slightly fast forwarded) which slowed me down when I tried a shotgun/try every combination approach to a puzzle I couldn't solve.
All in all this game is a fun and solid experience that is both relaxing and a bit of a brain teaser. There are some small quirks (like bombs burning the foilage) that I thought were a nice touch. I hadn't played a puzzle platform game like this in years and so this was a nice surprise in that it had a sort of old timey feel to it. For the price there seems to be a surprising amount of gameplay there, especially compared to the last few indie games I've bought, so I would definitely put this on my recommended list.

This isn't really a platformer (you don't have much control over the bombs) but it's more like The Incredible Machine or Lemmings. The bombs enter the level from a set point and you have a handful of tools you can use to send the bombs where you want them to go. Gravity is enough to get them started but when they stall out, they roll into each other and explode, which means the bomb in front gets a boost from the bomb behind it. This can create some very interesting and surprising situations, especially on levels where you have more tools available. (What tools you have varies from level to level.)
Ultimately the goal is to blow up all the rocks on the level that have gems in them so you can collect money from them and move onto the next level. As you beat levels you get experience points that help you unlock other kinds of bombs that have special abilities, as well as upgrades for bombs you already have.
Because it's a puzzle game, there are levels when you're probably going to get stuck. There are hints available for every level you can activate if you're at that point where it's going from fun to frustrating, but I haven't had that happen. (Yet.)
+Pros: Lots of levels with lots of possible solutions. A pretty concise tutorial and good controls.
-Cons: You cannot move tools around while bombs are moving. I understand why they did this but there are moments when it can slow down the pace of the game till you learn how it works.
If there was an Eh button, I'd use it. Overall my experience was positive, but deffinetly not the best.

Let me start off by addressing a few things ... This game is probably the most love/hate game of the series. I think it's due to a few things. One is the amazing 3 titles that spawned across Etzio's time line in the previous title Assassins Creed 2,the initial bugs that plagued the pc port of this game(which are now almost all gone), and the most hated of all...ubisofts game launcher UPlay. Im going to say that Uplay is by no means great but  it is possible to get it to work as intended, so I dont want to count it into this review.
So what makes AC3 so great?
Well for one the series has a great intro sequence, although some complain it is a bit long, it is essential to the development of the story. The main character you play in the story without giving much of the story away, really puts the assassins shoes onto a protagonist not commonly explored and I think is  on par with Etzio and Altair. The game is quite beautiful and does a great job of teaching you bits of history which sometimes spoil the outcome of many parts of the game by revealing too much. The combat system takes the good parts of the series and adds a new set of tools not seen before. Some will say the protagonist is not fleshed out as Etzio was but he is more like Altair in the way he kind of creates himself. Also ship battles are fun!
What makes it not a  10?
Generic enemies...only significant characters are diversified leaving crowds with very few models. An example is the native american models which are all bald old men except, for the main Indians who have long hair and are beautifully rendered. This game has tons of plot holes at one point you are rescued by assassins yet you are lead to beleive you were the last one this whole time and it never addresses them again. The combat system is a ♥♥♥♥♥ to learn simple enemies are easy to kill and fun but hard enemies♥♥♥♥♥♥me the hell off when your perfect counters just result in you dying wtf!!!*throw keyboard* The attempted house selling thing (not sure what to call it) is a pain to figure out and not very useful. You can find ridiculous amount of money in chests so looking for those is faster and 100x more profitable than selling things through your home store thing. Lastly there are some history hiccups in this game that can easily be avoided for example... right before you kill an important assassination target his bio tells you how George Washington treats his wound after he is injured and then he later dies. In the game you kill him straight up and it just leaves you kind of dumbfounded.
Overall:
Worth getting if you played the  previous ones. Definitely not worth jumping into it with out prior knowledge of the past games. Also DLC is alternate timeline so it is not required to play for story purpose. And lastly a tip for all of you that unlocked uplay costumes...they are not available until you finish sequence 7 your game is not broken.

I played this game for the first time somewhere around April, and I found it to be the work of a genius. Before going on with the review, there are some thing you should know about me. I love Half-Life, especially Half-Life 2. The game literally obssesed me. I finished the main game around 10 times and I spent countless hours reading all the possible pages on every possible Wiki about the game. I loved the world you were being immersed in.
In April, this game was loyal to the Half-life 2 unniverse, in the best way it could. The units, the building, everything looked exactly how it looked in the main game. It gave you the same feeling. There was no difference in seeing a combine shoot a rebel in Half-life 2 or in Lambda wars. This aspect of the game changed since April. I no longer feel the same Half life universe around me when I am playing.
The game feels buggier, even if it is 3 months later in development. I usualy play as the combine, so take note I will only talk about the changes suffered by the combine.
I was very excited to see what "vehicles" were added in the game. Whatever. I start an offline match, classic one, 1v1, combine vs rebels, me playing as the combines. First thing I noticed was the metrocop at the garrison. The took out the classic one with the 9mm pistol, which was very loyal to the half life universe, and they added some kind of combine police with a riot shield. I like the innovation these guys are coming with, but I don't like the way they are straying away from the original game. I do not remember not even one metrocop coming at me with a riot shield + it adds unncesarry details in the game. Like ordering the metrocops to stand in a line... With no use at all. They can easily be shot standing like that. I liked having the classic metrocop with the pistol, and I could upgrade it with bigger weapons.
I also saw a new "vehicle" factory. I was thinking that maybe they finally added the Combine APC, which could be a very important part in the game. In the original Half-Life 2 game, it was used by the metrocops to dispatch cops around the city. It could be used here to transport around 4-5 soldiers. Whatever. I built the vehicle factory, only to see the units you could build were the Manhacks, the rollermine, and scanners. The part with the scanners is very wrong. In april, the Scanners were build at the citadel, as it was in the original game. Why change the way it was? Why build them at the vehicle factory? No sense... Manhacks, same thing. In the original game, they were deployed by the metrocops... now you can build them at the vehicle factory?!! Wtf?! no sense again... The engine of the Scanners was modified, they no longer float realistically, they now move with no accelaration whatsoever.
No new buildings, except a generator for the Combine, which  takes energy from scraps. Again, a negative point. At least in April, the scrapt was something unique for the rebels, a team already with less content than the combine. Now the combine has access to scraps too...
If at least we would have vehicles...

Cities: Skylines is by far the best city simulation game that has been made so far, or is likely to be made in the near future. The level of detail and freedom of creative customization, in everything from individual pedestrian routes to entire neighborhoods and expressways, make Cities: Skylines a realization of everything that SimCity could have been and wasn't.
The positives of this game, compared to other city simulation games, include highly intracate traffic patterns and traffic flow (as the computer plots a unique route for every citizen in your city), the ability to freely place roads (unconstrained from 90-degree grids like older SimCity games), and even the ability to set different laws and regulations for different neighborhoods or suburbs. In addition to there being plenty of DLC (much of it paid, unfortunately), the Cities: Skylines Steam workshop is one of the most expansive collection of free mods and assets that I've ever seen for any Steam game, with over hundreds of thousands of workshop items available.
The negatives of this game include Paradox's paid DLC model, requiring users to pay to unlock things like trams, disasters, monorails, and winter weather. The game code is also poorly optimized with regards to memory allottment (especially if a huge number of Steam Workshop assets have been downloaded), and due to the game plotting individual paths for each citizen, users with older processors or RAM sticks may find that the game moves very slowly once their city reaches a high population.
Overall, I must recommend Cities: Skylines to anyone who has ever been interested in city simulation games. While I disagree with the concept of the paid DLC model, I have to make a reluctant exception in the case of Cities: Skylines. I am certainly not wealthy, and rarely spend any actual money on games, but Cities: Skylines is the ultimate city building game that I have waited for ever since I was a child playing SimCity 3000. So far, I have spent almost 2000 hours thoroughly enjoying every detail of Cities: Skylines, which is the only game I have ever spent more than 500 hours on, so it personally feels worth the money I've spent. If you are also planning to spend hundreds of hours on this game, the additional play abilities found in the DLC will probably be worth it. However, casual or occasional gamers may wish to skip the paid DLC and focus on the free Steam Workshop assets, which feature everything from unique skyscrapers to unique car models, buildable airports, a realistic overhaul of the metro system, and more. Cities: Skylines is probably my favorite game right now, with one of the best modding communities around, and I sincerely hope more and more people around the world come to enjoy this game.

Home isn't really a game in the classic sense, in much the same vein as Gone Home or Dear Esther. You walk around, you find things, you figure out the plot of the game after the fact.  Home's major twist is that your decision to pick things up, push things around, go through or ignore certain doors, ultimately decides what that overall narrative is.
If that kinda gameplay isn't your thing, of course you're going to hate it. As long as you know what the general idea is going in, I don't think you'll be too disappointed.  In a way, I kind of love the game not so much for its storytelling as its dependence on community-interpretation.  On their website, you can see everyone's analysis of what they thought was going on.
In some small way, it goes straight back to the Lovecraftian base fear of the unknown.  There are no exact answers, only an attempt to put together the pieces that are there.  I'm pretty sure there are no happy endings here, just a terrible situation.  I'm gonna do some more diving on another day, try and get the most benevolent ending I can, but I'm not sure such a thing is possible.

This is not a game of visceral horror and jump scares.  It is not a game with a concrete path and definitive ending.  HOME is a game of elegantly simple design that creates a sense creeping, uncertain horror that haunts you after it's over because you are acutely aware of not having all of the answers.  It tells a story, but not by itself.  You, as the player, very directly decide not only what happens in the present, but also what happened in the past.  You choose the paths to trase, items to take, and clues to follow, all the way up until the end where you piece everything together as best you can to tell your own version of this dark tale.

is a rougelike dungeon crawler with Minesweeper and RPG elements thrown in. You have four characters to play as, each offering a different playstyle. Your goal is to defeat the evil forces and reunite the land, which means going through countless dungeons. The game is rather challenging, sometimes frustrating, but highly addictive. Be ready to die often and make sure to save up your gold!
The story isn’t a major part of the game. You start off as Owin the paladin who has been tasked with the mission of defeating the creatures of darkness and reuniting the land, long torn apart. Along the way you’ll meet allies, some are unlockable as playable characters. Vlad the vampire, Elsa the witch and Simon the bard join forces with Owin to right wrongs and triumph over evil. It is a bit of a shame the story isn’t very fleshed out but the game is still fun regardless.
When I first booted up the game I thought that I might need a controller, however all you need is a mouse to get started. When you get into a dungeon you have a board that you need to click your way through to find a key to progress to the next level. It’s sort of like Minesweeper except you are given no hints about what each block is so it’s all random, just like the dungeons when generated. Clicking on a square can uncover a monster, a spell, food, goodies or the key. Each dungeon level has a certain amount of floors to visit and numerous monsters on each one to fight. There are also hideouts where you can rest every five floors, a few mini games and other nice bonuses. This is helpful since the farther you get into the game the harder it becomes and these safe spots can be lifesavers. The game also has a hunger feature, each level consumes one unit of food.  You can find more food on the floors and also buy some as well but if you run out you begin to starve which depletes your health.
You can fight monsters using a basic attack, a spell, or an item such as a bomb. All of the characters have four spells each which you unlock during the game, you must also unlock each playable character as well except for the paladin. Knowing when to fight, when not to fight and when to use a spell or item is crucial to surviving, your character starts off with armor that can only deflect a given number of hits and then your HP is affected and each character has different attack strength; sometimes it’s better for a weaker character to use a bomb or just avoid certain fights. There is a nice variety of times to play with that you find throughout the dungeons or you can buy them from the merchant in the dungeons but items do not carry over to the next dungeon. Weapons and armor you find to carry over and there is also a mansion to unlock which is like a home base where you can purchase permanent bonuses.
I was first drawn to the gis game because of the graphics before I even know what kind of game it was. They were colorful, crisp and kind of cute. Having played the game I am not at all disappointed. Each character and monster has their own unique look, animations are smooth, backgrounds are well-done, I found everything to pleasing to the eyes. The music is alright, it’s nothing too unique but it’s also not annoying. Each level has fitting background music that did not distract from the gameplay. There is also a little bit of voice acting, the characters say their catch phrases, some monsters squeak or groan, some NPC say a word to two. Nothing major but it certainly does add something to the game.
+ Very addictive and fun.
+ Good graphics and audio.
+ Items, bonuses, traps and such add a good system of checks and balances.
+ Each level gets increasingly longer adding new challenges.
+ Steam achievements.
- Can be frustrating since you die often.
- Game becomes a bit of a grind towards the end.
- No Steam trading cards.
I was pleasantly surprised by this game, it frustrates me often but I can’t stop playing and trying to unlock everything, the Steam achievements are a nice incentive to keep playing as well. I learned that this is apparently a port of a phone app game but I have not played that version nor does that affect this version of the game. While it might seem a little pricey, the game has a good replay value to make it worth it. If you enjoy a good dungeon crawler then I fully recommend this title for your Steam library.
8.5/10

I like Assassin's Creed, it's a bit of a guilty pleasure for me.
Unfortunately, this game has many of the bad aspects of Assassin's Creed and few of the good ones.
Climbing around historic landmarks is basically not there, since -sorry Americans- 18th century Boston simply is not as impressive a setting as Rome or Jerusalem. The main character has a pretty bland and unengaging personality and while the story of the American Revolution is pretty interesting for someone who is not very familiar with it, the real-world story is absolutely groan-worthy.
The gameplay is as you would expect it, the combat has been expanded a bit with new enemy types which makes it slightly more challenging than in the previous games. There are a lot of new activities like hunting, crafting and trading, but they all get old really quickly and only serve to pad the game length. Also, the game takes forever to get going and has tons of terrible tutorial missions (the ultimate low point is when you have to play hide-and-seek with some children). A good addition are the ship missions, which are really fun in the beginning, but drag out towards the end, since there is not enough depth to the ship combat.
A note about the DLC/Season Pass: It's quite fun, as it gives you crazy animal superpowers that you have to use to fight an insane George Washington, but it's not worth the price increase from the standard version.
Overall, I would not recommend this game. It's not worth spending a ton of time exploring the open world (believe me, I've done it), but the story is also not engaging enough on its own.

In Battlestation: Harbinger you navagate a ship from sector to sector exterminating bad guys in real time. Apon your death or victory, you earn exp that will unlock new starting ships, and ships to eventually add to your own in a new run.
Each ship has its own hard points for specific types of equipment; Primary Weapon, Secondary, and Hangers. However not all ships have access to the Hangers witch offer a variety of defensive and offensive fighter/drones to aid you.
Apon entering a new sector you will encounter a combo any of the following; Enimy ships, Enimy Starbase, Hidden Cashe, Ally ship or an Ally Starbase. On top of that, there are 4 types of sector; Normal sector that has no effects, Asteriod Belt with asteriods that crash into ships causing hull damage, Electrical Storm that drains shields and can cause you to be stuck there for a turn, or Black Hole that does a low amount of constant hull damage.
Once you clear a sector you will be rewarded with Scrap that is used to buy ships and equipment, and maybe an upgrade point for upgrading your current equipment, and a chance to get a new piece of equipment.
After a while you may end up with enough scrap to buy a ship to add to your fleet, with a maximum of 3 ships total. Those ships can be customised and upgraded as you see fit, and can be destroyed by the AI. However it is still game over if your starting ship is destroyed.
Overall its a solid game you can pop into and play a few min of and back out, or enjoy for an hours at a time.

Vivid historiacal characters (Cleopatra, Caesar...) and deities (Amun, Horus...). Stunning scenery. Intense combats. The assassinating system did change somehow (level barriers are really hard to get over...), but think about it: this is 49 B.C., the creed had just formed. Sometimes fightings are necessary instead of just assassinating all the time. You'll see how the first people of the creed gathered and learnt their ways of doing things.
The setting is Ptolemaic Dynasty - almost the end of ancient Egypt, which means that tombs of real pharaohs (or officials) throughout the ancient Egypt calendar, from Djoser to Smenkhkare, remain for you to explore. And these tombs are well-detailed, with hieroglyphic texts (fortunately Bayek knows how to read those lol), grave goods, mummies, and the four pots holding the organs... Have you ever wanted to dig into the three Pyramids in Giza? Or to get inside the Great Sphinx? Or to witness the mummification process? This is the game that can realize your wish. You'll even have the chance to face the deities themselves - Anubis, Sekhmet, Sobek, and so on - and get their theme outfits.
Okay this is not a Tomb Raider review (but again most of these are real tombs existing or existed) so besides that, great protray of famous cities - Alexandria, Memphis, Krokodilopolis... Also great portray of people's struggle in this time period, of Egyptians' anger and complaints about the invading Greek/Roman culture. People's everyday lives are simulated really well under the day and night system over this huge open-world map of Egypt.
Overall, a must-play for AC fans and for those who are into ancient Egyptian culture/mythology. I've played over 60 hours and this game still keeps giving me new surprises.

Dungelot: Shattered Lands is an interesting port from mobile that is a surprisingly decent title. I stepped into this game after seeing only a 5 minute review when I was looking for something completely different than the usual variety of games I inhale.
The game may seem like an easy clicker time sink while it is actually deceptively challenging and quite rewarding. It offers a variety of three different themes with an increasing skill level required and experience with the game. It allows you to grind by intentionally dying and earning gold to upgrade your mansion with some pretty worthwhile passives and yet is still possible to finish without.
I spent around 20 hours with this game for the $10 USD I paid for it, and while I feel like I got my money's worth from it, I am annoyed to see that it is a lot cheaper to purchase as an app for your phone vs steam. I would recommend giving the game a try if you have seen some basic game play footage and are looking for something a bit different.

This is an interesting mix of genres, with something approaching a light RPG with what amounts to a weird version of minesweeper. Each level of the Dungelot, you get a series of dungeon tiles that you need to dig out to find a key in order to exit to the next level. Sometimes under the tiles you might find items, pits or rather frequently, monsters. These monsters work like a reverse minesweeper, preventing you from uncovering the tiles they are adjacent to until they are defeated. The trick is that unlike normal RPGs, the monsters strike first and you have only a limited pool of armor and health. So there is a fine line between digging tiles, killing monsters and trying to exit to get to the next floor as soon as you can.
Generally speaking, this is actually a pretty fun mix and the game has an incredibly goofy, but quite charming, sense of humor. The first boss of the game is basically a gigantic zombie cow, whose only expression is basically a zombie moo equivalent. Unfortunately, I think the game does have some flaws and one of them is in the incredibly poor feedback during combat. Sometimes things just seem to happen, resulting in you losing health/armor from a fight, but seemingly not damaging or bothering the enemy that much. Usually this is because the enemy has dodge or your weapon has a miss chance, but there isn't good feedback as to why something happens. So you can click on something and discover that you've lost quite a bit of health, because the combat animations play so indistinctly and without giving a good indication what happened.
Additionally the game was recently patched adding a further complication, where some tiles can give you bonuses or (much more rarely) rewards if you dig them fast enough. A good example are the tiles that if you break, buff all the enemies in the area quite substantially for a period of turns. Similarly, there's a buff that if you reach fast enough can improve your attacks, but I will say these buffs are rare. The detrimental effects spawn much more commonly and this has greatly increased the games difficulty in places. Generally speaking, it's a bit counter intuitive, but there's not much of an incentive to engage with enemies if you can until the lowest levels of the dungeon you're on. Picking fights too early can cripple you towards the end, especially in the longer dungeons that can have 20+ floors to them.
Overall I think this is an entertaining and fun little distraction that I come back to for a while when I feel like playing something fairly light.

(Warning: I discuss spoilers. Play the game first if you're interested,  it takes 90 minutes.)
My approach to this game was wrong.
I had a restless night to kill, I had only my Macbook, and needed something graphics-lite I could play with my keyboard. Home seemed like the perfect fit.
It seemed set up as an adventure game with an easy interface. Great! I found myself quickly analyzing clues, trying to piece together what was happening. That being said, the game doesn't challenge you to *actually* understand much of anything - and so my character's frequent questions about what he was looking at just fed the sense of mystery.
I was expecting answers. That's not a good start.
The atmosphere is generally unsettling because the game teaches you very early on that the game's volume is on 5 and the game's audio jump scares are on THIRTY MOTHER♥♥♥♥ING TWO. I turned down the whole thing and ruined the atmosphere just to save myself a heart attack. But it's a cheap parlor trick - nothing ever comes out of the shadows, it's just noises.
There are many choices you can make. Do I pick up the bloody knife or leave it? Well, I seemed to be an amnesiac in an unknown environment with dead bodies everywhere, so yeah, I'll take the knife. I'd hate for something else to take the knife and kill me with it. My character then muses, "Did I really need this knife?" ..... Well now wait a minute, I thought I was being practical. Am I just being paranoid? Does the game think I'm a violent person now?
I picked up the knife, I picked up the gun, I picked up most objects that seemed useful. And some objects I decided seemed pointless wound up being typical adventure key items. Why am I given the choice to pick it up or not if I need it to progress? Seems strange. What do my choices even mean?
So I get to the end, ready for the story to come together. The game asks me if I find my wife. For some intuitive reason, I just don't get the feeling I do. So I answer no. I'm comfortable with that choice. But then the game asks me another 15 questions about the items I've collected and everything else that is going on. Well I mean, I'm not sure, I've only been playing for an hour. Is there a right or wrong answer? If I'm not sure, do I really have to pick yes or no?
I didn't have any solid understanding of what was happening throughout what I was experiencing, and I'm sure most people would agree with that - it's designed that way. So why then is the game quizzing you on this understanding at the end of the game? I never answered yes or no - I only answered,
or "Grrr, pff, I dunno, no?" It would take a clearer narrative to expect any clearer reaction, wouldn't it?
I mean, what arrogant self-assured idiot would go through an obtuse series of unrelated mysteries and think, "Dude, I know EXACTLY what's going on here"? There literally is no right answer, so attempting to decide what your choices meant within a meaningless context is itself an utterly meaningless action.
And of course, the few paragraphs of text that serves as the game's recapitulation and conclusion was the confirmation that I didn't know what I was talking about, because my choices as a whole didn't make any cohesive narrative sense, even for the ♥♥♥♥ing narrator. I remain just as confused now as I did while I was playing. Actually, more so.
I suppose that's the risk of an open-ended story, but it would have been nice to see the developer take the time to script his endings a bit more to ensure that most or all players would reach a conclusion that makes sense. I understand that western storytelling relies too heavily on clear denouements, but when it's the player dictating the storytelling, the ending feels more arbitrary than artistic.
So just to be clear, my recommendation is based on the fact that it's a cheap, interesting, and unique experience that you might not enjoy, but that's okay. It wasn't my cup of tea, but I'm glad I played it.

Home is a 2D Horror Game that proves you do not need realism in a horror game to have it be terrifying. You see, Home works on the same principle that many early horror movies did: Horror becomes more horrifying when you cannot see the threat. When it lingers around the outskirts of your vision, when you feel surrounded by darkness and evil, but it never actually steps in to harm you.
This game is an example of atmosphere done right.
Its controls are simple, its gameplay is easy to understand (if you're stuck, just go do everything that you can Interact with, that you haven't done yet) and there are branching story choices that for some people will dramatically change their interpretation of the game's ending.
I warn you, this is some dark, dark stuff - especially as you near the game's conclusion.
Home preys upon the pitch-blackness within your own imagination.
Above all, its strengths are Atmosphere and a Staggered Breadcrumb plot.
You will not find revolutionary gameplay here - this is a game whose gameplay serves its story and atmosphere, not the other way around.
It is very cheap, and it should be experienced. You'll probably have a better time than with many more expensive games.
Home is a bite-sized look at Atmospheric Horror that'll stay with you for a while; and you'll probably want to recommend it to your friends too - if only to hear their interpretations of the ending.

A Ninja, Wrestler, and Gorilla walk into a bar. That may seem like the start of joke but that situation is more than possible in Streets of Rogue.
That is the beauty of this title and its mad genius. This game is all about stories, ones you craft and that are usually insane in nature. Vampire Frank and his horrible cocaine addiction. Dr. Dissmelfunay(It’s Belgian) and his constant need to chloroform everybody. Perhaps something more “normal” with cops and robbers. It’s all there and Streets of Rogue wants you to play it with every toy in the toybox.
If that doesn’t sell you alone, then the news that you can play with up to three friends online or local co-op should. Now suddenly that Ninja/Wrestler/Gorilla combo can happen and probably will make a vicious team. To quote Bixby Snyder, “I’d buy that for a dollar!” Okay technically fifteen dollars but that’s beyond the point.
Dr. Dissmelfunay was my character and the start of an hilarious adventure into Streets of Rogue. I choose Doctor as my class primarily as a challenge unto myself. What could I get away with and how far could I go before somebody put a stop to my insanity? Turns out, pretty damn far! Why was this a challenge? Well, the Doctor class is a pacifist, which means he cannot use any weapons at all and his stats weren’t the greatest. He received double the bonus from using medkits, an item I found twice in my whole run. Finally his coup de grâce was his Chloroform which instantly knocked out enemies. It was his ace card and only attack aside from fisticuffs.
The good news is that most of the NPCs in Streets of Rogue are rather trusting and naive. Why is a stranger knocking on my door? Next thing they know I’m raiding their fridge for all the beer and sandwiches I can. Its morally wrong, but hey I’ve got to survive for the Resistance. Between selling weapons I didn’t need and robbing everybody in sight, I made it rather far and almost to the current end of the Early Access. Plot twist was that Streets of Rogue has modifiers that throw in chaos, such as riots, radiation flashes and robots with rocket launchers. What finally did in old poor Dr. Dissmelfunay was that there was three massive bombs to disarm in five minutes. Turns out the Doctor wasn’t good at breaching and entering quickly and thus his adventure ended.
That is the joy of this game though. I had a blast every minute, coming up with new ideas and strategies to use to get my missions accomplished. As the Doctor I had to think outside the box and use poisons, hire hoodlums and sometimes just beat the crap outta somebody. Did I die? Yes but I had blast, literally.
Speaking of the Resistance, the game has a new intro/tutorial since hitting Steam Early Access. Developer Matt Dabrowski was obviously in a snarky mood when he wrote out his tutorial. You are applauded for such things as following basic instructions. Beating someone to death and unlocking a door which makes someones head explode from excitement. In all it concludes with the death of two resistance members, which is terribly anti-productive, but you get the idea.
The story is fleshed out a bit more as well introducing, “The Mayor” character whom I am sure will have something to do with the big mission that we have been promised for a while now. It’s cute and all very tongue in cheek.
The reason this is all becomes so important, is the introduction of the Resistance base. It houses most of the new features. Streets of Rogue has now given a bit of progression to all aspects of the game such as unlocking classes. Accomplished with simple tasks like using only your fists for three levels. There are also chicken nuggets! That’s not a typo. Chicken Nuggets are currency you earn in game to unlock new traits and loadout/reward items back at the base. Letting you fine tune what you start out with or what kind of random skills/items you may come upon while playing the game.
The base also houses the Mutators, which is by far going to give the game some longevity. Mutators allow you mess with the game rules by giving everybody low health, disasters every stage, no weapons, rockets only. There is also an endless mode. You can also create your own Mutators for some chaos and fun. Other features that are present but locked off are the Create a Character feature. At this point, it’s purely conjecture, but I am very excited about this idea. Being able to perhaps choose negative and positive traits to form some unique classes sounds like a blast, especially if you can take those into online play.
Online play itself right now is a hit and miss. While the game does have a listing showing who is playing and whether their game is private or public, connection issues are standard and the game is suited probably best for playing with a close knit group of friends. This may change before the game hits final release. There is also a “Seed” npc which I imagine will allow you to share with others for Binding of Isaac type of action. This feature is currently locked as well.
Finally on more of the development side of things, Streets of Rogue now has a publisher, Tinybuild. This is fantastic news for the future of Streets of Rogue as this gives the developer more time to focus on finishing the game. While I may be a bit biased towards Tinybuild for whats it worth, they’re an excellent publisher and I have worked with them many times. You may know Tinybuild for publishing amazing titles such as Punch Club, The Final Station, Clustertruck, and Speedrunners.
The future is looking bright for Streets of Rogue, if you are on the fence about whether or not you want to get this game, I highly recommend it. As it stands in its current Early Access state, I have played this game many, many times. It’s well made and the developer is constantly taking feedback. I just can’t wait to see the final product and lead the Resistance to victory or more realistically blow everything up.

David. is a cute little game about a small cube named David. If you want to skip the lengthy part of my review and go straight to the pros and cons, you can find them below.
There isn't much of a story here. You're playing as the cute cube David who is destined to obliterate evil and destroy sin. To be able to do that a mysterious entity (which also narrates the game (intro and outro)) grants David a special power with which he may defeat the evils of the world.
The game is comprised of several levels you have to beat before going to the final boss, Sin. Every stage features a different kind of enemy/enemies or presents a different kind of challenge through enemy behaviour, environment or David himself.
There's always two difficulties for each level - "okay" and "very".
Okay-difficulty has you pitted against the misshapen geometry monsters with six hitpoints, so you may get hit five times before dying which makes the game a whole lot easier.
Very-difficulty however strips these hitpoints from you, effectively making you a onehit-target. This makes the game far more challenging. Especially the end boss battle against Sin takes some time before you can defeat it with only one hitpoint.
Gameplay wise the game's pretty simplistic but good. You can move up, down, left and right, you can click to charge your power and aim somewhere to slingshot it in that direction. Your power will then come back to you so you may do it again. Charging your power slows time which is essential for beating the whole game on "very". It's a nice game mechanic that I like.
The controls are responsive, the game runs well, no bugs, no crashes.
The music of the game is quite relaxing, even though the game itself can get pretty stressful. Although you might not hear a lot of the music because you're probably busy slowing time so you can plan your next move. That's what happened to me at least.
And there's not much to say about the game other than the above. Oh yes. It has hats in it. As a little reward for doing things. And a little secret.
So, go to the pros and cons:
Pros:
+ responsive controls, no crashes or performance issues
+ challenging gameplay
+ a lot of different challenges
+ relaxing music
+ the game's just cute and simplistic
+ Steam achievements (once you start trying to get them you wanna have 'em all)
+ hats!
Cons:
- it's a very short game (after 2.5 hours or so I unlocked every achievement)
- if you're bad at skill-based games like this you will indulge in pure rage sometimes
- nothing more, it's just short
Would I recommend this game? Yes.
It's a good 2-3 hours of fun. The price tag is a bit heavy though. Five bucks is a bit much to ask for a game that only lasts for a couple hours. So get it while the special promotion offer lasts or wait for a sale before you buy it unless you're extremely into this kind of game and wanna have it NOW.
