David. is a game that includes a period as part of its title.  We're going to pretend David. knows better and it's actually called David.  Argh!  That period there was to end the sentence not describe the title.   Moving on.  Let's discuss David.
Here's a bit of advice: if you're going to write a review that hinges on you spending two and a half hours to climb to the top of a leaderboard, best make sure the game will update your score and said leaderboard when you quit out manually rather than waiting for a game over.  Now, this statement should tell you three things.  One: this game is engrossing enough to keep playing for two and a half hours.  Two: while David is good fun, it is lacking some technical touches that can be frustrating.  And three: yes, I am petty enough to gloat about temporarily being the best David!  My name's not even David!
So, David is an interesting little shooter/platformer that invokes the vector graphics of ancient arcade games like Asteroids.  I'm not going to try and sell you on that.  I think you either know if that's a deal breaker, a nostalgia trip, or just a valid aesthetic choice you can live with.  What makes David interesting is its primary mechanic.  The game is frantically paced and the platforming is very loose and floaty.  However, you have the ability to charge up a shot of rainbow colored orbs and while charging the game will slow down, allowing you to get your bearings, aim, and dodge.  You'll often have to choose between spamming the charge to keep time slow or returning to heart attack pace to allow your orbs to return to you for another shot.  It works nicely and after a few tries, you'll no doubt find it simple and elegant.
The bulk of the game is the "story" mode.  The story being: you are a square (of course you are, you are playing a vector based shooter in the 21st century).  Evil rhomboids are invading, but you've got the rainbow balls to stop them!  This plays out over a handful of levels that are basically boss fights with a dash of puzzle.  Each of these can be quite tricky, though I dove in on hard where getting hit instantly ends your existence as a regular quadrilateral.  I'd actually recommend picking the hard mode right off the bat since it gives this short game a bit more weight and satisfaction.  That said, it's nice the option is there for a more casual experience.  One way or another, the reload time is fairly quick, so if you do die, you won't spend too much time waiting to get back into the action.
David also includes an arena mode where you can find an endless number of baddies.  I definitely recommend giving it a try since it adds some fun new mechanics, including a power-up and the ability to upgrade David with more projectiles and some new abilities.  The difficulty curve is a bit peculiar, however, since you upgrade David by spending points from your high score and, though the enemies are endless and do increase in volume for a time, the challenge does reach a plateau.  This creates a situation where getting a high score is more a matter of patience and attrition than skill as the more you win, the better a David you can build, so the more you win.  I guess that takes some of the glow out of being the best David, since even a schmuck like me can claw his way to the top.
In fact, in this mode, it could be argued the real enemies are your bodily functions (you cannot pause to pee) and boredom once you settle into a routine.  And perhaps your computer's memory.  Despite the extreme minimalist graphics, I had slowdown to almost unplayability once I'd been playing arena for long enough.  I suspect dead enemies weren't being properly recycled.  Of course, all of these issues will only be found by mad men, not anyone just casually playing the game.
This was the part of the review where I complained about things - lots of things because I'm difficult like that.  But I'm difficult for you, the reader who is maybe about to spend money on this pile of numbers in the shape of a game I'm writing about.
Thing is, there's a lot less to complain about now.  David's dev has been a real class act, lowering the price to a much more reasonable deal for the content, adding more content for free, and sanding down some of the rough edges.  You can rebind keys and alt + tab works right!  Joy!
That kind of attention alone makes me want to say emphatically: get this game!  It's earned it.
Yes, it's still missing volume sliders, resolution options, and a pause button.  Ah to have a pause button.
Sure the levels are short, but my bits still start to itch when I'm about to win, no?
That and I'm now only the third best David in the world.  Still, I can hardly blame David with a period for that.  That blame is squarely on the other two dudes who had lots of time to misspend.  And by blame I mean congratulations!  Probably.  I don't know, I'm still petty enough to mention this sort of thing in my review.  I'll get back to you.
Anyway, David: I had fun and if it looks like your kind of thing, I'd say it's now a pretty good deal for what's offered.

This Is The Police is very immersive. The graphics are intentionally minimalist, and you'll find that the gameplay can get repetitive, but there's a plotline that gets you interested, the gameplay is fun, and the characters are believable. Most of all, though, you feel like you're swimming in corruption. This is the grimy side of police work, and it's well written. It's a war filled with small victories and defeats, but no matter how hard you try, you can't change what things are.
The ending wasn't satisfying, and when the first major plotline was taken care of early I lost interest, only to discover new threads emerging. The one thing that I really dislike is that there's no randomness to the game - play it once and you've seen it all. Every case is the same, every false report is false every time. This Is The Police is a good game, but it's missing the things that would make it great.

One of the best roguelikes on steam! Why?
Characters-
Its got a lot of them, and they all suit different roles! Want to run around naked turning into other people? Use the shapeshifter. Want to just beat up anyone you see (and consume bananas)? Choose the gorilla. Want to be a cop and set the people straight? Go ahead. Ever wanted to be a zombie and command a horde of the undead? BECOME A ZOMBIE. The huge cast of characters is super fun, and you can move on to the harder ones after you start getting better at the game.
Levels-
Although kind of stale for now (only 4 levels atm, but with at least 2-3 stages on each) the levels are pretty large and a lot of the buildings give tons of opportunity for entry so you can accomplish your mission and move on to the next level. There are a large variety of building on each level, so the map (although randomly generated) feels more genuine instead of just copy paste copy paste.  Absolutely love the level and building design!
Difficulty-
It's a pretty hard game! I have only played singleplayer so I don't know how it varies with friends but I find the game to be a fun challenge. Depending on what character you use you can just rush the mission objectives and move on or you can stick around and loot a couple garbage cans and complete side missions for chicken nuggets (unlocks traits/items). If you are like me, you will die because you were saving all your healing items for the final floor instead of using it when you had 15 health and you walked into a bear trap that does 15 damage ;( feelsbadman
Overall- This game shows huge promise and I can't wait for more updates so I can keep on trying out new things! I give this game a 8/10, but once it is out of early access there will be plenty of content to allow for 100's of hours of gameplay.

Over the past couple of years, I was afraid that my love for gaming was going away forever. I'd buy, download, play anywhere from 15-45 minutes and sporadically, or never play again. Streets of Rogue has single handedly reaffirmed my love for gaming. I cannot put it down.
It is similar in some ways to Roguelands, another excellent roguelike game, but this one is a top down "3d" view where Roguelands is side scrollers. This game also has a lot of charm to it. Has a very retro feel (which as an old fogey I love). Each class has its unique skills, some better than others.
I believe the game goes for 14.99, I got it on sale for 11, and, had I known how good it was, would have been willing to pay double the current price. This is a rare early access that's good enough as it is.
Some people complain that it's easy to beat, and fear replayability, but I see it differently. For starters I can't even get past the first world (there are currently 3, and are going to be 5 or 6 total) and I already have 8+ hours in the game. WAY more than 15 dollars worth.
Plus since the game is simple, that means there is an insane amount of room for improvement, the potential is through the roof. not to mention the inevitable mods. I can't wait to see this game get better and better. My favorite game in at least 3 years.
Do I recommend it? Absolutely. If you enjoy retro games, roguelikes or the combination of the two, you can't possibly ask for more with Streets of Rogues. To put it simply, I absolutely love it.

It took me a while to decide whether to "thumbs up" or "thumbs down" this. It's definitely not a "thumbs up", I was sure about that. But is it worth a "thumbs down"? Too bad there is no neutral vote.
In the end, I went for "thumbs down". I haven't finished the game yet, but I'm close to the end (in the 'living castle'), and I may or may not finish it.
The game doesn't start off bad; the style is fun, and I really like how my little guy reacts when he enters a boss arena.
I even liked the bosses. This is rare, as bosses in most games tend to be just overpowered, frustrating garbage -- but the mini ninja bosses all work the same, and it's mostly a series of quicktimes that you just have to trigger in different ways and not fail 3 times. I can deal with that. Plus, you get that evil yoda cutscene at the end of the fight.
However, things really went downhill when they introduced the last enemy type -- samurai that basically drain my health items since they are hard to kill and deal damage that usually can't be avoided because by the time you see that attack starting you're already in an attack of your own trying to take that guy down. Sometimes you even get two of these.
Sow areas where annoying as hell -- with most of the drops being white, and the ground being solid white, things are impossible to spot. But that's
merely an annoyance. One of many, on top of those special samurai that don't show up all that often. Checkpoints are "one use", and once they introduced those samurai I didn't dare venture into unknown territory before activating a checkpoint.
I also started to spend a lot of time moving animals out of range of those resurrection guys that I might be encountering. Especially animals that produce any kind of special samurai.
As the game dragged along, doing the same things over and over and over again, always at risk to meet one of those almost unkillable samurai, I was finally getting into what seems to be the last level. Or close to it.
Except that I get those uber samurai in dual packs now. Or in a situation where I'm not allowed to do anything, but they can rip me apart no problem. Unless I drop to the floor where hordes of other enemies are waiting for me, in addition to those special samurai who will be following me.
Besides, I'm running out of health items... those guys need tons of them, and there are no fruits to be found in the castle so I can only use the few items that I have with me.
I also have too many characters ("friends") to choose from, without really knowing what they do. I've only ever used 2 of these -- one seems to be required to kill a certain type of enemy (or so the game told me), the other one has a ranged attack.
So, in the end, it kept turning into a pain to move along, and I might not even make it to the end. I cannot possibly give that a thumbs up.

Pretty nice strategy game that gives a couple of hours of fun before it gets repetitive, but mind you, those two hours will be epic. The game has reached that point in development where you are almost guaranteed no new content in updates, and instead only bug fixes, but honestly, I'm OK with that. There are a wide variety of units available to the three factions of the Half Life universe; the Rebels, Combine, and the Antlions. One faction in particular is rediculously overpowered, which forces multiplayer hosts to make players all play the same faction.
Besides the imbalanced units, the game is nice. The textures and models are the exact same as the ones in the original Half Life games, so don't expect any "next-gen" graphics or anything groundbreaking like that. Overall, gameplay is fun, but gets dry and repetitive a few hours in. I really want to give this game a higher score, but considering the combination of nasty GUI and balance issues, as well as a semi-broken singleplayer, I can't give it anything higher than a 6/10.

My only 3 complaints.
-My first complaint is that even when transitioning to systems and you choose where you pop out can vary widely. More often then not I find that I spawn right on top of or in VERY close proximity to everything around the center of the map. The reason it sucks is becasue once you hit stage 4 the 2-4 starbases with 1-4 ships quickly melt your fleet like there is no tomorow.

If you like roguelike space travel with sort of RPG elementsv and the ability to customize your ships loadouts its a pretty easy buy especially if you can get it on sale. I look forward to future updates where they add some features to the formation aspect, more ship, increased fleet size, more weapons (its pretty limited atm) and something that you can use your scrap for in the late game (kinda useless once youve unlocked all the ships) because managing to get 200k scrap banked away for points is annoying to say the least.

Vivid historiacal characters (Cleopatra, Caesar...) and deities (Amun, Horus...). Stunning scenery. Intense combats. The assassinating system did change somehow (level barriers are really hard to get over...), but think about it: this is 49 B.C., the creed had just formed. Sometimes fightings are necessary instead of just assassinating all the time. You'll see how the first people of the creed gathered and learnt their ways of doing things.
The setting is Ptolemaic Dynasty - almost the end of ancient Egypt, which means that tombs of real pharaohs (or officials) throughout the ancient Egypt calendar, from Djoser to Smenkhkare, remain for you to explore. And these tombs are well-detailed, with hieroglyphic texts (fortunately Bayek knows how to read those lol), grave goods, mummies, and the four pots holding the organs... Have you ever wanted to dig into the three Pyramids in Giza? Or to get inside the Great Sphinx? Or to witness the mummification process? This is the game that can realize your wish. You'll even have the chance to face the deities themselves - Anubis, Sekhmet, Sobek, and so on - and get their theme outfits.
Okay this is not a Tomb Raider review (but again most of these are real tombs existing or existed) so besides that, great protray of famous cities - Alexandria, Memphis, Krokodilopolis... Also great portray of people's struggle in this time period, of Egyptians' anger and complaints about the invading Greek/Roman culture. People's everyday lives are simulated really well under the day and night system over this huge open-world map of Egypt.
Overall, a must-play for AC fans and for those who are into ancient Egyptian culture/mythology. I've played over 60 hours and this game still keeps giving me new surprises.

Just to get this out of the way: this is a mobile game port. It's not a bad port, though. There are a few moments when it feels like a mobile game, but they are few and far in between. There is a lot to talk about here so lets get at it...
PROS:
1) Dungelot takes an idea from Minesweeper (yes, the original windows title from 1989) and it quite gracefully builds on the long forgotten game mechanic.
2) Art in Dungelot is really well polished. Extremely polished, actually. The whole game has been buffed to such an extremely bright shine that it is probably as good as you can get from a 2D game with bonebased animations.
3) The game feels good in large bites or in nibbles. You can play for 10 minutes or an hour and have fun. This design in this regard is pretty clearly for the "mobile" market, but games like this have a home on PCs too. Not all of us have the time (or attention span) to dedicated 4-5 hours in one sitting for Dota2 or something.
4) Gameplay is easy to learn and fun to play through. There is nuance and some tactical layers hidden under it's simplicity, but it isn't like Othello or Go, games that are classically "quick to learn, slow to master".
CONS:
1) As a mobile port the game is quite simplified. Perhaps too simplified for the PC, though. Clicking on everything is remeniscent of touch-screen gameplay and that at times can actually hurt the game. Complexity is not a virtue within it's own right, but just as a hammer doesn't need a wifi connection, but does well with the prybar to pull screws... Dungelot feels like a hammer without the prybar.
2) Menu Navigation is clumsy at times. When trying to vew my hero, i can accidentally click back to the main menu without realising how I did so. There is some nuance lost when porting to PC.
3) UI design is also...lacking. Opening up the "backpack" feels like a chore and simply "adds clicks" without adding depth. The bag only allows 4-6 slots and you can fit all 6 of them on the UI without much worry. This makes the whole "backpack" kind of a clumsy addition.
CONCLUSION:
I really like Dungelot. I am willing to say that for a PC port it is actually a fairly solid one and almost everything I see wrong with the game can be patched. I do hope that the developer cares enough about the PC community to patch the game with some PC appropriate fixes, but there is no way to know for sure. As I play the game I enjoy my experience and the little details that I may nitpick are overshadowed by what Dungelot does really well: feel fun to play. Over all it is a surprisingly well rounded game. It is a game that anyone can get into and enjoy and I think it deserves to be in the library of both casual and semi-serious gamers. Hardcore players will always have Dark Souls to enjoy, but games like Dungelot are great for everyone else. And that is the majority of gamers.
Purchased this at full price and feel very content with the 9.99 USD price point.

Dungelot: Shattered Lands is a roguelike dungeon-crawler with some mixed in RPG elements tied into the game. The game is simple enough to play, but can be fairly difficult sometimes. The game also has some very interesting mechanics that other games don't usually have. There are at the moment only 4 characters, although you really have to work hard in order to unlock them and play as them.
Dungelot: Shattered Lands is like no other rogue-like, dungeon crawler type of game. It has some really interesting mechanics tied into the game that really make this game unique and fun to play. First of all let's talk about the way that the game is played.
Basically your objective of each run is to get to the last floor and defeat the final boss in order to proceed. On each floor you are given a grid (5x5) and you will be at the door. You will be able to click on a tile to reveal what is on it, this could be a enemie, gold, a sack with a item or prehaps someone helpful. You're objective on each floor is to get the key, which is under one of the random squares in the grid, and get out of the floor to get to the next floor and the next until you get to the end. However, although this sounds easy and simple there are a few problems that you will most probably encounter throughout the game. First thing to worry about is your hunger, each time you go a floor you will lose one food. Although you can survive with no food and going down a floor, you will take some damage, so stacking food may be necessary for your survival. Along with the food that you will need, there are also enemies that you will encounter along your way. Because what is any rogue-like without it's enemies? At first you will find a very small amount of enemies that you might encounter, skeletons, bats and rats. But as you get into the other acts, there will be new enemies suited to that specific enviroment. These enemies will stand in your way, and will not let you proceed to certain blocks which may or may not have the key or something else under them. Killing them is essiential if you don't already have the key and there are no other tiles to look under. The combat system is turned based, so make sure you use your moves wisely. Although you can use as many items as you want and that will not count as your turn over. You can also find spells that will help you attack the enemie, and in some cases will heal you or do other things that might come in useful. The final thing that you will have to worry about is the traps that occur a little later in act I, these traps will be seeable, and will last a certain amount of turns until they are gone. Sometimes this cna leave you in a tricky situation whereby you are forced to step on a trap in order to obtain the key.
This game does so well by means of making you play just one more game until you have finally finished that one area. I'm not sure if it is just me, but this game can be fairly difficult at times. It took me about 6ish hours to complete Act I. The game is really addictive and really draws you in. I really like how unique this game is compared to other rogue-like games out there. This to me is something completely new and different to other games of the similar genre. I really like the way you play through the game, the way that most things are randomly generated and you never know where anything is until you reveal the tile you want to step on. There is a little bit of strategy involved in this game, you can salvage items to increase your bar at the bottom which will then increase the power of your spells. This is a new way of getting rid of junk you don't really need, instead of selling it to the next shop you might find you can increase the power of your spells which is way more useful. The only downside to this game that I found is that it can be rather fustrating sometimes you continously die on the same level over and over again.
The cartoonish like style to this game is really suiting the way that this game is played. Along with the story of the game, which as you would expect isn't too serious, this cartoon like feel to the game really fits in with the sort of casual way you play the game. All of the enemies and characters you meet look really nice and polished up, giving them that really nice look that most cartoon art styled games should have. The characters of the game seem to be really well animtated and produced much like the enemies are, but with a little more detailed payed attention to.
The music of this game is really suiting to where you are in the game. The title screen is a little creepy music that fits really well with the dark and gloomy colours of the castle in the background. It really does set the mood of the game to be one of them games that will keep you playing over and over again even if you keep dying. The sounds are fairly unique to each of the enemies that attack you, and the way that each character you play as has their own different sound to them. It is obvious that the developers really put a lot fo time and effort into making this game.
This is a solid rogue-like dungeon crawler game. Very unique and fun to play, it is also a great time killer if you are looking for one of them games that you want to play for a little bit. The art style and music are both really suiting to this type of game, the enemies are well balanced with each level they get increasingly difficult. Each character has their different strengths weaknesses so that you can play differently, although you will need to work hard to gain access to them.

Dungelot: Shattered Lands:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

We must rescue three of our friends; heroes just like you my dear Paladin. They are kept in captivity in highly dangerous dungeons. Are you up to challenge, my dear Paladin, because it is not going to be easy? Welcome to Dungelot: Shattered Lands!
Dungelot: Shattered Lands is an action /RPG / Dungeon Crawler game. At the start of the game, you will have one hero available to you, a Paladin. Later on, you will be able to play as a Vampire, a Witch and a Bard but you will have to beat dungeons and its bosses to unlock them.

As you enter your first dungeon, it will tell you how many floors it has (some dungeons have more floors than others) and what rewards you will earn if you successfully beat it. Each floor is divided into 25 squares. The door to the next floor will be on one of these square, but it is locked. The aim is to find the key to unlock the door to go to the next floor. How you do that is by clicking on the squares using your mouse and it will reveal what’s on the tile. You are probably not going to pick up the key on the first tile but you might get either a coin, a bag (which always has interesting goodies), a spell, food, or you might get nothing at all! But if you are lucky you will find an enemy. Make sure you pick up as much food as you can, as it will cost you one piece of food each time you go through to the next floor.
In regards to the combat phase - first of all, if you click on a tile and an enemy appears, you do not have to fight him straight away. In fact you might already unlock the door but if are like me, you might keep looking around in search of additional goodies. If you decide to engage in a battle, you just click on the enemy and it will start the turn-based fighting. Look at your inventory, you might have to pick up bombs, axes, knives and more to throw at your enemy and inflict greater damage. Let me be blunt here, you might die quickly in your first couple of tries. Before re-entering a dungeon, you will be able to use the coins you collect at the Armory to upgrade your hero weapons and armour.
I really like the randomly regenerated dungeons - it will keep you playing for hours and hours on end!

Negatives:

-	I would love to see additional heroes
Dungelot: Shattered Lands is definitely a game that should find is way into your game library.

Roguelands is a roguelike that offers challenging gameplay and a fair amount of depth, and enough unlockables (aquired after death, you can unlock races, hairstyles, etc) to keep the game from becoming stale or too fustrating after dying, with an acceptable RNG system in place to further add replayability. There are also multiple storylines (which are decent enough and add more content) and a somewhat barebones questing system.
The game's basics can be compared to Magicite, the dev's first game- but improved, tweaked, and faster, with perhaps more distractions. Player movement gradually scales with level due to directional jumping/dashing, and different melee and ranged weapons (2 for each from my understanding- ranged, melee, and magic) handle uniquely as well. Many different sets of armor and equipment are available, both through crafting and RNG drops - and at the end of a level, you can purchase random items, level up equipment or skills, and return back to your ship to craft, heal, etc. There is also a nice QOL feature, that you can gain warp points to start off again from your ship at further levels. The skills (tech) system also is interesting, and adds significantly more to the game, though it's also more or less reliant on RNG to get the ones you want. There's also a storage system available in the ship and at ends of levels, which can be used by all characters.

I really wanted to like This is the Police. The soundtrack is pure smoothe gold. The story and characters are unique and the writing is excellent; a lot of cynical, 2nd degree humor. So why am I not recommending it - with a very heavy heart?
The game is just not fun at all. You send cops to incidents, if you have enough. Sometimes they fail, sometimes they succeed, sometimes they die, sometimes you get a text based choice. After a few hours of play you soon understand that none of your choices have any effect on success/failure, there is a lot of RNG, and either way the game will progress and you cannot fail. 90% of the gameplay is this endless, most repetitive, driest grind.
The other bits unfortunately don't make anything better. There are criminal investigations which build on a very promising concept, your detectives pick up snapshots of what happened, and you have to put them back together in the correct order. Some of the snapshot are red herrings. Sounds great if executed properly, doesn't it?
Sadly, it's a miss. The snapshots are too poorly detailed and your info is lacking, so you need to work your way randomly, get frustrated, look up the solution on youtube, and then in half the cases realize you were going to fail anyway because you were missing a snapshot that you can never get in that playthrough.
There is also a poker mini-game where you always play first and your opponents fold randomly for no reason.
I would love to see more games like This is the Police. I would not have perservered for 20 hours if I didn't find the writing and music excellent, and the story worth progressing through.
I just honestly can't say I think it was worth the grind. It left me tired and bored more than excited. If the duration had been slashed in half, I think it would have been a better game.

David. is a platform based neo shoot-em up game which features a rather unique recharge to shoot mechanic. Like Superhot, before shooting, the game slows down, allowing you time to move and adjust accordingly.
The game’s graphics are simple, featuring a palate of about 64 colors. Every entity in the game is a polygon, and most are either triangles or rectangles. This in itself makes the game easy to run, and provides a retro feel and nostalgic throw back.
The story has to be implied, however, it isn’t a bad thing. The game has a mysterious vibe to it, exemplified in everything from the music to the some of the menu’s that illegible characters. The story, from what can be implied is somewhat biblical, as you fight the 7 deadly sins, and then sin itself. The action of shooting your projectiles is resembles a slingshot, like the one David used to take down Goliath in the Bible. While the rest is not clear, the game certainly feels complete.
While the main storyline is supplemented by a few Easter Eggs throughout the different levels, and an arena mode, the game feels short. Recently, they added a new set of levels which I have yet to play. The game does, however, do a very good job of personifying the main character, David, through subtle and discreet cosmetic features and movements.
One of the biggest issues, that is not really game breaking, but annoying is the fact that jumping through doors is very easy, even if you don’t mean to. Simply pressing the jump key while in front of the door instantly teleports you to the level. Additionally, some pieces will continue regularly for the split second you go to charge your shot.
All in all, this game is definitely worth the money. It is a fun and easy to learn game that invokes nostalgic emotions. While the game is relatively short, the game play is fantastic. Overall the game seems complete, and with the addition of new levels, I feel like the game can only get better. My rating is a 9/10 overall, the lack of ability to fully customize the settings means that some users may experience an nauseating play through, because of some of the bright flashes and glare effects.

The price drop finally happened (neat to know Valve enforces rules to prevent bait-and-switch launch prices still) so I've decided to update. It's still not amazing, but the game works well enough to be a good value. It grew on me a bit, and the promises of more content should improve things, but it's surprisingly short and easy once accustomed to the game.
David is a series of boss-rooms, contrary to my expectations. There is no real story, limited tactics, and not much replayability in the bosses. The particle shot system made me expect strategy on kills to gain particles, but nothing happens like that. Click-and-hold to charge, release to fire the particles in range. The only real tactical element is timing so that particles rebound into your range. Jumping is more like floating, and can be repeated infinitely to fly. With gameplay being the core, it could be better and more strategic. The awkward physics system driving everything means that dead enemies can still hit you for damage, and the biggest threats are the accelerating enemies offscreen.
The game is fairly short, and I have completed everything so far in around 2 hours. A fair amount of that time was adjusting to the controls, learning how to handle the physics and slowmo. I really don't like the comparisons to Shadow of Colossus. That game had personality to the bosses and stunning environments to tell a story. David is decent as a short game, but this is not a classic. David is Mega Man without the adventure areas or upgrades. Beyond price, my remaining criticism is that the game is not unique nor impressive. I purchased on a whim, and it's decent enough for that. It's not a game I'd mention to friends, but I can't really criticize the value anymore. If you are truly interested, the game is a good deal now. 50% off for 1.00USD recommended.

Five Nights at Freddy's 4 is easily the scariest game in the Five Nights at Freddy's series!
It makes you feel stressed out and worried! Not because of the graphics, not because of the nightmarish looking aniamatronics (which SPOILER ALERT: they literally ARE nightmares!), not because of the emotional story, no... it's because unlike every other previous installment, you NEED to listen for a specific game mechanic called breathing!
Now before reading this, I highly reccomend you check out the other games too! Doing that would help you understand the game mechanics a lot better! Unlike the previous installments, you are no longer static and need to move around the setting of the main game, like the first two games, Bonnie (now known as Nightmare Bonnie) comes from the left, and Chica (now known as Nightmare Chica) once again comes from the right. Also similar to the first two games: Foxy (now known as Nightmare Foxy) stays hidden and is more aggressive than the others, and you need to check on him frequently. Freddy (now referred to as Nightmare Freddy) behaves very differently from all he did in the other games, in fact, he shares almost 0 similarities to his original counterpart: basically, in this game he has three little companions that are housed within his mangled body, and in this game, you need to check behind you and watch your bed carefully, as his three mini versions of him will appear there very frequently! If you fail to check on them for too long, then Nightmare Freddy himself will jumpscare you, whether you check the bed or not.
And it sounds simple like the other games too, right? Like it'll eventually stop being scary after a while, right? HELL NO!!! Like I siad earlier, listening is a vital mechanic in Five Nights at Freddy's 4! When you go to check the doors, you need to listen VERY closely for three or four seconds, if you hear a creepy sound that resembles breathing, hold the door shut until you hear foot steps! If you don't then shine down your flashlight! If you just hear footsteps and/or any sound that's not breathing, DON'T HOLD THE DOOR SHUT! Because then Nighmare Bonnie and/or Chica will come closer! If you don't know what breathing sounds like, then search it up on YouTube. Now your probably wondering how this is any scarier than the previous games, well, in this game, unlike the breathing mechanic, the jump scares ARE REALLY FREAKING LOUD! And turning your volume loud enough to hear breathing or wearing headphones will only make it worse! So it will NEVER stop making you jump! And that's exactly why this game is scary and so hard! I can't even freaking get past Night 3!
But, that's what makes this a true and amazing horror experience! And that's why I reccomend it to anyone who wants a challenging horror game!

Easy to pick up, difficult to master.  The game is built on pretty simple mechanics - a turn-based strategic map to move around the galaxy coupled with real-time battles in any sector where you run into enemies.  There are also some anomalies, like black holes and asteroids, that make traversing the galaxy a little more challenging.  It's easy to pick a ship and equip it but there's a lot to learn to get good at the game.  Each ship has a set number of up to three different types of mount points for weapons and equipment.  Learning the strengths and weaknesses of each ship and weapon takes some time but the process is really fun.
You continue by fighting battles, completing missions, and collecting scrap and upgrade parts to buy new or upgrade existing items, and to add support ships to your fleet (which you also have to equip/upgrade).  As you gain experience, you unlock better ships, allowing you to survive into more difficult stages of the game.  There's a variety of alien races, each of which has a variety of ships and battlestations, so the gameplay doesn't get boring.
My overall conclusion: this is an incredibly fun game and I highly recommend it.  However, it's important to note that it requiress a bit of an investment of time and commitment to learning curve to get the most out of the game.  Anyone looking for an arcade-style space game like a twin-stick shooter should pass on this one.  However, if you're looking for a game that's relatively simple to get started yet offers a great deal of depth in learning to play well, this game is definitely for you.  If there were a rating system here, I'd give it 9/10.

Of all of the many, many, many roguelikes that have been published in the past half-decade Streets of Rogue is more faithful to the Great Old Ones (NetHack, ADOM, DC:SS) than all the rest in one key aspect: lateral thinking. Most older roguelikes had some element that would force the player to look through their inventory, their skills, or the dungeon itself to find a way to get around an enemy that was too powerful to defeat.
umping over a pit trap you found earlier,
rinking from a fountain and hoping desperately that it'll do something to save you from the angry horse that's been chasing you down the corridor, or
apping the right wand at the right time. There was always at least one moment (and if you played as a Tourist, every moment) where fighting the monsters was just not the right move.
That's something that seems to have fallen by the wayside in the new generation of roguelikes, but it is central to Streets of Rogue's gameplay. Each stage gives you a set of missions to complete, and often these missions don't require you to kill anyone. Have a mission to steal an object from a building full of armed guards? You could always kick in the door and try to fight them all, but you could also tamper with the air conditioner to spread a sedative through the building. Maybe you could decide to knock on the windows, and then sucker punch the guards one by one as they come to check out the noise. Maybe you've got more money than you really need, you could hire a few of the hobos around town to follow you around. When they fight the security guards, you sneak through the fracas and steal the object.
Streets of Rogue evokes the days when a roguelike meant a game where every key on the keyboard was a command, but it manages to keep everything contained with context menus and a mouse-interface.

What can I say? This game is a lot of fun. I've been playing nonstop since I got it and only stopped to make this review. It feels like a faster paced Monster Hunter, in the sense that you go out into a level and scavenge the world for materials to build more and better equipment. The game is a hardcore roguelike, and that means dying makes you lose all the items not kept safely away in storage.
The controls take a little getting used to, admittedly. While A and D do move the character left and right, you're going to be using Q and E more often to dash across the level. Dashing and jumping decrease stamina, but it goes down so slowly that you'd need to mash Q, E, and the space bar to deplete it at all.
Each level isn't a recolor of the previous one. While the level layout may feel same-y, the enemies and obstacles are different. Every level has a specific boss which can be triggered by doing some action a number of times. For example, in the jungle level there are vines everywhere, and running over the vines enough times spawns the boss. However, the number of times you need to do said action is inconsistent each time you go through, meaning that you may need to do the action only 4 times to 50 times.
One major complaint I have about the game is the cursor when outside of combat mode. It's small and blends into the background sometimes. I feel either increasing the size or giving it a fancy outline would fix that problem.
Overall, if you're a fan of Monster Hunter, and if you're a fan of roguelikes, then you'll love this game.

Grindlands would be a far more accurate name for this game. Do not buy if you're expecting a roguelike along the lines of Rogue Legacy, Binding of Isaac, or even this developers previous game, Magicite.
It is a basic roguelike but with one very big (and not good) difference. In between the create a new character bit and the perma-death/unlock new stuff bit is many, many, many hours of grinding the same levels over and over and over again. Grind XP to level your character up. Grind XP to level your gear up (but first grind tons of materials to play the RNG crafting game and hope it spits out a purple or yellow quality item). Grind chests hoping to get decent rings that actually have stats suitable for your character. Grind and grind some more. Then, finally, maybe you can make ultimate weapons and armour! Which obviously resets their level back to 1 because yet more gear XP grinding has got to be fun right?!?
Of course, all of this is assuming that you don't lose concentration for one second and die, permanently. Those tens of hours you spent grinding XP and obtaining legendary/ultimate gear? Pfft. Start again. Yes, ok, being that this is a roguelike you will level faster next time because of all the stuff you have stored on the ship, but it's still another looooong grind ahead.
This game needs either a softcore mode or for the amount of grinding to be turned way, way down. Certainly for single-player anyway. The (crude and buggy) multi-player support does make it a lot easier if you're the type that is fine with getting boosted by higher level players and/or trading items that have probably been cheated in with a character editor. Otherwise, not recommended unless you have a very high tolerance to frustration and boredom.

Scorecard:
Full review with screenshots:
Settings amount to music/sfx volume and generic Unity quality settings. High framerates (120-144+) are supported. Character animations & effects, pans & zooms, mouse cursor movement, attack and various UI animations all looked great at 120Hz. Resolution only adjustable via launcher (no on-the-fly window size adjustment) but alt-enter toggling and alt-tab work fine.
Meant for touch inputs but swiping only works on one screen. Hover doesn’t have any visual effect outside of the descriptions of skill descriptions (missing from status effects). Right clicking is used on monsters for their info pop-ups. Hotkeys were implemented, but the only useful one is Esc for backing up through menus; no other keys can be used to navigate. Mid-dungeon they're all spread out (1-4/C/I) and are of little use. A more logical layout could be ASZX matching the 2×2 skill UI, C left for crafting, and D and/or Shift for inventory. Opening and closing menus with keys is inconsistent, and some even queue inputs. I’m fine with an interface entirely for just clicking, but if you’re going to make the effort to add hotkeys, it would be nice if they worked properly.
It doesn’t utilize the horizontal space well at all. Depending on your run, you might make consistent use of items. Inventory in a pop-up means each item use requires an additional click, on top of two clicks to just view your items while it covers 40% of the play grid. The crafting menu is a click deep, and clicking blank space to cancel actions is inconsistent. There’s enough unused space to fit the inventory, crafting, volume/save/quit options all at once, but instead it's all in pop-ups. What was an already immensely click-heavy title, is made even more so. It’s required for mobile, but on PC it just lowers the speed of play and forces unnecessary player inputs.
It was initially advertised with the term "minesweeper", but that was removed recently, and I can see why. The similarities end at clicking a grid to reveal positive or negative outcomes. It’s a shame because not only do I love logic oriented games, I feel such an approach could have made the game vastly more interesting. Outside of following the idea that squares with the fewest uncovered squares surrounding should be uncovered first, as enemies lock said uncovered squares, there’s no strategy involved in revealing the grid. It’s just a click-fest until you’re forced to eliminate an enemy, or you find the key to open the door to the next floor.
Check full review for far more on mechanics; it's way above the character limit. Put simply: There's a 4 characters (2-3 more coming), tons of items/enemies/traits, a number of optional rooms/mini-games. There's a lot to manage and consider, but the core of play is pure RNG, which is often boring and unfair as a result.
Designs aren't very unique, but the visual style is cohesive and well executed. The characters/enemies are made up of many elements that squish around nicely, on top of their attack/damaged animations. This gives a dynamic feel to a title that could have been completely static; the same can be said for the UI transitions, and it all looks great at a high framerate. There are also a few comedic bits of written dialogue between the characters at the beginning, end, and upon reaching each of the regions.
The game progresses through 3 different regions with their own tilesets and additional enemies that fit each theme. An additional ice realm is teased after the final boss, and is confirmed to be coming at some point in a free update.
While the ambient music is nothing I’d listen to, I’d say it fits the aesthetic and does change to suit each environment and the menus. Almost every interaction and object motion has a sound effect, the most used having multiple variations, along with subtle changes between the regions. Characters have voice acting; 4-5 lines when selected in the menu, and a few for various events like passive skill triggers.
The art, animation, and visual presentation are very well done. There’s tons of items and enemies with traits to consider that play into each other, but the core play consists of a lot of meaningless clicking, made worse by a UI meant for mobile devices which forces unnecessary inputs. There’s little to no strategy for clearing the floor tiles, so whether or not you’re forced into fighting is completely random, on top of the random generation failing to create truly compelling encounters. You learn the enemy traits to clear floors quickly while avoiding the actions that will punish, not because there’s any time element, but just because you want to get through it faster. There are key items for the characters that are locked behind playthroughs that are already way too long to begin with.
I’m not the target audience for this title, but I’m sure some will enjoy it. I don’t feel it’s strategic or deep enough to really dig your teeth into, but the presentation is great, and I’ve sunk more time into titles far worse than this on mobile in the past. I appreciate that the title is on PC, but other than the high refreshrate support, it doesn’t really take advantage of the screen real  estate or input methods the PC allows for (slowing play considerably), while also being a title far more suited to the smaller bursts of casual play often seen on mobile. The PC version is also $10 with the iOS release at $4.
Among a few small bugs, there’s a significant issue with a number of achievements not triggering properly. There’s quality and good bit of content here, but I can only recommend it to those looking for a more casual dungeon crawling experience (not that it isn’t hard, but that the game is heavily reliant on RNG where mathematics/puzzle-solving would have been more suited) to be played in shorter bursts, and are okay with A LOT of clicking. I might have thought more highly of it had I played the 100 Floor Twitch Challenge build, or simply stopped sooner. Playing through till the final boss for review (still only ~25-40% of true completion), I found it tiring.

I'm a big fan of the original Dungelot on mobile.  When I saw this had come to Steam I had to check it out.
It may seem at the surface to be a simple game, but the game packs a lot of strategy.  The strength of the game is the fact that it is very easy to pick up and play.  Gameplay is simply entering a dugeon, traversing each level by clicking to reveal squares.  Your goal is to find the key and then you can leave, but along the way you might find treasure, traps or enemies.  And since the game is turn based, you choose how much you want to explore a level and even how many enemies you want to take on.  Once the key is revealed you are free to leave, but the temptation will be there to unveil every square.  And that is where the strategy comes in, if you try to reveal all the squares and fight every enemy you are likely not to get through the entire dungeon if you aren't careful.  This kind of choice offers a lot of replay-ability for what seems to be a simple game.
Adding; It is a game where you can get a quick round in, but will find yourself many times spending more time then you want to, while enjoying every moment of it.
The one negative I could point to is that the game does accommodate the touch screen much better then the mouse.  But because of how strong the gameplay is, it's easy to overlook this fact.

This is a tough game to rate.  Ultimately it is good and worth playing, though I would suggest to wait for a sale.
Pros:  The game has a beautiful unique artstyle, creative gameplay design and interesting story.  The music and how it is given to the player is spectacular.
Cons:  Your choices have too little effect on the outcome of the game.  As I played I kept thinking that I would replay the game and choose different options the next time, but seeing the ending I realized this would be pointless.
The developers also added a lot of loose strands of depth which were seemingly lost or never expanded upon.  You can bribe your officers not to snitch on you, but even if they do you just lose a small amount of your already marginal city paycheck.  There are multiple organizations which offer various abilities and services, but none of these matter and most are only available for a small part of the game.
And finally, a lot of actions and interactions are determined by hidden numbers.  What threshold does the game want exactly?  How did three drunk women kill 4 armed, professional police officers with a double barrel shotgun?
Obviously the con list is longer, but this is mainly because the story ending frustrated me somewhat.  The reality is, this game is good, special, unique and definitely worth your time and money if you like police, film noir or simply if it is on sale.

I originally passed on purchasing this game. The premise itself was very intriguing, but the actual gameplay reminded me of mobile-phone strategy games, and I never saw how people derive enjoyment from them.
It was on sale for Black Friday month, and I decided to take a chance on it.
I was surprised that the game is actually very fun to play, and isn't completely predetermined. It does require strategy, but it is not overbearing for those who are not masters in that genre. The game also makes you think ahead about your decisions, such as you might receive a call that could be serious, and want to send in a blitzkreig, only to find out your services are needed elsewhere, or miss out on an opportunity to make money on the side.
You are also given scenerios where you have to make a choice, but neither choice is treated as the games internal morally right decision. This is much more closer to reality than many other games that try to give you an oversimplified good guy vs bad guy dilemma. In many of these instances in this game, siding with one rewards you with one thing, and the other side punishes you.
All in all it is a fun game, and can be very enjoyable if you like these types of games, or need a break from fast paced games.

Quick Review: Buy it but buy it on a tablet
Long Review: Dungelot: Shattered Lands is a rather unique game that can best be described as a roguelike dungeon crawler with minesweeper mechanics thrown in. While that sounds like a massive headache it actually works fantastically well and makes for an easy to play yet surprisingly deep and addictive experience.
Also available on IPad it is actually the third in the Dungelot series. The first not surprisingly called Dungelot was released back in 2013 and was well received on mobile platforms. The sequel Dungelot 2 adopted a F2P model that was slightly less well received. Shattered lands returns to the first games pay upfront model and is largely more successful for it. The difference in prices between versions however is big with the Mobile version coming in at £2.99 or your regional equivalent and the steam version coming in at a considerably more expensive £6.99. Now while this game is definitely worth £6.99 as I am about to tell you I would 100% recommend picking this up on mobile as to be honest I actually found this game perfectly suited to playing on an iPad and actually preferred that version more.
The core game-play of Dungelot: Shattered Lands sees you explore dungeons made up of a number of different floors where you must find the key on each floor to proceed to the next. This is done by tapping to uncover squares which contain items and monsters. When a monster is uncovered you are unable break any adjacent blocks until it is dead which you may need to in order to search further. You do not have to kill a monster you uncover but if the key has not yet been found you may not have a choice.
Monsters get strong rather quick and often the deck is stacked against you. Monsters almost always attack first, they are littered with battle cries and death rattles and some make other adjacent monsters stronger. Really this game is a roguelike puzzle game and man is it fun.
As you progress you uncover a variety of different loot that help your adventure. Armour gives you extra buffs and abilities, all important food can be gained to stop hunger setting in as you lose a hunger point each floor, the usual life, armour and attack stats and a number of different offensive items. A personal favourite other item of mine is the lantern that reveals the location of enemies on the floor.
Each of the game characters that are unlocked as you progress also come with a number of different spells. The Paladin for instance has an instant damage or heal spell and the vegan vampire can cast a spell to move a monster to a different location (which is very handy to search nearby blocks without fighting overpowered mobs).
Another key mechanic comes in the form of salvaging which allows you to destroy an item to gain charge which increases the likelihood of gaining one off buffs and abilities. There is also a mood system in the game but honestly compared to the effect of other things its use is largely unimportant.
Every 5 floors you enter a merchant and there are other floors mixed in throughout the dungeon with other mechanics. The dungeons are all randomly generated which ensure that each run-through is a new experience.
In terms of the iPad version (which is by far the more sensible and in my mind better buy) it is a nice change of pace from the f2p offerings currently littering the ipad store. It is a nice change to have a decent difficulty curve and not be met by in game currency nonsense, stupid replenishing stamina and the ability to buy cheats. This is a proper and may I say very challenging game.
There are a few quality of life issues that I wish could be changed. Due to the nature of how the levels work there is a lot of wasted space at the edge of the screen. Why the inventories are not there as opposed to being on a separate screen is a bizarre move. Also I sometimes wished I had the option of playing as more characters from the start as opposed to unlocking one each act.
Overall though Dungelot: Shattered Lands is a great game the I would say is definitely worth considering on steam but an absolute must buy on iPad largely due to the touch controls being a more preferable way to play and the much more attractive price tag.
A KEY WAS PROVIDED BY THE DEVELOPER FOR THE PURPOSE OF THIS REVIEW BUT I AS NOT PAID IN ANYWAY. MY THOUGHTS AND OPINIONS ARE MY OWN.

Tiny Build had recently told me they were sending me out a code for Dungelot but as I hadn’t asked for it I really wasn’t too bothered, so when it arrived I thought I’d take a look but I still wasn’t sure if I’d write a review. I’m not big on games that move over from the mobile platform to PC as nine times out of ten they just don’t work for me. Dungelot has been a pleasant surprise in this respect, it’s not all that bad.
Dungelot is described as a hybrid between a dungeon crawler and minesweeper and it’s a pretty accurate description, but it’s far deeper than that. The game is played on a 5x5 grid that’s covered with rocks, as you uncover each square you might find one of a few things. Items, food, enemies or the dungeon key which is perhaps the most important thing, as opening the door to the dungeon takes you to the next floor. Enemies will restrict you from uncovering the squares around them until they are defeated but don’t be tricked into taking on every enemy as this is a quick way to die, rather avoid it if you can. Food is needed for progression as moving to another floor with no food will give you a penalty to your health and items offer a range of benefits to the player like bombs to fight enemies or buff giving potions. Items used correctly can be a life saver and you quickly learn to manage your inventory to match your style of play.
The game also has a selection of mini games and diversions to partake of which pop up as you quest, these are a nice little extra that keeps things fresh. All in all it’s an enjoyable experience to play with a fair bit of humour in the narrative too and while I’m not a huge fan of puzzle games which I would consider this to be I have found myself playing quite regularly. It also helps that the art is pretty good in its cutesy anime style, I’m a sucker for good artwork.
The heart of Dungelot is a mobile game no doubt, but it’s not a mobile game that needs you to keep playing every hour to collect something or do something, there aren’t even micro-transactions and this helps to make the experience a pleasurable one. I’m not being forced to play or strong armed into spending money, I can hop in as and when I please and have a quick blast. It doesn’t matter if I played an hour ago or a week, which probably makes me play it even more.
It’s not a hard game to understand, it’s a simple puzzle game that’s all about having a bit of fun. It’s enjoyable and the fact it came out on mobile first really doesn’t matter as this is just a puzzle game that happens to have been on mobile, it looks great and plays great on PC instead of being a bad port of a bad game which is what I’ve come to think of when I talk about mobile ports. There’s no earth shattering graphics or gameplay that reinvents the wheel, it’s a colourful, bright and fun little game that I highly enjoyed.

is a randomly-generated dungeon crawler with a very slight Minesweeper influence thrown into the mix. The game itself has been developed by Red Winter, a two man team, which also developed the previous Dungelot games.
The game is divided into three different acts and in each act you’ll unlock a new character. The available characters are: the paladin, the one you start with; the vampire, unlocked on Act I; the witch, unlocked in Act II; and the bard, unlocked on Act III. Each act has its own theme to it, its own unique tileset and its own enemy types. The premisse of the game is pretty simple, in each act there is a final dungeon, with a special boss, and it is your task to complete this dungeon and defeat the boss.
The gameplay and combat is pretty simple and straightfoward and, in this case, I think that simple gameplay benefits the game. Each dungeon has several floors, depending on the difficulty of the dungeon, and each floor is divided in squares, only having one that has been revealed which is the floor exit. To use this exit you need to find the hidden key on this floor. Clicking on one of the squares will use one turn and it will reveal what was in that square. It could be an enemy, it could be a pit, it could be loot or the key you’re looking for.
This is where the game gives you freedom to maneuver. You can choose to find the key as fast as possible and proceed to the next floor or you can keep exploring and get all the loot there is to find and defeat all the enemies, which grants you a reward. Sometimes you’ll be forced to just find the key and get the hell out of there because you need to reach the end of the dungeon. If you die before completing the dungeon that is it, you have to start over from the first floor. Some dungeons might also contain mini-games that range from having to guess which of 3 chests contains an item to repeating a certain melody played by some statues. If you fail to succeed in these mini-games however, you’ll be punished but, if you choose to do so, you can just proceed to the next floor ignoring this entirely.
The gold you acquire on the dungeons allows you to buy things like weapons, special items and food. Food is a key component on this game because, each time you go down a floor you’ll consume 1 food, so if you run out of food you’ll start loosing health as you go down the dungeon. One other very important aspect of the game is your armour. Armour allows you to block attacks thus not loosing health but loosing armour instead.
However, the gold you acquire isn’t tied to a specific dungeon or level, soon enough you’ll unlock the ability to purchase permanent upgrades that affect all your characters which incentives saving gold during your runs in order to purchase permanent upgrades adding an element of progression to the game.
This is an amazing game to play on either long or short sessions and I highly recommend it to any fans of dungeon crawlers, roguelikes, roguelites or whatever.

I have a new game under the category of ‘favorites’ on Steam. That’s how much I think of Red Winter Software’s Steam debut title, Dungelot: Shattered Lands. I had an inkling during my research of the game that I was going to enjoy this one and it has proven me to be correct. I generally try to avoid allowing myself to have preconceptions about games before I feature them on the site but in this case I found it very difficult. I’m traditionally not a huge fan of Minesweeper which is one of the natural inspirations for this game but I have to admit that that aspect of the game really works for it. The dungeon crawler – action RPG aspects of the game mesh very well to create an interesting game that was able to keep me captivated throughout my playtime.
The game offers players a very thorough challenge. Although the presentation may make the game appear easier or more hand-holdy than other dungeon crawlers it takes incredible use of strategy to delve deeper and deeper into the game once you have successfully completed the game’s tutorial-like difficulty levels. Players have to advance through a number of floors – varying by the dungeon – in order to advance. You begin with the armor, health and weapons and must search for more otherwise you’ll ultimately lose as enemies become stronger. Generally I notice whenever I gain a new achievement and to my surprise on my first session I was more than a little surprised that I walked away with ten of the fifty two on offer such was the attention that the game itself held for me. I was also a big fan of the art style used both graphically as well as audibly. I felt that both worked to aide the game’s immersion.
If there were things that I would advise the developers to add to the game I would begin with Steam trading cards. This will help foster a greater purchase base for the game because without a multiplayer aspect you’re not going to get people playing so that they can play with their friends. I feel that trading cards will increase the number of people buying the game. Another extrinsic value that I would like to see is a slight lowering of the price. Don’t get me wrong at $9.99 I feel that the value is there for people like me that would really enjoy the game but for those that are on the fence that price is a tad high especially if you have an ability to purchase the iOS game at $2.99. Another small issue is the UI. It’s a little clumsy and could have been built better. Only minor tweaks need to be made but it would make a world of difference.
Dungelot is a game that I know I will return to weeks and months, perhaps even years from now. It’s a very fresh and energetic take on the dungeon crawler and action RPG genres. Who knew Minesweeper could be so much fun? It’s easy to learn yet requires some serious thought to master.

Now, the way the narrative works is a sort of unspoken agreement between the developer and yourself; the yes/no question/answers leading to the maker putting words for the plot changes into your mouth. Largely, this fits okay, butsuddenly "realising" it's all a dream was a little odd. The open interpretation AND the choice to change the plot allows for a strange and dynamic relationship between the two is ultimately a fairly unique feature if one that's a little bit subtle to mention. It's certainly not lacking a plot despite how much some may say.
This is not a game to play as a speedblitz or one to play to win. It's closer to Gone Home than most exploration/adverture games. Maybe not even a game, but there's nothing wrong with that. It is cheap as chips and pixel games are lovely to play, especially when they're in this style.

There's also the attempt to give it replay value but if you play it No Stone Unturned on the first playthrough then the exploration element is largely done with.

Cities: Skylines is a fun and challenging city builder, the gap that SimCity left has been correctly filled by this game.
At first it's quite hard to build a sustainable city, but through determination and alot of trial and error you'll find this to be very amusing.
To keep up with the demands of your growing city whilst coping with the garbage and traffic jams is probably the hardest challenge. Alot of my cities start out small, and once they get bigger, roads and even whole neighbourhoods are removed to keep traffic flowing.
I do not own any of the DLC's but Steam Workshop provides many buildings and small modifications to the game.
Unlimited money might seem fun, but after a while it gets stale. But be sure to give it a try if you want to build your dream city without limitations!
In my opinion the game has little downsides.
This game is a must buy for all old school SimCity players, but wait for any summer or wintersale to pick it up cheaper.

A few notes for the beginner:
- For starting weapons focus on range, shield damage, and hull damage. For starting upgrades focus on # of fighters and/or # of projectiles (burst)... though the Laser Cannon is an all-round excellent weapon.
- Picking up items is done in Engineering: Drag from Space to Cargo.
- Upgrade points (green) should be used to spec your ships for specific roles.
- Fill your ship's equipment hardpoints and then save up for the next ship... but make sure to have spare change for some equipment on that ship as well.

Pros :
+Seriously awesome graphics: to all those who say that the game
have awesome graphics but somehow the lack of facial details or the not-so-real-ness of them makes it look sorta fake, well, if any of you know a bit about modelling characters that are to be used in games, you'll know that they have a size limit and a face limit. In lay man's words, the more the 'faces'(i'll explain below what i mean by faces here), the larger the size. So now there's like a LOT of npcs in the game by default, not to mention the ones that randomly spawn in and around you as bandits or bronze/iron/cedarwood carriers. You'll need a MONSTER of a graphics card/processor if you wannna render those without a lag, and also, the game size will shoot up to somewhere close to(or north of) 120gb.
Now, coming to faces; in any character-creation software that you might use(well in most of them atleast, like Maya, Blender, etc..), each shape you create is basically a polygon in 3 dimensions. As we all know, polygons have sides, and edges. These sides are called faces. The more they are, the more 'rounded' the figure looks and the more space it takes up on your HDD.
So ya, basically, the current level of facial detail is the best the can manage by prioritizing optimal performance.
+Really good combat mechanics. Some say it's broken, but then again, you can only expect so much from ubi coz in the previous versions of AC, you just press E(counter) and thats it, fight won. In here, you need to have atleast a bit of skill because firstly, you needa get a lock on your opponent(that, or be good enough to keep rotating your fov and keeping him in your screen at all times and not missing a swing/powerattack at him). After that, just spamming the attack key doesnt help, nor does holding the block key do anything substantial. You needa keep dodging, hitting, kiting, and not missing power attacks to actually win a fight against a good opponent. Also, you cant just waltz into a high level area and assasinate the entire region with your hidden blade. All of the above was said assuming you're playing at high difficulty. This game is amazing. Or at least it would be if the publisher would stop ♥♥♥♥ing up the game's economy, and the devs would actually fix the game's core issues. However, for a casual player, giving Tera a try for the gameplay, specifically the combat, is worth it. However, getting invested in the game is hard for me now. I have no drive to play anymore. I've spent 2200 hours in the game since it came on steam, and at least 800-1200 before then. I'm writing the review right before the "Guilded Age" update comes out and I haven't played actively since the beginning of the "Secrets and Shadows" update.
EME = publisher
BHS = dev
These are some reasons I'm quitting the game for:
1. EME has no idea how to manage a game economy. Every issue with in-game resources is met with: "Oh, [insert item here] is rare? Let's make an event that will give everyone thousands of them." Not to mention bringing back "limited time" or "exclusive tournament reward" cosmetics in an event, for free, not that it negatively affected me, I got quite a few of them for cheap during that time. It just goes to show how stupid it can get.
2. EME has no QA. Every single time there is a new patch. There will be game breaking bugs guaranteed, even though we're getting the 2 months after zero-day version of the Korean game. Not to mention every event will also have either a bug that (surprise) breaks the economy by flooding the market with whatever rare item they're giving out in stacks anyways due to a bug in the event rewards, or more likely just flat out not work at all.
3. Bluehole can't fix the goddamned performance issues in their game. It doesn't matter what kind of killer rig you've got, if it's not a 2770k and a gtx 680 ti, it'll run like♥♥♥♥♥♥ and even if you have that exact setup, it'll run like♥♥♥♥♥♥anyways. There haven't been any optimizations for newer arcitectures so that old hardware still runs the game best, albeit still poorly relative to other games. I see players of other games like PoE, TF2, CSGO, and Payday, off the top of my head, complain about a game's performance, but Tera is on a whole new level. I'm talking about you're never hitting 60+ fps unless literally nothing is going on. If you're in a fight, and you have a pretty beast rig, even with some important graphics tweaks, it's a 20 fps slideshow unless you have everything turned down through config files. It's been 5 years, Bluehole, fix your ♥♥♥♥ing game.

Roguelands is my baby. I've been following it since its announcement, and I bought it as soon as I could, given my affection for Magicite (a game I wished I could have bought, but this is better). Roguelands is a roguelike, and prides itself on replayability. Unlocks come with dying, and each one is better than the last (Unless you're a prune who always goes with the same build). Recently I’ve started playing Roguelands, a neat game by the makers of Magicite; Sean Young. An early access title that packs a punch!
The game has the same general art style as Magicite, a game that took many by surprise for its fun and difficult gameplay, it’s crafting mechanics and it’s price point. Well he’s back again, with Roguelands a somewhat spiritual successor to Magicite.
Roguelands takes place on an intergalactic scale, with a meshing of most things with a hint of technology. Be it an Aethermage, a commander or a Datamancer. The variety in builds lends itself greatly to the online multiplayer aspect of the game.
Being able to create a character from many different races, appearance variants, starting boons and classes allows you to really min-max your set up for singleplayer and multiplayer. What this allows is for you to really make characters that feel unique, say a Royalite Gunner or a Human Aetherknight. This variance in gameplay and styles lends a sizable portion of depth to an otherwise simple looking game.
The game also features a full bodied crafting system, with the ability to collect things in maps and turn them into emblems, potions, armor etc. This again allows a real depth to the personality and mechanics of ones character, maybe you want to play a datamancer in heavy armor, or an Aetherknight in light dex boosting armor. A system in place that adds a greater depth to the already unique game.
Beyond that, there is also a shop inside your ship where you can spend several types of currency. There is Credits, the general currency that can be used to buy ship decorations among others and world currency that your ship collects for you that can be used to buy items for yourself. Another system in place that allows great customization as well as varied depth.
The combat can be a bit simple at times, especially in the beginning but don’t let that hold you back. What Roguelands lacks in story and “HD graphics” it embraces and overcomes with character and charm. Combat can be summed up as 1 button attacks for awhile, which can feel very tedious. Characters can gain augments and skills to alter their loadout as well as weapons of different sorts.
Q and E dash your character using energy, while Space allows jumping multiple times, again costing energy. Beyond that, there is a mana system reserved for abilities you use while wielding your weapon. Outside of combat 1-6 serve as hotbar positions, while in combat they serve as skill slots. This simplicity makes the combat very easy to get into, and difficult to master.
Overall with my short time playing Roguelands and it being in Early Access! It’s a very deep game, that will continue to get better. I look forward to the future of it and shall continue to play it.
I give it a 7/10 in it’s current state, and say that it’s not for all gamers; especially those weary of early access. But, the game has an already tremendous depth and will continue to be quite enjoyable as it progresses. If you have friends, or aren’t afraid to make some than I think it’s an easy buy at $9.99.

Streets of Rogue is an amazing Rogue-Lite game with many unique ideas. You make your way through randomly generated maps with randomly generated tasks while it's always left upon you how to approach them.
At the beginning of each playthrough you must pick one of many different characters which have a big impact on the way you will play the game as each of these characters have unique abilities and advantages.
