Should this be on my phone instead of my PC? Oh yeh, I have a Windows phone and there is about as much support for it as there an existing Steam app. In all seriousness, other than the name being a good joke when describing the game itself, there us some fun times to be had here.
I’m going to start with calling Dungelot a grind. That’s coming off of saying that Battle for Blood wasn’t a true grind. Dungelot is a bit more blatant in its grind… that is unless I’m playing the game wrong.
*An hour or three bits of gameplay later…*
Turns out, yes I was playing it wrong. Dungelot is a item-driven game, but it is more correctly a progress-driven game. What I mean is that you don’t have to fight all the enemies and from what I’ve come to experience, it can actually be better for you if are able to grab all of the loot without encountering any enemies. This is seriously counter-intuitive for the likes of me. This is especially true when you make me a paladin and then have me walk past hordes of undead to beat a dungeon. You simply need to get to the bottom of the dungeon without dying of HP lose or starvation. The kicker is, while you may progress in the game by getting to the end, if you kill everything on a floor you are rewarded with a chest that can have some pretty useful loot. Is this the only way to get certain items? I’m not really sure. I also can’t remember where I got some items and that kind of frustrates me since killing a lot of things in this game is a gamble that I don’t like to take. Who cares if you have a lot of items if you don’t have the HP to make it to the end?
The first few dungeons or so are rather simplistic and they move up in difficulty quickly (especially if you’re trying to kill a lot of things). You’ll be walking around these RNG’d dungeons trying to get to the last level and while concept sounds easy enough I want to emphasize the “walking” bit. If you go around clicking around all willy-nilly, you will end up regretting it sooner rather than later. There are enemies that benefit greatly from being surrounded by other blocks and some enemies get buffed when you kill others. If you let too many of them gather and you haven’t discovered the key to the door for that level yet, you could be in for some work. There are some baddies that will take damage for other monsters and some that get buffed when you kill other monsters as well. So there may be only one block left and you may have to kill more than just one monster to get there.
Naturally, the more you play, you’ll get a pretty good idea of which ones should be dealt with when you encounter them. There are some that are on my “kill on site” list, but even those enemies are spared sometimes if I don’t need to take the chance. If I can get the key, I’ll just grab it and peace out of the level as quick as possible. Is there a reason for killing things other than a random chance at an item? Kind of… if you like temporary buffs and achievements. I hate to admit it, but I’m a mild fan of both. I’ll probably end up going back through just to finish out some achievements. That will come later though. I’ve got three continents to save from… peril? Well, three main bad guys at least. I’ve also got more of this game to figure out.
Score: Tasty!
Dungelot is a genuinely fun game to experience. While I get frustrated with how some encounters/dungeons end, with the way the game is built I know that there was definitely something I could have done differently to save myself. There’s been a few circumstances where I just had some bad luck here and there, but so far the game is rather fair in comparison to other roguelikes. Dungelot has a fun aesthetic going for it making playing and losing an almost pleasant experience. It’s a fun title that most should enjoy as a nice relaxing break from the normal go-go-go of games today. There’s also some endless levels who just fall in love with the gameplay. Not my thing since the devs take 90% of my winnings from there. *Fist shaking!*

Anyway.. done with this one.

WELL, just bought this game as an off chance, I Dont usually buy early access games in fear of them not ever finishing it BUT I just couldnt resist. Within the first 15mins of the game I could tell this game is HEAVILY inspired by the Super Nintendo game.. Secret Of Mana. The enemies, their attacks, music, temples, the spells you get to learn, even bosses (the water temple boss). THIS is NOT a bad thing that the game borrows from Secret Of Mana, cos that game was certainly one of the Super Nintendo's BEST action rpg games. The only main difference so far is that there's NO ring menu for item usage, the main chararcter you control dont look nothing like Randy off S.o.M, and the story is slightly different.
I can see the game has a few issues it needs to still iron out for what content has been released so far but these are so minor it won't spoil your gameplay, someone needs to re-read this games english script and alter it cos things spelt wrong and sentences not making full sense are in this game, for example.. Wish spelt as Whish .. and talking to the water temple woman certainly needs reworking text wise. I'm now only just beaten the two werewolf monsters and saved the water temple princess and have stopped to write this review for the game so here are my marks so far..
Graphics: 8/10 (Because of visible glitches, and the damage pop could look a lot more colorful and flash with crit hits also.)
Music/Sound Effects: 9/10 (I noticed a few minor jumps in the music and whilst loading areas, this though could be my laptop and not the game itself, not sure really.)
Story: 10/10 (I'm loving it so far, makes me want to go play 'Secret Of Mana' all over again, hahaha!)
Over All: Id certainly recommend this to my friends, in fact.. i'm just about to head on over to a facebook page thats dedicated to final fantasy and spread the word of this game to them, they are ALL Secret Of Mana fans. i'm also going to cover a mini-review on my website.
Suggestions to the devs: Please dont think im making these suggestion out of spite or they are meant in any negativity against your game, it's constructive ideas for you to think about adding to your game to make it even MORE appealing, so..
1. Make damage pop more flashy.. IF you take a look at 'Dawn Of Mana' on the PS2 and see how the damage pops on that, I think that type of effect would look FANTASTIC in this game of yours, look on Youtube.
2. Get someone in to rework the English dialogue and spell check for mistakes.. Whish?
3. Maybe introduce items menu, with potions etc.. maybe use the F-Keys, F1, F2 etc.. to use the items.
4. have enemies drop items, like hp potions etc. by doing this it will give your game more content also, like item shops.
5. give your game a coin currency, again for buying items in shops etc.
6. get some side quests put into the game, with rewards like currency, items, etc. even if you only do like 3 to 5 side quests per chapter.. it adds more depth to your game and interaction with npcs.
There's probably loads more I could write here but dont want to overwhelm you, in ANY case, this is a fantastic game and look forward to MANY more updates for it.. good luck on getting this project finished.

Divinia Chronicles: Relics of Gan-Ti is an ARPG where you're going to play as a guy from a village in a middle of the forest that in the begining he doesn't know anything about his fate but his during the adventure will discover it.
At the first sight, the game has remembered me the Wii version of Legend of Zelda
The game is in early acces now, but you can play five chapters and try some of the features and contents.
In the first chapter, the game introduces you the story and characters.
In the second one, you are going to learn how to fight, and solve some puzzles.
In the third one, you are going to awake a fairy that will teach you how to use magic powers and you will fight to your first boss.
These three chapters are a sort of tutorial, the adventure really begins in the fourth one.
The game unblocks chapters when you arrive to some checkpoint and you can not save during them.
The character is easy to control using keyboard and mouse. WASD to move and mouse to fight using one button for hit and one for block.
The graphics are nice anime style. There are full of colours and animations are normal for a game of these characteristics. The scenarios are quite good (the game uses source engine), water effects are good and the enviroment changes a little bit during night and day. Maybe developers must improve the models of the characters, they are a litlle bit simply, specially the enemies (there are three types: squirrels, frogs and plants). They must be better, because all of them  are low detailed and have the same look and textures.
The map is a little bit complex. I miss a little map of the area in the corner of the screen and some sort of quick travel because I spent a half of time walking around between the main sites of the map.
The game is very linear and there's no side-quests, but it's well written and its story seems long enough (I have only play the first three chapters) to give you some hours of entertainment.
You improve your skills fighting, each enemy gives you points of expirience that raise your level but I haven't been able to find new equipment (you change the sword between chapter two and three) so it neither seems there is inventory management or traits/abilities/skill point. Maybe in the next chapters this point changes,I hope so.
Music and sound are quite good, there are some qualilty tunes and sfx.
The game has no achievements neither trading cards, I encourage to developers to add them in next releases
The game needs some work but developers are working hard on it so I think it is a good choice to play, if you like Zelda style role games.

Builds up on everything that made Witcher 3 a great game. This is a true open world game, in which your game is actually open for you to tackle the problems in diffrent ways including some sandbox-ish physix that encourage you to experiment.
The world is the biggest world in any video game. It is fair to say that part of it is useless desert but even the useful part of the map is bigger than Witcher 3, and more diverse. The game is extremely beautiful and ancient Egypt is a pleasure to explore and its misteries to uncover. You really feel like a tourist and after finishing it I feel like I explored all of Egypt.
The horse is responsive, the climbing and parkour-ing is natural and fluid. You can also climb any terrain now, and the horse can jump extremely large distances, cross medium-depth waters and even jump into canyons.
The combat si extremely thoughtful. It isnt necessarely difficult along the game but if you really want a challenge you can visit the gladiator colloseum or elephant events. Not only the combat is good and diverse with plenty of enemy types but the horse combat is super cool as well, being able to rotate on the horse to shoot and swing at the enemies chasing you while the horse is sprinting forward is perfectly done and action-movie-esque.
The stealth section is taking inspiration from AC Unity, Deus Ex and Dishonored, with several ways to enter a secured zone without being noticed. This is where your eagle shines, his job being to scout for enemy sentries, hidden pathways, caverns and treasures.
The draw distance is amazing, way better than Witcher 3. Also features a Photo Mode which is amazingly satisfying to use to capture amazing moments especially whit the great draw distance and amazing acrobatic combat and movement.
Also has plenty of weapon variety, each type of weapon with diffrent handling and use and each weapon with diffrent stats and enhancements like bleeding, burning etc. That applies to bows as well as tools.
You can also tame wild animals to have pets that help you in combat which is a nice addition. Also the game now features tombs inspired by Tomb Raider games. They are short, one puzzle or platforming section leading to the treasure. They are not hard but they contribute to the authenthicity of ancient Egypt. Also the side activities are far superior to Witcher 3's. I mean The Witcher has Gwent which is fantastic, but little else but AC Origins has gladiator fights, war elephant fights, hippodrome chariot races, tombs. Also every question mark in W3 is usually a monster nest or something similar, really simple, but here, any question mark can vary from an wild animal lair to a whole fortification waiting to be thrown into chaos with slaves and animals to be released, captains to be killed and treasures to be looted.
The swimming sections are also better than Wither 3's because it's more beautiful and it now features a fully developed underwater combat.  Also the naval combat is similar to Black Flags but it doesn't overstay its welcome.
Storywise it's debatable if it's as good as AC II but if not, it defeneatly comes close.
These are just on the top of my head but I'm sure you will have many more things to praise about this game by the time you're done with it.

Up until recently, I've been happy with the FNAF storyline. The lore was deep, the clues were clever, and all in all it was an enjoyable romp... but, I can't help but feel like this game ends in the worst way possible. I don't find a lot of pleasure in progressing through a mystery, wracking my brain to put the loose pieces together, staying up for hours trying not to die of a heartattack in my chair, only to be met with a brick wall at the end of things. It's like telling a disjointed story for 4 chapters and the final pages are all blank. Sort of like "The hero stood before the keep with his sword drawn. As the dragon rose up from behind the spires he could hear the princess calling his name from the highest tower. Steadfast and diligent, the hero began to cross the drawbridge, inching closer and closer to the dr-" and then nothing.
The story stops mid-scene. There's no rising action or climax, just a bunch of unanswered questions.
I can totally get behind creativity, and every one has a different method of story telling, but what makes a story is a beginning, middle and end. No offense, but I don't find omission of an ending to be a creative means.
I understand that Scott is hesitant to release the ending because of his anxiety revolving around the fan base response, but completely cutting out the ending isn't the way to go about this. Any writer worth his salt should present their stories as they intended, and I don't think that this was meant to be swept under the rug and over-shadowed with a plush-doll RPG. I'm hoping that the details with either be revealed in movie form, or through the game in an update later, but I'm not going to hold my breath.
To be honest, this is why I stopped watching M. Night Shamalananananan movies... when you go through all of this without a proper pay off, you're left feeling like you've wasted your time, energy and money. If this is the kind of storytelling we can expect in the future, I'm afraid I'll have to decline further indulgence in the series.
I mean, I'm the type of person who hates the idea of unfinished games hitting the market, and I steer clear of a lot of indy titles for that reason. With FNAF, I thought was being immersed in a grand mystery that would inevitably end with the facts being laid out. While it's fun to speculate, there's no real substitution for directors intent. I wanted to see how this story was supposed to end, not leave it up to kids on YouTube to theorize and rant about for views. Overall, with this being the final chapter and no conflict resolution, I'm concerned that further games and tales will end this way.
At the end of the day, I play other people's games for entertainment and storytelling. As it stands, this story is unfinished, disjointed and any conclusions are just speculation from reddit and youtube.
If you had asked me if I would recommend any game from the series before this point, I would have been able to put forth a great review and sing high praises, but now, I wouldn't recommend it to anyone simply for the fact that all they're going to get for their troubles are panic attacks and a deep sense of disappointment.
The way this series has allegedly ended has made me reconsider seeing the movie or purchasing any further work from this developer or any other indy developer. I would love to get the time and the $30.00+ I've spent on these games back, but that's how we learn. We gamble and we lose. Next time, I'll exercise more caution when delving into the indy community, if I even decided to gamble again. I also cannot recommend to friends, family or anyone else that they play these games, see the movie or go for the new RPG.
I wouldn't recommend dry-humping over actual sex, so I can't recommend a game that gives you mental blue balls.

What I did like about the game is that while finding clues, your character will sometimes propose questions that basically ask you how he should interpret them. You can make him start to feel guilty, as if he's done something wrong, or you can project that onto other characters. This seemed to play a big role in how your character inevitably decides how to handle what he's discovered, and inevitably deciding how the story will end.
Like for many other reviewers, that still didn't feel like enough. You never find out the truth of what happened, only your interpretation based on what you observed. I admit, in retrospect it's clever and almost enough. But I wanted to KNOW what happened; so I was left feeling unsatisfied.

Dungelot is a fun time waster that combines Minesweeper's game mechanic with a rogue-like game play. The game offers enough variety to stay interesting for quite a long time and the pace that it unlocks new content is just right.
The presentation of the game is cartoon-ish and well made. The sounds and voices suit the setting. The graphics have a distinguished style. There is a certain humour in the writing and it doesn't try to be too funny, but adds a nice amount of silliness to the game.
The main game mechanic (clicking on blocks to uncover what they hide) is clearly 'borrowed' from Minesweeper, but the game play is entirely different. If you want to buy this game to play a fantasy version of Minesweeper you will be fairly disappointed. That being said the game play is a solid rogue-like that offers enough variety and strategic decisions to stay interesting for a longer time.
Overall the game is very well made and balanced. The only problem is the price point of 10$ which is a bit too much for what the game has to offer. I can recommend the game when it's on sale or if you really liked the free version.
Edit: The game just got its second update and the devs are really listening to suggestions and problems with the game (as little they might be). This is very great to see for a mobile port as they often don't get much attention after being released on Steam. Another plus on the list :)
Edit 2: Some achievements are broken and the developer seems to not care about it after the initial patches anymore. For over two weeks no replies to forum threads and yesterday a 'patch' was released without a note that just makes things worse. They added a new 'feature' to the game though. Sadly it seems like the game is stuck in a half working state and chances to see it fixed don't seem too good right now. I'll change my recommendation for the game and will wait for a proper fix or at least an explanation from the dev.
Edit 3: The same day that I changed my review, the dev (finally) fixed the problems and posted a patch note. Game fully recommended again :)

Having been largely unaware of the Dungelot series, I wasn't entirely sure what to make of the mashup design when I first saw it advertised on Reddit. As it was, the developers had launched an ongoing Twitch event that involved key giveaways; I figured I'd try to snatch a key and see what the fuss was all about.
Red Winter has impressed. Before I comment further on the game itself, allow me to share a quick story. After tabbing through several streams over the span of an afternoon, engaging with streamers and other players alike, I simply hadn't any luck winning distributed keys. I decided to reach out to the Dungelot team on their official Facebook page and inquire into the length of the event, in hopes that they intended to keep it going for a few more days. A mere fifteen minutes after I sent my message, a member of their team responded with gratitude for my interest in the game and four free keys to use for my wife and I, as well as two friends. This isn't something you see very often and it was entirely unexpected (despite the random giveaways that had been done throughout the day). This alone has earned my respect and admiration for Red Winter Software.
That said, don't be deceived by the colorful animations and quaint humor: this game
challenge you. Sure, as soon as you loot the current floor's key, you can move on whether or not you've cleared the floor but the game is still designed in such a manner as to stack the odds against you. As you're unable to clear tiles adjacent to monsters you've yet killed, it becomes a game of strategy -- more so given the nature of many of the monsters and their de/buffs. Mechanics are not overwhelmingly difficult to learn and while the crafting + vendor system is a bit simplistic, the variation of loot adds a layer of intrigue (and addiction to clearing each floor, I might add).
I'd be remiss if I didn't acknowledge how pleasantly surprised I was with the lore and NPC interactions as well.
For a dungeon crawler, this is easily my best experience to date and I would wholeheartedly recommend this game. I look forward to adding more to my review as I invest more time into the game but at this very moment, it gets a 10/10 from me.

Looks like an interesting resource management game, it actually thinly-veiled propoganda masquerading as a noir story, which itself is masquerading as a game. Nothing you do matters, yet you can constantly lose by doing the most ordinary things. That's fine, Papers Please did that, and it was pretty good. Note that in Papers Please, you only go back one day, and the gameplay is very very simple. Here, your win conditions for events are so arbitrary that doing anything is a failure, there's incredibly long and drawn out badly-narrated cutscenes that you can skip (but if you do, then there's no point to the 'game'), and then when you inevitably go back to try again you end up more frustrated because literally everything that the game tells you is a choice, is actually just pre-scripted nonsense.
You can tell there was an attempt to be realistic, and to provide some sort of political and/or social commentary, but it just completely fails to actually say anything other than what might as well be "Nothing matters, kill yourself." I'm not even trying to be edgy here, this game takes the RNG from Tharsis and combines it with the cyncism of Papers Please, and then vacuum seals out all of the fun, choice, or reward. I'd actually recommend you try just a single hour of this game to experience how insanely depressing it is, but also to experience the apex of horrendous voice acting. Immediately refund, of course, unless you're a masochist, in which case I'm glad you've finally found the perfect game.
I couldn't make it through the first month of the game, I might find myself going back since I have nothing to lose having spent three and a half hours on it already. To be fair to the game, it has decent graphics (though I hate minimalist art styles) and sound, and I can appreciate what they were trying to do to with the gameplay and story, but it just isn't compelling enough to sell the concept. There's absolutely nothing to lighten up the mood, so you get so burnt out on all the cartoonishly dark rubbish going on that you end up feeling like you shouldn't even care, and that's why I stopped playing.

Unfortunately this review is in the negative.
My interest piqued by the interesting concept and good reviews on Steam, I decided to buy the game and give it a whirl. Though the game gets one hooked quite easily with the intriguing gameplay and story, soon after you start playing you slowly start to find out that the gameplay is not quite as deep as you thought it would be. On top of that the days you spend sending around police/detectives become quite tedious, without any way to fast forward time, and you lose interest in properly reading each crime that is reported. That being said, just when you really think about stopping to play, there is a development in the story, which changes a tiny bit of the gameplay, making it bearable again.
However, what really killed it for me, was the ending. The one I got was very unsatisfactory, which was fine, as it could be a result of my own poor choices. But even though the game forces you to make tons of decisions throughout the game, some internet research to see if I could have done things differently, turned up that there are only two really different endings, and they are still extremely similar. Wish I could say more, but don't want to spoil. Please do google it if you're interested, you'll be negatively surprised.
The game has so much potential: the strategizing with regards to the cops you send out, the personalities/skills of each cop, political intrigue, ties with criminal enterprises, crime solving puzzles, etc., but unfortunately, each and every one of the aspects is lacking in depth and execution. On top of this the story turns out lackluster and the voice-acting is sub-par. I got the feeling the makers got tired of building the game at the halfway point, and decided to stick to a simplified version of the story they wanted to tell, and to leave out loads of features they had initially planned for. Real shame!

Divinia Chronicles: Relics of Gan-Ti is an early access Action RPG with a bit of puzzle and substantial amount of story. Above is a short video of my first half hour of game play. Below are my initial thoughts on the game and purchasing recommendation.
was provided a preview copy from Team Monkey and for that we thank them.
This game has potential and the opportunity to be relatively good if the final product is slightly more polished. The initial mechanics are a bit rough in many areas, control, combat, and overall flow of game play. If the developers were not actively addressing these concerns openly I might be inclined not to suggest this game. The developers have been very active in updating the news for what they are improving, and most of my concerns are on their list. The one issue I did have is that between zones or chapters the loading screens seem to remove you from the experience a bit.
That being said, the game is a cute ARPG with similarities to The Legend of Zelda (Ocarina of Time or Majora's mask) in terms of it's feel. There are puzzles and combat, a seemingly large map, and multiple chapters of story which seem deep enough. Be prepared for the atypical JRPG dialogue, it makes more sense than some, but is clearly a translation that doesn't always match up. The story initially is intriguing and mysterious.
The combat is lacking, but again development is planning to improve this aspect. Currently it's sort of a repetitive experience with some variation in attacks at a higher level. The AI isn't extremely skilled and fights feel more like a task than a combat engagement. The combat controls and movement controls have some to do with this problem, and with some refinement they could be solid for the games purpose.
I'll say if you are willing to watch the game develop and help attempt to shape it's future a bit then it's worth picking up. The potential to be a fun Zelda-esque game is there, but as their early access description says, this is a small passionate development team. This is one you should pick up if you want to see this type of Action RPG developed further and refined into a finished product.

Here is my First Part of My Playthrough of this game:
Okay people.. Here's the deal.  I just finished what there is of early access in about 2.5 hours, and I received two phone calls during my play that totalled at least 30 minutes.  What this means is that for $15 USD, you'll only be getting about two hours worth of content until more content is released as the development continues on this game through its early access period.  Please keep in mind that I bought this game on it's first day of early access launch and that there may more much more content available by the time you are reading this review.  (The early access launch date for this game was October 7, 2015)
What this is available is plenty fun and the graphics are of a cartoony but very nice style that I like quite a bit.  There are some things I like and things I would love to see added to this game from what I've experienced so far in the first couple of hours on early access launch day...
Part 2 (of 4):
What I like:
- Very nice graphics with smooth textures that draws you into the world.
- Smooth animations and fluid movement controls
- Nice story, though it does seem to be of typical RPG fashion.. the same kind of story that we've all seen and can predict 1,000 times before.  ..Still, it's a fun and well done story.
- The combat engages you and requires much more skill and involvement then typical turn based RPG games.  This one is very action oriented and I love that!
- The music is very peaceful and nice
What I'd love to see:
- This RPG game lacks a skill progession system at the current time and there's no way to upgrade skills or stats at any time, even after you level up it's all automatic
- An RPG game without loot?  UGH.  No inventory?  UGH.  No cool weapons and armor and potions and junk loot to pawn at a shopkeeper in town?  Major UGH!  Please add all of this to this game please!  I want gold and loot galore!
- No ability to select a class, profession or even change what you look like.  While this isn't a requirement, it would be nice to be able to have a few options even if they have no bearing on the story of the game.
- Game currently on its launch day of early access is way too short!  I want more!!
Here is Part 3 (of 4):
So, as you can see from the lists above.. this game is easy enough to like and have fun with for what it does offer, I really just want to see so much more!  Mainly more content right now because I was enjoying it and want to see more of this story!  And I really want to able able to get loot and weapons and armor and have an inventory like any other RPG game!  Being able to upgrade skills and choose new attacks at level up etc is also something that really feels like it's missing right now.
Whether or not the developers have any intention of adding anything that I want to see is unknown to me at the moment.  What I can say is that this game is nice, but until it offers more content then it current does on early access launch day (October 7, 2015), most people might want to hold off with their purchase.  I like it so far alright, but want to see more story content as well as more classic RPG loot and progression added soon.
Here is Part 4 of 4:
Here is my ratings at this point:
VALUE:  15/40  This score could be so much higher if only we had more content and if there were more skills and progession like skill points and if there was loot and gear to choose from and shops to buy and sell it.  Just more content in the story to make this a 6 or 8 or 10 hour game would help my value score as well.  Right now, it's just too little for your dollar in my opinion, even though what is there now is fun.
FUN:  25/30  I can't knock this important aspect of my scoring table.  This game is really fun right now, even though once you master the combat it gets a little tedious.  But isn't almost any RPG kinda like that?  I like it right now.. just wish there was more conent and depth.
CONTROLS & BUGS:  20/20  For an early access game, this game plays without even a hitch.  You can change your controls layout now to whatever you prefer and it works very fluid and smoothly.
GRAPHICS & SOUND: 10/10  A very nice art style and sound/music for a low budget RPG.  This one is an easy 10.
TOTAL SCORE ON EARLY ACCESS LAUNCH DAY:  70% (70 out of 100)  This score will likely only go up as the development continues for this game thoughout its early access.  More content will only increase the value score which is by far the lowest score on this EA launch day.

David is a small, hollowed out square, with a special power. David contains several little ovals, which he can fling at enemies. He has been tasked with fighting and destroying evil, which he does by destroying 12 (very large) bosses. Presumably David's story is based on the biblical David, as you are a tiny hero taking on humongous foes, and the developer is quite clearly Christian (in addition to fighting sin, Jesus is the first thanked in his acknowledgements).
The boss fights are fast-paced and frantic. They're also very challenging and often frustrating when playing on the high difficulty (which you have to do, in order to get to the final boss). After playing the first boss, you'd be forgiven for thinking that the game will become repetitive quickly, and while this is true to a certain extent, the bosses in David are actually fairly original and varied. There are an impressive array of novelties that make each boss fight unique and feel fresh. For example, in one of the bonus boss fights, your ellipsoidal ammunition no longer follows you, meaning you have to go to it, and fire it from where it lies. Little variations like this really keep the game fun.
The downside is that this game is extremely short. Even with the arena mode, I would not expect more than a few hours. Five dollars is not an unreasonable asking price for something so different from the usual fare, but if you're uncertain, you can pick it up on sale. It is worth a try.

Many of the other reviews go over the content of the game; so I figured I'd give a slightly different angle. The game most certainly is a good game, as others have stated, but for the price I payed for it. I payed $1 for it, which is well worth it. If I didn't already own the game I would be willing to pay up to $2 to own it, but not more.

David is a 2D arena shooter where you control a little floaty cube called David. David can slide from side to side and can jump repeatedly in mid-air, giving him a levitation ability but with a constant gravity pull. To attack an enemy, you click and hold on David to enter a slow-motion state where David charges his attack. His attack shoots a sphere in the direction you are pointing; this sphere being composed of smaller spheres that orbit David. How big your shot is depends on how many of the small spheres are within a certain boundary around David at the time you release the shot.  After firing, you need to wait for the spheres to come back to orbit around David before shooting again.
The game has two modes. The main mode has you entering constrained arenas to fight bosses, and each boss has a certain gimmick that makes it unique. You will need to beat each boss twice, once with 7 hit points (easily managed) and 1 hit point (where the real fun is!). All the bosses are accessible at any time, except the final boss which requires that you successfully beat each minor boss at both difficulties.
There is also an arena mode where enemies keep coming at you while you accumulate points. The points allow you to upgrade David to last longer in the next run.
The game is definitely worth a purchase. It's a steal at $1, so get it while the offer lasts.

This is a horrible game: The keyboard controls for movement go from sluggish to erratic in a nano second, the mouse controlled slingshot is not intuitive and the fact that the cursor has to touch your David to load a new shot combined with the erratic movement makes every shot a chore. I can imagine it works much better with touch controls but then this is a very poor port and no thought has gone into a new control scheme.
Since enemies swarm you immediately you have to stay off ground as much as possible and here comes the next problem: The camera zooms in on your character when you're in the air, so most of the time you can't even see the enemies.
The config menu is just a sad joke: Anti aliasing on/off and that's it.
The final icing: The game can't be paused. Hitting escape brings you back to the level select screen.
Fantastic game. Beautiful looking and very fun to play. A little on the short side but for the price, I would def recommend it.

I am a big fan of FTL and the comparisons to that game are defintiely what brought me here. Having put a few hours into the game I do not think those comparisons are warranted. Unless I am missing something there is nothing that keeps you from simply retreating and returning to any conflict as many times as you like so it is not really all that rougelike and the most strategic decision I make in most battles is how to maximize my starting distance from the enemies. It is not a braindrain and the need to precisely target enemies is just not there, So not like FTL, but I still really like it.
Most games I feel like I can get into the developer's heads and figure out what I am supposed to do, but this game is not one of them. I do not understand the ship progression at all. I feel like the number 11-13 ships are way better than the number 21 ship for example. When you jump to a new sector you cannot neccessarily see if anyone else is jumping into it and this can result in massive ambushes that you have to run away from, so there are plenty of situations that I assume are just unwinnable. Also the experience system is not balanced in terms of time invested and the whole thing is very grindy and slow to start. These are minor complaints though because I really love the core of the game.
I particularly like the end-game. Once you get your three ships and you have filled all the slots you can upgrade some guns, but if you lose the ship you lose those upgrade points which are much scarcer than the regular currency. Instead I have been buying the super advanced weapons at the top of the purchable weapon list that are just brutal. I expect there could be some expansions in the future that would allow some custumization as well. I would recommend this game, but understand that its nowhere near as full and intricate as FTL. It is a 3 ship fleet simulator with some RNG elements and very little customization or variation between the ships.

The game is beautiful it ran 720p 30 FPS on the 360 and if your rig is moderate it can kill this game. Got 1080p 60FPS no problem on a gtx 750ti and an I3-4170 processor with hyperthreading. I was able to run it at 1536p 60FPS on High settings so that sould tell you something. Overall the story is great and should not be looked over.
Gameplay: Classic Assassins creed you will be jumping, climbing, stabbing, sychronizing viewpoints etc. So what makes this game special from the past games? Well besides new weapons, new parkour abilities, etc. its the open world. In the American Revolution setting you can go to Boston, New York, the Frontier as the main locations. You can hunt animals and there is also Naval Combat but its in missions and not free roam (If you want that go play Black Flag). Multiplayer returns as well and like the multiplayer from Brotherhood and Revelations its fun and intense so do not skip over it. Gameplay is once again a reason to buy this game.
Bad Stuff: Besides a few flat characters I really don't have anything to complain about the game is Very good. I will say the first three hours of the game is a glorified tutorial that'll make even the biggest AC fan cringe. It uses that to set up the story and its worth getting through.
Final Verdict: Back in 2012 I thought this game was worth 60$ so at 20$ on steam you need to add it to your collection right now. DO IT!

Being a F2P game, I thought Tera had one of the fairer business models. The cash shop was mainly for skins, different mounts, other cosmetic items. Sure there were items that boosted stats(crit inners), but most, if not all can be bought in game with gold or aquired from other means. Special events like the "Mongo Hunt" also let players stock up on things that would cost an arm and a leg normally.
Even with the game being heavily instanced, the world was free roam and different zones varied greatly from one another. Leveling is incredibly easy and straight forward, leaving most of these areas empty. Getting to the cap, 65 is easy, but be prepared to hit a wall. RNG enchanting to higher and higher sets of gear, farming for feedstock to try enhancing that weapon you've failed on five times in a row, it soon becomes a pattern of doing the same couple of dungeons and your daily quests. A guild system rework and a new 30 man raid are in the pipes to be added soon, so maybe that will change things up.
I'd reccomend Tera overall, just be ready for the late game grind and repition.

Home is a 2D side scrolling mystery story based game. You'll walk left and right, open doors and find clues. The clues help you find out why you woke up in someone else's house and what has happened to your wife Rachel. Objects you can interact with will have an outline when you walk next to them. You will collect items, but have no inventory. The game spans a few locations and each location has several different rooms. Two houses, woods, a sewer system and a factory. There are locked doors and you'll need to find keys, hairpins and other ways to open them. After each location, the character will reference objects that you found and ponder what they could mean.
The art style is very pixelated for better or worse. It doesn't feel too detailed. The only animation is the character's walk animation. Everything else is a static object. The game is very story based and you will be reading a lot. My only problem with the dialog is that it has its own screen. It takes me out of the game when it has its own screen. As game calling itself horror, it is all at night and your character is carrying a lantern. While you come across pixelated horror such as dead night watchmen and read about it, there is no threat. So its not scary. Nothing is out to get you. There is no pressure.
As you search through the locations you'll tackle a few light puzzles to progress forward. You'll find dead bodies and read through text about how rancid trash is and some back story about your character. Even with no map, I don't feel like I ever got lost. Most things you find, you get a choice to take it or not. Find a bloody knife, do you take it or leave it? Normally the choice would be laughable. Of course people want to take it. Well everything you take leads up to something and what you take and the story molds itself nicely to what you have and don't have.
That's really what this game excels at, an interactive story that molds itself to your choices. Do you uncover a pair of bodies? Do you take a video tape that is potential evidence? Do you read a letter that you find hanging out of a mailbox? Did you find a list of names or not?
Home can be played in an hour or so. My second time through I speed ran it in about 20 minutes. There are many different endings depending on the choices you made. Even with different endings, I don't feel like the game is worth replaying. Its over too quick to give impact to any ending. The game feels like there wasn't much effort put in. Everything is text, no real animation. I'm reading emotions rather than seeing the graphics convey the emotions. Television and video games are visual mediums. I should be seeing things, not reading them. I wouldn't be so harsh on the text if it didn't have its own dedicated screen to take me out of the game.

Builds up on everything that made Witcher 3 a great game. This is a true open world game, in which your game is actually open for you to tackle the problems in diffrent ways including some sandbox-ish physix that encourage you to experiment.
The world is the biggest world in any video game. It is fair to say that part of it is useless desert but even the useful part of the map is bigger than Witcher 3, and more diverse. The game is extremely beautiful and ancient Egypt is a pleasure to explore and its misteries to uncover. You really feel like a tourist and after finishing it I feel like I explored all of Egypt.
The horse is responsive, the climbing and parkour-ing is natural and fluid. You can also climb any terrain now, and the horse can jump extremely large distances, cross medium-depth waters and even jump into canyons.
The combat si extremely thoughtful. It isnt necessarely difficult along the game but if you really want a challenge you can visit the gladiator colloseum or elephant events. Not only the combat is good and diverse with plenty of enemy types but the horse combat is super cool as well, being able to rotate on the horse to shoot and swing at the enemies chasing you while the horse is sprinting forward is perfectly done and action-movie-esque.
The stealth section is taking inspiration from AC Unity, Deus Ex and Dishonored, with several ways to enter a secured zone without being noticed. This is where your eagle shines, his job being to scout for enemy sentries, hidden pathways, caverns and treasures.
The draw distance is amazing, way better than Witcher 3. Also features a Photo Mode which is amazingly satisfying to use to capture amazing moments especially whit the great draw distance and amazing acrobatic combat and movement.
Also has plenty of weapon variety, each type of weapon with diffrent handling and use and each weapon with diffrent stats and enhancements like bleeding, burning etc. That applies to bows as well as tools.
You can also tame wild animals to have pets that help you in combat which is a nice addition. Also the game now features tombs inspired by Tomb Raider games. They are short, one puzzle or platforming section leading to the treasure. They are not hard but they contribute to the authenthicity of ancient Egypt. Also the side activities are far superior to Witcher 3's. I mean The Witcher has Gwent which is fantastic, but little else but AC Origins has gladiator fights, war elephant fights, hippodrome chariot races, tombs. Also every question mark in W3 is usually a monster nest or something similar, really simple, but here, any question mark can vary from an wild animal lair to a whole fortification waiting to be thrown into chaos with slaves and animals to be released, captains to be killed and treasures to be looted.
The swimming sections are also better than Wither 3's because it's more beautiful and it now features a fully developed underwater combat.  Also the naval combat is similar to Black Flags but it doesn't overstay its welcome.
Storywise it's debatable if it's as good as AC II but if not, it defeneatly comes close.
These are just on the top of my head but I'm sure you will have many more things to praise about this game by the time you're done with it.
Totally recommend!

Steam is home to a lot of crap, and I do mean a lot.. But it also is home to a number of hidden gems that no one really talks about much.
Mini Ninjas is one of those gems. A bit of an imperfect one, sure, but a gem nontheless. And like many hidden gems, it doesn't get a whole lot of attention.
The game is kinda an action adventure game, with small elements of RPG and stealth. You play the role of a ninja named Hiro, who is tasked with finding all his lost friends and saving the world while he is at it. A lot of pressure, I know, but then you are a ninja with the power to control the elements, so it shouldn't be too hard (Which kinda is a problem for the game, I'll explain later)
Being that you play the role of a ninja, stealth is a tool you'll be making a lot of use out of. As some might indicate, however, the stealth aspect of the game isn't really all that advanced, and oftentimes isn't used to avoid fights so much as it is to get the first strike in any given fight (or outright kill everyone in a patrol before they even have time to react). While it is possible to avoid fights, you won't want to in the early game, because you need to fight to gain XP and level up. Otherwise, the road ahead will be awfully harsh to those who don't kick enough butt. While quietly avoiding fights isn't encouraged (At least in the early game), the stealth system does indeed work very well, and in the late game, where  by then you are already maxed out, it becomes much more viable.
When the time comes to fight, however, it is a mixed bag. Combat is simple, with a few basic attacks, a block breaker, and even a super move that can cause all sorts of pain for those unlucky to be the target of it. You also have a selection of items that can make fights go more smoothly, such as pepper bombs and potions that make arrows bounce off your face. However, the problem is that it IS simple, even to the point of simply mashing the two buttons until everyone is dead before moving on to the next fight. I myself don't mind it, but those seeking a deeper combat system might not enjoy the game as much.
Sure, as you progress through the game you'll unlock more ninjas to fight with, each having their own style (Such as the fat ninja's brute force hammer skills that can make fighting larger enemies blindingly easy, or the archer ninja's ranged combat skills). However, I never really did bother to use any of them besides the ninja you start with. In DK 64, the devs made it so that you had to use all the Kongs in order to beat the game, so you couldn't just march through the whole game with Donkey Kong the whole time. Not so much here, where you can get through the entire game without changing ninjas ONCE. Maybe on hard mode, you would have to swap out ninjas more often, but on normal mode it is rather pointless for the most part, and in some cases even more fun, since fighting larger enemies feels more satisfying when you have to put up a real fight to take them down, rather than swapping over to fat ninja and just wailing on them, stun locking them to death. And even moreso, the starter ninja is the only one who can use magic, and as you progress through the game, you'll learn how important magic is.
So, the combat is ok at best, the whole 6 ninja team gimmic is iffy when you can go through the whole game with the main star of the game just fine (and possibly makes the adventure so much more interesting and challenging), and stealth early on, while it does play a considerable role in the game, is mostly used for ambushing more than avoiding conflict altogether. And yet... I love this game.
Maybe it is because it reminds me of the glory days, back when we had games like Banjo & Kazooie 1 & 2, Conker's Bad Fur Day, Jak and Daxter... You know those kind of games? The ones where you feel like you are on a real adventure throughout an interesting, if sometimes even strange, world waiting to be explored. You start out in your humble village, venturing out chapter after chapter on your way to the big bad guy himself, taking out his generals and anyone else who dares to get in your way, while at the same time taking a moment to explore the area for goodies and new spells to unlock. It helps that the world and the music that fills it is quite appealing, making the journey all the more enjoyable. That, and it is around 9-10 hours on my first playthrough, so you get your money's worth for sure. Gotta love a game that keeps you busy for a nice long while.
As much as I'd like to yammer on and on, I'd like to wrap it up as a game that, while the gem is a bit cloudy, it is a gem nontheless, and a shame that it isn't more popular, let alone given a respected sequel (instead getting spinoffs on the Kinect and a Ipad runner.. Yeah, kinda a sad fate for the ninjas if you ask me).

This game should be pulled for misadvertising, because if you think a game solely about Ninja would contain stealth, then you'd be wrong. Sure, there are stealth mechanics, sure, some areas give you paths to sneak past enemies, but if you want to rescue animals and gain XP, the only way you'll do that is by charging in and killing everything you see. You in fact lose out if you stealth.
This game is about as barebones as it gets. Despite being a linier game split into levels, the end of each level tell you how many collectables you managed to snag on your way there. This includes: freed animals, flowers, Jinzo statues, spell scrolls, and money. "Great", you might think, "Lots of replayability!" Well, you'd be wrong. Freeing animals gives you XP, collecting plants gives you ingredients with which to craft potions (which I have yet to need), scrolls give you new spells, and the statues? Well, they're purely collectables - all of which, as far as I can tell, have absolutely no reward for collecting them all. There are no achevements, either on Steam or in-game, and aside from your base stats which are improved automatically when you level-up, there isn't anything they could offer in the way of a reward anyway. And yes, you read that correctly: money is a commodity. It's that useless.
Mini Ninjas is an empty, soulless (albeit cute) journey down a long woodland-themed corridoor, with no real incentive to stray off the beaten path besides completionism. Fighting is just mashing 'attack', with special attacks or spells that one-hit-kill. The only reason you'd need to switch characters is to kill the heavy enemy (which is only easily killed by your heavy ninja) or cast spells, which only the default character can. The English voice-acting also seems to be have been assigned exclusively to one guy.
So what's good? Well, the art-style is lovely. The mixture of ambient Japanese dialogue and English cutscene dialogue is nice. You can control animals, which is oddly rare in games... And that's about it.
CONCLUSION: It pains me to say this about anything in the Ninja genre, but I recommend giving this title a miss, unless you're buying it for a child - the cartoon violence, quirky designs and easy controls make this a good entry-level romp through ancient Japanese culture.

Loved David. when it was an incredibly cheap indie game out there, bought it without thinking because it had some amazing recommendations by some intelligent people, enjoyed it thoroughly and then voted for it on Greenlight. David. is the quintessential action game, distilled from decades of Mega Men, Street Fighters and other games where tactical thinking is as important as good reflexes. It is distilled to almost complete abstraction and yet it has both spirit AND character with enemy behaviours standing in for elaborate art direction and animations and the poor little David with his Halo the only little glimmer of hope in a universe consumed by darkness. This is it, this is the game where you don't get bogged down with having to wrestle with unrealistic motivations of the bad guys or the artificial dilemmas of your hero, this is all about brutal fighting to the death, all about movement, positioning, being cool under fire, knowing when to bait them, knowing how to avoid succumbing to your fears. David is, in case I wasn't entirely clear, very very good. Get it.

What a great little game for 8€. I expected a SPAZ clone but this is much more, a game that has come into it's own since the project first started. An interesting cross between FTL and SPAZ.  The game is slower even in the real time battles giving you time to make a more strategic choice of placement rather than twitch ability.  There is a decent variety of turrets for ships, all of which can be upgraded in a variety of stats throughout the game, including some support-only turrets.  You gain experience throughout the game, whether you win or lose the scenario, which in turn potentially unlocks new starting ships.  There are three main difficulties, but I have yet to actually beat easy, though I have seen the final sector.  It is roguelike in the sense that if your ship is destroyed the game ends regardless of how much of your fleet remains.  Really nice for essentially being an upgraded port of a mobile game.
Also, you get carriers.  I love having a carrier with drones.
UPDATE: I've played enough to beat normal a couple of times and even finished hard once.  I have unlocked all but four ships.  Still quite enjoyable if you prefer a slower paced game and the ship combinations give it a decent amount of replayability if you don't just want to min/max.

This game is best described as a mashup of Gratuitous Space Battles and FTL. The graphics and sounds are not as good as GSB, and the rogue-like, perfectly balanced micromanaging of FTL is not present. However, it has elements of both of those games, combining two enjoyable things into one, though not being as highly proficient at either. This is not a knock on the game, it's just where it lands on the spectrum.
I like how the game handles the tactical combat interface. Your ships act how you want them to act. They go where you tell them and attack in the desired order. The only problem is that there is almost no depth to combat. Yeah, you can change where your ships land in the sector, or position them in a minorly superior way, but it does not make much difference. It operates such that you optimize your ships while traversing a map (FTL), but then order them around precisely in real time battles (like GSB). The game consists of 4 procedurally generated sectors (FTL), though each particular sector is wide open for combat (like GSB).
The game becomes far too grindy at times due to poor pacing. There are major spikes and valleys in the opponents difficulty even in neighboring sectors. One second you are destroying face, and the next you are scurrying back to your battlestation to repair. This would be fine, but it is often expensive to upgrade or purchase additional firepower. This sends you grinding around safe parts of the map when you should be getting rewarded for exploring more. This problem worsens as you go on.
The deeper you get into the game, the more boring it gets. I often have my fleet at maximum capabilities in the first map. What this means is that I have no way of improving my ships, and if the enemies keep getting strong, there is no possibility of victory. The game needs tweaks. It's not horrible as it is, but it could be a lot more. This feels more like an early release, at least from a PC standpoint. It is obvious that the game is a port from a mobile platform, that's its ideal niche.

For those looking for something along the lines of FTL, this game did not even come close for me. I felt like all I did was just click on places to go, the combat seemed arbitrary and very easy. Without any form of pausing, and very weak mission parameters (mainly, go here, destroy stuff, return), I failed to see where the "tactical" portion of the game came in. Feels like mobile game fluff with a sci-fi skin.

The ever emotional yet conflicting end to the Desmond Saga. This is popularly referred to as the 'last good AC'. The argument being that future AC games lack the 'present day' element that linked the player to the experiences of Desmond.
AC3 is a game that stands out. Not only because Connor is so unlike the previous or proceeding protagonists, but also due to his character arc being the first in the series to introduce the grey areas in the Templar-Assassin war. Not only is this the first game to have a first playable Templar - Haytham Kenway is also really hot and classy. (hehe)
The previous Templar villains were classic - hardcore maglomamaniacs - easy to hate and deliciously cruely. But this AC introduces hesitation to dislike. The Templars are truly working for a better cause - following a noble Grandmaster of Haytham - who is compassionate and non-racist in his views. The Templars want what is best - which was not so clearly the case in the previous games.
This raises question of how America could have been in the now - could Native Americans not be second class citizens as they are today? Could the American Revolution been less violent and more diplomatic - resulting in the first era of democratic relationships between enemies? Would George Washington be less of a hero he is idealised and lorded over as he is portrayed to be as he is today?
AC3 truly brings out the questions in life - would things have been better if Templars ruled? Are they truly evil? Do the ends justify the means? Are Templars methods something that could be condoned? We had always and still been playing arcs that saw us vehimently rejecting Templars and everything they do. We understand their methods are harsh and perhaps cruel, but will this be the best and only way?
Do they Assassins really have the right answers to life?
As continued in AC3 novel Forsaken - another masterpiece - AC Rogue, AC Black Flag and perhaps even Unity, Ubisoft has taken the questions even further, expanding and also adding to the richness of the AC world with thoughts on 'Who is truly good or evil?' and also the darkness of the AC franchise. Not only does this make you LURVE the characters even more than you would already do, but also make you immerse yourself in history and art and politics.
Gameplay wise, this game revolutionized (another revolution) the system and made it more flexible and dynamic. Connor is also the first in AC protagonists to be able to climb trees. And don't question why his father can't.... Combat is more fluid and even enjoyable - sometimes you just want to go on a killing spree through town. Despite this - do not fear - you can still die and stealth is still important for an Assassin. Although, the constraints are annoying, it adds to the element of the shadows that the Assassin wars wage in history.
The open world is almost as annoying as it always famously is - loads of collectibles and the Cheevo for collecting and doirng everthing is there - so good luck with that - even i havent got 100% sync on the bloody naval mission.
Naval missions are a new thing (yay) - kicking off a chapter of AC games for naval warfare. This prototype maybe quite the dinosaur, but it is an interesting development from land-based combat.
Annoyingly, the tunnel system can be foregone with horse travel, but then, its entirely up to you if you want to get lost in the dark.
Overall, a blessed improvement for the AC franchise - for the day of course - and a brilliant story arc. Though you might find Connor a tough person to like - come on, if your father is the enemy, mother murdered, people not even considered citizens and you have to continue living with all that on top of the fact that you have to kill your own father....who found out his own father was betrayed and killed too - you wouldn't be a happy-go-lucky person like Ezio was.
Ezio was a nobleman, grew up with his family and had his mom and sister with him, found love eventually and had a family. Connor never had a chance - not to mention that he is a Native at a time when slavery was still around....
All in all, a great game, though annoying for perfectionists, it is splendid in comparison to previous games

There are a lot of positive factors in AC3 that you can work with: A large, well-crafted world; open-world content; smooth combat system; great story related to the American Revolution; Naval combat. All of this provides a great deal of potential for this game, but there's not enough refinement in the whole package to make this game great.
The world is sometimes seemingly too big with not enough to do. You travel very large distances toward your next main objective marker between missions, only because you haven't discovered the fast travel point yet. The wilderness looks really nice, and that's great, but there's very little to do in it. The open-world content is almost exclusively put in the city settings, but they impact your character and story in no significant way. It's basically all the bad about open-world, and none of the good.
The combat and naval battles are quite good. However, there simply isn't enough of either unless you go out of your way to make it happen. The whole game feels like you move from point A to point B (or attack X groups of enemies) until you trigger the next cutscene to advance the story. But even the story becomes tarnished because it keeps breaking immersion by going back to the whole overarching present-day story.
Assassins Creed 3 is a deeply flawed game that, despite it's shortcomings, still manages to be a good experience.

UPDATE: I gave the game another go, I managed to beat the game with all the Satanic animatronics crawling in the vents. The trick is shut off everything after finishing a task (use silent ventilation, it works even if the terminal's off), wait for the creepy-crawly noises to go by when you use the flashlight, then rinse and repeat while quickly referring to the motion detection system. I still don't think it's a worthwhile experience overall, unless you're 12 years old, screamishly neurotic, or obsessed with FNAF's cryptic depths. I cheated my savefile so I could buy the security puppet (and see all the hidden lore in the minigames), and it's remarkable how Scott was able to render things in such different styles, whether it's 2D retro, 3D photorealistic, the 1950s informercials.
I've played to Friday, and I'm just not enjoying the game whatsoever. Even in the "this is intentionally awful, lol" sort of ironic sense.
There's so much for me to comment on what's unenjoyable/nonsense - but I'll first focus on the bread and butter gameplay, which is the sitting at a terminal in some cramped room part, fending off whatever animatronics are allowed to roam in the grid-like ventilation.
I hated the basic premise of pressing buttons on a menu to do tasks that a simple automated macro can solve. Press X menu entry (like printing menus), listen to some sound effect play with no progress bar, then rinse and repeat for all the other menu entries until you can sign off for the night. Meanwhile, this is a world where you have animatronics who can move, decide for themselves, crawl through vents and speak synthesized voices. If anything, the same technology can go towards automating the pizzeria's menial tasks.
That alone isn't interesting by itself, so you also have to juggle fending off against the rogue animatronics who appear as minute blips on the ventilation map. Your only real defense is aiming your flashlight down the two vents to your side. Why is the flashlight fixed on where you look? I'd be holding the light down the vent with one arm, while typing commands in the terminal with the other.
Or hell, if these animatronics are so scared off by the light, I'd just smuggle in another flashlight (with some duct tape), tape these flashlights by the vents, and then there'd be no game.
What especially annoyed me was the in-game advertisements that get in the way when you buy a sponsorship for some extra cash. Supposedly, you have a crude terminal that can display text graphics with a PC speaker - yet graphic ads are capable of interrupting your work on such a mission-critical interface, complete with theme music. It's so bad your character is basically paralyzed by adware, not even able to look left or right while the ad struts its stuff ("Please wait 5 seconds.."). It's so bad that when you click away from the ad to get back to the actual terminal, the screen you were just on half the time is non-functional, and you have to change to a different menu and back again, just to get it working.
Alright, so let me look at it from a gameplay level. You want to fend off the animatronics with the tools at hand, and rely on reacting to the auditory cues when you aren't able to look at the motion sensors. But it's hard to distinguish which direction the ventilation noises are coming from, even when you have the terminal and fan shut-off. For instance, I thought I heard something on my left, turned to look, shut off my stuff-- nothing, then looked back at the terminal only to have Baby make that generic shrieking sound that all the other animatronics make when they jump-scare you.
You have the option to use the silent ventilation, but it's pointless when your terminal makes noise anyway, and when the other options usefully serve to distract the animatronics/notify you of their locations.
And when you die, it's a waste of time to have to wait for the game over screen to pass, click through the "Warning, jumpscares!", the cutsy opening screen, continue game, the cutsy pizzeria management stuff -- just to get back for another attempt. You can sustain the mood much better if you cut out all the waiting.
Let me focus on the pizzeria management stuff. It feels like a tacked-on element from an unrelated game -- it's like The Sims, where you're buying furniture and accessories for the house, only you never get to see the actual sims enjoying your efforts.. (the player is too busy in some survival horror game).. only just an end-of-day profit report where you hope the lawsuit lottery doesn't hit you. Feels very engaging, yes?
The only part I actually enjoyed was the Fruity Maze Arcade minigame, when you collect the powerups and watch them work in conjunction to suck in the fruit at the speed of sound.
The most egregious feeling I've felt playing this game, other than eventually feeling bored enough to not want to continue to its end - and it is something I can't place it on anything specific - was that I wasn't really engaged with a living, believable virtual world, but rather I was going through the motions of the game's deterministic mechanisms (as in, you pull a lever and a thing happens). You press X in reaction to Y being present. If Springtrap is in the vent, look left for a few seconds to make him go away, so you can go on with crossing off a checklist, one by one. You'll see this quality too with the other entries in the FNAF series, and it's best emblified by that FNAF 2 GIF where the poor security guard is spazzing out between wearing a mask, winding the box, shining the flashlight, rinse and repeat. I think someone has managed to make a PowerPoint presentation of the first FNAF game.
A few more notes - when I was doing the animatronic inspection (it was picked up from a shady back alley, then some guy on a cassette asks you to play weird f--- sounds to it so you can mark yes on the checklist, so you can have one more Satanic creature in the vents the next night, and remember to taze it in the balls if it even looks at you funny), I failed one. I didn't know what to look for, apart from thinking that well, the animatronic shifted gazes this one time I looked away at the checklist, so maybe there might be a few more steps.. nope. Baby snapped into lunging at me a few seconds after its changed pose, I failed the salvage (you need to complete all of them for the good ending), and I have it roaming the vents with the others for no reward. There's no way to retry it (conveying a clarity of understanding is not one of this game's strengths), other than starting a new game, or happening to backup your savefile for every night.
A better game would be if it were like a cross between Alien: Isolation and Silent Hill, and you were able to prepare your character for what would happen every night. Having a set amount of time to roam the halls, arrange the furniture, lock any doors, and obtain what tools you'll need for your own pizzeria (you're the owner of a franchise building). Being able to upgrade the terminal, the surveillence, the doors. Suffering penalties (losing money, risk of getting fired or bad reviews for the business) if you damage the animatronics or the building. Think of that scene from Straw Dogs when Dustin Hoffman had to prepare himself at night for the attackers coming into his house, you'll get my idea. You'll hide under desks you've arranged, or stack chairs against a door, crawl in panic through the open vents.. scream as you jab an animatronic in its eyes with a taser prod.
Is it horror? Is it terrifying? Interesting and worthwhile to play as the game currently is? Fun, fun, fun, fun, fun (like the Kazoo Kid says)? No. For me, it is just mind-numbing, even factoring in all the cryptic lore that has the Game Theorists mentally masturbating over the out-of-place details.

I am enjoying this game, and I don't regret purchasing it.  I can't recommend it though in its current state.
First the good.  The art style is fantastic.  From the characters to the bosses to the tiles everything is very detailed and beautiful.  Animations are very well done.  The level of challenge seems decently balanced.  You can make choices that really hinder your progress or that make the game relatively easy.  It's not too difficult but not too easy for the average player.
The bad, however, heavily outweighs the good.  Itemization feels very unbalanced.  One of the first unlockable weapons has such powerful abilities that it will carry you through the entire game.  Halving damage and parrying are infinitely more powerful than a 1 in 20 chance of a modest effect, especially when your damage is tied more to your character itself than the weapon's damage.  Add the fact that the later weapons are two-handed, which incurs an accuracy penalty and sacrifices the ability to use shields, and they are all but worthless.  Armor is similar.  You can fight through the most difficult dungeons to obtain character specific armor that once again gives modest effects, only to discover the more easily obtainable armor is superior.  This could all change if proc chances were much higher, but as it stands be prepared for let downs on discovering new items.
The quest system doesn't make sense at times.  You have 3 quests active at a time, and those quests change depending on the area you are in.  When you complete a quest a new one takes its place until all quests are exhausted.  It can be confusing and annoying to kill 30 goblins and have a quest pop up to kill 30 kobolds, only to find out that the kobolds you already killed don't count.  The kobolds in the next act won't count either, as quests are not global.  The quests do not have a counter, so you have to count them yourself or just be surprised.    Global quests or simply listing all of the areas' quests from the start would go a long way toward alleviating this issue.  Of course there's also the bug of some quest achievements not registering at all once you've completed them.
The game is simply riddled with bugs.  None that I have encountered have been game breaking, ie corrupting, but they are enough to make the average player move on.  Some bugs are benign, such as bomb upgrades not working until you restart the game.  Others range from confusing to very annoying.  If you are fast clicker you may find yourself frequently exiting dungeons or restarting when bugs won't let you click tiles or your dungeon is a solid black screen.  Maybe you'll get lucky though and recreate the infinite crafting bug or the bug that allows your Paladin to have first strike and infinite spells for the entire dungeon.
Sadly this game has all the signs of a money grab iport.  If you have a lot patience, then this game can be very enjoyable.  Otherwise give it a pass or watch to see if the devs fix the problems.

Runestone Keeper is a clone of the original Dungelot, but has added more content and deeper gameplay. It can be arduous to play, while Dungelot is light and fun, progress and unlocks are more consistent.

This game is very simple and very fun to just mess around with.
Being able to create simple beats and feel like you have control over how the song plays out is a cool idea and is brought out well considering. It is easy to go in and create a beat of your own with and you do not need to be a wiz with music making to do it well.  However this is where the negatives start to kick in.  In the game you go between 4-5 different instruments and create beats with essentially 4 different notes....and that's it really. There are bonus loops or instruments that can appear and give you the option of changing your current instrument with the new one or have the option of selecting new music in general.  Besides this there is no other way to make or alter music.  This is where the simplicity will be seen as a negative.  You are not able to fade music in or out, change the BPM, and there is no way to edit your samples the way YOU want after you create them.  The game will automatically edit the samples together which may make your song sound better or worse.  It is a shame that if you want to make advanced samples or create your own songs your out of luck really.  It took me 3 hours to go through the entire "story" section but I will say I had a lot of fun playing through it.  Even though you have limits to the kind of music you can make it is still a fun expereince that is worth that little bit of money it costs to play it.  People looking for an advanced music maker to make samples and great tracks would probably get nothing from this, but for players looking for a simple and fun music creation game to mess around and have fun with then there is nothing wrong with this game.  Did I forget to mention any song you finish you can save and export it to your music library on you computer to listen to whenever you want (even if the songs are just 1 minute long).  A lot of neat ideas in this game I just wish there would be options for more advanced options to give people freedom to create even more awesome tracks.    However because the game only costs a couple of dollars my negatives really are just minor.        Cosmic DJ get's a 7/10 From me. It may be a hidden object game, but the obscurity of some puzzles, especially related to the inventory, puts Salem Witch Trials on the difficulty range of some old point ‘n’ click adventure games. If you expect an easy HOG, buckle up.
Midnight Mysteries 2: The Salem Witch Trials was the game that introduced the plot-driven lightweight adventure game format to this franchise of hidden object games. It did so with a unique approach, so there are many differences compared to other similar games on today's market.
For one, the plot is thick and difficult to follow: the author we met in the first game is contacted by another ghost, the spectre of Nathaniel Hawthorne, who asks him to get to the bottom of the mystery of the titular witch trials. This task quickly gets a lot more complicated after we get entangled in family dramas, feuds, and even a legal dispute with the local Indian tribe.
Gameplay mirrors this complexity. Hidden object scenes take a secondary role to classic point ‘n’ click game elements, including item combinations within the inventory. Progress requires the player to listen to the story to decipher where to go next. So, in short, it isn’t meant for the HOG rookies, and even veterans may find a decent challenge in it.
